title: DUET: Decoupled Upper- and Lower-Body Execution for Task-Agnostic Humanoid Loco-Manipulation
summary: Changing a humanoid robot's manipulation policy should not require retraining the controller that maintains the robot's balance. This study introduces DUET, a decoupled execution framework that enables locomotion and manipulation controllers to operate simultaneously by combining their commands only at the robot interface. A reinforcement-learning locomotion policy controls the 12 leg joints and a waist yaw joint, tracking planar velocity, turning rate, and pelvis height from deep crouching to upright standing on a 23-degree-of-freedom Unitree G1. The 10 arm joints are excluded from the action space, while their positions and velocities are included only as observations, so that any compatible manipulation policy that generates arm-joint targets can control the upper body, and the locomotion policy keeps the lower body stable without requiring shared training or direct coordination. This study demonstrates the modular approach on hardware by pairing the same locomotion checkpoint with two different vision-language-action models, GR00T N1.7 and pi0.5. In simulation evaluation, the locomotion controller kept the robot's lower body stable with no falls while tracking the commanded planar velocity, yaw rate, and pelvis height with errors of 0.186 m/s, 0.142 rad/s, and 0.016 m, respectively. Ablation studies identify the upper-body pose curriculum as the dominant component, and removing this training step reduces episode survival from 20.0 to 7.4 seconds and increases the fall rate to 6.06 per environment minute. Robustness tests show no falls under pushes of up to 1.0 m/s within the trained payload range, and no falls at twice the payload limit for pushes below 0.7 m/s. These results show that a manipulation policy can be exchanged without retraining, restarting, or otherwise touching the layer that keeps the robot upright.

title: Stress-Query and Temporal Reliability of Vision-Language Models as copilots in Autonomous UAV Navigation
comment: Paper accepted at the Latin American Robotics Symposium LARS 2026
summary: Integrating Vision-Language Models (VLMs) into autonomous UAV navigation enables high-level semantic reasoning but introduces critical temporal bottlenecks that can destabilize flight control. This paper presents a systematic benchmark that evaluates the operational trade-offs among model scale, hardware constraints, and flight reliability. By subjecting the system to extensive stress tests on both a high-performance workstation and a constrained integrated-graphics laptop, we isolate the kinetic impact of inference latency against reasoning accuracy. Our findings reveal a performance dichotomy: lightweight models struggle with structural hallucinations that break deterministic state machines, while heavyweight models induce trajectory overcorrections due to inference lag. We demonstrate that a mid-weight architecture strikes the optimal balance, successfully rehabilitating navigation in degraded environments without compromising real-time stability across different hardware profiles.

Introduction Traditional autonomous navigation tasks in Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs) have relied on conventional perception pipelines that utilize rigid computer vision architectures and sensor fusion. While these geometric systems are highly reactive, their performance degrades significantly in uncertain environments, such as when navigation markers are severely damaged or visual cues are ambiguous. In contrast, the rapid development of Vision-Language Models (VLMs) represents a paradigm shift levine2016end . By incorporating multimodal semantic reasoning into the perception process, UAVs can interpret high-level contextual information in complex scenarios. This approach bridges the gap between rigid pixel-level processing and contextual scene understanding, enabling UAVs to conduct a more intelligent secondary assessment of their surroundings. However, the transition of VLMs from cloud-based APIs to real-time embedded robotic control presents profound operational challenges. The main obstacle is the bottleneck between model scale and inference time limits. Models with many parameters exhibit robust reasoning but impose inference latencies that often exceed several seconds on edge hardware, decoupling the control loop and causing severe deviations in the physical trajectory. On the other hand, lightweight edge-optimized models minimize latency but often suffer from structural distortions, failing to maintain the rigorous formatting schemes, such as JSON outputs, required by classical deterministic controllers. While previous research has explored end-to-end visuomotor policies levine2016end or reinforcement learning kober2013reinforcement , there is a critical gap in the empirical understanding of the exact time limits and trade-offs that dictate when a VLM mathematically breaks an autonomous control loop. The evaluations are executed within a high-fidelity Software-In-The-Loop (SITL) Gazebo simulation, subjecting multiple visual architectures to incremental stress tests under both structured and severely degraded environments, as shown in the proposed diagram in Figure fig:architecture . The main contributions of this paper are summarized as follows: A comprehensive quantitative benchmark that evaluates the real-time operational limits of varying VLM parameter scales (from 1.8B to 11B) in closed-loop UAV navigation systems natively available at . The conceptualization and empirical measurement of the Temporal Reliability Boundary, demonstrating how excessive hardware-induced latency directly correlates with physical trajectory overcorrections in real-time edge robotics. A systematic stress-testing protocol that varies asynchronous query intervals to isolate the critical trade-off between semantic reasoning capabilities and structural output hallucination rates in degraded environments. The identification of an operational "Sweet Spot" in mid-weight VLM architectures, establishing a blueprint for maximizing visual navigational recovery without compromising the strict timing requirements of deterministic FSM controllers. Related Works Reliable navigation in complex aerial missions requires the capacity to perceive, interpret, and respond to environmental information in real time. Traditional unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) systems address this challenge using computer vision, sensor fusion, and deterministic control strategies, which provide robust performance in structured environments. However, their effectiveness declines significantly when visual cues are ambiguous, partially occluded, or degraded. These conditions reveal the inherent limitations of purely geometric perception methods, which restrict their ability to support advanced decision-making or navigational recovery chang2023gpsdenied . Recent advances in multimodal learning have introduced Vision-Language Models (VLMs) as a paradigm for incorporating abstract semantic reasoning into robotic perception systems. Models such as CLIP radford2021clip , BLIP-2 li2023blip2 , and LLaVA demonstrate strong capabilities in visual understanding and zero-shot reasoning by integrating advanced visual encoders with large language models touvron2023llama . Although these architectures have shown promising results on static, open-ended tasks, their application to dynamic, real-time autonomous systems is limited by significant inference latency and the lack of mathematical guarantees. To achieve both flexibility and deterministic safety in robotics, hybrid architectures that combine learning-based components with classical control systems have been extensively investigated. Previous research on visuomotor policies levine2016end and reinforcement learning kober2013reinforcement has demonstrated the effectiveness of data-driven approaches for sequential decision-making. Nevertheless, these methods generally function within narrowly defined action spaces and do not address the challenge of integrating large, free-form generative models into safety-critical, asynchronous control loops. Asynchronous control loops. System Overview and Benchmarking Framework To systematically evaluate the impact of Vision-Language Model scaling and cognitive latency on real-time autonomous flight, an exhaustive benchmarking framework was developed. The evaluations are executed within a fully physics-accurate Software-In-The-Loop (SITL) stack running PX4 Autopilot, ROS~2 Humble middleware, and Gazebo Harmonic (Figure fig:frames ). Hybrid Advisory Architecture The testbed operates under a decoupled hybrid control paradigm, deliberately separating low-level kinetic stability from high-level generative reasoning. The fast control layer consists of a deterministic Finite State Machine (FSM) operating at 30--50~Hz. This layer utilizes classical OpenCV-based pipelines to extract fast visual primitives (lines, simple geometric gates) and pushes immediate velocity setpoints to the flight controller via MAVROS, ensuring constant aerial stabilization how its represented by the Figure fig:simulation_environment ). The slow generative layer functions as an asynchronous advisory copilot. Camera frames are periodically offloaded to a local VLM deployment running varying architectures via Ollama. By decoupling these layers, the FSM can maintain flight stability even while the VLM resolves queries that take several seconds. To combat desynchronization during these inference windows, the framework automatically triggers adaptive speed scaling (slowing the UAV geometry while awaiting insights) and records positional snapshots to enable Latency-Aware Backtracking if semantic target areas are breached during computation. Structured Reasoning Evaluation To quantify the reliability of generative models functioning as robotic operators, a strict structural contract was enforced. VLMs are queried through predefined spatial prompts and are required to output exclusively in a deterministic JSON schema (e.g., boolean flags for primitive detection, explicit strings for turn left, and float values for confidence). This interface allows the benchmark to mathematically isolate and track silent autonomous failures: Format Error: The model returns unparsable syntax or conversational structures instead of the requested JSON. Logic Error: The response maintains valid syntax but hallucinates parameters or semantic conditions unsupported by visual evidence. Outputs failing this structured validation are immediately discarded by the FSM, inherently penalizing the model's mission effectiveness. VLM Variable Scale and Cross-Hardware Deployment Protocol To assess the trade-offs associated with deploying vision-language models (VLMs) at the robotic edge, three generative models representing a range of capabilities and parameter sizes were evaluated: Moondream (1.8B), LLaVA-LLaMA3 (8B), and LLaMA 3.2 Vision (11B). In recognition of the significant computational constraints of onboard unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) systems, the benchmark employs a physical multi-tier hardware setup. The evaluation utilizes the models across two distinct physical operational environments (Table tab:hardware_specs ). The High-Performance environment employs an unrestricted desktop computing architecture to establish theoretical performance baselines. In contrast, the Constrained Profile assesses the models natively on a resource-limited mobile GPU architecture. This deliberate physical contrast enables empirical quantification of the architectural requirements necessary to meet the Temporal Reliability Boundary for safe autonomous recovery. to the Temporal Reliability Boundary for safe autonomous recovery. Evaluation Scenarios os Test Evaluation The models were deployed across a matrix of incrementally complex operational scenarios simulating autonomous delivery, infrastructure inspection, and Urban Search and Rescue (USAR). The missions range from simple street-tracking (Mission 1) to multi-stage altitude sweeping and dynamic semantic identification across structures (Mission 3). A comprehensive Full Run sequential challenge evaluates energy and persistent context capability across all tasks (Figure fig:missions ). To promote reproducibility and statistical reliability, each experimental configuration was evaluated using a comprehensive experimental matrix. Mission~1 was designated as the baseline challenge because it encompasses the essential trajectory-following and semantic recovery tasks within a controlled environment. For each Vision-Language Model (VLM) and hardware profile, the asynchronous semantic query interval was systematically varied across the set s. Each stress condition was independently repeated five times, resulting in 30 autonomous executions per model configuration. The effect of computational and communication delays on closed-loop control performance has been extensively examined in networked control systems. Previous studies have shown that delays must remain below system-dependent admissible bounds to preserve control performance and stability lian2002network,kim2003maximum . This challenge is especially significant in the context of vision-based UAV navigation, where delays in perception and processing have a direct impact on controller tuning, trajectory tracking accuracy, and the boundaries of system stability humais2022delay . title: A Heterogeneous UAV UGV Methodology for Aerial Tracking of Mini Autonomous Cars
comment: This paper was accepted at the Latin American Robotics Symposium LARS 2026
summary: Aerial tracking of autonomous ground vehicles can provide useful situational awareness in environments where fixed external perception infrastructure is unavailable. However, visual-only tracking from an unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) is limited by camera field of view, viewpoint changes, occlusions, and temporary loss of target visibility. This paper presents a heterogeneous UAV--UGV methodology for aerial tracking of small-scale autonomous ground vehicles in simulation. The system is implemented in ROS~2 and Gazebo Sim using a Tello-like UAV equipped with a front-facing RGB camera and multiple LIMO-like unmanned ground vehicles (UGVs). Three approaches are evaluated: a training-free color-marker baseline, a YOLO-based visual baseline, and a proposed UAV--UGV fusion method. The proposed method uses the same visual detector as the YOLO baseline, but combines visual detections with UGV state information to maintain the target estimate during visual gaps. The methods are evaluated across four scenarios: single-car tracking, crossing trajectories, occlusion, and UAV-assisted awareness. Results over 600 simulation runs show that the proposed fusion method achieves nearly continuous track coverage across all scenarios while reducing localization error relative to the YOLO baseline. Compared with the visual-only YOLO approach, the fusion method reduces RMSE by 37.3\%, 64.2\%, 62.6\%, and 61.8\% in the four evaluated scenarios, respectively. The method also enables conflict-awareness lead times of 10.20~s in the crossing scenario and 9.07~s in the UAV-assisted awareness scenario. These results indicate that heterogeneous UAV--UGV fusion can improve aerial tracking continuity and robustness when visual observations are intermittent.

Introduction sec:introduction Heterogeneous robotic teams combine platforms with complementary sensing, mobility, and computational capabilities. In air--ground systems, unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) provide an elevated viewpoint and wide-area perception, while unmanned ground vehicles (UGVs) offer stable ground-level motion, longer operational persistence, and direct interaction with the environment. This complementarity has motivated increasing interest in UAV--UGV cooperation for inspection, mapping, monitoring, search-and-rescue, and collaborative autonomy zhou2026airgroundsurvey,miller2022airground . Aerial tracking of autonomous ground vehicles can be particularly useful in environments where fixed external perception infrastructure is unavailable. This aerial perspective allows the UAV to simultaneously monitor multiple vehicles, detect potentially hazardous situations, and provide complementary information for trajectory coordination. This capability can support fleet monitoring, collision prevention, large-area inspection, and assistance to ground vehicles whose perception is limited by obstacles, short-range sensors, or unfavorable environmental conditions. Despite these advantages, purely visual tracking is limited by the camera field of view, viewpoint changes, partial occlusions, and target appearance variations. These limitations become more critical in multi-robot scenarios where ground vehicles may cross paths, become partially occluded, or enter shared areas where early conflict awareness is required. Real-time object detection has become a standard component of robotic perception systems. The YOLO (You Only Look Once) family is widely adopted because it combines accurate object localization with real-time inference redmon2016yolo . Recent implementations such as YOLOv8 provide practical training and deployment pipelines for robotic applications jocher2023yolov8 . However, continuous target awareness cannot be achieved through visual detection alone. Visual observations become unavailable when the tracked UGV leaves the camera field of view or becomes temporarily occluded. Under these conditions, a UAV relying only on visual perception loses the target despite the detector providing accurate observations whenever the vehicle is visible. This paper proposes a heterogeneous UAV--UGV methodology for simulated aerial tracking of small-scale autonomous ground vehicles. The system employs a mini UAV with a front-facing RGB camera to observe UGVs in a ROS~2 and Gazebo Sim environment. Three tracking approaches are evaluated. The first is a training-free color baseline. The second is a visual baseline based on YOLO. The third is the proposed heterogeneous UAV--UGV approach that integrates visual perception with information shared by the ground vehicle. This comparison isolates the contribution of heterogeneous cooperation to aerial target tracking.Figure~ fig:methodology_framework summarizes the proposed heterogeneous UAV--UGV tracking methodology. The simulated environment provides two complementary information streams. The first is the UAV front RGB image. The second is the UGV state information. The RGB stream is processed by both visual baselines. The proposed method combines visual detections with UGV state information to estimate the target position when visual observations become unavailable. This design isolates the effect of heterogeneous information on tracking continuity. The main contributions of this work are: A ROS~2/Gazebo Sim methodology for heterogeneous UAV--UGV aerial tracking of small-scale autonomous ground vehicles. A comparison between a color-based visual baseline, a YOLO visual baseline, and a UAV--UGV fusion approach. An evaluation across four scenarios: single-car tracking, crossing trajectories, occlusion, and UAV-assisted awareness. Experimental evidence that the proposed fusion method increases track coverage to nearly 100 while reducing localization error across all evaluated scenarios. Related Work sec:related_work UAV Target Tracking UAV target tracking has been studied as both an active and passive perception problem. In active tracking, the UAV adjusts its motion to maintain the target within its field of view, while passive tracking focuses on estimating information about the target from the available observations. State-estimation and fusion strategies, such as Kalman filtering, particle filtering, and learning-based tracking, are commonly used to improve robustness under noisy or intermittent observations wu2025uavsurvey . Vision-based UAV tracking systems often combine object detection with temporal filtering. Barisic et al. presented a vision-based system for real-time detection and following of UAVs using YOLO and a Kalman filter, showing that combining visual detections with dynamic estimation improves tracking stability barisic2022uavfollowing . These works support the idea that visual detections are useful but should be complemented with temporal state estimation. YOLO-Based Robotic Perception YOLO is a family of single-stage detectors capable of estimating object locations and classes within a single inference step redmon2016yolo . Its balance between detection accuracy and processing speed makes it particularly suitable for robotic applications requiring real-time visual perception. YOLOv8 is distributed through the Ultralytics framework, which provides pretrained models, training utilities, and deployment tools jocher2023yolov8 . Recent work has analyzed YOLOv8 and reported its practical advantages for real-time object detection, including its anchor-free design and efficient training pipeline yaseen2024yolov8 . In UAV applications, YOLO-based detectors have been used for flying-object detection, small-object recognition, and lightweight onboard perception. Reis et al. evaluated YOLOv8 for real-time flying-object detection and emphasized challenges related to small target size, motion, occlusion, and cluttered backgrounds reis2023flyingobjects . These challenges are also present in UAV--UGV tracking, where temporary occlusions or field-of-view limitations may interrupt visual observations of the target. Heterogeneous UAV--UGV Cooperation Heterogeneous UAV--UGV systems have been studied for cooperative localization, mapping, planning, and semantic collaboration. Recent surveys describe air--ground heterogeneous systems as a promising robotic paradigm because UAVs and UGVs provide complementary capabilities in perception, mobility, and mission execution zhou2026airgroundsurvey . Other works have explored air--ground cooperation for semantic mapping and navigation, where aerial perception provides information that improves ground-robot decision-making miller2022airground . However, it remains important to evaluate under controlled conditions to what extent shared UGV state information can preserve aerial tracking continuity during temporary visual loss. The present work follows this research direction but focuses specifically on aerial tracking of small-scale autonomous ground vehicles. Unlike a purely visual method, the proposed approach uses the same visual detector as the YOLO baseline and combines visual detections with UGV state information, including position, orientation, and velocity, to maintain continuous tracking during temporary visual loss. This design isolates the contribution of heterogeneous fusion from the contribution of the learned detector. Methodology sec:methodology The proposed methodology (Figure fig:methodology_framework ) is implemented in ROS~2 Jazzy and Gazebo Sim. The simulated heterogeneous team consists of a mini UAV and one or more UGVs. The UAV is equipped with a front-facing RGB camera and observes the UGVs from an elevated viewpoint. The UGVs follow predefined trajectories according to the selected scenario, while the UAV provides aerial visual information. The simulation considers a Tello-like UAV and an Agilex-like UGV. The tracking pipeline contains four main modules: Scenario controller: generates the motion patterns for each experimental scenario. Visual detector: processes the UAV RGB stream and outputs target detections. Tracking module: converts detections into estimated target states and maintains tracks. Experiment logger and evaluator: records samples and computes coverage, localization error, and conflict-awareness metrics. Three tracking methods are evaluated. These include a color baseline, a YOLO visual baseline, and the proposed UAV--UGV fusion approach, as described in the following subsections. Color Baseline The color baseline is a training-free visual method. It detects a colored marker placed on the top of the LIMO using RGB thresholding and connected-component filtering. This method is included as a classical baseline because it does not require a learned detector or a training dataset. However, it is expected to be sensitive to viewpoint changes, marker visibility, lighting, and geometric projection errors. YOLO Visual Baseline The YOLO baseline uses a trained YOLOv8 detector to identify the LIMO marker from the UAV RGB image. The model is trained using images collected from the simulation environment. To avoid inaccurate labels caused by simple geometric projection from the front camera, the final dataset labels are generated from the visible marker in the RGB image. During evaluation, YOLO detections are converted into estimated target positions using a bounding-box-based front-camera range model. This method represents a learned visual baseline: it can localize the target accurately when the marker is visible, but it does not use UGV state information when detections are absent. Proposed UAV--UGV Fusion Method The proposed method uses the same trained YOLO detector as the YOLO baseline. Therefore, both methods share the same visual perception capability. title: AutoPruner: Agentic Depth Pruning for Vision-Language-Action Models
summary: Layer pruning reduces the size and inference cost of vision-language-action (VLA) models, but selecting a deployable configuration requires deciding both which layers to remove and how to recover task performance. These decisions depend on the model and task, and a failed trial can reflect either the deletion set or insufficient recovery. We present AutoPruner, an agent-driven framework that jointly searches pruning structures and recovery recipes through closed-loop experimentation. Offline layer interventions measure changes in action output to provide functional evidence. An LLM agent combines this evidence with evaluation history and retained diagnoses to propose deletion sets and recovery recipes within a search budget. Each proposal is executed and evaluated on the target tasks, and the resulting feedback guides the next experiment. Across OpenVLA-OFT, StarVLA, and FastWAM on four LIBERO suites, AutoPruner removes 16.7--87.5% of backbone layers while maintaining task success above 90%, with measured inference speedups of up to 2.50$\times$. Further analysis shows that functional probes identify action-sensitive layers despite high representation similarity, and that recovery can make previously failing structures viable.
full_text: AutoPruner overview. (a) Manual pruning requires repeated human tuning. (b) AutoPruner selects pruning structures and recovery strategies using probes and closed-loop feedback. (c) Results on LIBERO Object show parameter and latency reductions across three robot policies. fig:teaser Layer pruning reduces the size and inference cost of vision-language-action (VLA) models, but selecting a deployable configuration requires deciding both which layers to remove and how to recover task performance. These decisions depend on the model and task, and a failed trial can reflect either the deletion set or insufficient recovery. We present AutoPruner, an agent-driven framework that jointly searches pruning structures and recovery recipes through closed-loop experimentation. Offline layer interventions measure changes in action output to provide functional evidence. An LLM agent combines this evidence with evaluation history and retained diagnoses to propose deletion sets and recovery recipes within a search budget. Each proposal is executed and evaluated on the target tasks, and the resulting feedback guides the next experiment. Across OpenVLA-OFT, StarVLA, and FastWAM on four LIBERO suites, AutoPruner removes 16.7--87.5 of backbone layers while maintaining task success above 90 , with measured inference speedups of up to 2.50 . Further analysis shows that functional probes identify action-sensitive layers despite high representation similarity, and that recovery can make previously failing structures viable. Introduction Vision-language-action (VLA) models rely on billion-parameter backbones whose memory and computation requirements constrain robot deployment~ kim2024openvla,black2024pi0,starvla2026 . Runtime techniques including token skipping and computation caching can reduce inference cost without shrinking the stored model~ jiang2025lightvla,xu2025vlacache . Layer pruning instead removes transformer blocks, reducing model size and backbone computation~ men2025shortgpt,yang2025efficientvla,fan2020layerdrop . The challenge is finding a deletion set and recovery recipe that preserve task success on the deployment. Structure and recovery are coupled. A deletion set that initially disrupts behavior may become viable after recovery. In our experiments, two deletion sets exhibit a reversal in observed task performance after the same recovery procedure. Immediate pruning damage alone therefore cannot determine the preferred deployment configuration. Feasible structures also vary across models and tasks: some tolerate long contiguous deletions, while others require preserving sensitive internal layers. These observations motivate joint selection of deletion sets and recovery recipes for each deployment. Single-layer measurements guide this selection, while task evaluations reveal the combined effect of deleting multiple layers and recovering the policy. Each trial may require recovery training and hundreds of closed-loop rollouts. When performance falls short, the next decision is whether to revise the deletion set or try another recovery recipe. Failure alone cannot distinguish an unsuitable structure from insufficient recovery; previous trials provide context for choosing the next step. As Figure~ fig:teaser (a) illustrates, manual pruning requires repeated human intervention to interpret results and rerun experiments. We therefore treat pruning as an iterative experimental process in which previous trials determine the next structure–recovery configuration to evaluate. We introduce AutoPruner, an agentic framework that jointly searches deletion sets and recovery recipes for a target deployment, as shown in Figure~ fig:teaser (b). Layer interventions measure changes in action output, providing functional evidence for initial proposals. AutoPruner uses an LLM agent to integrate functional measurements, trial history, and diagnoses, jointly revising deletion sets and recovery recipes through closed-loop task feedback within a search budget. Model-specific tools execute proposals, and closed-loop evaluation identifies configurations meeting the target success threshold. The user selects a passing configuration for export as a physically pruned checkpoint with its evaluation records. We evaluate pruning and recovery on OpenVLA-OFT~ kim2025openvlaoft , StarVLA~ starvla2026 , and FastWAM~ yuan2026fastwam . On OpenVLA-OFT Object, the pruned policy retains four of 32 backbone layers with 92.6 success, reducing parameters from 7.71B to 2.05B and latency from 102 to 41 ms. Further analyses examine functional layer evidence and recovery-dependent pruning depth, while a logged OpenVLA-OFT search demonstrates proposal revision using task feedback. Our contributions are threefold: We formulate deployment-specific VLA depth pruning as a sequential decision problem over layer removal and recovery, guided by closed-loop task performance under a search budget. We develop AutoPruner, an agentic framework that integrates functional measurements, retained diagnoses, and tool execution to revise deletion sets and recovery recipes through experimental feedback. We evaluate pruning and recovery across three heterogeneous VLA systems on four LIBERO suites, removing 16.7--87.5 of backbone layers with inference speedups of 1.11--2.50 while maintaining measured task success above 90 across all twelve deployments. Related Work Agentic Model Optimization ReAct grounds language-model decisions in tool feedback~ yao2023react , and Reflexion retains textual reflections on task feedback to guide later attempts~ shinn2023reflexion . This pattern has been extended to score-guided optimization, code search, automated experimentation, and full machine-learning pipelines~ yang2024opro,jiang2025aide,lu2024aiscientist,ren2026autoresearch,trirat2024automlagent . Agentic methods have also been applied to compression. ProfilingAgent reasons over static cost metrics and runtime profiles to plan layer-wise structured pruning and post-training quantization~ jafari2025profilingagent . Agent-guided pruning selects layers from weight-activation and gradient sensitivity profiles, using self-reflection and checkpoint rollback across iterations~ kodathala2026llmcompress . These systems score a fixed compression operator against static accuracy or perplexity proxies. AutoPruner instead jointly selects deletion sets and recovery recipes using functional measurements and closed-loop task success. Efficient Vision-Language-Action Models Compact VLAs such as TinyVLA and SmolVLA reduce model size or action-generation costs~ wen2025tinyvla,shukor2025smolvla , while OpenVLA-OFT and FAST improve action decoding or representation~ kim2025openvlaoft,pertsch2025fast . Quantization reduces inference memory~ kim2024openvla , and SQAP-VLA combines it with visual-token pruning~ fang2025sqapvla . LightVLA and VLA-Pruner prune visual tokens~ jiang2025lightvla,liu2025vlapruner , and VLA-Cache reuses token features across control steps~ xu2025vlacache . DeeR-VLA uses early exits~ yue2024deervla , while MoLe-VLA and DySL-VLA dynamically skip layers~ zhang2025molevla,yang2026dyslvla , retaining backbone layers in the model. EfficientVLA prunes layers in a training-free manner from input--output hidden-state similarity and reuses diffusion-head features~ yang2025efficientvla . Removed capacity is typically restored by retraining a small set of parameters or by distilling from the dense model~ houlsby2019adapters,hinton2015distillation,rusu2016policydistillation , as in LLM-Pruner, which pairs structural pruning with low-rank adaptation~ ma2023llmpruner . GLUESTICK recovers pruned VLA policies through training-free weight-space correction~ jabbour2025dontrunscissorspruning . These methods apply recovery after the deletion set is fixed. AutoPruner incorporates recovery into the search, evaluating deletion sets together with recovery recipes on the target tasks. AutoPruner proposes deletions from the action changes caused by individual layer bypasses, and exports policies meeting the deployment success threshold with the selected layers physically removed. Method As shown in Figure~ fig:framework , AutoPruner closes the pruning and recovery loop with an LLM agent. The LLM agent acts as the proposal controller, selecting the next deletion set and recovery recipe from the accumulated evidence and recovery library. Tools prune, recover, and evaluate each policy. Feedback guides subsequent proposals toward deeper pruning under a success threshold and a round budget. title: GeoForward: Geometry-Guided Cross-View Alignment for Feedforward 3D Gaussian Splatting
summary: Feedforward 3D reconstruction has largely followed an {appearance-driven paradigm}: multi-view images are encoded into visual representations, cross-view correspondence is implicitly inferred from learned features, and 3D primitives are subsequently predicted from these representations. However, calibrated cameras and sparse metric measurements already provide explicit constraints on where the same physical point should appear across views. We propose a novel paradigm, \textbf{Geometry-Conditioned Feedforward Reconstruction}, in which metric geometry establishes cross-view correspondence before the 3D representation is formed, while learned visual features refine rather than discover this correspondence. Based on this paradigm, we introduce \textbf{GeoForward}. Sparse LiDAR points are unprojected into 3D and analytically projected across calibrated cameras to provide metric correspondence anchors. A bounded continuous local search then refines these anchors using visual features, and the resulting geometry-conditioned representation is fused with global multi-view context from VGGT. The shared representation drives separate metric-depth and Gaussian-attribute prediction, establishing a direct path from explicit geometry to both Gaussian centers and spatial attributes. A sparse 3D refinement module subsequently improves local attribute compatibility while preserving the geometrically determined centers. For temporal reconstruction, endpoint Gaussians are composed using vehicle masks and motion priors. On nuScenes, GeoForward achieves the lowest cross-camera depth-consistency error and Chamfer distance among the compared methods while maintaining competitive reconstruction quality. These results demonstrate that explicitly conditioning correspondence formation on metric geometry provides an effective alternative to purely appearance-driven feedforward 3D reconstruction.
full_text: Feedforward 3D reconstruction has largely followed an appearance-driven paradigm : multi-view images are encoded into visual representations, cross-view correspondence is implicitly inferred from learned features, and 3D primitives are subsequently predicted from these representations. While effective, this paradigm leaves a fundamental source of information underexploited: calibrated cameras and sparse metric measurements already provide explicit constraints on where the same physical point should appear across views. We propose a novel paradigm, Geometry-Conditioned Feedforward Reconstruction, in which metric geometry establishes cross-view correspondence before the 3D representation is formed, while learned visual features refine rather than discover this correspondence. Based on this paradigm, we introduce GeoForward. Sparse LiDAR points are unprojected into 3D and analytically projected across calibrated cameras to provide metric correspondence anchors. A bounded continuous local search then refines these anchors using visual features, and the resulting geometry-conditioned representation is fused with global multi-view context from VGGT. The shared representation drives separate metric-depth and Gaussian-attribute prediction, establishing a direct path from explicit geometry to both Gaussian centers and spatial attributes. A sparse 3D refinement module subsequently improves local attribute compatibility while preserving the geometrically determined centers. For temporal reconstruction, endpoint Gaussians are composed using vehicle masks and motion priors. On nuScenes, GeoForward achieves the lowest cross-camera depth-consistency error and Chamfer distance among the compared methods while maintaining competitive reconstruction quality. These results demonstrate that explicitly conditioning correspondence formation on metric geometry provides an effective alternative to purely appearance-driven feedforward 3D reconstruction. Introduction sec:introduction Feed-forward 3D reconstruction has recently emerged as a promising alternative to optimization-based scene reconstruction, enabling 3D representations to be predicted directly from multi-view observations without per-scene fitting~ smyzanowicz2024splatter,charatan2024pixelsplat,chen2024mvsplat,tian2025drivingforward . A central challenge in this setting is establishing reliable correspondence across views: observations from different cameras should describe the same physical surface and therefore produce geometrically compatible representations. Existing approaches typically address this challenge by learning cross-view relationships from visual representations, where image features implicitly encode correspondence cues before 3D geometry is decoded. This appearance-driven formulation has achieved impressive performance, but it leaves an important source of information underexploited. In calibrated autonomous-driving platforms equipped with sparse LiDAR, metric measurements already provide physical constraints on where a scene point observed in one camera should appear in another. This motivates a fundamental question: can metric geometry directly participate in cross-view correspondence formation before 3D representation prediction? Existing feed-forward reconstruction methods incorporate geometric information through different mechanisms, including learned depth prediction, explicit depth-hypothesis reasoning, or geometric foundation models that infer multi-view structure from images~ charatan2024pixelsplat,chen2024mvsplat,wang2024dust3r,wang2025vggt . These approaches demonstrate the power of learned visual representations for recovering geometry, but the correspondence underlying reconstruction remains primarily obtained through visual inference. In driving scenes, sparse LiDAR and calibrated cameras provide a complementary opportunity: instead of requiring a network to discover all possible cross-view associations from appearance, metric observations can provide a physically grounded initialization that narrows the correspondence search space. We introduce GeoForward, a geometry-conditioned paradigm for feed-forward 3D reconstruction, as illustrated in Fig.~ fig:teaser . Different from appearance-driven correspondence learning, GeoForward first establishes metric cross-view correspondence using sparse LiDAR measurements and calibrated camera geometry. A LiDAR-supported point in a reference view is unprojected into 3D and projected into context views, providing an explicit correspondence anchor. Since sparse sensing, calibration errors, and discretization introduce residual uncertainty, a bounded continuous refinement module further adjusts the correspondence using local visual features. In this way, geometry constrains where cross-view evidence should be associated, while learning determines how the local correspondence should be refined. The geometry-conditioned representation is then used for Gaussian scene reconstruction. GeoForward fuses the aligned features with global multi-view context from a frozen VGGT encoder~ wang2025vggt and jointly predicts metric depth and Gaussian attributes. The depth branch determines Gaussian centers through camera unprojection, while the attribute branch predicts spatial extent, opacity, and appearance conditioned on the geometry-aware representation. Beyond initial prediction, a sparse 3D neighborhood refinement module improves local attribute compatibility while preserving the predicted Gaussian centers. For dynamic driving scenes, endpoint Gaussian representations are further composed at arbitrary query times using vehicle masks and motion priors~ yu2026recondrive,he2026dynamicvggt,song2026envision4d . We evaluate GeoForward on two large-scale driving-scene benchmarks, nuScenes~ caesar2020nuscenes and Waymo~ sun2020scalability . Experiments demonstrate that explicitly conditioning correspondence formation on metric geometry improves cross-view geometric consistency while maintaining competitive rendering quality. These results suggest a complementary direction for feed-forward reconstruction: rather than relying solely on learned appearance-based association, available metric information can directly participate in forming the 3D representation. Our contributions are summarized as follows: 0pt 0pt 0pt 0pt 0.5em We propose a geometry-conditioned paradigm for feed-forward 3D reconstruction, where sparse metric geometry constrains cross-view correspondence before 3D representation formation, reducing ambiguous visual matches and anchoring depth and Gaussian prediction in metric space. We introduce GeoForward, which combines LiDAR-based correspondence initialization with bounded visual refinement and propagates geometry-conditioned features into Gaussian geometry and attribute prediction. We introduce sparse 3D attribute refinement to improve local Gaussian consistency without modifying geometrically determined centers, and demonstrate improved cross-view reconstruction quality on nuScenes and Waymo. Related Work Feed-Forward 3D Scene Reconstruction Recent advances in feed-forward reconstruction aim to predict 3D scene representations directly from multi-view observations, avoiding expensive per-scene optimization. DUSt3R learns pairwise point maps from image pairs, while VGGT extends this idea to jointly estimate depth, point maps, camera parameters, and point tracks from multiple views~ wang2024dust3r,wang2025vggt . InfiniDepth further explores continuous coordinate-query decoding for high-resolution geometric prediction~ yu2026infinidepth . Building on these geometric representations, recent works investigate feed-forward Gaussian reconstruction. MVSplat, AnySplat, and IDESplat predict Gaussian representations directly from images, improving reconstruction efficiency and scalability~ chen2024mvsplat,jiang2025anysplat,long2026idesplat . For autonomous driving scenarios, DrivingForward, DGGT, and StreetForward incorporate camera poses, temporal information, and dynamic scene modeling into feed-forward Gaussian reconstruction~ tian2025drivingforward,chen2026dggt,yu2026streetforward . DynamicVGGT and Envision4D further extend feed-forward reconstruction toward temporal prediction and future scene generation~ he2026dynamicvggt,song2026envision4d . Other approaches improve multi-view representation through 3D latent structures, uncertainty-aware canonical representations, or sparse 3D queries, including UniSplat, CanonicalGS, and PointForward~ shi2026unisplat,xu2026learning,chi2026pointforward . ReconDrive further combines VGGT representations with hybrid Gaussian prediction and velocity-based temporal composition for driving scenes~ yu2026recondrive . Although these methods achieve impressive reconstruction quality, cross-view consistency is mainly obtained through learned visual representations and implicit feature interaction. GeoForward complements this direction by introducing explicit metric constraints into the cross-view association process before Gaussian prediction. Metric-Guided Multi-View Geometric Reasoning Metric measurements provide an important source of geometric constraints for multi-view reconstruction and depth estimation. Previous works incorporate sparse geometric priors into multi-view stereo through sparse cost-volume construction or depth hypothesis refinement~ qi2022sparse,poggi2022multi . In autonomous driving, LiDAR measurements are particularly valuable due to their accurate metric information, and several approaches explore LiDAR-guided geometric prediction. DriveMVS uses sparse LiDAR observations to anchor depth hypotheses and incorporate geometric cues into feature fusion, while DrivingDepth leverages sparse LiDAR measurements to calibrate monocular depth estimation through metric correction~ sun2026lidar,huang2026drivingdepth . Related LiDAR-camera fusion methods further combine sparse depth measurements with image features for dense depth estimation~ fu2019lidar,wei2023real . These approaches demonstrate the effectiveness of metric information for reducing geometric ambiguity. However, existing methods primarily introduce geometry as a constraint on depth estimation or feature enhancement, while the cross-view association underlying representation prediction is still largely determined by learned visual similarity. GeoForward explores a different use of metric information by treating sparse LiDAR measurements as geometric anchors for cross-view feature alignment. Rather than predicting correspondence purely from appearance or depth hypotheses, GeoForward establishes geometry-aware associations through calibrated projection and refines them using local visual evidence. Methodology sec:geoforward_method 5pt plus 2pt minus 1pt 5pt plus 2pt minus 1pt 3pt plus 1pt minus 1pt 3pt plus 1pt minus 1pt 0pt Overview. GeoForward reconstructs a Gaussian scene from calibrated surround-view images and sparse LiDAR depth observed at two endpoint timestamps. Camera intrinsics and camera-to-reference poses transform all observations into a common reference-ego frame. The key idea of GeoForward is to convert sparse metric measurements into explicit cross-camera feature correspondence before Gaussian prediction. As illustrated in Fig.~ fig:geoforward_overview , a LiDAR-supported pixel in a reference camera is first projected into a context camera using calibrated geometry, providing a metric correspondence initialization. A bounded learned offset then refines this correspondence using local visual evidence. The resulting aligned features are combined with global multi-view features from a frozen VGGT encoder~ wang2025vggt and shared by the depth and Gaussian-attribute prediction branches. Finally, a sparse 3D refinement module improves local attribute compatibility while preserving the predicted Gaussian centers, and endpoint Gaussians are composed at arbitrary query times for dynamic-scene rendering. Sparse LiDAR is used at both training and inference. Metric-Guided

title: Language-Forcing: Advancing Humanoid Loco-Manipulation via Semantic Alignment of Whole-Body World Action Models
comment: 9 pages of main text, 31 pages of appendix
summary: World Action Models (WAMs) jointly predict robot actions and future observations. However, their visual prediction objectives do not explicitly distinguish task-relevant transitions from incidental scene changes. For whole-body policies, this distinction matters because task progress depends on coordinated changes in body pose, contact, and object state. We introduce LANGUAGE-FORCING, a training strategy that uses language to emphasize task-relevant changes in the future visual representations of a whole-body WAM. Given paired current and ground- truth short-horizon future frames, a frozen vision-language model assesses task progress and predicts plausible subsequent state changes. We encode these descriptions with a frozen text encoder and align their embeddings with intermediate, action-conditioned future-visual features, complementing the original visual and action prediction objectives. All auxiliary components are used only during training, introducing no additional inference overhead. On HumanoidArena, LANGUAGE-FORCING achieves an average success rate of 79.17%, exceeding the strongest competing policy by 9.46 percentage points and the same WAM without language alignment by 10.77 percentage points. Across five real-world tasks, language alignment raises average success from 53.33% to 71.33% over the same WAM baseline.
full_text: 10pt plus 2pt minus 2pt 8pt plus 2pt minus 2pt 6pt Experiments sec:experiments We evaluate on HumanoidArena and five real-world tasks. The ablations examine the content of the language targets, their correspondence with the observations, and the future visual information used during training. Experimental Setup sec:experimental_setup Benchmark and metric. HumanoidArena wang2026humanoidarenabenchmarkingegocentrichierarchical evaluates humnanoid whole-body policies on seven tasks. The human-object interaction(HOI) tasks including Football, DoubleDesk, and P PBox; the human-scene interaction(HSI) tasks including OpenDoor, SitSofa, Boxing, and VisNavi. All policies use SONIC for motion tracking during evaluation. We evaluate each task under the base mode and three out-of-distribution (OOD) modes: lighting changes (visual), altered appearance or distractors (semantic), and object positions outside the training range (execution). Each mode uses three rollout seeds and 20 trials per seed, giving 240 trials per task and 1,680 trials in total. We report success rate (SR), with equal weight for the four settings, and the unweighted mean across tasks (AVG). We report the success rate (SR) over all 240 trials for each task and average success rate across all tasks. Baselines. We compare with established visuomotor policies, including ACT zhao2023learningfinegrainedbimanual , Diffusion Policy (DP) chi2023diffusionpolicyvisuomotor , and a flow-matching policy (FM) lipman2023flowmatchinggenerativemodeling . We also evaluate recent vision-language-action (VLA) models: intelligence2025pi05visionlanguageactionmodelopenworld and GR00T N1.7 nvidia2025gr00tn1openfoundation . Representative WAM baselines include LingBot-VA li2026causalworldmodelingrobot , Fast-WAM yuan2026fastwamworldactionmodels , and GigaWorld-Policy 0.5 ye2026gigaworldpolicyefficientactioncenteredworldaction . GigaWorld-Policy 0.5 also serves as the base WAM for . ACT, DP, FM, and are reevaluated under the same protocol. Training. Training demonstrations contains 200 successful episodes per task, for 1,400 episodes in total. All methods use same training data and action interface. We match the observation sources, initial configurations, rollout seeds, and success criteria within each evaluation setting. Each model is trained for 50K updates using its architecture specific preprocessing and optimization settings. We initialize from GigaWorld-Policy 0.5 and adapt its action interface to the whole-body representation in Section~ sec:preliminaries . The WAM receives images and five frames at offsets in the 50 Hz trajectory. The models with and without Language Forcing use the same initialization, humanoid adapters, training data, and base optimization settings; the added language loss is the only difference. We use the final 50K step exponential moving average (EMA) weights for evaluation. All ablations retain this training budget. Data partitions and model-specific settings are provided in Appendix~ sec:implementation_details . Policy Performance sec:main_results Overall performance. achieves the highest average SR of (Table~ tab:main_results ), exceeding the strongest baseline, GR00T N1.7, by percentage points. The results cover both object interaction and scene interaction, which require different combinations of locomotion, body positioning, and manipulation. Effect of Language Forcing. Compared with the same WAM without Language Forcing, our method raises average SR by percentage points. Language-Forcing improves performance on tasks involving object motion, such as Football and DoubleDesk, as well as body positioning in SitSofa and navigation in VisNavi. The base WAM already learns to predict future observations. Adding task-relevant semantic supervision and future-state predictions as supervision for its visual features further improves the policy, without changing its inference procedure. The ablations below examine what makes this language supervision useful. Task-relevant spatial focus. Figure~ fig:spatial_focus expands the representation visualization in Figure~ fig:teaser (b). With Language Forcing, responses focus on the ball in Football and the punching bag in Boxing, and on the manipulated object and interacting hand in DoubleDesk and P PBox. Without Language Forcing, responses are more dispersed over background regions. These qualitative examples support the task-relevant focus of the learned visual features, complementing the performance gains in Table~ tab:main_results . Language-Forcing Design Analysis sec:ablations We first investigate different language supervision targets, their correspondence with observed transitions, and the frames used for visual prediction. Then we study the effects of alignment depth and language-loss weight, and compare performance with different numbers of demonstrations. r 0.48 3pt 0pt Language supervision on HumanoidArena. Left: alignment targets with identical VLM image inputs. Right: matched versus within-task shuffled descriptions. WAM training images are fixed. fig:language_supervision_ablation Task relevant semantics versus image captions. We compare task instructions, captions of the future image, and the descriptions used by Language Forcing as alignment targets (Figure~ fig:language_supervision_ablation , left). For both captioning and Language Forcing, the VLM receives the current and future images. The caption prompt asks for a description of the future scene. Language Forcing asks the VLM to assess progress and predict future states. The WAM's visual targets and task-instruction conditioning remain unchanged. Captions improve SR over training without language alignment, while Language Forcing adds a further percentage points. Task instructions give the lowest SR among the three language targets. With the same observations available to the VLM, language about task progress and future states provides more effective supervision than a description of the future scene alone. Matching language to observations. We shuffle language descriptions across trajectories of the same task (Figure~ fig:language_supervision_ablation , right). The descriptions remain relevant to the task, but are no longer paired with the observations used to produce them. Matching each description to its original observations improves SR by percentage points over shuffling. Thus, descriptions of the same task cannot be used interchangeably for language alignment. The language needs to reflect the robot actions and object states of the corresponding observations, where the robot and objects may be at different stages of the task. Predicting future frames. We keep the language descriptions fixed and change the images used for future video prediction. Every setting uses five image inputs, with frames repeated when necessary. Repeating the current image in all five positions yields SR. Including the current image, one intermediate frame, and the endpoint increases SR to , while using three intermediate frames raises it to , with the current image and endpoint unchanged. The latter comparison isolates the benefit of including more images of the motion before the endpoint. Language provides task-relevant semantic supervision and describes future states, while the intermediate frames show how the robot and objects move. The improvement from these frames explains why future video prediction remains useful alongside language alignment. The frame offsets and repeated inputs are listed in Appendix~ sec:implementation_details . With the language descriptions and training images fixed, we next examine where to apply alignment and how to weight the language loss. Alignment layer. We apply language alignment at five blocks of the visual expert, keeping (Table~ tab:ablation-alignment-depth , left). All five improve upon the WAM without Language Forcing, and block 22 achieves the highest SR. Moving alignment from block 22 to block 29 reduces performance, so a layer closer to the visual output is not necessarily a better choice for language supervision. We use block 22 in ; block indices are zero-based. Language-loss weight. With alignment at block 22, we vary the weight of the language loss relative to the visual and action losses (Table~ tab:ablation-loss-weight , right). SR peaks at and decreases at larger weights. At , performance approaches the WAM baseline. Language alignment therefore benefits action modeling at a moderate weight, but increasing its contribution to the training objective does not produce a larger gain. We use in . Data efficiency. We compare the WAM with and without Language Forcing using the same subsets of demonstrations and 50K training updates (Table~ tab:ablation-data-efficiency ). Language Forcing improves SR at every training-set size. With of the demonstrations, the WAM with Language Forcing reaches SR, compared with for the WAM trained on all demonstrations without language alignment. This corresponds to comparable performance with fewer demonstrations in this experiment. The gains also persist as more demonstrations become available. From to of the training set, Language Forcing maintains an improvement of around 10 percentage points. The benefit therefore extends beyond training with very few demonstrations: adding more robot data does not remove the gain from language supervision. The VLM extracts task-relevant semantic information from the recorded images, providing additional supervision without collecting new robot demonstrations. Real-World Experiments sec:real_world_experiments We evaluate on five real-world tasks and compare with the same WAM without Language Forcing, GR00T N1.7, and Fast-WAM. The comparison with the same WAM examines whether language supervision improves physical task completion under the same training and deployment settings. The robot hardware and deployment workstation are described in Appendix~ sec:implementation_details . Tasks and evaluation. The tasks in Figure~ fig:real_exp require different combinations of locomotion and object interaction. Box transport combines carrying with walking, while food preparation involves several objects. Visual navigation requires reaching a visually specified target. Moving a clothes rack and opening a door require coordinated body motion and hand contact. The task instructions are fixed across methods: Carry the box, Prepare the food, Navigate to the target, Move the clothes rack, and Open the door. Each method is trained with demonstrations per task, for demonstrations in total. We evaluate each policy over trials per task under held-out initial configurations, giving trials per method. Trials vary box and rack positions, food objects and poses, navigation targets, and doors and handles. All methods use the same demonstrations, instructions, observations, and evaluation scenes. We report success rate for each task and the mean across the five tasks. Whole-body task completion. Language Forcing improves all five tasks and raises average SR from to (Table~ tab:real_world_results ). Food preparation shows the largest gain, at percentage points. The improvements extend from navigation, where progress means reaching a target location, to manipulation, where completion requires changing the state of an object. The comparison with the same WAM shows that task-relevant semantic supervision complements action and future-frame prediction and improves real-world task success. Deployment efficiency. With KV caching and quantization, policy inference takes \,ms on a RTX4090 24G GPU. Language Forcing is used only during training, so our method does not add computation at inference. More details are given in Appendix~ sec:deployment_details .

title: MicroSplat: Towards Automating 3D Small-Scale Reconstruction
summary: Reconstructing sub-millimeter detail of small objects underpins tasks such as circuit-board defect detection, specimen digitization, and archiving. 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) makes photorealistic reconstruction possible from posed images alone, but macro optics violate two conditions it depends on. The field of view (FOV) and the depth of field (DoF) shrink to millimeters, so viewpoint error can take a sample out of frame, and only a thin focal plane is sharp in frame. Existing automated macro-capture rigs handle the shallow DoF with per-view focus stacking, but typically rely on classical photogrammetry and offline, human-in-the-loop processing. We present MicroSplat, which generates a 3DGS using a low-cost consumer microscope on a manipulator arm. After a single up-front object-localization step, the system runs unattended. It performs calibration, plans collision-free viewpoints, captures and fuses a focal stack at each viewpoint, segments the object across all views, and optimizes a 3DGS model warm-started with the arm's own poses. We further compare against blur-aware 3DGS methods, which infer sharp scenes from defocused images, and find that measuring sharpness with a controlled focal sweep outperforms inferring it. We provide real and synthetic datasets (including robot and camera parameters) and the fitted 3DGS reconstructions.
full_text: Reconstructing sub-millimeter detail of small objects underpins tasks such as circuit-board defect detection, specimen digitization, and archiving. 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) makes photorealistic reconstruction possible from posed images alone, but macro optics violate two conditions it depends on. The field of view (FOV) and the depth of field (DoF) shrink to millimeters, so viewpoint error can take a sample out of frame, and only a thin focal plane is sharp in frame. Existing automated macro-capture rigs handle the shallow DoF with per-view focus stacking, but typically rely on classical photogrammetry and offline, human-in-the-loop processing. We present MicroSplat, which generates a 3DGS using a low-cost consumer microscope on a manipulator arm. After a single up-front object-localization step, the system runs unattended. It performs calibration, plans collision-free viewpoints, captures and fuses a focal stack at each viewpoint, segments the object across all views, and optimizes a 3DGS model warm-started with the arm's own poses. We further compare against blur-aware 3DGS methods, which infer sharp scenes from defocused images, and find that measuring sharpness with a controlled focal sweep outperforms inferring it. We provide real and synthetic datasets (including robot and camera parameters) and the fitted 3DGS reconstructions. Introduction Centimeter-scale objects resolved at sub-millimeter detail are the working domain of a range of inspection and digitization tasks: defect detection on printed circuit boards (PCBs) and solder joints, the digitization of insects and biological specimens, and the archiving of coins and other small artifacts~ fu2023pcbicp,lu2023solderjoint,macdonald2017coins,doan2024insectscanner . 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS)~ kerbl20233dgs makes photorealistic reconstruction possible from posed RGB images alone, but macro optics break two of its working assumptions at once. The field of view and the depth of field (DoF) both shrink to millimeters, so viewpoint error decides whether the sample is in frame at all; and within a single exposure only a thin focal plane is sharp, so recovering sharp detail requires an explicit strategy. Two families exist: focus stacking, which recovers sharpness before reconstruction by combining multiple images per viewpoint, and blur-aware methods, which recover a sharp scene from defocused images during the reconstruction phase. Systems that automate macro capture, such as the Orbitoscope~ ylinampa2026orbitoscope , already handle the shallow DoF with per-view focus stacking, positioning their sample by hand at a fixed orbit center. What they do not produce is a Gaussian Splat; these systems reconstruct with classical photogrammetry and rely on offline, human-in-the-loop processing. The manual efforts that do create a Gaussian Splat require labor-intensive hand-masking of hundreds of images to suppress floater artifacts (spurious semi-transparent Gaussians) induced by blurred backgrounds~ bittel2025macro . MicroSplat Project page (includes interactive viewer): . Code: pairs a robotic manipulator arm (KUKA iiwa14 R820) with a low-cost consumer microscope as its end-effector ( ). We leverage the arm's repeatability to enable microscope calibration and precise microscope placement for focus stacking. Our use of a low-cost microscope introduced noise in both our images and poses. We developed several engineering solutions such as a human-in-the-loop object-centering pipeline, SfM initialization with robot pose and camera intrinsics, and Gaussian-fit-based window selection for focus stacking to make our pipeline robust to this noise. To summarize, we make three main contributions: An autonomous capture-to-reconstruction pipeline, in which, after calibration and object-centering, the system captures data and generates a 3DGS model of a small object. We also extensively evaluate the impact of key engineering choices in our pipeline (object centering and robot pose SfM initialization) through ablations and comparison to baselines. A comparison against blur-aware 3DGS methods, in which we benchmark our focus-stacking approach on synthetic data using ground-truth in-focus renderings, and show that when a controlled robotic focal sweep captures sharp detail from every viewpoint, measuring sharpness directly outperforms inferring it from defocused images during reconstruction. A reconstruction dataset of eight real objects and eight synthetic objects, spanning a wide range of attributes. The dataset contains information on scans, 3DGS reconstructions, initial robot arm poses and camera intrinsics. For each synthetic object we additionally release the Blender scene and object mesh, along with both the shallow-DoF focal stacks and the corresponding fully in-focus renderings, which serve as ground truth. , released under CC BY 4.0. The rest of the paper is organized as follows: covers related work, details our method's hardware, calibration, planning, and reconstruction stack, and presents experimental results. Related Work sec:related We now review existing systems for automated 3D capture, highlighting the gap in small-scale capture that our system targets. Automated Capture Rigs 3D reconstruction is an essential tool used across a wide range of domains such as film, video games, virtual and augmented reality, medical imaging, and robotics. Neural rendering has emerged as a powerful approach to this problem, with Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF)~ mildenhall2020nerf and 3DGS~ kerbl20233dgs being commonly adopted over classical photogrammetry for their ability to produce photorealistic novel-view synthesis from posed images alone. With so many applications relying on 3D reconstruction, much work has focused on automating the data collection process. For example, the Google Scanned Objects dataset demonstrated a custom enclosure with structured light and machine vision cameras capable of generating high-fidelity 3D models for over 1,000 household items for the downstream task of robot learning~ downs2022google . More recently, automated pipelines have moved toward reconstructing objects directly with 3DGS from RGB images alone, without the depth or structured-light hardware these earlier systems require~ qiu2025omniscan, strong2024nextbestsense, jiang2024fisherrf, pan2022activenerf . For example, Omni-Scan~ qiu2025omniscan used a bi-manual robot to rotate a grasped object in front of a fixed RGB camera, merging two scans into a 3DGS model. To isolate the object from the gripper and background, it prompts SAM~2~ ravi2025sam2 with foreground cues and scores the resulting candidate masks. We similarly use SAM 2 for object mask generation in MicroSplat. Small-Scale Reconstruction Beyond standard objects, there is great interest in applying 3D reconstruction to resolve sub-millimeter detail as well. In electronics and semiconductor manufacturing, high-fidelity reconstructions of PCBs, microcontrollers, and solder joints enable automated defect detection and quality control~ fu2023pcbicp, lu2023solderjoint . Similar techniques are used to digitize insects and biological specimens in entomology, to archive coins, engravings, and other small artifacts in cultural heritage, and to characterize surface morphology in materials science~ macdonald2017coins, gallo2014multifocus, doan2024insectscanner, spp_gaussian_splatting_2024 . Small-Scale Capture and Sharpness Recovery Hobbyists such as Danny Bittel have shown that Gaussian Splatting of small objects is possible with manual macro photography~ bittel2025macro , using focus stacking~ wang2011focusstacking to overcome shallow DOF: a series of images are captured from a single viewpoint while the camera steps along the optical axis, and the resulting slices are fused into one all-in-focus composite. Manually producing such a capture, however, faces two bottlenecks. First, at macro working distances, both FOV and DOF are small, so precise viewpoint control is essential. Second, masks are necessary since blurred backgrounds lack geometric cues, causing background-colored floater artifacts that forced Bittel to hand-mask hundreds of images. Several works do automate this capture process for small samples via focus stacking~ gallo2014multifocus, latapie2024pearls, ylinampa2026orbitoscope . Closest to this work, Orbitoscope~ ylinampa2026orbitoscope uses a custom six-axis gantry with a dedicated stacking axis for per-view focal stacks. Its viewpoints are fixed and the sample is manually positioned at the orbit center with intersecting laser pointer. We take the complementary approach of leaving the sample untouched and adjusting the viewpoints (i.e., the robot's motion) to the estimated sample center. All of these autonomous systems for small-scale objects, however, reconstruct with classical photogrammetry rather than Gaussian Splatting. To our knowledge, MicroSplat is the first fully autonomous pipeline for small-scale objects that goes from robotic data collection to a 3DGS model without human intervention after setup. An alternative to capture-time focus stacking is to recover sharpness during reconstruction: Deblurring 3DGS~ lee2024deblurring3dgs and its successors~ peng2024bags, lee2025cocogaussian jointly estimate a blur model and a sharp scene from defocused images. However, with a robot arm we can capture in-focus detail directly from every viewpoint rather than inferring it. We compare these methods in Section~ sec:comparisons . At this scale, the shallow DoF prevents any single image from being fully in focus ( ), and the capture precision required is impractical to achieve manually. We present a robotic pipeline that autonomously performs image acquisition and 3D Gaussian Splatting reconstruction. title: ChairNav: Cross-Embodiment Pre-training and Personalization for Long-Horizon Wheelchair Navigation
summary: Developing autonomous electric wheelchairs capable of long-horizon sidewalk navigation is critical for accessible personal mobility, yet existing approaches either focus on indoor map-based navigation or rely on expensive, complex sensor stacks to achieve full autonomy. In this work, we propose to tackle outdoor sidewalk navigation by leveraging visual navigation foundation models and large-scale navigation datasets, which offer strong generalization using lightweight hardware. To this end, we present ChairNav, a novel framework that adapts a general visual navigation model into a personalized electric wheelchair navigation system using a three-stage data pyramid. To address the scarcity of in-domain data, ChairNav first pre-trains on large-scale cross-embodiment datasets transformed into the wheelchair domain, followed by mid-training on a small number of wheelchair demonstrations to eliminate remaining domain gaps. Finally, a post-training stage refines the deployed model from user interventions to personalize its behavior. We deploy ChairNav on a commercial electric wheelchair equipped with an RGB-D camera and an onboard NVIDIA Jetson compute module. Experimental results validate the effectiveness of each stage in our data pyramid: pre-training reduces lateral ADE by 18%, and post-training increases the mean distance between user interventions from 29.2 m to 57.4 m. Further evaluation on kilometer-scale urban sidewalk routes shows that our system operates autonomously for 93.4% of total driving time, demonstrating its potential for everyday accessible mobility. Demo video and more details are at https://vail.cs.ucla.edu/ChairNav/.

To this end, we present ChairNav, a novel framework that adapts a general visual navigation model into a personalized electric wheelchair navigation system using a three-stage data pyramid. Finally, a post-training stage refines the deployed model from user interventions to personalize its behavior.
