title: RoMo-GS: Efficient Online 3D Gaussian Splatting for Robot Mapping via Exposure-Integrated Motion Blur
summary: Online 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) is emerging as a practical way to build a representation for robotics applications. However, deploying it on real-world platforms exposes multiple challenges. Rapid maneuvers of a robot induce motion-blurred images, which corrupt the reconstructed geometry and cause camera pose drift. Furthermore, the number of Gaussians grows without bound during continuous online mapping. In this study, we present RoMo-GS, an online 3DGS system designed to address these challenges. Instead of averaging N discrete sub-frames as in prior motion blur-aware 3DGS, we analytically integrate each projected Gaussian over the exposure interval, yielding an O(1) complexity per Gaussian. Building on this, we bound the Gaussians' growth with a Hessian-based pruning score, while jointly refining pose, velocity, and Gaussians with Adam and an online LM step over the Gaussians. On multiple public datasets and a self-collected dataset, RoMo-GS matches or exceeds offline deblurring 3DGS methods in rendering quality while running 15--150x faster, and operates online at competitive quality with about 20% fewer Gaussians than the online 3DGS baseline.
full_text: Experiment sec:experiment Experimental Setup For evaluation, we use three public datasets: the Deblur-NeRF~ ma2022deblur synthetic dataset, ETH3D~ schops2019bad , and TUM RGB-D~ sturm12iros . To validate our framework with diverse real-world motion blur induced by different robots, we captured custom indoor sequences using a Boston Dynamics Spot quadrupedal robot, a Franka Emika robot arm, and a handheld platform. We report , , and scores, running speed, and the number of Gaussians. All experiments are conducted on a single NVIDIA RTX A6000 GPU. Deblur 3DGS Comparison We compare our method against existing offline global-optimization motion-blur-aware baselines: BAD-Gaussians~ zhao2024bad , Deblurring 3DGS~ lee2024deblurring , ~ seiskari2024gaussian , BAGS~ peng2024bags , and CoMoGaussian~ lee2025comogaussian . The evaluation uses the Deblur-NeRF~ ma2022deblur synthetic dataset and the camera-shaking sequences of ETH3D~ schops2019bad . We omit the Deblur-NeRF real-world sequences as ORB-SLAM3 fails on them. Hessian-based pruning is disabled here so that the comparison focuses on the deblurring quality. Quantitative results appear in and ; qualitative comparisons are shown in . On the Deblur-NeRF synthetic dataset, BAD-Gaussians attains the best overall metrics. It is the only method that performs photometric bundle adjustment, allowing it to correct the noisy ORB-SLAM3 trajectory through global optimization. We therefore treat it as an indirect upper-bound reference and primarily compare against the remaining methods, which share the same front-end poses. Among those, our framework reaches the highest and , demonstrating robust deblurring even under severe motion blur and inaccurate initial poses. Our method also completes running in under one minute, against 10--60 min for the offline baselines. is slightly higher, reflecting a marginal loss of perceptual sharpness which is expected from online, sequential optimization compared with offline, global refinement. For ETH3D, clean ground-truth is unavailable. We therefore use the outputs of BAD-Gaussians ( 4 hours of offline optimization) as a reference, while noting that this introduces a bias toward multi-sample rendering. Due to the aggressive camera motion, Deblurring 3DGS, GSOM, and BAGS fail to handle motion blur in . Deblurring 3DGS even fails to optimize on the second sequence, presenting a limitation of the kernel. Ours attains the best and among the baselines and a comparable to , with the fastest optimization. Achieving the best on these challenging real-world sequences indicates that our motion-blur model avoids the discretization artifacts of multi-sample and remains robust under real-world motion. In , Ours produces fidelity comparable to CoMoGaussian, whereas the remaining baselines yield blurry renderings. Online 3DGS Comparison We compare our method with existing online including RTG-SLAM~ peng2024rtg , GS-ICP~ ha2024rgbd , MonoGS~ matsuki2024gaussian , Photo-SLAM~ huang2024photo , HI-SLAM2~ zhang2025hi , and MODP~ wu2025monocular . Additionally, we include tttLRM~ Wang2026TTTLRM , a recent feed-forward Gaussian reconstruction method, for a comprehensive comparison. We evaluate on the TUM~ sturm12iros real-world dataset and our custom dataset. The deblur model is disabled in this experiment, as clean ground-truth is unavailable, and the baselines do not target motion-blurred input. Therefore, we leveraged the original input RGB images as the ground-truth reference, as in previous online Gaussian Splatting methods. Quantitative results are reported in and , and qualitative results on the custom dataset are shown in . Details about the custom dataset are provided in App.~ . On both TUM and our custom datasets, the rendering quality of GS-ICP and Photo-SLAM remains degraded, a trade-off for their fast optimization speed. tttLRM and GS-ICP show a higher number of Gaussians than the others, indicating limited online density control. MonoGS and HI-SLAM2 attain competitive metrics with a small number of Gaussians, but at the cost of the slowest running speed and a long post-optimization stage. Ours achieves comparable quality with MODP, while retaining 20 fewer Gaussians, which follows from the Hessian-based online pruning. Ablation Studies Comparison with Multi-Sample Rendering subsubsec:ablation_blur To isolate the contribution of our exposure-integrated blur formulation, we compare it against the discrete multi-sample strategy of GSOM~ seiskari2024gaussian and a no-blur baseline, all within the same framework. We evaluate on the ETH3D dataset with multi-sample variants at and . reports the quantitative results and shows the qualitative comparison. Rendering Quality. The w/o blur reduction baseline yields the worst scores across all metrics, and multi-sampling improves them. Our exposure-integrated blur is slightly behind multi-sampling on and but beats the variant on . This perceptual gain arises because the pseudo ground truth is generated by BAD-Gaussians, which itself uses discrete multi-sampling and therefore biases the evaluation. In , our model produces cleaner reconstructions than the multi-sample variants while requiring fewer Gaussians to represent the scene; the multi-sample variants spawn additional Gaussians to compensate for the temporal gaps caused by discrete rasterization. Running Speed. The no-blur baseline is the fastest, while our model incurs an overhead from evaluating the two terms of Eq.~ during the rasterization pass. Unlike multi-sampling whose cost scales as , ours runs in regardless of , keeping it viable for online framework. Effect of Hessian-based Online Gaussian Pruning We ablate the Hessian-based pruning ratio on the dog park custom sequence (3000 frames, 4 loops). plots the Gaussian number over frame index and reports the final counts. For and MODP, the Gaussian number grows without bound, while at , the count plateaus near frame 1000, around the first loop closure. This confirms that our score retains the Gaussians anchored to each keyframe and drops the redundant ones. For HI-SLAM2 and MonoGS, the Gaussian number fluctuates due to the absence of robust online density control. We also run an experiment with a controlled Gaussian count of 150K for RoMo-GS, compared to Deblurring 3DGS ( 169K). As shown in , increasing the Gaussian count consistently improves the quantitative metrics, while LPIPS remains higher than Deblurring 3DGS. We attribute this gap to per-Gaussian time averaging before alpha compositing, which may slightly smooth object boundaries and thus penalize LPIPS. Additional Comparison with MODP on Blurry Scene On and , RoMo-GS matches MODP while using 20 fewer Gaussians. To show clear qualitative improvements of RoMo-GS on severe motion blur, we report an additional experiment on the ETH3D dataset. As shown by the comparison at and , RoMo-GS is particularly beneficial for online mapping under rapid camera motion. Complete System Ablation Study We additionally ablate deblurring, pruning, joint pose/velocity, and the online step to evaluate the complete RoMo-GS pipeline on the ETH3D dataset as in . The evaluation metrics get worse when we remove each module of RoMo-GS, except for Hessian-based pruning. Tracking Accuracy We additionally evaluate the tracking accuracy on the TUM~ sturm12iros dataset. Specifically, we compare the of the from the Gaussian-jointly-optimized poses against native ORB-SLAM3~ campos2021orb , which serves as the input pose stream to our mapper. On average, is reduced by about 2 and by about 0.4 . While the improvement is modest, it confirms that jointly optimizing the camera state with the Gaussian map not only sharpens rendering but also provides a marginal refinement of the front-end pose estimates.

title: Time-JEPA: Grounding Video World Models with Physical Time Series
summary: Video world models learn how visual environments evolve by predicting missing or future content. However, physical-state information can provide useful context for predicting how environments evolve. Prior work incorporates this information through different mechanisms: domain-specific physical laws can complicate multi-domain training, while supervision on individual frames or frame pairs gives limited attention to how physical state evolves over time. We introduce Time-JEPA, which fine-tunes a video world model using low-dimensional, temporally aligned physical time series as auxiliary supervision. Physical time series connect video representations with physical state at corresponding temporal positions, encouraging the model to preserve how physical state evolves. In multiple domains including autonomous driving, robot manipulation, and human motion, Time-JEPA improves current-state decoding, multi-horizon future-state prediction, and kinematic reconstruction over matched video-fine-tuned controls across both condition and state-variable distribution shifts. Multi-domain training provides aggregate gains over matched single-domain training in all three tasks. External evaluations further suggest that time-series supervision improves sensitivity to physical anomalies and the representation of physical interactions, including in unseen scenarios. Aggregate gains on a second video backbone indicate that the method can be applied to more backbones. These results suggest that physical time series help video world models better understand the physical world.

Introduction sec:intro Video world models learn how visual environments evolve by predicting missing or future content. Common approaches include masked video autoencoders, which reconstruct hidden pixels tong2022videomae,feichtenhofer2022spatiotemporal , and latent-prediction video models such as V-JEPA bardes2024vjepa,assran2025vjepa2 . V-JEPA builds on the joint-embedding predictive architecture (JEPA) assran2023ijepa to predict masked spatiotemporal target representations from visible video context. The resulting representations encode objects, motion, and events. However, predicting how an event unfolds also requires information about physical state. A car can follow the same turn at different speeds and produce different future motion, and visually similar grasps can involve different joint configurations or forces. The speeds, joint configurations, and forces in these examples form part of the physical state and help video world models understand how events unfold. Prior work incorporates physical state into video world models in two main ways. Some methods use physical laws or system-specific dynamical priors to constrain how physical state evolves leguen2020phydnet,mao2026piwm . Because these constraints rely on domain-specific formulations, equations, and knowledge, one training design cannot easily cover multiple domains. Moreover, certain physical constraints can make the model focus on the dynamics they describe and miss other changes in videos. Others use geometric structure, motion cues, or privileged state as prediction or alignment targets to capture different aspects of physical state mustafa2024dynamics,shang2025roboscape,shen2026phantom,zeng2026phylatent,yan2026psgjepa,wen2026xpjepa . This way reduces reliance on explicit physical laws. However, this way often focuses supervision on individual frames or frame pairs, giving limited attention to how physical state evolves within a video’s full temporal context. Besides, such methods often require additional input signals, making the training setup more complex. Therefore, overcoming these limitations requires a common interface and readily available data that can serve as physical state. We introduce Time-JEPA, a method that aligns physical-state with the temporal structure of video. We apply a shared interface for multiple domains and use physical time series that sensors often easily provide alongside video. It is noted that time series only serve as auxiliary supervision during training and video remains as the model's only input during evaluation. We evaluate Time-JEPA in multiple domains including autonomous driving, robot manipulation, and human motion. Compared with matched video-fine-tuned controls, Time-JEPA improves current-state decoding, multi-horizon future-state prediction, and kinematic reconstruction. The gains hold under two levels of out-of-distribution evaluation: unseen test conditions, and state variables not used as auxiliary training targets. Multi-domain training provides aggregate gains over matched single-domain training in all three tasks. External evaluations further suggest that time-series supervision improves sensitivity to physical anomalies and the representation of physical interactions, including in unseen scenarios. Aggregate gains on a second video backbone indicate that the method can be applied to more backbones. These results indicate that physical time series help video world models better understand the physical world. We make two contributions: Physical time-series supervision for video world models. We introduce Time-JEPA, which combines latent prediction with temporally aligned physical time-series supervision through a shared interface. We set up in-distribution (ID) and out-of-distribution (OOD) settings at two levels, including conditions and variables. Datasets and toolkit in multiple domains. We construct datasets for multiple domains including autonomous driving, robot manipulation, and human motion. We develop a toolkit for video world models that combines current-state decoding, multi-horizon future-state prediction, and kinematic reconstruction to more thoroughly assess their ability to represent physical states, including physical relations and state evolution. Related Work sec:related_work Predictive video representations and world models. Video world models learn representations of visual environments through pixel reconstruction or latent prediction. For pixel reconstruction, masked video autoencoders tong2022videomae,feichtenhofer2022spatiotemporal reconstruct hidden pixels, and VideoMAE~V2~ wang2023videomaev2 scales this objective through dual masking. For latent prediction, V-JEPA~ bardes2024vjepa follows JEPA~ assran2023ijepa and predicts target-encoder representations at masked spatiotemporal positions. V-JEPA~2~ assran2025vjepa2 and V-JEPA~2.1~ murlabadia2026vjepa2_1 develop this family for motion understanding and dense feature extraction. InternVideo-Next~ wang2025internvideonext combines reconstruction and latent prediction. Dreamer~ hafner2020dreamer and iVideoGPT~ wu2024ivideogpt learn action-conditioned dynamics for control and interactive video prediction. Time-JEPA builds on V-JEPA's masked latent-prediction objective and adds time-series supervision during fine-tuning. Signals for visual learning. Prior work uses auxiliary supervision from scene state, egomotion, and other modalities to shape visual representations chen2020learningbycheating,agrawal2015moving,gupta2016crossmodal . One route incorporates physical equations or dynamical priors into latent prediction, as in PhyDNet~ leguen2020phydnet and PIWM~ mao2026piwm . A second route adds prediction or alignment targets, including physical state in Dynamics Mapping~ mustafa2024dynamics , depth and keypoint trajectories in RoboScape~ shang2025roboscape , and V-JEPA-derived latents in PHANTOM~ shen2026phantom . PhyLatent~ zeng2026phylatent and PSG-JEPA~ yan2026psgjepa add physical-state supervision to action-conditioned JEPA prediction, while JEPA-x~ wen2026xpjepa couples visual and physical trajectories through cross-modal future prediction. Time-JEPA uses low-dimensional, temporally aligned physical time series as auxiliary supervision through a shared interface across autonomous driving, robot manipulation, and human motion. Sensors or synchronized annotations supply these time series, and the encoder uses video as its only input during fine-tuning and evaluation. Evaluating physical information in video representations. PHYRE~ bakhtin2019phyre and CLEVRER~ yi2020clevrer evaluate physical reasoning about interacting objects and collision events. Physion~ bear2021physion tests future-contact prediction, and GRASP~ jassim2024grasp evaluates intuitive-physics properties with matched possible and impossible videos. Studies of self-supervised video predictors examine intuitive physics and probe physical-state information in frozen video representations garrido2025intuitivephysics, joseph2026interpretingphysics,punzo2026videophysics . Our evaluation combines continuous current-state decoding, kinematic reconstruction, and multi-horizon future-state prediction with external tests on GRASP and Physion. Method: Time-JEPA sec:method Overview. We propose Time-JEPA, a fine-tuning approach that uses temporally aligned physical time-series supervision to encourage predictive video representations to preserve information about physical state as it evolves. As shown in Figure~ fig:time_jepa_overview , Time-JEPA couples two learning paths through a shared online video encoder. The predictive video representation module builds on V-JEPA and predicts latent representations at masked positions. An exponential-moving-average (EMA) target encoder computes these representations from the full clip. The physical time-series preparation module maps synchronized measurements to video time, and the physical time-series supervision module regresses the aligned state from full-clip video features. Both objectives update the same online encoder, coupling masked latent prediction with tubelet-level physical-state supervision. The physical time series provide auxiliary supervision during fine-tuning, and video remains the encoder input throughout fine-tuning and evaluation. Predictive Video Representation sec:method_preliminaries The predictive video representation module builds on the masked latent-prediction objective of V-JEPA~ bardes2024vjepa . For each clip, the online encoder transforms a masked video view into latent patch tokens. Its final-layer representation indexes these tokens by temporal position and spatial patch location. The predictor estimates latent tokens at the masked positions. The EMA target encoder processes the full clip and provides the corresponding latent tokens. The JEPA loss measures prediction error at the masked positions and updates the online encoder and predictor. The exponential moving average updates the target encoder parameters from the online encoder. Physical Time-Series Preparation sec:method_state_targets The physical time-series preparation module maps physical time series from sensors or synchronized annotations to the encoder's temporal grid. These time series record measurements such as vehicle speed, robot joint configuration, and human joint angle over time. We associate each sampled video time with nearby physical measurements using timestamps or frame indices, then group the aligned measurements according to the encoder's tubelet structure. Within each tubelet, we pool each type of physical measurement across its sampled times. We then normalize the pooled measurements to place different numerical scales in a common space, producing a sequence of tubelet-level state values. This preparation aligns each temporal video feature with the corresponding physical measurements even when their sampling rates differ. Appendix~ app:time_series_preprocessing gives the shared alignment, pooling, validity, and normalization details. Physical Time-Series Supervision sec:method_time_supervision In the physical time-series supervision module, we process the unmasked video clip with the shared online encoder. The online encoder's final layer organizes patch tokens along temporal positions and spatial patch locations. title: Learning to Compose: Recursive Self-Improvement of Shared Executable Stacks for Zero-Shot Long-Horizon Robot Manipulation
summary: Individually competent robot skills can fail when composed: tools may lack a required capability, completion signals may misrepresent physical progress, and one skill may leave a state that violates its successor's prerequisites. We introduce Recursia, a recursive self-improvement framework that treats the shared executable stack, rather than individual task programs, as the persistent unit of improvement. The stack integrates tools, skills with execution contracts, handoffs, and verifiers. Source-side execution traces guide failure attribution and the generation of missing tools or repairs to existing shared components. Generality checks, mechanism tests, and paired selection and regression gates determine which changes become the next parent. The resulting stack is frozen and reused through declarative task adapters, allowing source-derived changes to support new compositions without target-side code repair. Experiments cover LIBERO-Pro Long simulation and a physical Franka FR3 equipped with a Franka Hand. In simulation, Recursia improves success over ASPIRE by 5.8 percentage points under Pos perturbations and 15.1 points under Task perturbations. Across three physical compositional target tasks, it improves mean success over the Skill Document Only baseline by 40 percentage points. Analyses of constituent execution, candidate rejection, and inference drivers distinguish local mechanism improvements from complete task success and characterize the cost of feedback-conditioned orchestration. These results examine shared executable interfaces as a concrete mechanism for compositional transfer in robot programming.

We introduce , a recursive self-improvement framework that treats the shared executable stack, rather than individual task programs, as the persistent unit of improvement. In simulation, improves success over ASPIRE by 5.8 percentage points under Pos perturbations and 15.1 points under Task perturbations. Across three physical compositional target tasks, it improves mean success over the Skill Document Only baseline by 40 percentage points. Analyses of constituent execution, candidate rejection, and inference drivers distinguish local mechanism improvements from complete task success and characterize the cost of feedback-conditioned orchestration. These results examine shared executable interfaces as a concrete mechanism for compositional transfer in robot programming. Introduction sec:introduction Long-horizon robot manipulation demands more than a repertoire of individually capable skills~ mees2022calvin . Executing a pick-and-place action, for instance, is insufficient if it leaves the environment in a state that violates the preconditions of the subsequent skill~ xu2026baton . Grounding high-level language plans in skill affordances and perceptual geometry is therefore critical for physically feasible execution~ ahn2022saycan,huang2023voxposer . The central question is how skills acquired on source tasks can be composed to reliably solve previously unseen long-horizon target tasks. Coding agents provide a natural testbed for studying this compositional generalization~ liang2023code,mu2024robocodex,capx2026 . Language-model-generated programs can invoke perception and control APIs, implement feedback loops, and reuse procedural abstractions~ liang2023code . RoboCodeX further decomposes multimodal instructions into object-centric manipulation units and synthesizes control code~ mu2024robocodex , while ProgPrompt incorporates state-feedback assertions and recovery actions into generated plans~ singh2023progprompt . Skill-library systems such as Voyager store executable procedures and use environmental feedback for extension~ voyager2023 ; ASPIRE combines execution feedback, program refinement, skill discovery, and evolutionary search for manipulation~ lu2026aspire . Lifelong Robot Library Learning expands skill repertoires from accumulated experience~ tziafas2024lrll , and Uni-Skill requests new skill implementations when existing ones fall short~ uniskill2026 . CaP-X examines how abstraction levels, perceptual grounding, and structured execution feedback affect the reliability of embodied coding agents~ capx2026 . Although these capabilities make program improvement a promising route to transfer, reliable composition depends not only on the generated task program, but critically on the shared interfaces it invokes: tools, skill contracts, inter-skill state transfers, and verification logic. Thus, the central object of study shifts from how an agent writes a program to which reusable execution semantics that program inherits. We identify four key obstacles to reliable composition: (1) Tool insufficiency, where a task requires a reusable capability absent from the initial API; (2) Semantic misalignment, where an existing tool returns normally despite failing to reach its requested pose of the next tool in the skill; (3) State incompatibility, where a skill's terminal state violates its successor's preconditions~ xu2026baton ; and (4) Verification brittleness, where incorrect checks advance an unfinished task or disturb a completed goal. These failure modes correspond to different interfaces in a hierarchical controller: tool execution, skill completion, inter-skill state transfer, and verifiers. Prior systems acquire and reuse executable skills from experience~ voyager2023,tziafas2024lrll,lu2026aspire , and execution-guided self-debugging demonstrates that failed programs yield useful repair evidence~ chen2024selfdebug . The Darwin G\"odel Machine extends this to persistent self-modification evaluated on coding benchmarks~ zhang2025dgm . We investigate how repairs to shared interfaces with multiple layers can be validated and retained across tasks. We hypothesize that a repair at a shared interface should improve multiple compositions, whereas a task-specific patch should benefit only the trajectory in which it is written. We examine this hypothesis through simulation and physical-robot experiments on long-horizon compositions. We propose , a framework that targets compositional generalization by treating the shared executable stack as the primary object of persistent improvement. A coding agent can add missing tools, repair skill contracts, or improve handoffs and verifiers. Each modification becomes part of a versioned implementation reused by subsequent source tasks and frozen during target-task execution. Specifically, is stack-aware and validation-gated. Source-side execution traces identify the first violated requirement, attributing failures to specific repair layers. This attribution proposes a mechanism for change but does not itself establish efficacy. Candidates must satisfy restrictions on task-specific specialization, survive paired comparisons with the parent stack, and pass the validation gate with selection gate and regression gate. Accepted changes are retained with their failure class, validation evidence, and code version. Task variation is expressed through declarative adapters. At deployment, the frozen stack relies solely on permitted robot observations; evaluator-side ground truth used during source diagnosis is never an input to the deployed policy. Our contributions are threefold: (1) We formulate skill composition as the persistent improvement of a shared executable stack integrating tools, skills with execution contracts, handoffs, and verifiers, and enable the generation of previously absent tools. (2) We introduce a failure-attributed improvement procedure that localizes repairs to specific stack layers and validates shared patches through generality and regression gates. (3) We evaluate frozen-stack transfer to long-horizon compositions in LIBERO-Pro Long simulation and on a physical Franka FR3 robot, comparing with skill-library and skill-document baselines and analyzing compositional execution, validation decisions, and inference strategies. Method sec:method Problem Formulation sec:formulation Let denote the source dataset available for improvement and the target dataset used for frozen transfer. denotes one task. The goal is to obtain an executable shared stack through debugging with . After accepted modifications obtained from , the executable stack is where contains tools, reusable skills, handoff mechanisms, and verifier mechanisms. Learning and debugging occurs through changes and modifications to executable code; the foundation model is held fixed within a comparison. The declarative adapter provides object descriptions, support or destination descriptions, relation types, and goal dependencies. A shared executor composes calls to these components using and the available observation history . We use zero-shot compositional transfer to mean that target-task compositions do not provide feedback for stack modification, and the frozen stack is executed without target-specific code repair. Source and target tasks may share objects, relations, or individual skills. Four-layer Shared Executable Stack sec:stack Tool. Tools expose reusable perception, geometry, planning, or execution operations. Their interfaces specify inputs, coordinate conventions, observable completion conditions, and resource limits. The tool set is extensible. When an attributed source failure reveals that no available operation can satisfy a required capability, the agent proposes a new shared tool rather than embedding a task-specific workaround in the adapter. A proposal defines the missing capability, an interface, the permitted observations it consumes, and tests of its intended behavior. New tools are assembled from the permitted lower-level operations and are registered only after validation. Tool generation cannot introduce privileged sensing at deployment or alter the external evaluator. We distinguish these additions from repairs to existing tools in the experimental analysis. Figure~ fig:shared-stack-details illustrates representative interfaces. Skill. A skill with execution contracts is represented by where defines observable prerequisites, is a parameterized program, specifies evidence required at completion, and bounds resource use. Preconditions and postconditions refer to task arguments and measured geometry, not identities of benchmark tasks. Execution returns evidence and a reason for termination, allowing the caller to distinguish a completed motion from an established task relation. Contracts are executable checks, not formal guarantees of correctness in unobserved states. Handoff. The completion of one skill does not imply readiness for the next: A handoff updates the state used by the successor, checks its prerequisites, and checks previously achieved relations that later actions could disturb. Depending on the observed failure, the shared executor may re-observe, invoke a bounded recovery, or stop. Recovery must establish the missing prerequisite before execution resumes. For instance, a completed release motion requires a subsequent retreat before the next grasp becomes executable. The handoff makes this transition explicit. Verifier. The verification layer evaluates object identity and task-relevant relations from permitted observations and execution history. The external evaluator independently measures its errors; the internal evaluator's own output is never used as the ground-truth success label. The external evaluator's role is distinct from a motion tool's arrival check: reaching a pose does not establish that the intended object is supported by the intended surface. The external verification uses support geometry and object identity across observations to decide whether the evidence permits advancement or recovery. Together, these levels define the unit of reuse. A validated tool can serve several skills, a skill can appear in several goal sequences, and a handoff or relation check can apply across tasks. Figure~ fig:shared-stack-details shows four representative shared interfaces. The layers group responsibilities within one executable stack. Failure-Attributed Improvement Procedure sec:repair The executor run source rollouts and records actions, observations and robot state. Source diagnosis use simulator ground truth to distinguish failure mechanisms, while the deployed stack remains restricted to permitted observations. The attribution procedure identifies the earliest supported violation of an execution requirement and records its stage, evidence, and affected component. It distinguishes an absent capability from an incorrectly implemented one. The coding agent receives this evidence and proposes a candidate modification . title: Relational Spatial Alignment for Vision-Language-Action Models
summary: Spatial understanding is essential for robots to perceive their surrounding environments and execute actions. Existing approaches typically encode 3D awareness into vision-language-action (VLA) models by directly aligning their representations with pre-trained 3D foundation models. However, we observe that such direct geometric feature alignment essentially exploits 3D foundation priors as a form of low-rank regularization in the feature space, resulting in severe rank collapse of the pre-trained VLA representations. In contrast, we shift the focus from enforcing point-wise equality to aligning pair-wise relationships. We propose a representation-alignment method that enables the injection of 3D spatial awareness without compromising the model's original expressivity. Extensive experiments on public benchmarks, our new spatial reasoning benchmark, and real-world manipulation scenarios demonstrate that our approach effectively incorporates 3D spatial representations into VLA reasoning, achieving robust performance and enhanced spatial awareness across diverse manipulation tasks.

Introduction Spatial understanding is fundamental to robotic manipulation, enabling robots to interpret their environment from multi-view RGB observations, estimate distances, localize objects, and infer 3D structure either explicitly or implicitly. Traditional approaches~ dexnet2, dope typically follow a reconstruction-before-action paradigm, in which an explicit 3D scene is first reconstructed and then used for downstream tasks such as path planning and control~ octomap,voxblox . Inspired by the success of end-to-end learning in natural language processing~ gpt4 and autonomous driving~ uniad,end2endsd , recent attention has shifted toward Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models, a unified end-to-end learning framework for embodied AI. To incorporate spatial awareness, some prior methods~ perceiver,3dvla,voxposer,pointvla follow the reconstruction-before-action paradigm by leveraging explicit spatial representations, such as depth maps or point clouds, as additional inputs to VLA models. However, such approaches often depend on pre-scanned environments or high-quality sensor observations, both of which can be unreliable in real-world scenarios due to sensor noise, reflective surfaces, and occlusions. Consequently, such methods remain limited in constrained environments and struggle to generalize to open-world problems. To avoid reliance on explicit 3D representations, recent works~ spatial-forcing, rocket shift the focus to encode implicit 3D geometric structure within the latent space. Building on recent advances in 3D foundation models~ dust3r,spann3r,vggt , this approach transfers geometric knowledge into VLAs through feature-level distillation. While these approaches bypass the need for explicit 3D representations, the underlying mechanism of this latent geometric transfer remains underexplored. More importantly, it raises a fundamental question: Does injecting spatial awareness into the VLA with direct feature alignment compromise its original semantic-level representational capabilities? In this work, we systematically investigate the direct feature alignment between 3D foundation models and 2D VLA models. Our analysis suggests that direct spatial alignment does not necessarily lead to genuine 3D understanding. Instead, it primarily behaves as a form of low-rank regularization. Specifically, we observe a substantial collapse in the numerical rank of the VLA feature space after alignment (Fig.~ fig:teaser (b); see Sec.~ sec:motivation ), indicating a significant loss of representation capacity. Consequently, experiments across diverse benchmarks show that models trained with direct spatial alignment suffer from degraded generalization performance. To overcome these limitations, we propose a new paradigm of relational spatial alignment that aims to distill 3D awareness into 2D VLAs while preserving their expressivity. Motivated by the observation that 3D foundation models encode spatial structures through cosine similarity (i.e., the attention maps) between corresponding features, we argue that effective spatial understanding can be achieved by aligning pair-wise relationships rather than enforcing point-wise equality. By supervising relative similarities instead of absolute feature directions and norms, our method allows the 2D VLA representations to maintain their native feature coordinate system, with 3D knowledge being encoded in its feature similarity. (Fig.~ fig:teaser (a)). Theoretically, we demonstrate that this relational alignment objective is inherently rotation-invariant: The optimization objective remains strictly unchanged under arbitrary orthogonal transformations within the latent feature space, which is crucial for preventing the feature collapse. To practically instantiate this paradigm, we introduce RIGID: Rotation-Invariant Geometry Distillation, which implements the relation alignment paradigm and formulates the geometry knowledge transfer as an Optimal Transport problem over spatial attention distributions. Compared to direct feature supervision, RIGID improves spatial awareness while maintaining the numerical rank of the learned representations, effectively preventing capacity collapse. Extensive experiments on both simulated and real-world robotic tasks demonstrate that RIGID achieves state-of-the-art performance, exhibiting better robustness and open-world generalization than direct feature alignment. Related work Recent advancements seek to enhance the spatial grounding of vision-language-action (VLA) models by directly incorporating geometric information. One main stream of methods embeds raw 3D observations, such as depth maps or point clouds, directly into the input space. Frameworks including 3D-VLA~ 3dvla , 3DS-VLA~ 3dsvla , PointVLA~ pointvla , 3D-CAVLA~ 3d-cavla , GeoVLA~ geovla , FALCON~ falcon , and BridgeVLA~ bridgevla align these 3D inputs with 2D backbone or action experts to unify perception and manipulation, while 4D-VLA~ 4d-vla extends this by stacking multiple depth maps for temporal context. Another paradigm utilizes auxiliary explicit 3D cues instead of raw sensory data. For instance, SpatialVLA~ spatialvla applies Egocentric 3D Position Encoding, and TraceVLA~ tracevla leverages visual traces. Furthermore, approaches like ReconVLA~ reconvla , DreamVLA~ dreamvla , and GuidedVLA~ guidedVLA enforce 3D representation learning by employing explicit 3D feature reconstruction as an auxiliary supervision signal. Although these models provide precision in handling height variations and object posing, they suffer from substantial data dependencies, as they often require high-fidelity 3D annotations or depth estimations that are frequently noisy in real-world environments. Recent advances in 3D reconstruction have enabled the end-to-end learning of multi-view geometry~ dust3r,mast3r,spann3r,vggt,pi3,amb3r,depthanything3 . These methods typically employ transformer-based architectures to infer geometric properties such as point maps, depth, and camera parameters from multi-view images. To circumvent the dependency on physical 3D sensors or explicit annotations, recent vision-language-action (VLA) models leverage these learned geometric cues for implicit spatial grounding. Methods such as Evo-0~ evo-0, evo-1 and GeoAware-VLA~ geoaware-vla directly integrate geometric features generated by 3D foundation models into the VLA backbone. Conversely, techniques including Spatial Forcing~ spatial-forcing , ROCKET~ rocket , and GLaD~ glad leverage feature distillation. They align the intermediate latent states of the VLA with the geometric embeddings of a frozen teacher model (e.g., VGGT) to acquire spatial awareness. However, this feature integration or direct alignment across different modalities can potentially compromise the 2D image-derived representations acquired during large-scale pre-training, such as semantic understanding and general reasoning abilities, thereby degrading the overall robustness of the model. Relational Knowledge Distillation (RKD)~ rkd is built upon the knowledge distillation (KD)~ kd , which focuses on transferring knowledge from the teacher model by distilling the in-batch structure. While traditional RKD methods primarily focus on single-modality and inter-instance associations, our approach targets the latent feature alignment between VLA models and 3D foundation models in spatial through multi-view inputs. title: EndoVLA-OOV: Language-Conditioned Out-of-View Target Acquisition in Robotic Endoscopy
summary: The scan-then-revisit workflow of upper gastrointestinal endoscopy requires bringing a previously observed suspicious region back into view for closer inspection. Acquiring such targets requires translating anatomical and appearance descriptions into camera motions from partial observations of a confined, deformable environment. We present EndoVLA-OOV, a language-conditioned vision-language-action policy for out-of-view target acquisition in robotic endoscopy. The policy adapts a pretrained backbone to continuous two-degree-of-freedom distal bending commands and combines initial, intermediate, and current images to guide search. To support policy learning, we provide an open-source VLA dataset containing 1,050 episodes across six tasks and approximately 262k observation-action pairs. Physical evaluation spans wet-lens and low-light conditions, two unseen stomach phantoms, and cross-embodiment transfer to an unseen ex-vivo environment. In the cross-embodiment evaluation, the full-data policy achieves 93.3% target acquisition success (28/30). In a controlled training-data comparison, expanding the corpus from 312 to 1,050 episodes increases acquisition success from 40.0% to 90.0% under the same model, training, and test configuration. Instruction and observation interventions further support the use of language and temporal context in the evaluated acquisition tasks. These results support language-guided endoscopic revisitation across the evaluated environments and robot embodiments and demonstrate the benefit of expanded task-specific demonstrations.
full_text: Robotic endoscopy, vision-language-action policies, out-of-view search, continuum robots, domain adaptation. Introduction Upper gastrointestinal endoscopy combines systematic mucosal inspection with focused examination of suspicious regions. Screening protocols organize stomach coverage into anatomical stations and recorded views, providing a spatial framework for inspection and subsequent review~ yao2013endoscopic,bravo2025gastrohun,veitch2015optimizing . Quality standards emphasize careful examination and photographic documentation~ beg2017quality,bisschops2016performance , and a study of systematic image acquisition reported an association between more gastroscopy images and detection of clinically significant gastric lesions~ lee2020taking . These practices motivate robotic assistance that links a region of interest to the camera motion needed to inspect it. After an initial scan, an operator can specify an anatomical station and target appearance, and ask the robot to bring that target back into view for closer examination. This scan-then-revisit workflow creates a specific control problem: language-conditioned acquisition of an initially out-of-view (OOV) target (Fig.~ fig:workflow ). The instruction supplies a semantic goal, while the current image shows only a local portion of the stomach. Bending changes the visible folds, distances and illumination, and successive views reveal different parts of the target's surroundings. Successful acquisition therefore involves choosing camera motions from partial observations until the requested target becomes visible. Once acquired, the target supports image-space feedback for centering. Flexible endoscope operation combines insertion, axial shaft rotation and two distal bending degrees of freedom (DoFs). Robotic assistance has introduced motorized steering, lumen centralization and feedback control to support camera positioning~ pullens2016colonoscopy,gafford2018fuzzy . Visual servoing provides a general framework for converting visible feature errors into corrective motion~ chaumette2006visual . OOV acquisition extends the observation requirements of this interface: the policy uses the requested region, target appearance and previous observations to guide motion toward a target that becomes visible later in the trajectory. In this work, autonomous commands act on the two distal bending DoFs, while insertion and shaft rotation remain fixed throughout autonomous model trials. This defines a bounded action interface for studying acquisition in stomach phantoms and ex-vivo organs. Vision-language-action (VLA) models connect semantic requests to robot commands. RT-1 learns language-conditioned actions from robot demonstrations~ Brohan-RSS-23 ; RT-2 transfers web-scale visual-language knowledge into control~ pmlr-v229-zitkovich23a ; and OpenVLA demonstrates adaptation and generalization across downstream tasks~ pmlr-v270-kim25c . Cross-robot datasets and generalist policies extend this shared experience across tasks and embodiments~ o2024open,Ghosh-RSS-24 . These pretrained representations provide visual and semantic priors beyond the available endoscopic demonstrations. This is relevant to low-light views with reduced contrast and wet-lens views with droplets and reflections, where target appearance shifts from the high-light, dry training condition. Broad pretraining therefore motivates our choice of a VLA backbone for language-guided OOV acquisition under appearance change. The physical evaluation measures transfer across appearance, organ geometry and robot hardware. To support embodied learning in this setting, we provide a VLA dataset containing 1,050 episodes across six tasks and approximately 262k pairs. EndoVLA-OOV adapts the pretrained action-chunk backbone~ pmlr-v305-black25a through low-rank updates~ hu2022lora and a continuous two-component action head. Its visual input combines an initial global view, an intermediate observation and the current frame. Action chunks represent a sequence of future bending commands, following a widely used approach to visuomotor sequence prediction~ Zhao-RSS-23,black2024pi_0 . Together, the task interface, temporal observations and adaptation procedure form a domain-specific recipe for instruction-conditioned endoscopic acquisition. We study transfer using two robotic embodiments: R1 denotes the 6 mm platform used for demonstration collection and baseline evaluation, and R2 denotes the 3.9 mm platform used for cross-embodiment evaluation. Experiments on R1 examine acquisition and composite finding-and-tracking (FT) under lighting and wetness changes and across two unseen phantoms and ex-vivo tissue. Experiments on R2 examine acquisition in an unseen ex-vivo environment and the effect of expanding the training corpus. Competing-target instructions and contextual-view interventions assess how language and temporal images guide the policy's search. The transition from target acquisition to centering also motivates a clear account of feedback timing. A model that processes an input every seconds has perception rate . A chunk of actions gives a theoretical maximum chunk-equivalent control rate when all actions are consumed between successive processed observations; the chunk shares one input. Our common 300-input benchmark reports both quantities. This distinction connects action generation to the fresh-observation updates needed for precise centering and informs a future architecture that combines VLA acquisition with a low-latency visual controller. The Supplementary Information provides full data distributions, robot and annotation details, exact prompts, offline diagnostics and supplementary camera-control experiments. The contributions of this work are: An embodied endoscopic dataset: We provide a VLA dataset linking language, endoscopic observations and recorded robot states to continuous two-DoF bending actions. Its 1,050 episodes span six tasks and approximately 262k pairs, covering both target tracking and OOV acquisition. This resource provides a shared data and control basis for developing and evaluating instruction-conditioned endoscopic policies. Temporal-context VLA control for OOV acquisition: We introduce EndoVLA-OOV, which translates anatomical and appearance descriptions into continuous distal steering by conditioning a pretrained action-chunk policy on initial, intermediate and current views. Physical instruction and observation interventions support target selection through language and the use of contextual images during search. This formulation extends language-conditioned endoscopic assistance to targets beyond the current field of view. Transferable acquisition across endoscopic embodiments: We demonstrate that a VLA policy adapted on R1 acquires language-specified targets on R2 in an unseen ex-vivo environment. Target acquisition reaches 93.3 on R2, and a controlled training-data comparison raises acquisition from 40.0 to 90.0 with corpus expansion. These findings support reuse of the acquisition policy across the evaluated endoscopic platforms and identify demonstration coverage as a practical means of improving transfer. Related Work Robotic Endoscopy and Target Acquisition Robotic endoscopy supports camera positioning and instrument manipulation within a confined anatomical workspace. Endoluminal platforms provide coordinated actuation for interventions such as endoscopic submucosal dissection~ chiu2025prospective,arezzo2024endoluminal , while steering systems use motorized bending and image feedback to regulate the viewing direction~ pullens2016colonoscopy,gafford2018fuzzy . Visual servoing expresses a camera-positioning objective through measured feature errors and their relationship to motion~ chaumette2006visual . These approaches connect an observable image-space goal to corrective commands, making them relevant to lumen centralization and the centering of visible targets. For endoscopic revisitation, acquiring a requested target supplies the visual reference needed for this local feedback stage and links anatomical inspection to focused camera control. Language-conditioned endoscopic policies extend this interface by allowing an operator to specify the feature to follow. EndoVLA~ pmlr-v305-kit25a combines a vision-language backbone with supervised and reinforcement fine-tuning for tracking tasks, predicting discrete directional or stop commands from the current image and prompt. This work establishes a direct connection between semantic target descriptions and endoscopic motion. EndoVLA-OOV addresses the preceding acquisition stage: the requested target begins outside the field of view, and the policy steers through successive observations until it becomes visible. Continuous bending actions and temporal visual context support this formulation. Table~ tab:prior summarizes the task, action, data and evaluation scope of the two approaches, positioning language-guided acquisition within the broader endoscopic control workflow. Language-Conditioned Control and Visual Context Language-conditioned control links semantic descriptions to spatially meaningful robot behavior. SayCan combines language-derived task proposals with robotic affordance estimates~ brohan2023can ; CLIPort couples semantic representations with spatial action prediction~ shridhar2022cliport ; and VIMA uses multimodal prompts to specify manipulation tasks~ pmlr-v202-jiang23b . PerAct represents language-conditioned actions in a voxel-based spatial representation~ shridhar2023perceiver , while VoxPoser composes language-driven three-dimensional value maps~ pmlr-v229-huang23b . Together, these methods connect what an instruction requests to where and how the robot acts through complementary representations of task intent, geometry and action. In endoscopy, anatomical-region and appearance descriptions similarly specify a target for camera motion. This connection motivates treating the instruction as part of the control problem, with acquisition measured for the requested target. Semantic navigation extends language-conditioned behavior to goals encountered after a sequence of observations. LM-Nav grounds instruction landmarks through pretrained language, image-language and navigation models~ shah2023lm . VLFM combines observed geometry with a language-grounded value map to select exploration frontiers~ yokoyama2024vlfm . These approaches make observations gathered along a route useful for deciding where to search next. We draw on this relationship between semantic goals and accumulated visual evidence when formulating endoscopic OOV acquisition. Distal bending reveals different folds and surfaces, so the current image represents one part of the scene traversed during search. Temporal visual context offers a way to relate that local view to the preceding trajectory while preserving the requested target as the search objective. Pretrained VLA Policies and Cross-Embodiment Transfer Pretrained robot policies share representations across tasks and adapt them to a deployment interface. RT-1 learns language-conditioned control from robot demonstrations~ Brohan-RSS-23 , while CLIP and PaLM-E establish complementary connections between visual observations, language and embodied inputs~ radford2021learning,pmlr-v202-driess23a . RT-2 incorporates robot actions into vision-language training to transfer semantic knowledge to control~ pmlr-v229-zitkovich23a , and OpenVLA provides an open pretrained policy with downstream adaptation~ pmlr-v270-kim25c . The family couples a vision-language backbone with continuous action generation, with emphasizing generalization through heterogeneous training~ black2024pi_0,pmlr-v305-black25a . Low-rank adaptation provides an efficient parameter-update mechanism for such specialization~ hu2022lora . These studies motivate adapting shared visual-language representations to endoscopic imagery and a compact distal-bending action space. Training diversity and embodiment coverag

title: SARAM: Sparse Adapter Allocation with Reuse and Merging for Lifelong Robot Learning
summary: Lifelong robot learning requires acquiring new tasks sequentially without forgetting earlier ones. With large pre-trained vision-language-action (VLA) backbones, adapter-based methods effectively mitigate this challenge. However, their task-specific adapters and selection modules accumulate with the task stream, creating a scalability challenge in on-disk storage and deployment cost under fixed onboard resource budgets. We propose SARAM, a lifelong learning framework that limits storage growth while keeping GPU memory and per-step inference cost independent of the task stream length. For each new task, SARAM reuses frozen adapters from previous tasks and introduces new adapters only at sparsely selected layers, with a duplication penalty encouraging them to capture information not already represented by the adapter library. At deployment, a compact signature derived from backbone activation statistics identifies the task once per episode, and the corresponding task update is merged into the backbone, leaving only the backbone in the control loop. Across four LIBERO suites, SARAM matches or exceeds adapter-based baselines while adding up to 4.5x less on-disk state per task. GPU memory usage and control frequency remain comparable to those of the backbone as the task stream grows. Experiments on a real UR5 arm with a different backbone further demonstrate retention throughout a sequential task stream.
full_text: Lifelong robot learning requires acquiring new tasks sequentially without forgetting earlier ones. With large pre-trained vision-language-action (VLA) backbones, adapter-based methods effectively mitigate this challenge. However, their task-specific adapters and selection modules accumulate with the task stream, creating a scalability challenge in on-disk storage and deployment cost under fixed onboard resource budgets. We propose , a lifelong learning framework that limits storage growth while keeping GPU memory and per-step inference cost independent of the task stream length. For each new task, reuses frozen adapters from previous tasks and introduces new adapters only at sparsely selected layers, with a duplication penalty encouraging them to capture information not already represented by the adapter library. At deployment, a compact signature derived from backbone activation statistics identifies the task once per episode, and the corresponding task update is merged into the backbone, leaving only the backbone in the control loop. Across four LIBERO suites, matches or exceeds adapter-based baselines while adding up to less on-disk state per task. GPU memory usage and control frequency remain comparable to those of the backbone as the task stream grows. Experiments on a real UR5 arm with a different backbone further demonstrate retention throughout a sequential task stream. INTRODUCTION sec:intro Robots deployed in real environments need to learn new tasks continually~ liu2023libero , yet onboard hardware imposes fixed budgets on storage, memory, and compute. Learning tasks sequentially causes catastrophic forgetting~ goodfellow2013empirical,wang2024comprehensive , where acquiring a new task degrades performance on previously learned ones. Existing approaches address this through replay, regularization, or architectural isolation, which require storing past demonstrations, provide weaker protection against forgetting, or leave progressively less free capacity for new tasks, respectively~ chaudhry2019tiny,saha2021gradient,kirkpatrick2017overcoming,mallya2018packnet . With large pre-trained vision-language-action (VLA) backbones~ kim2024openvla,black2024pi,brohan2023rt , recent methods~ liu2024tail,romer2026clare,lei2025dynamic increasingly adopt lightweight adapters such as LoRA~ hu2021lora . The backbone remains frozen, while each task learns its own adapters, which are then frozen so that later training cannot overwrite them. By freezing the backbone and task-specific adapters, these methods effectively preserve previously learned tasks. However, task-specific adapters must be selected at deployment, and the oracle task ID is typically unavailable. Instead, the robot receives the current observation and language instruction, from which the appropriate task-specific adapter must be identified. Recent methods~ romer2026clare,lei2025dynamic dynamically select task-specific adapters from the current input during execution. By design, the adapters and selection modules therefore remain active in the control loop, increasing GPU memory and per-step computation as tasks accumulate. As illustrated in Fig.~ fig:motivation , this accumulation appears along two axes. During training, task-specific adapters, selection modules, and associated state accumulate on disk as new tasks are learned. At deployment, the adapters and selection modules must remain available on the GPU and are used throughout the control loop. Both axes therefore grow with the task stream, conflicting with the fixed resource budgets of onboard robot hardware. Can a VLA policy learn new tasks continually while keeping its deployment cost independent of the task stream and limiting task-dependent storage growth? To address this, we propose , a lifelong robot learning method that addresses the two axes at their respective stages: storage as tasks accumulate, and deployment cost at execution. During learning, each new task first reuses a linear combination of frozen LoRA adapters from previous tasks, then adds new adapters only at layers selected under a sparsity penalty. A duplication penalty discourages the new adapters from reproducing what the reused library already expresses. The newly allocated adapters and combination coefficients are frozen after training, so later tasks cannot overwrite previously learned parameters. Because every per-task update stays linear in the weights, it can later be folded into the backbone rather than evaluated as a separate module. then removes task selection from the control loop. After each task is learned, the demonstrations are passed through the adapter-free backbone and its layer-wise activation statistics are summarized into a compact task signature. These frozen-backbone statistics provide task-dependent signatures without requiring a learned selection module. At deployment, the initial observation and instruction are summarized in the same way, matched against the stored signatures, and the selected update is merged into the backbone before execution. The episode therefore runs on a single backbone, with no task-specific adapter or selection module inside the control loop, keeping GPU memory and per-step inference cost at the backbone's level regardless of the number of learned tasks. We evaluate on four LIBERO suites against adapter-based methods~ lei2025dynamic,romer2026clare and standard continual learning baselines. attains the highest final success rate and AUC on all four suites while requiring up to less on-disk state per task than adapter-based baselines. At deployment, remains at the backbone's level in both GPU memory and control frequency: after ten tasks it runs at 15.2\,Hz with 748\,MB of GPU memory, identical to the backbone alone. By contrast, CLARE and DMPEL grow to 922\,MB and 829\,MB of GPU memory and slow to 10.1\,Hz and 5.0\,Hz after ten tasks, respectively. On a seven-task real-robot stream with a different VLA backbone, ends the stream at the same success rate it reached when each task was learned, showing that the method transfers to a physical robot and a different backbone architecture. We summarize our contributions as follows: We propose , an adapter-based lifelong robot learning method that limits per-task storage through adapter reuse, sparse allocation, and compact task signatures in place of learned selection modules. At deployment, task signatures move selection outside the control loop, and the corresponding task update is merged into the backbone to keep GPU memory and per-step inference cost independent of the number of learned tasks. On four LIBERO suites, attains the highest final success rate and AUC while requiring up to less on-disk state per task, and real-robot experiments with a different VLA backbone demonstrate applicability beyond simulation. RELATED WORK sec:related Lifelong Robot Learning. Lifelong robot learning~ thrun1995lifelong,liu2023libero studies how robots can learn new tasks sequentially while retaining those learned before. A central challenge, shared with continual learning in general~ wang2024comprehensive , is catastrophic forgetting~ kirkpatrick2017overcoming , where learning new tasks degrades performance on earlier ones. Existing approaches address this problem through replay, regularization, or architectural isolation. Replay methods retain past demonstrations for later training~ chaudhry2019tiny , which incurs storage overhead and can be undesirable when past demonstrations cannot be retained. Regularization methods such as EWC~ kirkpatrick2017overcoming avoid storing past data but often provide weaker protection against forgetting. Architectural-isolation methods such as PackNet~ mallya2018packnet protect previous tasks by reserving separate capacity, but the available capacity becomes increasingly constrained as more tasks are learned. In robot manipulation, LIBERO~ liu2023libero provides a standard benchmark for evaluating sequential task learning and retention. Adapter-Based Lifelong Robot Learning. With the emergence of large pretrained VLA policies~ black2024pi,kim2024openvla,intelligence2025pi,brohan2022rt,brohan2023rt , recent work has increasingly adopted lightweight adapters for task-specific adaptation while keeping the backbone frozen~ liu2024tail,romer2026clare,lei2025dynamic . After each task is learned, its adapter is frozen, preventing later training from overwriting previously learned task parameters. This provides strong retention, but requires maintaining additional task-specific parameters as the task stream grows. When the oracle task ID is unavailable, CLARE~ romer2026clare and DMPEL~ lei2025dynamic dynamically select or combine task-specific modules from the current input using learned discriminators and a router, respectively. These input-dependent mechanisms remain active during control, causing task-specific storage and deployment cost to grow with the task stream. Resource-Efficient Continual Learning. Recent work beyond robotics has explored reducing the parameter growth of adapter-based continual learning. Some approaches compress task-specific adapters into a shared low-rank representation or merge multiple task updates into a shared model~ kaushik2026shared,qiao2026merge,fukuda2025adapter . These methods reduce parameter growth, but typically update shared parameters that also represent previously learned tasks. Their evaluation settings typically do not consider task selection from observations and instructions at deployment. In contrast, keeps previously learned task parameters frozen, reuses past adapters through combination coefficients, and adds new adapters only at layers retained by sparse allocation. It further replaces learned selection modules with task signatures and merges the corresponding task update into the VLA backbone before execution, so only the backbone runs during control. METHOD sec:method Problem Setting sec:setting We follow the lifelong imitation learning setup of LIBERO~ liu2023libero . A robot learns manipulation tasks sequentially with a single policy conditioned on observations and language instructions. Each task comes with a language instruction and a demonstration dataset , where each episode contains a sequence of observation--action pairs. Past datasets are not available unless the method stores them itself, at its own storage cost. After each task is learned, the policy is evaluated on the current task and all tasks learned so far. At deployment the task identity is not given, so the policy receives only the current observation and instruction. The objective is therefore to acquire each new task while retaining performance on earlier ones. Overview sec:overview addresses the two growth axes at their respective stages: disk storage during learning, and GPU cost at deployment. Each new task first reuses the frozen adapters of past tasks (Sec.~ sec:prefit ). A sparse adapter allocation then adds new capacity only at layers selected under a sparsity penalty (Sec.~ sec:allocation ), and a duplication penalty keeps that capacity from re-expressing what the reused adapters already provide (Sec.~ sec:training ). At deployment, every per-task update is linear in the weights, and the task is selected once per episode from frozen-backbone activation statistics (Sec.~ sec:selection ). The selected update can therefore be added directly to the backbone weights, and the episode runs on a single backbone (Sec.~ sec:merging ), holding GPU memory and per-step inference cost at the backbone's own level. title: Dream What I Can: Sparse Visual Planning for Long-Horizon Robot Manipulation
summary: Video models provide rich priors for generalizable robotic manipulation, but plausible visual futures are not always executable. We introduce DreamCan, a hierarchical policy that grounds video models through sparse visual planning: a high-level planner adapted from a pre-trained video model and a low-level visuomotor policy. Rather than predicting dense trajectories, the high-level planner generates sparse visual subgoals that balance reachability and task utility. From offline, action-free robot videos, we estimate these quantities and use dynamic programming to select subgoal sequences without manual annotations. The resulting subgoals are more reliably attained than uniformly spaced alternatives, and the full system outperforms language, dense-video, and uniform-subgoal planners, reaching high planning success rates on Language-Table tasks and 91.2% success on LIBERO-Long with a 0.1B-parameter low-level policy. Additional suboptimal videos and test-time compute further improve success. The system also performs challenging real-world bimanual tasks, including box folding and packing with unseen object combinations. More results are available at https://dreamcan.github.io/.

Right: with our subgoal sequences, our parameter-efficient low-level policy can achieve comparable performance with large VLAs or WAMs on LIBERO-Long, and can scale with test-time compute and suboptimal data. fig:teaser Video models provide rich priors for generalizable robotic manipulation, but plausible visual futures are not always executable.
