The system also performs challenging real-world bimanual tasks, including box folding and packing with unseen object combinations. More results are on https://dreamcan.github.io/ . Introduction The promise of video models for robotics lies not merely in predicting how the world may evolve under interaction, but in revealing intermediate outcomes through which a task can be accomplished. For manipulation, this knowledge extends beyond the task semantics readily expressed in language: visual predictions can depict contact, fine adjustment, and detailed configurations connecting a scene to a desired outcome. Video therefore offers an expressive medium for planning interactions whose geometric and physical details are cumbersome to specify in words. Yet a plausible visual future is not necessarily one a robot can realize. We argue that a visual plan should specify intermediate outcomes that support execution, rather than every intermediate frame. A goal image prediction may leave too much for the controller to solve, while a dense trajectory prescribes overly constrained motions that can be hard to realize by the controller. We thus propose sparse visual planning: learning to predict a sequence of subgoal images that both (i) makes meaningful progress towards achieving the task and (ii) remains executable by a low-level subgoal-conditioned policy. We formalize these principles through reachability, which estimates how readily one visual state can be attained from another, and task utility, which measures progress toward the instruction. Under a fixed subgoal budget, a good subgoal sequence plan should reward terminal utility and penalize difficult transitions. Utility directs the plan toward task completion; reachability determines its intermediate steps. This formulation echoes SayCan’s decomposition into task relevance and robotic affordance~ saycan , but does not require a predefined vocabulary of language-labeled skills. Instead, intermediate objectives can be discovered from video datasets, allowing them to reflect visual configurations useful for execution rather than language-based task decompositions. We term our approach , a sparse visual planner that generates policy-aware sequences of visual subgoals. Given a dataset of robot manipulation videos, we first learn two complementary value functions from the action-free data: a reachability value, estimating whether one visual state can be reliably reached from another, and a task utility value, measuring progress toward task completion. We instantiate reachability with goal-conditioned offline RL~ iql,park2023hiql under sparse rewards, and estimate utility using a task-progress model~ liang2026robometer or a VLM. We then jointly use these two values to automatically annotate each video with a sequence of visual subgoals that balances local reachability with global task progress. The resulting subgoal sequences are used to fine-tune a pretrained video generation model, WAN-2.2~ wan2025wan , to predict sparse visual subgoals from the current observation and language instruction, serving as the planning output of our model. These predicted subgoals can be subsequently executed by a goal-conditioned low-level policy. Through extensive experiments, we show that \ consistently outperforms alternative planning representations, including language plans, dense video predictions, and uniformly sampled visual subgoals. On three challenging Language-Table tasks~ lynch2023interactive , \ achieves substantially higher planning success rates than the prior state-of-the-art method~ vlp . On LIBERO-Long~ liu2023libero , our hierarchical system achieves a 91.2 success rate with only a 0.1B-parameter low-level policy. We further show that \ benefits from scaling suboptimal action-free video data on RoboMimic-MH Square~ robomimic , without additional policy training, as well as from increased test-time compute on Language Table~ lynch2023interactive . The sparse planning representation also naturally supports language-guided steering at test time, enabling users to specify preferred plans. Finally, on a suite of challenging real-world tasks, our system demonstrates effective manipulation under contact-rich interactions, long horizons, and combinatorial generalization using a bimanual robot platform, while maintaining fast closed-loop replanning at 1.03s per planning step on an RTX 5090 GPU. Our contributions are: (i) We propose , a sparse visual planner for robot manipulation that learns from action-free video datasets using automatically discovered subgoals that balance reachability and task utility; (ii) We integrate \ with a goal-conditioned policy to form a closed-loop hierarchical manipulation system, and demonstrate strong performance across simulated benchmarks and real-world contact-rich tasks; and (iii) We show that the proposed sparse planning framework scales effectively with both suboptimal video data and test-time compute, while supporting language-guided plan steering at inference time. Related Work Keystate Planning for Robot Manipulation Tasks Sparse temporal abstractions have long been used to reduce the redundancy of dense robot trajectories. Keystates can be obtained from manual annotations~ akgun2012keyframe,wgobench , embodiment-specific signals such as actions, proprioception, gripper states, and unsupervised objectives based on temporal structure, reconstruction, or information-theoretic criteria~ gregor2016variational,eysenbach2019diversity,pertsch2020keyin . However, these approaches either scale poorly or rely on signals unavailable in video-only data. VLMs can instead identify semantically salient task stages~ wang2024vlm , but semantic salience does not guarantee executability. Several works directly use visual subgoals for planning and control. KeyIn~ pertsch2020keyin discovers keyframes through prediction and reconstruction, SuSIE~ black2024susie generates subgoal images through a pretrained image generator, and LBP~ liu2025lbp predicts latent subgoal sequences using fixed temporal supervision. In contrast, we construct sparse visual subgoals by balancing task utility and reachability, favoring states that are both reachable and useful. World Models for Robot Manipulation Tasks World models support robot control by predicting future dynamics. Latent models such as Dreamer~ hafner2023dreamerv3 and TD-MPC~ hansen2024tdmpc2 enable policy optimization or model-predictive control, while visual models such as UniPi~ du2023unipi , UniSim~ yang2024unisim , and other works~ gao2025flip,zhou2026gem predict future observations for action generation or interaction. More recent world-action models jointly model visual futures and actions~ li2025unifiedvideoaction,ye2026dreamzero , with Fast-WAM~ yuan2026fastwam improving inference efficiency. Our work instead focuses on the temporal granularity of explicit visual planning. Rather than predicting dense trajectories, we generate sparse subgoal images supervised by reachability and task utility. This reduces prediction overhead, enables test-time search, and enables learning from suboptimal datasets. We further decouple the planner and policy, allowing them to communicate solely through subgoal images without sharing gradients or features. This modular design enables either component to be independently replaced or upgraded. Preliminaries sec:preliminary We consider a language-conditioned visuomotor manipulation, where the robot observes an image and an instruction , and produces a low-level action chunk to complete the task. Rather than predicting actions directly, adopts a hierarchical architecture. The high-level sparse visual planner, denoted by , predicts a short sequence of future visual subgoals: which are executed by a goal-conditioned policy : where denotes the actual subgoals used as conditions. The policy repeatedly generates actions toward the current subgoals, while the planner is periodically re-invoked from the latest observation for closed-loop replanning. Importantly, and are decoupled. The planner is trained solely from video trajectories , while the low-level policy can be any compatible goal-conditioned policy trained independently. Unlike tightly coupled world-action models, they share neither gradients nor hidden representations; their only interface is the generated subgoal images. This modular design allows either component to be replaced or improved independently. Motivation: What Makes a Good Visual Plan? We use Push-T~ florence2022implicit to illustrate why choosing an appropriate planning representation is nontrivial (Figure fig:motivation ). The robot must push a T-shaped block into a target pose, requiring both geometric precision and appropriate contact changes. A natural choice is language. A language planner might say ``Push the T shape from left to right " or ``rotate the T and then move it into place''. However, such descriptions leaves ambiguous where to contact, which direction to push, and which intermediate configurations to reach. As an alternative, a dense video planner can predict the entire future trajectory frame by frame, providing richer geometric guidance, but frame-by-frame prediction is prone to accumulated errors, can conflict with the actual execution trajectory after deviations, and is expensive to generate. A seemingly simple alternative is to uniformly sample a few future frames. However, temporal spacing does not imply good subgoals: selected frames may capture uninformative motion, regress in suboptimal demonstrations, miss important contact changes, or be difficult for the policy to reach. A useful visual subgoal should balance two properties: reachability, whether it can be reliably reached from the preceding states, and task utility, whether it makes meaningful progress toward completion. Nearby states may be easy but uninformative, while distant states may be useful but unreachable. This trade-off motivates our formulation for selecting sparse visual plans. sec:method In this section, we first introduce the reachability and task utility value functions, then use them to annotate sparse visual subgoals for training the sparse visual planner. title: Learning Waypoints and Passage Events for Decentralized Multi-Quadrotor Trajectory Planning
summary: Multi-quadrotor passage planning requires coordinated spatial routes and passage times under vehicle dynamics and actuation constraints. Optimizing these decisions jointly couples temporal allocation, nonlinear motion, and inter-vehicle interactions, creating a computational challenge for local trajectory generation. We propose a learning-optimization framework that predicts spatial waypoints and ordered passage events for independently solved quadrotor planners. A common physical time grid aligns the vehicles, with intermediate events fixed by the networks and terminal progress optimized locally to permit different completion metrics. Differentiable sequential convex programming incorporates rigid-body dynamics and rotor-thrust bounds, allowing collision and completion gradients to train both networks through the generated trajectories. In a two-quadrotor evaluation across 24 layouts, the adapted policy passes physical feasibility and sampled separation checks in all five held-out layouts. Their mean completion metric decreases by 1.52% relative to the inherited policy. The median forward time is 21.01 ms on the held-out exchange layout with matching numerical trajectory references. These results demonstrate that learned spatial and event parameters can coordinate independent rigid-body planners while preserving local vehicle constraints in the evaluated scenarios.
full_text: Multi-quadrotor passage planning requires coordinated spatial routes and passage times under vehicle dynamics and actuation constraints. Optimizing these decisions jointly couples temporal allocation, nonlinear motion, and inter-vehicle interactions, creating a computational challenge for local trajectory generation. We propose a learning--optimization framework that predicts spatial waypoints and ordered passage events for independently solved quadrotor planners. A common physical time grid aligns the vehicles, with intermediate events fixed by the networks and terminal progress optimized locally to permit different completion metrics. Differentiable sequential convex programming incorporates rigid-body dynamics and rotor-thrust bounds, allowing collision and completion gradients to train both networks through the generated trajectories. In a two-quadrotor evaluation across 24 layouts, the adapted policy passes physical feasibility and sampled separation checks in all five held-out layouts. Their mean completion metric decreases by 1.52 relative to the inherited policy. The median forward time is 21.01\,ms on the held-out exchange layout with matching numerical trajectory references. These results demonstrate that learned spatial and event parameters can coordinate independent rigid-body planners while preserving local vehicle constraints in the evaluated scenarios. Multi-robot planning, quadrotors, differentiable optimization, event timing, sequential convex programming. Introduction Multi-quadrotor passage planning concerns the coordinated motion of several vehicles through prescribed gates toward individual targets. Such tasks arise in swarm racing and navigation through cluttered environments, where vehicles share limited passage space~ shen2023,zhou2021ego . Successful traversal requires each trajectory to satisfy vehicle dynamics and each pair of vehicles to maintain suitable separation. Spatial route selection and passage timing therefore form a common planning problem for coordinated flight. The central computational difficulty is the coupling between passage timing, vehicle motion, and inter-vehicle separation. Changing an arrival time changes where a vehicle meets its neighbors, and generating the corresponding motion requires satisfying nonlinear attitude and actuation constraints. Solving these decisions jointly introduces temporal variables and interaction constraints into the trajectory optimization. This coupling motivates three complementary approaches: direct optimization, learned motion generation, and hybrid learning--optimization planning. Optimization-based methods provide explicit representations of trajectory objectives and physical constraints. Minimum-snap and MINCO formulations exploit polynomial structure for efficient trajectory generation~ mellinger2011,wang2022minco , while complementary progress constraints (CPC) optimize ordered waypoint completion together with motion~ foehn2021,shen2023 . Decentralized planners such as MADER and Robust MADER incorporate shared trajectory information into local collision handling~ tordesillas2022,kondo2024 . The resulting formulations make passage allocation and inter-vehicle coupling explicit, identifying the decisions that a learned planner can help organize. Learning-based methods offer a direct mapping from observations to motion decisions. Sensor-to-trajectory policies have been trained through privileged imitation learning for high-speed flight~ loquercio2021 , and differentiable simulation has supplied analytical gradients for quadrotor control from states and visual features~ heeg2025 . Their training objectives encode desired behavior in network parameters and support rapid inference. For constrained multi-vehicle passage, this motivates learning spatial and temporal decisions together with a physical trajectory-generation model. Hybrid learning--optimization methods provide a mechanism for coupling neural predictions to constrained planning. AllocNet predicts segment durations for a differentiable trajectory quadratic program~ wu2024 , Jiang et al. jointly learn waypoints and time allocations~ jiang2025 , and Marino et al. combine learned multi-UAV trajectory parameters with a differentiable correction layer~ marino2024 . These approaches show how optimization gradients can shape planning parameters during training. Inspired by these approaches, we learn spatial and event parameters to coordinate independently solved rigid-body trajectories on a shared time grid. This design involves three linked challenges. First, pairwise separation must be evaluated at common physical times even when the vehicles complete their routes at different times. Second, the trajectory layer must incorporate nonlinear rigid-body motion and rotor-level limits while retaining usable derivatives for network training. Third, independent local solves need spatial and temporal decisions that respond to neighboring vehicles. A suitable hierarchy must therefore connect synchronized event allocation, constrained local motion, and inter-vehicle learning within one training objective. We propose a learning--optimization framework that connects these three requirements through spatial waypoints and passage events. As illustrated in Fig.~ fig:architecture , shared networks use the vehicle state, known gate locations, and current relative neighbor positions to predict waypoint centers and ordered intermediate events. Independent differentiable CPC-based planners then generate trajectories on a common physical grid, and the outer objective evaluates collision and completion costs across the resulting trajectories. This hierarchy makes learned event allocation the connection between multi-vehicle coordination and local physical planning. The framework has three main technical contributions: A shared-grid event representation organizes spatial targets and passage timing for independent local planners. Continuous intermediate timestamps parameterize interpolated passage constraints, and the final CPC progress distribution remains a local decision variable. This construction supports common-time interaction evaluation together with vehicle-specific completion metrics. A differentiable sequential convex programming (SCP) trajectory layer incorporates rigid-body dynamics and individual rotor-thrust limits. Local approximations of the dynamics and terminal progress yield convex conic subproblems whose parameterization satisfies disciplined parametrized programming. The layer provides a constrained trajectory map through which waypoint and event predictions can be trained. An outer coordination objective adapts both networks through independently generated trajectories. Collision penalties act on synchronized vehicle positions, and the completion term links the learned parameters to local progress. This objective makes inter-vehicle behavior part of parameter learning while keeping the trajectory solves independent. The numerical evaluation examines coordination, physical feasibility, and computation within a two-vehicle setting. Gate-perturbation and goal-exchange layouts test spatial and temporal adaptation, a frozen-policy experiment examines thrust-difference regularization, and selected finite differences check the network derivatives. Warm-reference forward timings characterize the solver's computational cost. Together, these experiments assess the framework through trajectory behavior, local constraint satisfaction, and measured planning cost. Related Work Waypoint Timing and Trajectory Optimization Polynomial minimum-snap trajectories provide an efficient representation for quadrotor flight through waypoint sequences~ mellinger2011 . MINCO provides a compact polynomial representation with efficient spatial--temporal deformation and supports geometrical and dynamic constraints through trajectory optimization~ wang2022minco . CPC models ordered completion through continuous progress variables and jointly optimizes passage allocation and vehicle motion~ foehn2021 . Shen et al. extend this principle to a swarm racing task~ shen2023 . Our formulation retains complementary progress only for the final event and uses learned continuous timestamps for intermediate events, which restrict the feasible trajectories to those compatible with the assigned passage times. Decentralized Multi-Vehicle Planning MADER generates trajectories asynchronously using enclosing polyhedra, optimized separating planes, and collision checks against other agents' committed trajectories~ tordesillas2022 . Robust MADER extends trajectory sharing with delay checks and a two-step publication scheme to accommodate communication delays in dynamic environments~ kondo2024 . EGO-Swarm combines gradient-based local planning, collision-risk penalties, and lightweight topological trajectory generation for decentralized navigation in cluttered environments~ zhou2021ego . These methods make exchanged trajectory information part of decentralized collision handling. In our formulation, current relative neighbor positions condition the shared networks, and synchronized local trajectories enter the outer collision objective during training. Learning with Differentiable Planners Differentiable MPC learns controller costs and dynamics by differentiating the KKT conditions of a convex approximation at a controller fixed point~ amos2018mpc . AllocNet predicts segment durations and differentiates through the fixed-duration trajectory QP~ wu2024 . Jiang et al. combine depth-based waypoint prediction, time allocation, and differentiable minimum-snap optimization~ jiang2025 . Marino et al. predict MINVO control points and a learned collision constraint from point clouds and communicated features, then use an OptNet-based QP layer during imitation learning~ marino2024,amos2017 . These works establish the broader learning--optimization architecture. Our focus is the event representation and the separation of outer inter-agent collision learning from local rotor-level planning. For interacting aerial systems, learned model predictive games project neural reference strategies into dynamically feasible trajectories and train with game objectives~ papuc2026 . DiffCoord differentiates a distributed ADMM--DDP pipeline to learn problem and solver parameters for cooperative trajectories~ wang2026 . Our local optimizers interact through shared observations and the outer training objective. This choice reduces explicit coupling in each local solve, while leaving collision avoidance dependent on the learned policy and numerical validation. Learning also connects visual observations to aerial motion. Loquercio et al. train a sensor-to-trajectory policy through privileged imitation learning in simulation for high-speed flight~ loquercio2021 . Heeg et al. train quadrotor control policies using analytical gradients through differentiable dynamics and learned visual-state representations~ heeg2025 . These studies provide context for trajectory-level learning and dynamics-based policy gradients. The present formulation learns spatial and event parameters from state observations through differentiable local optimization. Problem Formulation We consider a multi-quadrotor racing scenario in which vehicles traverse prescribed gates and proceed to individual terminal targets. Each quadrotor has real-time access to its own state and the race-gate positions, and observes the current relative positions of neighboring quadrotors. These local observations provide the spatial information used to coordinate passage timing and generate dynamically feasible trajectories. title: Localization and Neural Splatting on the Edge: An FPGA Scene Memory for Robots
summary: Resource-constrained robots and autonomous vehicles need scene memories that localize a camera and render nearby views without a desktop GPU. Scene-coordinate regression (SCR) and 3D Gaussian splatting (3DGS) fit because they avoid an SfM stage, but ACEsplat-style pipelines are GPU-centered, and moving them to an edge FPGA is hard because SCR is pose-sensitive and 3DGS rendering is irregular and capacity-sensitive. We present LENS, an edge scene-memory acceleration system on the AMD KR260 that brings an ACEsplat-style workload to a low-power FPGA/ARM platform. Rather than proposing a new scene model, LENS co-designs the two dominant kernels with the board data path: an INT16 SCR accelerator that preserves pose accuracy, and a bit-exact fixed-point ordered 3DGS renderer that rewrites alpha transmittance as a log-sum-exp recurrence and removes provably useless streamed Gaussians. All LENS latency, power, and quality results are board-measured. The SCR engine preserves DSAC* localization accuracy at 25.42 ms, the on-board renderer reaches 34.11 dB on Cambridge against ACEsplat's 33.20, novel-view synthesis on RealEstate10K reaches 27.84 dB against 26.11, and all ten Wayspots scenes reach the ACEsplat rendering target. LENS wins performance per watt over a Jetson Orin NX on every deployment task, by 1.9x to 5.7x at about a quarter of the power, and is faster in absolute latency on localization and Wayspots rendering. On-device training reaches ACEsplat-level quality but not the GPU's time or energy, marking the remaining boundary for a future training accelerator.

Scene-coordinate regression (SCR) and 3D Gaussian splatting (3DGS) fit because they avoid an SfM stage, but ACEsplat-style pipelines are GPU-centered, and moving them to an edge FPGA is hard because SCR is pose-sensitive and 3DGS rendering is irregular and capacity-sensitive. Introduction Edge autonomy is increasingly limited by what a system can remember under its own power and thermal budget. A mobile robot revisiting a building, or an autonomous vehicle returning to a mapped route, needs more than a single pose estimate. It needs a scene memory that can answer two questions locally: where is the camera in this place, and what would the scene look like from a nearby view? Visual localization has been studied through direct pose regression, prioritized 2-D/3-D search, dense matching, hierarchical retrieval and matching, and SfM-backed maps kendall2015posenet,sattler2017active,brahmbhatt2018mapnet,taira2018inloc,sarlin2019hloc,schonberger2016sfm . Today, however, localization plus rendering is usually built around GPU-backed reconstruction and neural scene optimization. Such systems are powerful, but they are difficult to carry into small platforms that must localize, render, and reason while sharing watts with sensing, planning, and control. SfM-free neural scene pipelines offer a promising alternative. Scene-coordinate regression (SCR) predicts dense 3-D coordinates from image pixels shotton2013scrf,brachmann2017dsac,brachmann2018dsacpp,brachmann2021dsacstar . ACE makes this per-scene relocalization practical within minutes brachmann2023ace . On the rendering side, neural radiance fields mildenhall2020nerf,barron2022mipnerf360 and 3D Gaussian splatting (3DGS) kerbl20233dgs have made view synthesis a useful scene-memory interface, and recent Gaussian SLAM systems use explicit Gaussians for tracking and mapping matsuki2024gaussianslam,keetha2024splatam . Autonomous-driving scene models have also adopted Gaussians for surround-view dynamic reconstruction and urban scene understanding zhou2024drivinggaussian,yan2024streetgaussians,zhou2024hugs . ACEsplat combines SCR and 3DGS into a pipeline for localization, reconstruction, and novel-view synthesis without an offline SfM stage acesplat2026 . The algorithmic story is attractive for autonomy: the same scene representation can support both relocalization and visual prediction. The deployment story is harder. General FPGA DNN frameworks show that quantized neural inference can be efficient on reconfigurable logic venieris2016fpgaconvnet,sharma2016dnnweaver,umuroglu2017finn,wang2017pipecnn , and recent neural-rendering accelerators target NeRF and 3DGS kernels wang2023moth,lee2024gscore,wang2025famers . LENS targets a different composition of constraints. SCR is a dense CNN, but its output is geometry, not a class score; small coordinate errors can become large pose errors, so the convenient INT8 path used by many embedded neural accelerators is not automatically safe. The 3DGS renderer has the opposite structure: it is irregular, view-dependent, and dominated by sorted per-pixel Gaussian contributions. A small tile capacity makes the renderer fast but inaccurate; a faithful renderer must carry long Gaussian tails through a low-power memory system. For edge autonomy, success is therefore a system property: pose accuracy, render quality, latency, power, and board data movement must hold together. The question is not simply whether ACEsplat can run on an FPGA, but which parts of a neural scene-memory pipeline can be made accurate, which parts can be made fast, and which limits remain visible only on the board. We answer this question with LENS (Localization and Embedded Neural Splatting), an embedded-FPGA scene-memory system for resource-constrained edge autonomy. LENS runs on an AMD Kria KR260, a W-class Zynq UltraScale+ platform xilinxkr260 , and compares against a Jetson Orin NX edge GPU. It keeps SCR accuracy-first through INT16 custom logic and moves 3DGS rendering into a bit-exact fixed-point log-sum-exp datapath. This paper makes a hardware-system claim: an SfM-free localization and rendering pipeline can serve as an edge scene memory only when arithmetic, representation, and board-level data movement are co-designed. Our contribution is threefold: A board-measured edge scene-memory system. We map SCR relocalization and 3D Gaussian rendering to a KR260-class FPGA/ARM system and report accuracy, latency, and power with explicit board/GPU/emulator provenance. An accuracy-gated SCR accelerator. We show that INT16 custom logic, low-rank encoder decomposition, and DSP double-pumping can preserve DSAC* pose accuracy while reaching 25.42 ms on board. A bit-exact fixed-point LSE 3DGS render datapath. We replace the loop-carried alpha update with a fixed-point log-transmittance add, add a provably bit-exact stream truncation that removes 24 to 60 percent of streamed Gaussians, and reach ACEsplat-level reconstruction, novel-view synthesis, and Wayspots rendering on board at a performance-per-watt advantage over a Jetson Orin NX. Related Work localization and scene coordinates. Visual relocalization spans direct pose regression, structure-based 2-D/3-D matching, visual odometry/SLAM, and SfM-backed maps kendall2015posenet,sattler2017active,brahmbhatt2018mapnet,taira2018inloc,sarlin2019hloc,sarlin2020superglue,murartal2015orbslam,murartal2017orbslam2,engel2018dso,teed2021droidslam,schonberger2016sfm,lindenberger2021pixsfm . These methods differ in how much geometry is stored explicitly and how much query-time matching is required. Scene-coordinate methods predict dense correspondences and solve pose with robust geometry, from regression forests and DSAC/DSAC++ to DSAC* and ACE shotton2013scrf,brachmann2017dsac,brachmann2018dsacpp,brachmann2021dsacstar,brachmann2023ace . LENS keeps this relocalization model and studies the hardware mapping when pose accuracy, not classification accuracy, is the acceptance criterion. scene representations. Neural scene representations have moved from NeRF-style implicit fields to factorized, baked, voxel, and hash-grid variants mildenhall2020nerf,barron2022mipnerf360,chen2022tensorf,yu2021plenoctrees,reiser2021kilonerf,garbin2021fastnerf,hedman2021snerg,fridovichkeil2022plenoxels,muller2022instantngp and to explicit 3D Gaussian splatting kerbl20233dgs . Most accelerate a single render or train kernel, often as ASICs, while a deployed scene memory must preserve pose accuracy, render quality, latency, and power on the same board. Workload and System Partition LENS targets the ACEsplat-style deployment workload, not a new scene model. The workload exposes one localization service and two rendering services. For localization, an ACE-style SCR network predicts a dense 3D scene coordinate for each image pixel, and a DSAC*-style robust PnP solver estimates the 6-DoF camera pose from the resulting 2-D/3-D correspondences. For reconstruction and novel-view synthesis, scene-coordinate predictions initialize Gaussian centers; the Gaussian colors, opacities, covariances, and rotations define the explicit scene field rendered from a requested view. The two kernels pull in opposite directions. SCR is a regular CNN, but its output is metric geometry, so small coordinate errors can move PnP hypotheses across inlier thresholds. 3DGS rendering is irregular, depth-ordered, view-dependent, and capacity-sensitive; dense scenes carry long per-tile Gaussian tails. title: Structure over Reasoning: Unified Zero-Shot Navigation with a Small Vision-Language Model
summary: Vision-language navigation is moving into photorealistic, physically simulated scenes, where the leading zero-shot agents put a vision-language model in the control loop to choose every move and stop. Robots favour small models, whose abilities are uneven: Qwen3-VL-4B can judge whether a single view looks like the goal, but its route reasoning is at chance, its distance estimates nearly constant, its stop votes unreliable. Our agent therefore asks it two perceptual questions per step, which direction looks like the goal and whether the view justifies stopping, plus one gated frontier query on route-bearing instructions, and treats the answers as evidence, not actions: a route-blind semantic field over a bird's-eye map accumulates the directional scores through a tempered update, a skeleton graph supplies frontiers and geodesic distances, and a two-stage terminator turns stop votes into termini through a trail-consistency gate and a budget-forced return. With every baseline re-run in one installation at one budget, the agent exceeds all four zero-shot baselines of the VLNVerse subset in mean success on both granularities, though the paired interval against the strongest coarse-grained baseline includes zero. Termination is the dominant lever in ablation, thirteen attempts to give the model more of the navigation establish no reliable gain, and the agent runs on a Unitree Go2 quadruped with off-board inference. Code, per-episode logs and a robot video will be released at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/structure-over-reasoning-PAGE.

Code, per-episode logs and a robot video will be released at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/structure-over-reasoning-PAGE . Introduction Vision-language navigation asks an agent to follow a natural-language instruction to a goal it has never seen. The field is moving from panoramic graphs into photorealistic, physically simulated scenes such as VLNVerse vlnverse2025 , where the leading zero-shot agents place a vision-language model in the control loop and let it decide each move and each stop from panorama, history and full instruction zhou2024navgpt,chen2024mapgpt,long2024discussnav,qiao2025opennav . The recipe needs no training, but it assumes a model large enough to reason about a whole route from a few images and to judge, from a single view, whether the goal has been reached. A robot cannot always afford one: a cloud model adds latency and recurring cost, an onboard one must fit limited memory and compute. Qwen3-VL-4B qwen3vl2025 occupies GB and answers a step of our agent in seconds on an , against seconds when asked to reason at length. A smaller model does not make every part of navigation slightly worse; some parts fail while others hold. Shown one view and the goal phrase, the 4B model can usually tell whether that direction looks like the goal; across the variants we tried, its route reasoning over candidate directions stays at chance, its distance estimates are nearly constant, its grounding finds the right category but not the instance the instruction names, and its fine-grained stop votes fall within three metres of the goal less than a third of the time. A small-model navigator should use what stays reliable and move the rest into structure the model only feeds. Our agent asks two narrow perceptual questions, which of twelve directions looks like the goal and whether the view justifies stopping, and treats the answers as evidence and proposals, not actions. A bird's-eye occupancy map built from depth supports a skeleton graph whose frontier nodes are the only sub-goals the agent adopts, the moves being chosen among the benchmark's waypoint candidates, and a route-blind semantic field over the same map accumulates the directional scores with a tempered update, so that the field, not the model, remembers where the goal probably is. When a fine-grained instruction carries route clauses the model may also propose a frontier through a chain-of-thought query wei2022cot , gated and coupled conservatively; on coarse-grained instructions, which name only the destination, or without a usable proposal, the field drives alone. A stop vote is likewise checked against the trail's evidence rather than executed, and an episode nearing its budget without an accepted vote walks back to the best position seen. One policy with a single granularity-specific parameter serves both. Among the components removed in our ablations, termination produces the largest drop in success. On fine-grained instructions an agent that never stops and walks the full forty-step budget of our ablations passes within three metres of the goal in of episodes but succeeds in ; the full terminator raises this to in about half the steps. Reaching is not solved either, since even that agent stays beyond three metres in more than a fifth of episodes, but the gap shows that nearing a good position and ending there are separate problems. The ablations agree elsewhere: the field and the route channel contribute nearly additively, and the terminator is the largest single lever. Thirteen attempts to hand responsibility back to the model, from longer route reasoning and sub-goal decomposition to grounding-based final approach and model-selected return positions, establish no reliable gain, and two lose beyond the run-to-run spread. Throughout, the model supplies local evidence and structure mediates it. The contributions are fourfold. First, a decomposition of zero-shot navigation around a small vision-language model into a route-blind semantic field, a skeleton graph and a gated route channel, with the field update, the coupling and the action utility in closed form and one policy for both granularities. Second, a two-stage terminator with a trail-consistency gate and a budget-forced return proved affordable under the benchmark's displacement protocol, with an ablation that quantifies each stage. Third, on the official VLNVerse subset, with every zero-shot baseline re-run in one installation at the same thirty-step budget, the agent exceeds the strongest baseline in mean success by points on fine-grained instructions, with lower navigation error and higher path efficiency, and by on coarse-grained ones, all three-run means, and runs on a Unitree Go2 quadruped. Fourth, ablations and thirteen attempts to give the model more of the navigation, mapping what this model and prompt family support reliably and what still needs explicit structure. Related Work Vision-language navigation. The task was introduced on panoramic graphs of real buildings anderson2018r2r and extended to finer-grained instructions ku2020rxr , object-centric goals qi2020reverie and continuous environments krantz2020vlnce , where trained agents pair a waypoint predictor with a learned policy krantz2021waypoint,an2024etpnav,an2023bevbert or train a vision-language-action model end to end zhang2024navid,cheng2025navila . VLNVerse vlnverse2025 moves the task into a physics-based simulator with real-scale scenes and two instruction granularities; we adopt its official evaluation subset and protocol without change. Zero-shot navigation with language models. A line of work replaces the trained policy by a language model that reads a textual description of the panorama and the history and chooses among candidate directions zhou2024navgpt,long2024discussnav,lin2025navcot , with a map-like textual memory in MapGPT chen2024mapgpt , open-source models in continuous environments in Open-Nav qiao2025opennav and sub-task decomposition in InstructNav long2024instructnav . For object-goal search, language models score frontiers zhou2023esc,yu2023l3mvn,yin2024sgnav and vision-language embeddings build value maps over the explored area yokoyama2024vlfm ; VoroNav reasons over a reduced Voronoi graph with captions of far-sighted views wu2024voronav , which our skeleton graph and frontier captions resemble. Two things separate our agent from this family: the model never chooses a waypoint, since it scores sectors and proposes frontiers while a belief over the map decides where to go, and it never decides to stop on its own, since its vote is verified against the trail; Section~ shows that with a 4B model both restrictions are what make the agent work. Semantic maps and stopping. Occupancy grids elfes1989occupancy,thrun2005probabilistic , frontier-based exploration yamauchi1997frontier and semantic exploration policies chaplot2020semexp are the classical basis of our map, and open-vocabulary maps huang2023vlmaps show that language-conditioned scores can be written into spatial memory; our field differs in being a probability distribution over reachable cells, updated by tempered exponential evidence accumulation and blind to the route. When to stop is a known weakness of VLN agents, addressed by progress monitors ma2019selfmonitoring and backtracking ke2019tacticalrewind on the panoramic graph; the VLNVerse baselines execute the model's stop directly vlnverse2025 . We keep the vote as a proposal, add two cheap verifications and quantify each. Method sec:method Task formulation. VLNVerse places a cylindrical agent in physically simulated interior scenes rendered at real scale in Isaac Sim 6.0.1 and evaluates instruction following at two granularities: fine-grained instructions describe the route clause by clause and end with the goal; coarse-grained instructions name the goal object and its surroundings without a route. At each step the agent observes a twelve-view RGB and depth panorama and its pose, and moves by selecting a waypoint from the toolkit's waypoint predictor. We use the benchmark's Tel-Hop protocol: the agent is teleported to the chosen waypoint, and only the terminus is checked against the physical scene. An episode ends when the agent stops or its budget of steps is exhausted, and succeeds if the final position is within m of the goal. Overview. The design rests on one division of labour: the model answers local questions, structure handles the global problem. Shown a single view and the goal phrase, Qwen3-VL-4B can say whether that direction looks like the goal and whether the view justifies stopping; asked which candidate direction continues a route, it answers at chance level (Section~ sec:negative ). The agent therefore asks only the local questions and writes the answers into a semantic field over a bird's-eye map that is route-blind by construction, so that it cannot become a second, failing route reasoner. Where to go next and when to end the episode are decided from geometry and bookkeeping: a skeleton graph supplies frontiers and distances, a utility over the waypoint candidates picks the move, and a terminator verifies each stop vote against the trail (Fig.~ fig:arch ). Bird's-Eye Map and Skeleton Graph In each of the twelve depth views, which span the full circle with a ninety-degree horizontal field of view each, every column is reduced to the nearest surface whose height lies within an obstacle slab around the camera, which gives a range scan around the agent, with a column that sees only floor or ceiling counted as free to the trusted range, and the scan is integrated into an occupancy grid elfes1989occupancy,thrun2005probabilistic with a trusted range . Free cells reachable from the agent's position form the support of everything that follows, and denotes the geodesic distance between two cells of , infinite when no free path connects them. The geodesic ball uses the benchmark's success radius m, so that every readout of the field measures mass that would count as success. title: HAVANA: A Hierarchical Video-Action Model for Vision-Language Navigation
summary: Vision-Language Navigation (VLN) requires long-horizon instruction-consistent planning and short-horizon local planning in current geometry. Video-action models (VAMs) offer a promising way to learn predictive representations for navigation. However, existing VAMs jointly predict visual futures and local trajectories in a single process, even though they operate at different paces: future prediction remains stable across multiple updates while local trajectories must react to fresh observations. To bridge this gap, we introduce HAVANA, a dual-system VAM that decouples predictive reasoning from reactive local planning. A slow system produces a compact language-conditioned latent plan from observation history, while a fast system combines the latest plan with the current observation to generate local trajectories. Their asynchronous execution enables rapid adaptation without repeated future prediction, and no future video is generated during inference. Experiments on OmniNavBench demonstrate state-of-the-art navigation performance over prior baselines, while real-world deployments further show robust generalization to unseen environments across different robot embodiments. Our code and checkpoints will be available at https://github.com/Anastasiawd/HAVANA.
full_text: HAVANA separates predictive reasoning from reactive local trajectory prediction. The illustrated previous works include two designs: joint generation of future videos and trajectories ( 1), and trajectory recovery from generated videos via inverse dynamics ( 2). HAVANA learns compact instruction-conditioned latent plans through history observations. Its two systems run asynchronously, allowing each plan to guide multiple local trajectory updates from fresh RGB-D observations. Future-video generation is omitted during inference. Introduction sec:intro Vision-Language Navigation (VLN) requires an embodied agent to follow natural-language instructions through sequential interaction with its environment~ Anderson2017VisionandLanguageNI . Recent approaches~ Zhang2025UniNaVidAV,cheng2025navila,Wei2025StreamVLNSV directly predict actions or local navigation goals from instructions and observation histories. This leaves future route consistency implicit: when the next instruction-relevant landmark is not yet visible, a locally plausible action does not guarantee reaching the scene expected by the instruction. Learning to predict future semantics provides an additional supervision for this correspondence and has been shown to improve navigation on longer routes~ li2023vln-sig . Video-based World-Action Models (WAMs), also referred to as Video-Action Models (VAMs)~ pai2025mimicvideo,Yuan2026FastWAMDW,wang2026unified , introduce predictive capability by learning future visual states together with actions. For VLN, however, long-horizon instruction-consistent planning and short-horizon local path planning require different information at different rates. To follow instructions beyond the current field of view, long-horizon planning requires semantic reasoning about future observations and route progression, whereas local trajectory generation needs to continuously adapt to latest observed geometry to avoid obstacles. This conflict leaves open how those representations should be organized for navigation across different temporal scales. Existing fast-and-slow VLN frameworks~ wei2026ground, zhu2026fsd demonstrate the benefits of separating reasoning from execution. They typically condition a trajectory policy on latent goals and current observations, with its planning interface learned through pixel-goal grounding and trajectory supervision. We instead investigate how future visual prediction can ground a reusable planning interface in anticipated route progression. Such instruction-conditioned guidance can remain useful across multiple trajectory updates, while each local trajectory prediction must account for newly observed geometry. We therefore ask: how can low-frequency future visual prediction guide high-frequency trajectory generation from fresh observations? We introduce HAVANA (HierArchical Video-Action Model for NAvigation), a dual-system framework that reuses predictive latent plans for local trajectory prediction. The slow system uses a pretrained Vision-Language Model (VLM) to encode observation history and language instructions into planning states. Joint future-video and long-horizon waypoint supervision grounds these states in visual evolution and intended motion. The lightweight fast system combines the latest latent plan with the current RGB-D observation to generate short-horizon trajectories, which a tracking controller converts into velocity commands. Both systems run asynchronously, allowing the fast policy to incorporate new observations between planning updates while reusing latent route guidance, without video generation. Our contributions can be summarized as follows: We propose HAVANA, a dual-system VAM for VLN that decouples low-frequency predictive reasoning from high-frequency reactive trajectory prediction. We learn plan representations through joint future-video and waypoint supervision, augmented with an instruction-ranking objective that encourages instruction-consistent predictions over conflicting alternatives. We transfer trajectory prediction priors learned from language-free expert data to language-conditioned navigation through predictive latent plans, enabling local trajectory prediction without video generation. Related Work sec:related_work Video-Action Models for VLN Video-to-Action Models. Video-based planning uses generated visual futures as intermediate plans for action execution. UniPi~ du2023learning formulates control as text-conditioned video generation followed by inverse dynamics. ImagiNav~ chen2026imaginav extends this paradigm to navigation through subgoal-conditioned egocentric videos, while NavDreamer~ huang2026navdreamer selects imagined visual plans and reconstructs executable 3D waypoints. These approaches provide explicit visual foresight, but action recovery depends on the geometric consistency of generated videos. Iterative video generation also increases the cost of replanning from new observations, complicating high-frequency closed-loop control. World-Action Models. World-action models (WAMs) integrate predictive visual representations with action learning. DreamZero~ Ye2026WorldAM and AstraNav-World~ Hu2025AstraNavWorldWM jointly model future visuals and actions, while WAM-Nav~ yang2026wam uses asymmetric joint diffusion for long-horizon actions and short-horizon visual foresight. WorldVLN~ Zhao2026WorldVLNAW decodes predicted latent world transitions into waypoints, and SparseVideoNav~ Zhang2026SparseVG reduces inference cost through sparse future prediction. Other approaches retain predictive supervision while avoiding explicit future-video generation at inference: Fast-WAM~ Yuan2026FastWAMDW uses video co-training to improve direct action prediction, whereas ForeWAM~ Huang2026ForesightWS exposes latent future context to an action decoder. AHA-WAM~ Cai2026AHAWAMAsynchronousHW separates low-frequency world planning from high-frequency action execution for robotic manipulation. These advances establish predictive representations as useful control signals. For VLN, a key design question is how instruction-conditioned visual and motion foresight can provide reusable route guidance across successive reactive control updates. Hierarchical VLN Frameworks Inspired by fast-and-slow dual-process theory~ kahneman2011thinking , hierarchical navigation frameworks separate deliberative reasoning from reactive execution. At the reactive level, ViNT~ Shah2023ViNTAF learns transferable visual navigation representations, NoMaD~ Sridhar2023NoMaDGM employs diffusion policies for local trajectory generation, and FlowNav~ Gode2024FlowNavCF uses flow matching Lipman2022FlowMF . DualVLN~ wei2026ground combines a slow VLM planner producing pixel goals and latent planning features with a fast diffusion policy Cai2025NavDPLS for asynchronous navigation. FSD-VLN~ zhu2026fsd extends this separation to aerial navigation, while NavForesee~ liu2026navforesee combines hierarchical language planning with short- and long-horizon visual prediction. In VLN, route planning must preserve instruction intent over a longer horizon, whereas local control must adapt to current observation. HAVANA connects these roles through language-conditioned predictive latent plans learned with future video and waypoint supervision. A separately trained reactive policy reuses these plans alongside real-time RGB-D observations, enabling asynchronous control without video generation. Method sec:method As shown in Figure fig:pipeline , HAVANA is a dual-system framework that separates long-horizon semantic reasoning from short-horizon trajectory generation. The two systems operate asynchronously: the slow system continuously updates the high-level plan, while the fast system reacts to current observations using the most recently available plan. The predicted trajectory is subsequently tracked by a model-predictive path-integral (MPPI) controller Williams2017ModelPP . This design preserves the semantic and predictive world modeling while retaining the responsiveness, geometric awareness, and closed-loop safety required for embodied navigation. Latent Planning with the Slow System Our slow system is designed around a simple observation: a navigation representation should not only describe where the agent should move, but also anticipate how the visual scene will evolve along that motion. Direct waypoint supervision provides a compact geometric learning signal, yet it does not explicitly encourage the multimodal representation to model the future consequences of a navigation decision. The trajectory queries are explicitly supervised by future robot poses, encouraging them to form a compact structured representation of the intended motion. Thus, the trajectory latents are shared by waypoint prediction and video generation. title: GOFusion: Real-Time Gaussian-Occupancy Submap Fusion for Fisher-Informed Autonomous Robot Navigation
comment: 8 pages, 7 figures, 4 tables. Paper under review
summary: In this letter, we present GOFusion, a real-time visual mapping system for autonomous robot navigation that anchors Gaussian primitives to local occupancy maps, providing both spatial awareness for path planning and high-fidelity appearance that enables information-driven robot navigation. GOFusion builds 3D Gaussian maps from pose estimates and local occupancy maps obtained via visual-inertial SLAM and enables pose corrections to maintain both geometric and visual consistency. Furthermore, it restricts the 3D Gaussian Splatting optimization to active submaps to bound GPU memory usage. Building on the appearance-rich Gaussian map, we introduce a rasterizer-integrated Fisher approximation that quantifies per-primitive sensitivity online, serving as an information-driven heuristic for Gaussian pruning and next-best-view planning. We evaluate GOFusion on public datasets and in real-world drone flights. It not only outperforms several baselines in mapping quality, but also achieves real-time, high-fidelity and uncertainty-aware mapping at scale. Finally, we demonstrate fully autonomous drone exploration for Gaussian map refinement using the proposed Fisher-informed heuristic. Code is available at https://github.com/Bennnoo/GOFusion. We provide a supplementary video demonstration at https://youtu.be/pLQKbxQvb6I.
full_text: Experiment and Results sec:experiments Experimental Setup We evaluate the proposed method on two public datasets and a real-world flight, comparing against state-of-the-art baselines throughout. TUM RGB-D~ sturm2012benchmark provides real-world indoor sequences with motion-capture ground-truth trajectories, while the uHumans2~ rosinol2021kimera offers larger-scale synthetic environments with dense ground-truth geometry. The flight experiments additionally demonstrate real-time exploration of unknown, larger-scale environments, with the proposed Fisher information guiding view selection to refine the reconstruction. All experiments run on a workstation with an Intel Core Ultra 9-285K CPU, 96 GB of RAM, and an NVIDIA RTX 4090 GPU with 48 GB of VRAM, which also serves as the ground station for the outdoor flight A fully onboard configuration at reduced resolution is shown in the supplementary video due to space limitations. . In the real-world experiment, we used a self-built quadcopter with a MicroStrain 3DM-GX5-25 IMU, a custom stereo rig of two ZED X One GS cameras, and a Jetson Orin NX with 16 GB of unified memory, running visual-inertial SLAM alongside a PX4 flight controller. In contrast to the public datasets, which provide low-resolution RGB and depth images at , our outdoor-flight experiments use images Depth images are processed by the ZED SDK (v5.4, NEURAL PLUS mode). See stereolabs.com . at Hz together with IMU measurements at Hz . For DiskChunGS~ feldmann2026diskchungs , we supply depth directly to bypass its stereo-depth network without loading or executing it. Unlike several baselines that evaluate only on valid-depth regions, we compute , and over the full image for all methods, since regions without depth returns are still rendered. This is why our reproduced scores for some baselines fall below the numbers reported in their papers. We further measure RMSE, the number of Gaussian primitives, and peak GPU VRAM usage. Mapping (Mapp. FPS) reports mapping throughput and full-system (Full-FPS) the full tracking-and-mapping pipeline, both excluding the post- refinement. Evaluation of Mapping Quality TUM RGB-D res:tum_rgbd On TUM RGB-D~ sturm2012benchmark , we first evaluate reconstruction quality using ground-truth camera poses to isolate Gaussian mapping from trajectory estimation. Numbers are averaged over ten runs across all scenes in Table~ tab:gt_pose_mapping . Both configurations, with and without depth and normal supervision, take the top two places on PSNR and LPIPS at competitive mapping FPS. Although our image decomposition produces more primitives than wei2024gsfusion , the memory footprint grows far more slowly, with 5.3 times as many primitives at 0.9 times the VRAM. The reason our SSIM falls behind keetha2024splatam is likely its D-SSIM loss term and a three-times-larger primitive count. Interestingly, depth and normal supervision trade a small drop in RGB scores for better geometric consistency and map completeness. We further discuss this observation in Sec.\, subsec:ablation_depth_normal . uHumans2 In extension to Sec.\, res:tum_rgbd , we next evaluate our method against a comparable set of baselines on uHumans2~ rosinol2021kimera as a full-mapping system with estimated camera poses, in which SLAM also affects reconstruction quality. As shown in Table~ tab:uhumans_cross_method and Fig.\, fig:uhumans2_demo , our method leads on all rendering metrics across all four sequences and achieves the lowest ATE on the three long ones. Although we generate more Gaussian primitives, our memory footprint remains lower than that of peng2024rtgslam and feldmann2026diskchungs . This highlights the benefit of our system design that anchors occupancy and Gaussian primitives to share submap frames. Confining the optimization to the active submap guarantees 's scalability and enables consistent reconstruction across large environments where several baselines fail to complete sequences or suffer from trajectory drift. As observed in Sec.\, res:tum_rgbd , adding depth and normal supervision during 3DGS optimization does not necessarily improve rendering quality, since it regularizes the reconstruction toward geometric consistency. Self-Collected Outdoor Flying Data We benchmark all methods on 16 self-collected outdoor flight sequences The supplementary video shows the outdoor flight experiment. with challenging real-world illumination. Table~ tab:realworld_16_run reports the mapping performance in two settings. In the offline setting, all methods use camera poses from our SLAM output after bundle adjustment (BA) , which are held fixed as pseudo-GT poses and also fixed during global 3DGS refinement. In the online setting, we report metrics obtained with live SLAM pose estimates and incremental 3DGS optimization before and after global 3DGS refinement. SLAM runs on the resource-limited onboard platform, while the 3DGS optimization was executed on a ground station. As in the previous sections, a similar conclusion on mapping performance can be drawn from the offline evaluation, with zhu2025loopsplat and feldmann2026diskchungs additionally failing to complete all sequences. Our offline configuration with RGB-only supervision performs best on PSNR and LPIPS, as shown in Sec.\, res:tum_rgbd . For online, real-time drone navigation, our method adaptively skips frames to avoid blocking, thereby consuming fewer frames than offline baselines. Despite this, it already surpasses most offline baselines in rendering quality with global 3DGS refinement across all submaps (i.e.\,post-global), whereas those baselines were evaluated offline with BA-refined poses. Under identical online conditions, it also surpasses most offline baselines in memory usage with BA-refined poses. Since our incremental 3DGS optimization (i.e.\,pre-global) runs only on the current submap to bound computation and keep the system real-time, the rendering quality drops but still exceeds~ peng2025gpsslam, peng2024rtgslam . This is sufficient during flight, where navigation plans on the occupancy layer and view selection relies on Fisher information rather than on rendering fidelity (see Sec.\, sec:fisher_eval ). This quality gap closes after a few passes of global optimization. In addition, we found that a larger Gaussian count, which results from denser keyframe selection and a finer occupancy resolution (e.g., m ), does not translate into a proportional memory cost, since offline holds roughly ten times as many primitives as huang2024photoslam at less than twice its VRAM. Ablation Studies subsec:ablation Submapping and Joint Optimization subsec:ablation_submap_joint_opt We study the submap-based map representation and joint Gaussian-pose optimization on uHumans2~ rosinol2021kimera , using only RGB supervision. As shown in Table~ tab:ablation_submap_gradient , partitioning the map into submaps improves every rendering metric, slightly raises full-system FPS, and reduces peak memory, since only the active submap carries training buffers. Because each submap covers a small region, its local Gaussians stay consistent with the underlying geometry, where a global pose correction is applied to all of them at once. Besides, the joint optimization yields further gains across all rendering metrics at no cost in full-system FPS, and lowers the ATE of the single map but not of the submaps, whose poses are already well constrained by loop closure and submap alignment. Depth and Normal Supervision for 3DGS subsec:ablation_depth_normal We further investigate the impact of geometric supervision through depth and normals in . Fig.\, fig:abl_depth_normal illustrates exemplary RGB renderings alongside their rendered normals from novel viewpoints on uHumans2~ rosinol2021kimera . Accordingly, depth and normal supervision consistently maintain surface geometry and substantially improve novel viewpoints, while the RGB renderings remain comparable. As discussed in park2025dropgaussian , regularizing the 3DGS optimization toward geometric consistency prevents overfitting to the training-view appearance, which matters more for robot navigation than training-view rendering quality. However, this comes at the cost of a slight drop in rendering quality on the training views in our experiments, as shown in Table tab:uhumans_cross_method . Consequently, the weights for depth and normal loss terms in have to be carefully balanced. Evaluation of Gaussian-Map Fisher Approximation sec:fisher_eval Pruning of Weakly-Constrained Gaussians subsec:experiment:pruning In this experiment, we evaluate the proposed online Gaussian-map Fisher approximation as a pruning heuristic to remove weakly constrained Gaussians (see Sec.\, subsec:fisher_pruning ), comparing rendering quality before and after pruning on four uHumans2 sequences~ rosinol2021kimera . We evaluate our pruning heuristics against two baseline pruning scores: a random pruning strategy that replaces the entries of in with random values from a fixed seed, and an offline score recomputed over all keyframes after merging the submaps as in hanson2025pup3dgs , which serves as the reference pruning strategy. Fig.\, fig:fisher_pruning shows rendering quality as a function of the pruning ratio during online Gaussian mapping. Our online Gaussian pruning using the proposed Fisher approximation achieves pruning quality comparable to the offline reference, while both clearly outperform the random baseline as pruning becomes more aggressive. Since the offline reference is only available after the session ends, our online Fisher-based heuristic offers a practical alternative for Gaussian pruning. Next-Best-View Selection subsec:experiment:nbv We then show that the Gaussian-map Fisher approximation can also select the next-best-view for map refinement in a real-world autonomous flight, while the occupancy map supports collision-free path planning. To achieve the best mapping performance, the visual-inertial runs onboard, while the ground station maintains the hybrid map and evaluates candidate views offboard. Fig.\, fig:realworld_nbv_scene provides a scene overview while the drone was transiting between two next-best-view candidates. To examine how a selected view improves reconstruction, we compare maps reconstructed from observations accumulated before and after its visit, using the same fixed final estimated trajectory. Both maps are rendered from the same candidate camera pose and intrinsics. As shown in , the visit improved both local detail and reconstruction completeness. The displayed high-response regions in the Fisher uncertainty map also become more localized, with remaining responses concentrated around vegetation and object boundaries. These qualitative results support the ability of Fisher-informed next-best-view selection to identify informative views that improve 3DGS reconstruction quality and reduce map uncertainty.

title: Precision Cotton Disease Management: Leveraging UAV Imagery and Custom YOLO Deep Learning Framework for Enhanced Detection
summary: Cotton sustains the textile economies of over 80 countries with an annual yield of 113 million bales, yet 30-60% of yield losses are still attributed to viral, bacterial, and fungal diseases that remain undetected until manual field scouting. To address this critical issue, the integration of Unmanned Aerial Vehicle (UAV) imagery with deep learning offers a scalable early-warning system; however, existing models suffer from low early-stage accuracy, poor transferability, and high computational cost. In this paper, we propose Cotton-Vision, a fully convolutional single-stage detector that synergizes three lightweight architectural innovations: Ghost Bottleneck modules for a 20% parameter reduction, Efficient Channel Attention (ECA) for adaptive feature recalibration, and Cross-Stage Partial (CSP) fusion for enriched gradient flow. The network is trained on a novel dataset collected across seven cotton fields in the Punjab province of Pakistan, comprising over 2,700 high-resolution drone images. Extensive data augmentation (rotation, shear, exposure, and saturation) expands the dataset to 11,704 training samples. On a held-out test set, Cotton-Vision achieves a precision of 97.7%, a recall of 77.7%, an mAP@50 of 85.6%, and an mAP@50-95 of 76.6%. These results represent a 10-20% improvement in precision, recall, and mAP over state-of-the-art baselines, including YOLOv5, YOLOv8, YOLOv11, YOLOv12, RT-DETR, and RF-DETR. Through a comprehensive ablation study, we demonstrate that each proposed architectural enhancement contributes to the model's superior performance, yielding a 12-16% mAP improvement over the baseline architecture. Our findings confirm that this synergy of lightweight and attention-based modules provides a robust, computationally viable solution for early cotton disease detection.

title: AeroDASH: Asynchronous Vision-Language-Action Control for Continuous UAV Flight
summary: Onboard inference latency creates a mismatch between the trajectories predicted by vision-language-action (VLA) policies and the ongoing motion of unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs). We present AeroDASH, an asynchronous VLA framework for continuous language-conditioned flight. A B-spline policy is initialized through supervised fine-tuning on expert demonstrations, providing continuous trajectory references in position and yaw. During execution, trajectory fusion removes the expired prediction prefix and connects the remaining segment to the active reference with derivative continuity while limiting trajectory deformation. To account for deviations induced by asynchronous execution, execution-aware group relative policy optimization (GRPO) further adapts the policy using trajectory-level rewards. On the UAV-Flow test set, AeroDASH achieves a success rate of 76.56%, exceeding OpenVLA-UAV and AeroDASH w/o GRPO by 38.1 and 20.1 percentage points, respectively. Execution experiments show that AeroDASH sustains motion during inference and reduces acceleration, jerk, and speed fluctuations relative to asynchronous tracking of waypoint sequences. We further demonstrate language-conditioned flight with onboard inference and asynchronous trajectory execution. The code will be released upon acceptance.
full_text: Onboard inference latency creates a mismatch between the trajectories predicted by vision--language--action (VLA) policies and the ongoing motion of unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs). We present AeroDASH, an asynchronous VLA framework for continuous language-conditioned flight. A B-spline policy is initialized through supervised fine-tuning on expert demonstrations, providing continuous trajectory references in position and yaw. During execution, trajectory fusion removes the expired prediction prefix and connects the remaining segment to the active reference with derivative continuity while limiting trajectory deformation. To account for deviations induced by asynchronous execution, execution-aware group relative policy optimization (GRPO) further adapts the policy using trajectory-level rewards. On the UAV-Flow test set, AeroDASH achieves a success rate of 76.56 , exceeding OpenVLA-UAV and AeroDASH w/o GRPO by 38.1 and 20.1 percentage points, respectively. Execution experiments show that AeroDASH sustains motion during inference and reduces acceleration, jerk, and speed fluctuations relative to asynchronous tracking of waypoint sequences. We further demonstrate language-conditioned flight with onboard inference and asynchronous trajectory execution. The code will be released upon acceptance. Introduction sec:introduction Language-conditioned flight requires an unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) to ground natural language instructions in visual observations and translate them into continuous three-dimensional motion. Vision--language--action (VLA) models have emerged as a promising paradigm for this task, learning to map visual observations and language commands directly to robot actions. However, continuous UAV flight imposes a stringent execution requirement that goes beyond discrete action prediction: the flight controller needs a temporally smooth reference between successive policy updates, with high-order derivative continuity across all degrees of freedom in the vehicle's flat-output space. Current VLA approaches for UAVs predict discrete waypoints or pose targets, leaving the system without a continuous reference between updates. Onboard inference latency further exacerbates this gap: during VLA inference, the UAV continues to move, so each delayed prediction is conditioned on a stale observation and arrives after part of its intended horizon has elapsed. Existing asynchronous execution strategies address this mismatch at the position level only, without enforcing the high-order derivative continuity that UAV flight controllers require across the flat-output space. Abrupt transitions in these derivatives produce large jerks that can destabilize the vehicle. A second gap lies in the mismatch between open-loop training and closed-loop execution. Supervised fine-tuning trains the policy to match individual predictions to expert demonstrations but does not directly evaluate the complete trajectory produced by asynchronous execution. To overcome these challenges, we present AeroDASH (Fig.~ fig:aerodash-overview ), an asynchronous VLA framework for UAVs that sustains continuous language-conditioned flight under onboard inference latency. To address the first gap, the VLA policy predicts control points that define a cubic B-spline over the quadrotor's four-dimensional flat-output space, providing an analytically differentiable reference throughout each inference interval. When a delayed proposal arrives, the portion preceding the scheduled switch time is removed and the remaining segment is refitted to enforce high-order derivative continuity with the active reference. The fusion formulation enforces continuity of the trajectory reference at switching boundaries while penalizing deviations from the retained prediction. To address the second gap, we introduce execution-aware post-training with group relative policy optimization (GRPO). We optimize the policy using trajectory-level rewards that measure agreement between the complete trajectories produced by asynchronous execution and expert demonstrations. We design an asynchronous B-spline fusion mechanism that aligns delayed predictions with execution time and enforces continuity at switching boundaries while limiting trajectory deformation. We introduce GRPO post-training with trajectory-level rewards computed from asynchronously executed trajectories to improve agreement with expert demonstrations. Related Work sec:related_work Vision-Language-Action for Drones General-purpose VLA frameworks learn language-conditioned robot actions from diverse embodied demonstrations~ zitkovich2023rt2,kim2025openvla, black2025pi0,bu2025univla . For UAVs, existing work spans long-horizon language-guided navigation and fine-grained flight control. AerialVLN~ liu2023aerialvln studies navigation toward a distant goal, whereas UAV-Flow Colosseo~ wang2025uavflow pairs individual flight instructions with pilot demonstrations and trains VLA policies to predict UAV poses. Its Flying-on-a-Word tasks require the flight path to follow the spatial relationships specified by the instruction, making the executed path relevant in addition to the final position. Reinforcement learning extends VLA training beyond demonstration imitation. SimpleVLA-RL~ li2026simplevlarl applies outcome-driven reinforcement learning to OpenVLA-OFT, using online trajectory sampling and exploration to improve manipulation performance and generalization. Its formulation provides feedback on the consequences of sequential actions, rather than supervising each prediction solely against demonstrated actions. In aerial navigation, EG-GRPO~ chen2026eggrpo augments online rollouts with expert data to guide exploration and improve alignment with fine-grained instructions. These studies establish reinforcement learning as a means of improving instruction-conditioned behavior, while AeroDASH focuses on the effect of asynchronous execution on the resulting flight trajectory. The policy predicts B-spline control points and receives GRPO updates from closed-loop trajectory returns. This training objective evaluates successive predictions through their execution outcomes, complementing the temporal alignment and trajectory fusion discussed next. Asynchronous Trajectory Execution Optimization-based trajectory generation provides a foundation for continuous UAV flight. Minimum-snap methods~ mellinger2011minimumsnap penalize high-order derivatives of polynomial trajectories to generate smooth motion through prescribed waypoints. Richter et al.~ richter2016polynomial develop an efficient formulation for jointly optimizing polynomial segments and allocating their durations. MINCO~ wang2022minco further supports efficient trajectory optimization under geometric and dynamic constraints. These methods optimize flight trajectories from planning objectives and constraints; AeroDASH instead uses optimization to correct a trajectory predicted by a language-conditioned policy while limiting changes to its shape. Receding-horizon planners update trajectories as the flight state evolves. B-spline-based systems exploit local support and analytic derivatives for online kinodynamic replanning~ usenko2017replanning,ding2019bspline, zhou2019robust,zhou2021egoplanner , while FASTER~ tordesillas2022faster maintains a committed trajectory during successive planning cycles. These mechanisms allow flight to continue during planning. For a VLA, however, a prediction is conditioned on an earlier visual observation and may arrive after part of its intended execution interval has elapsed. Maintaining an executable trajectory during inference therefore does not by itself resolve how the delayed prediction should be aligned and connected to it. RTC and REMAC address asynchronous execution through action generation. RTC~ black2025rtc guides new predictions using overlapping actions, whereas REMAC~ wang2026remac learns delay-aware corrections and preserves the executed prefix during sampling. Both promote consistency between successive predictions, but neither explicitly imposes velocity and acceleration matching at the switching boundary. AeroDASH aligns delayed B-spline predictions with execution time and refits the remaining curve to match the current reference's position, velocity, and acceleration while limiting deformation. GRPO post-training further adapts the policy to asynchronous execution using closed-loop trajectory returns. Method sec:method Figure~ fig:aerodash-training outlines AeroDASH's training and execution pipeline. Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) initializes the B-spline policy from expert trajectories. Because the UAV continues moving during inference, optimization-based fusion aligns delayed proposals with execution time and connects them continuously to the active reference. GRPO then adapts the policy to accumulated closed-loop deviations using trajectory-level rewards.
