title: T(R,O) Grasp++: Cross-Embodiment Dexterous Grasping in Cluttered Environments at Scale
summary: Dexterous grasping in cluttered scenes remains a central challenge in robotic manipulation, as it requires high-dimensional hand coordination under complex object-environment constraints. To address this problem, we introduce one of the largest simulation benchmarks to date, comprising around 0.5B grasp annotations across eight dexterous hands and approximately 50K objects. Furthermore, we propose T(R,O) Grasp++, a scalable diffusion-based framework for cross-embodiment dexterous grasp synthesis in cluttered environments. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our model significantly outperforms existing baselines, achieving an average success rate of 88% across eight dexterous embodiments. Meanwhile, our pipeline achieves only 0.3s inference latency while improving inference sample efficiency by over 10 times.
full_text: Dexterous grasping in cluttered scenes remains a central challenge in robotic manipulation, as it requires high-dimensional hand coordination under complex object-environment constraints. To address this problem, we introduce one of the largest simulation benchmarks to date, comprising around 0.5B grasp annotations across eight dexterous hands and approximately 50K objects. Furthermore, we propose Grasp++, a scalable diffusion-based framework for cross-embodiment dexterous grasp synthesis in cluttered environments. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our model significantly outperforms existing baselines, achieving an average success rate of 88 across eight dexterous embodiments. Meanwhile, our pipeline achieves only 0.3s inference latency while improving inference sample efficiency by over 10 times. Introduction sec:intro Dexterous grasping in cluttered environments is essential for practical robotic manipulation. However, it remains challenging due to the high-dimensional action space and complex interactions among object, hand and surrounding environments. Existing methods typically generate multiple grasp proposals directly in the scene and rely on collision checking or grasp scoring to select executable grasps~ zhang2024dexgraspnet, zhang2025contactdexnet, hgcnet, fang2025anydexgrasp, DDGC, multimodal2021, zhang2025cadgrasp . However, previous works have three key limitations. First, the proposal-and-selection paradigm suffers from low inference sample efficiency. Since the relations among the hand, object, and surrounding environment are not sufficiently encoded, many generated proposals are either in collision or dynamically unstable, requiring a large number of candidates to obtain a single successful grasp. Second, model performance is limited by insufficient data scale and diversity. Existing datasets are limited in object and embodiment diversity, with redundant annotations concentrated on a small set of objects~ zhang2024dexgraspnet, zhang2025contactdexnet . Third, existing grasp representations are insufficient. Prior methods either rely on hand-specific representations, such as hand joint values~ zhang2024dexgraspnet, hgcnet or predefined grasp templates~ fang2025anydexgrasp, zhang2025cadgrasp , which limit generalization across hands, or adopt object-centric representations for grasp optimization~ zhang2025contactdexnet, jiang2021graspTTA , which is computationally expensive. To address these limitations, we first construct a large-scale dataset across multiple embodiments for dexterous grasping in cluttered environments. Our benchmark contains around 0.5B grasp annotations in common manipulation scenes, with hierarchical difficulty scores that enable fine-grained evaluation across varying grasp difficulties. In addition, we propose Graph++, a unified grasp representation that models spatial transformations among environment, robot, and object. Built upon Graph++, our Grasp++ model performs unified diffusion-based cross-embodiment grasping synthesis. In extensive experiments, our model achieves an average success rate of 87.96 across eight dexterous hands, an inference speed of 0.34 seconds on an NVIDIA 4090 GPU, and over 10 higher inference sample efficiency than existing baselines. In conclusion, our contributions are summarized as follows: (1) We construct a large-scale cluttered-scene dexterous grasping benchmark with 53,675 objects, around 0.5B grasp annotations, and difficulty scores for evaluation under varying grasp difficulties; (2) We propose Grasp++, a scalable diffusion-based framework that integrates object-environment geometry with hand kinematics for cross-embodiment grasp synthesis in cluttered environments; (3) We conduct extensive simulation and real-world experiments, where Grasp++ significantly outperforms all baselines by over 30 , while achieving fast and sample-efficient inference; (4) We present the first scaling study for cross-embodiment dexterous grasping, leveraging our large-scale benchmark to reveal how performance scales with training object diversity and model capacity. Related Works sec:rw Dexterous Grasping Dataset sec:2.1 Creating large-scale datasets for dexterous grasping is challenging due to the high-dimensional hand action space and complex hand-object contacts. One line of work constructs such datasets through optimization-based synthesis, where grasp poses are directly optimized with force-closure, contact, penetration, and stability objectives~ zhang2024dexgraspnet,zhang2025contactdexnet, wang2022dexgraspnet, pmlr-v205-wu23b . Another line of work trains grasping policies in simulation and rolls out on large object sets, collecting successful executions as grasp annotations~ zhang2024graspxl,casas2024multigrippergrasp, pmlr-v205-chen23b . In our work, we train reinforcement learning policies for each dexterous hand and use successful rollouts to annotate 444 million grasps across large-scale object datasets. As shown in Tab.~ tab:dataset , our dataset covers 53,675 objects and 8 dexterous hands, while additionally providing per-grasp difficulty scores and a mount link to approximate real-world hand-arm deployment. Learning-based Dexterous Grasping Synthesis sec:2.2 Learning-based frameworks for dexterous grasping synthesis can be categorized into single-object and scene-aware approaches. Single-object methods typically predict or optimize grasp poses for an isolated target object without modeling environment constraints~ zhang2025contactdexnet, wei2024dro, fei2025t, wan2023unidexgrasp++, shao2020unigrasp, xu2024manifoundation, dfc, li2023gendexgrasp, attarian2023geometry, khargonkar2023neuralgrasps . While these methods achieve promising results in single-object settings, their inference sample efficiency drops substantially when applied to real-world cluttered environments, as many predicted grasps suffer from severe collisions with surrounding objects or environment. In comparison, scene-aware methods further incorporate environment constraints into grasping synthesis~ zhang2024dexgraspnet, zhang2025contactdexnet, hgcnet, fang2025anydexgrasp, pmlr-v205-chen23b, chen2025clutterdexgrasp, pmlr-v270-wang25l, pmlr-v155-breyer21a . Despite their progress, existing methods still face limitations in both task setting and grasp representation. In terms of task setting, existing methods generate grasp proposals over the entire scene and then rely on collision checking, grasp scoring, or feasibility filtering to select executable grasps~ zhang2024dexgraspnet, zhang2025contactdexnet, hgcnet, fang2025anydexgrasp, DDGC, multimodal2021 . While suitable for open-world scene grasping, this setting suffers from poor sample efficiency in target-object grasping, as many generated proposals correspond to irrelevant objects or collide with the surrounding environment. As for grasp representation, prior methods either directly predict hand-specific joint values~ zhang2024dexgraspnet,fang2025anydexgrasp, chen2025clutterdexgrasp , which limits cross-embodiment generalization, or rely on object-centric predictions that require additional slow optimization to recover executable joint configurations~ zhang2025contactdexnet, zhang2025cadgrasp . To overcome these limitations, we propose Graph++ as a unified grasp representation across embodiments, enabling direct grasp prediction on the target object in cluttered environments within a unified framework. Benchmark sec:benchmark We present a large-scale benchmark for cross-embodiment dexterous grasping in diverse cluttered scenes, with grasp difficulty assessed by object-level graspability and scene-level clutter complexity to support fine-grained evaluation across varying grasp difficulties. Our dataset comprises 53,675 objects from UniDexGrasp~ xu2023unidexgrasp and ObjaverseXL~ deitke2023objaverse , including diverse cluttered scenes in tabletop, shelf, and box settings (as shown in Fig.~ fig:teaser ). Across eight dexterous hands, we annotate around 0.5B valid grasp samples in simulation. Object Collection and Scene Synthesis sec:3.1 We collect 13,049 objects from the UnidexGrasp dataset~ xu2023unidexgrasp and 40,626 objects from the ObjaverseXL dataset~ deitke2023objaverse . For training, we use dexterous grasp samples in cluttered scenes across all dexterous hands on 47,737 objects. For testing, we use the remaining 5,938 unseen objects to construct cluttered environments for each dexterous hand. In each scene, 15 to 25 objects are randomly placed on a supporting plane. We construct three common manipulation environments: tabletop, shelf and box, with environment scale randomly sampled within predefined ranges. Dexterous Grasp Annotation sec:3.2 To efficiently annotate dexterous grasps across robotics hands, we adopt a three-stage annotation pipeline. First, we train embodiment-specific reinforcement learning policies to roll out power and precision grasps on floating objects. Second, we generate stable object poses by randomly sampling initial object poses and dropping the objects onto a tabletop in simulation. Each floating-object grasp is then transformed according to the resulting object pose, and candidates with tabletop penetration are filtered out. Finally, we construct diverse cluttered manipulation scenes across tabletop, shelf, and box settings by placing additional obstacle objects outside the 2D convex hull of the hand-object grasp configuration to avoid collisions. In this way, we annotate approximately 1K grasps in clutter per target object for each dexterous hand. To better reflect real-world deployment constraints, we attach a cylinder mount link to each palm to approximate the connecting arm segment and include it in collision checking, ensuring sufficient clearance for both the hand and its mounting structure. Our RL-based annotation pipeline supports scalable data generation through massively parallel simulation. On an NVIDIA RTX 4090 GPU, a trained policy generates 216 grasp annotations per second while also achieving a higher filtering success rate compared with optimization-based methods~ li2023gendexgrasp, chen2024bodex . Hierarchical Difficulty Annotation sec:3.3 Beyond grasp annotations, we further assess the execution difficulty of each grasp to support fine-grained evaluation across varying grasp difficulties. Specifically, object-level difficulty captures the intrinsic graspability of the target object, estimated by the number of RL optimization steps required for reliable grasping. Environment-level difficulty measures local clutter around the target object based on obstacle proximity and spatial enclosure. We combine these two factors as an overall difficulty score for each grasp annotation. Detailed definitions are provided in the Appendix. Dexterous Grasp Evaluation in Simulation sec:3.4 We evaluate dexterous grasps in Isaac Gym simulation. A grasp is considered successful if it is collision-free with the surrounding environment and lifts the target object above a predefined height threshold. The hand is initialized at the outer grasp pose, driven to the inner grasp pose with position control, and then lifted upward. For consistency, we use the same simulation protocol for both training data filtering and model evaluation across our method and all baselines. Grasp++ T(R,O) Grasp++ for Dexterous Grasping in Clutter sec:model Given point-cloud observations of the target object and the surrounding environment, denoted as and , together with the URDF description of an arbitrary dexterous hand, our goal is to learn a unified model that predicts link-wise transformations representing a valid and collision-free grasp in a cluttered environment. Finally, the predicted link poses are converted into executable joint values by solving a real-time inverse-kinematics retargeting problem using Pyroki~ kim2025pyroki . title: DialogMem: Evaluating Dialogue-Grounded Embodied Memory in 3D Environments
summary: Embodied agents in human-centered environments require memory that integrates what they observe with what humans tell them over time. However, existing embodied memories are built primarily from visual experience, leaving open how dialogue with humans can be grounded in the objects encountered throughout that experience. We introduce DialogMem, a two-phase benchmark in which agents build memory from time-aligned streams of posed RGB-D observations and dialogue, and later use it for instance-level object navigation and question answering (QA). DialogMem provides 142 episodes across 27 real-world 3D scenes, with 14,193 QA pairs and 11,890 navigation instructions. We evaluate nine memory representations within a unified framework of memory formation, evidence retrieval, and reasoning for task outputs. In experiments, appending dialogue to visual memory at evaluation time substantially improves QA but yields negligible navigation gains, suggesting that relevant dialogue is present in memory but not grounded to specific objects. Controlled diagnostics show that navigation improves with link quality but falls short of ground-truth object-level memory even under perfect linking. Retrieving the correct object entry and recovering its spatial location remain further bottlenecks. These results identify three bottlenecks for dialogue-grounded embodied memory: grounding and organizing dialogue at object-level entries during formation, retrieving the correct entry, and localizing it accurately.
full_text: Embodied agents in human-centered environments require memory that integrates what they observe with what humans tell them over time. However, existing embodied memories are built primarily from visual experience, leaving open how dialogue with humans can be grounded in the objects encountered throughout that experience. We introduce , a two-phase benchmark in which agents build memory from time-aligned streams of posed RGB-D observations and dialogue, and later use it for instance-level object navigation and question answering (QA). provides 142 episodes across 27 real-world 3D scenes, with 14 , 193 QA pairs and 11 , 890 navigation instructions. We evaluate nine memory representations within a unified framework of memory formation, evidence retrieval, and reasoning for task outputs. In experiments, appending dialogue to visual memory at evaluation time substantially improves QA but yields negligible navigation gains, suggesting that relevant dialogue is present in memory but not grounded to specific objects. Controlled diagnostics show that navigation improves with link quality but falls short of ground-truth object-level memory even under perfect linking. Retrieving the correct object entry and recovering its spatial location remain further bottlenecks. These results identify three bottlenecks for dialogue-grounded embodied memory: grounding and organizing dialogue at object-level entries during formation, retrieving the correct entry, and localizing it accurately. Introduction Humans build memories of their environments through extended experience. They remember which objects they observed, when and where they encountered them, and what others told them about those objects. Embodied agents operating in human-centered environments need a similar capacity: integrating perceptual evidence, trajectory context, and dialogue-derived information into persistent memory. Embodied memory research has made rapid progress in turning long streams of visual experience into persistent representations. These representations support navigation~ wani2020multion, khanna2024goat , question answering~ majumdar2024openeqa, hu20253dllm , and object search~ yadav2025findingdory , and are often queried at evaluation time by a vision-language model (VLM)~ bai2025qwen3, hurst2024gpt . Yet most existing benchmarks~ majumdar2024openeqa, khanna2024goat, yadav2025findingdory, hu20253dllm and methods~ gu2024conceptgraphs, yang20253d build memory primarily from RGB-D observations and agent poses, without explicitly retaining dialogue-derived information. We therefore ask: when experience also includes dialogue, how should embodied memory be organized so that a VLM can both recall what was said and localize the objects it refers to? To address this, we introduce , a benchmark for evaluating how well agents build memory from time-aligned streams of posed RGB-D observations and dialogue, and later use it for instance-level object navigation and question answering (QA). Navigation and QA probe two distinct aspects of dialogue-grounded memory: spatial grounding of referenced objects and semantic access to what was said about them. provides 142 episodes across 27 real-world 3D scenes, with 14,193 QA pairs and 11,890 navigation instructions. Each episode is split into two phases. In Phase~1, the agent traverses a 3D environment while receiving time-aligned streams of posed RGB-D observations and dialogue turns, forming memory over an extended multimodal experience. In Phase~2, the resulting memory is queried by navigation instructions and questions that draw on three types of memory content: perceptual content capturing object appearance and spatial relations, episodic content from the trajectory, and social content from dialogue. Each query refers to a target object using one or more of these content types. Both tasks require identifying the referenced object. Navigation further requires recovering its spatial location, while QA requires retrieving information about the target. We evaluate nine memory representations on , spanning raw stream storage, structured visual memories~ gu2024conceptgraphs, yang20253d , and dialogue-augmented variants that either append dialogue at evaluation time or link dialogue turns to memory entries during formation. All representations use the same VLM reasoner~ bai2025qwen3 , enabling controlled comparison of memory representation and retrieval. Across all memory representations, navigation and QA exhibit a clear asymmetry: dialogue substantially improves QA but yields negligible navigation gains. Neither evaluation-time appending nor simple formation-time linking reliably grounds dialogue-derived information in the objects it refers to. A controlled sweep over link quality shows that navigation improves as links become more accurate, yet even perfect links fall short of ground-truth object-level memory. Controlled diagnostics further reveal substantial bottlenecks in retrieving the correct object entry and recovering its spatial location. Changing the reasoner does not close the gap. These findings motivate object-centered memories that ground and organize what agents observe and what they are told around the correct object entries during memory formation. provides a testbed for measuring progress on this goal, together with the retrieval and localization bottlenecks it exposes. Contributions. We formulate dialogue-grounded embodied memory as forming persistent memory from posed RGB-D and dialogue streams, retrieving relevant evidence, and reasoning over it for embodied tasks. We introduce , the first benchmark that treats dialogue as a persistent memory source jointly grounded with visual experience and evaluates the resulting memory through both navigation and QA. We evaluate nine memory representations under a common reasoning framework and introduce controlled link-quality and oracle probes that decompose failure into dialogue--object grounding, entry retrieval, and 3D localization. Related Work in Embodied Tasks. Language has been widely used as an interface for embodied agents~ thomason2020vision, gao2022dialfred, padmakumar2022teach , including navigation instructions, task guidance, clarification, and human-agent collaboration. However, these settings typically treat dialogue as task-time context rather than as content to be retained across tasks. In contrast, treats dialogue as a memory source during memory formation, requiring agents to ground dialogue-derived object information in perceptual and spatial experience for later navigation and question answering. Memory Benchmarks. Prior embodied memory benchmarks have made important progress in testing memory over long-horizon visual experience. Evaluation targets include object locations~ wani2020multion, khanna2024goat , spatial layouts~ pasukonis2022evaluating, pleines2025memory, zhu2023excalibur , and temporal observation history~ majumdar2024openeqa, min2024situated, hu20253dllm, yadav2025findingdory . The input streams in these benchmarks are largely limited to visual observations and poses, leaving out dialogue-derived object information such as aliases, usage patterns, and corrections. Consequently, these benchmarks primarily evaluate perceptual and episodic memory, leaving social memory largely unexplored. treats dialogue as a persistent memory source alongside visual experience, thereby extending embodied memory evaluation to include social memory. Table~ tab:benchmark_comparison summarizes this distinction. 3D Scene Representations as Embodied Memory. Recent 3D scene representations, such as semantic maps~ huang2023visual , 3D scene graphs~ gu2024conceptgraphs , and dense 3D representations~ yang20253d, hong20233d , can serve as embodied memory for downstream tasks by organizing past RGB-D observations into persistent spatial structures. Recent systems often pair such representations with VLM reasoners~ bai2025qwen3, hurst2024gpt , using retrieved visual or spatial evidence for tasks such as object localization and navigation. However, these representations are typically constructed from visual observations alone, leaving open how dialogue-derived object information should be incorporated into object-level memory. Embodied Memory Formulation sec:formulation We formalize embodied memory to provide a unified framework for describing and comparing the memory representations evaluated in this work. Input streams and memory. We consider an embodied agent operating in a 3D environment over timesteps . At each step, the agent receives an input tuple: where is an RGB-D frame, is the agent pose, and is the dialogue content aligned with time , when available. The agent constructs or updates an internal state , referred to as its embodied memory, updated incrementally by an update function : Retrieval and reasoning. At evaluation time, given a query , a retrieval function selects task-relevant evidence . A reasoner then produces the output . The form of depends on the task, such as a target location for navigation or an answer for question answering. This formulation is agnostic to how is represented, allowing it to take the form of either raw observation streams or structured visual representations, such as scene graphs and 3D spatial representations. DialogMem sec:benchmark instantiates the preceding formulation in real-world scanned 3D environments, where agents must integrate perceptual, episodic, and social memory content for downstream navigation and question answering. Task Overview. The two-phase structure separates memory formation from memory use, so that downstream performance reflects what the agent has retained rather than what it can infer from the current observation (see Figure~ fig:overview ). Phase 1: Memory formation. The agent receives posed RGB-D observations and dialogue streams over an extended traversal. The goal is to construct a memory that covers three types of memory content. Perceptual content captures object appearance and spatial relations, originating from RGB-D observations. Episodic content comes from the trajectory and captures when and how often each object was observed. An instruction such as ``go to the sofa'' further defines a navigation segment, associating objects with segments and supporting references such as ``the chair you saw on the way to the sofa.'' Social content comes from dialogue and captures human-provided object information, including ownership, aliases, usage patterns, and updates or corrections. Phase 2: Memory evaluation. Phase~2 evaluates whether the agent can retrieve and use the memory content formed in Phase~1. It consists of two task types grounded in the same Phase~1 episode: navigation and question answering. In navigation, starting from its Phase~1 endpoint, the agent receives a natural language instruction that identifies a target object and navigates to its location, e.g., ``Go to the cabinet where Amelia keeps snacks.'' In question answering, the agent first identifies a target object using Phase~1 memory evidence and then answers a question about that object, e.g., ``Who owns the bed with two lamps?'' Benchmark Construction Environment and metadata. We build on 27 scenes from the HM3D validation split~ ramakrishnan2021habitat , using object annotations from GOAT-Bench~ khanna2024goat . is an evaluation-only benchmark: following prior embodied QA evaluation practice~ majumdar2024openeqa , all baselines use pretrained models without training or fine-tuning on . For each scene, we use an LLM (GPT-4o~ hurst2024gpt ) to generate scene-specific resident profiles. Each profile specifies a resident's name, relationship to others, and speaking style, giving dialogue generation a consistent set of speakers. For each annotated object, we construct perceptual memory content by parsing GOAT-Bench descriptions into attributes and spatial relations. title: Self-Crystallizing Behavior Trees: Amortizing Foundation-Model Reasoning into Deterministic Control for Autonomous Drones
summary: Classical robot control, Finite State Machines and Behavior Trees (BTs), is deterministic and inspectable but fixed at design time: it fails on situations its designers did not anticipate. Foundation models can synthesize new control logic at runtime, at a cost in latency and non-determinism hard to accept in safety-critical aerial systems. Existing LLM-driven approaches keep the model in the loop permanently and discard what it produces. We propose Self-Crystallizing Behavior Trees (SCBT), in which the foundation model is a compiler rather than a runtime. When a BT node fails, an LLM proposes a minimal, mission-agnostic subtree patch; CMA-ES tunes its parameters in simulation; a contextual bandit decides whether a stored patch or a new LLM call is worth its cost; and a three-stage admission pipeline (static check, invariant-monitored replays, an empirical margin over the unpatched tree) admits only patches that demonstrably recover. Admitted patches are stored in a fleet library and, once the LLM call rate decays, crystallized into a deterministic BT that no human wrote. We implement SCBT on Microsoft Project AirSim with a schema-constrained LLM pipeline (Gemini 3.1 Pro) and a lockstep simulator. Over three seeds of a 20-episode learning phase with wind-gust and battery failures, SCBT used $11\pm1.4$ LLM calls against 26 for whole-tree regeneration and 22 without a library, with 0.33 calls per episode in the second half. The crystallized trees, 28 and 33 nodes with two patches each, reached $97\pm2\%$ mission success with no learning running, against 12\% for the unpatched tree and 98\% for a hand-coded expert tree, and reproduce decision traces exactly when re-ticked offline. Two negative results: replay admission rejected useful wind recoveries by attributing wind-induced geofence excursions to the patch, and a static-only ablation generalized better to held-out failures.
full_text: Self-Crystallizing Behavior Trees: Amortizing Foundation-Model Reasoning into Deterministic Control for Autonomous Drones Classical robot control architectures, Finite State Machines (FSMs) and Behavior Trees (BTs), are deterministic, inspectable, and fast, but fixed at design time: they fail on the long tail of situations their designers did not anticipate. Foundation models can synthesize new control logic at runtime, at the price of latency, cost, and non-determinism that are hard to accept in safety-critical aerial systems. Existing LLM-driven approaches keep the model permanently in the loop and discard what it produces after each use. We propose Self-Crystallizing Behavior Trees (SCBT), in which the foundation model is a compiler rather than a runtime. When a node of a vehicle's BT fails, an LLM proposes a minimal subtree patch in a constrained, mission-agnostic grammar; CMA-ES tunes the patch's continuous parameters in simulation; a contextual bandit decides whether a stored patch or a new LLM call is worth paying for; and a three-stage admission pipeline (static check, invariant monitors over randomized replays, and an empirical margin over the unpatched tree) admits only patches that demonstrably recover. Admitted patches are stored in a fleet library indexed by failure context and, once the LLM call rate has decayed, crystallized into a conventional deterministic BT that no human wrote. We implement SCBT on Microsoft Project AirSim with a schema-constrained LLM pipeline (Google ADK, Gemini~3.1~Pro) and a lockstep simulator. Over three seeds of a 20-episode learning phase with injected wind-gust and battery failures, SCBT used LLM calls against 26 for whole-tree regeneration and 22 for patching without a library, with 0.33 calls per episode in the second half. The crystallized trees, with 28 and 33 nodes and two patches each, reached mission success on the curriculum with no learning component running, against 12 for the unpatched base tree and 98 for a hand-coded expert tree; re-ticked offline against recorded observations they reproduce their online decision traces exactly. Two negative results are reported: replay admission as parameterized rejected useful wind recoveries because it attributed wind-induced geofence excursions to the patch, and the static-only ablation generalized better to held-out failures as a consequence. behavior trees, large language models, contextual bandits, CMA-ES, UAV, neuro-symbolic AI, lifelong learning, simulation-based verification Introduction sec:intro For half a century robot behavior has been specified explicitly, first as FSMs and, over the last decade, as BTs~ colledanchise2018bt,iovino2022survey . These architectures are attractive precisely because they are closed: every branch can be inspected, every transition is deterministic, and the controller runs at a fixed rate on embedded hardware. The same closedness is their limitation. A BT cannot execute a branch that was never written, and in open environments the set of situations that require a branch is effectively unbounded. We call this design-time rigidity. Foundation models offer an apparent escape: LLMs write robot programs from natural-language goals~ liang2023cap , generate BT XML on demand~ izzo2024btgenbot,zhou2024llmbt , ground plans in perceptual affordances~ ahn2022saycan,huang2023voxposer , and coordinate heterogeneous teams~ mandi2024roco,chen2024scalable . But these systems share a structural assumption: the model stays in the control loop for the lifetime of the system, and what it produces is discarded after use. For aerial robots this has three consequences. Latency: in our implementation a single structured proposal from a frontier model takes 31--105\,s (two schema-constrained calls); a vehicle in a wind gust cannot wait for it. Cost: operating cost grows with activity. Non-determinism: two flights under identical conditions may execute different logic, which defeats the certification argument that makes BTs acceptable in the first place. The two camps are usually framed as a trade-off between adaptability and determinism. We argue the trade-off is an artifact of when the foundation model is invoked. If the model is called only when the existing control structure fails, if what it produces is verified and retained, and if a learned policy stops calling it once stored structure suffices, then adaptability is paid for once, during a learning phase, and the deployed system is an ordinary deterministic BT. Approach SCBT assigns each mechanism to the job it is suited for: The LLM proposes structure: given a failed node and its context, it emits one minimal, local, mission-agnostic patch in a constrained grammar. Structure synthesis is discrete, symbolic, and rare. CMA-ES tunes parameters: each patch declares its uncertain numeric ports as tunables with bounds; these are optimized against simulated replays before admission. A contextual bandit selects: among stored patches that match the failure context and the option of a new LLM call, with the call's cost in the reward. A three-stage admission pipeline gates library entry: static check against the grammar and the vehicle's capability manifest; invariant monitors over randomized replays; and an empirical success margin over the tree as it currently stands. A deterministic BT executes: the vehicle controller is always a plain BT ticked in lockstep with the simulator. No neural component is in the tick path. Contributions The SCBT framework: failure interception, a mission-agnostic patch grammar with anchor-port references, a context-indexed fleet library, bandit-based selection with an explicit LLM-call arm, and replay-based admission with CMA-ES tuning (Sec.~ sec:framework ). An implementation on Project AirSim with a schema-constrained ADK agent pipeline, a lockstep tick loop at real time whose decision traces are an exact function of the observation sequence, and a failure-injection curriculum calibrated against the simulator's measured response (Sec.~ sec:impl ). An evaluation against hand-coded, regenerate-on-failure, and five ablated baselines over a frozen phase in which all learning is disabled, with an exact decision-determinism test, and an analysis of what the admission pipeline caught and what it wrongly rejected (Secs.~ sec:exp ,~ sec:results ). Related Work sec:related Classical Control Architectures FSMs require transitions from every state to handle global events, so transition count grows quadratically with state count~ colledanchise2018bt . BTs~ ogren2012uav,marzinotto2014unified standardize the node interface to a ternary status and decouple nodes; the survey by Iovino et al.~ iovino2022survey documents the gains in modularity and reactivity and the persistent limitation that BT structure is fixed at design time. Learned BTs via genetic programming~ colledanchise2019learning,iovino2021gp or learned leaf policies~ pereira2015framework learn from reward alone and are sample-hungry when the needed structural change is semantically obvious. Foundation Models for Control Synthesis Code as Policies~ liang2023cap prompts an LLM with a robot API to write programs; SayCan~ ahn2022saycan and Inner Monologue~ huang2022inner ground plans in affordances and feedback; VoxPoser~ huang2023voxposer composes LLM reasoning and VLM grounding into value maps; VLA models~ brohan2023rt2,kim2024openvla map pixels to actions. Closest to us are BTGenBot~ izzo2024btgenbot , which fine-tunes small LLMs to emit BehaviorTree.CPP XML and validates it syntactically and in simulation, and LLM-BT~ zhou2024llmbt . These regenerate structure on demand and do not retain, verify against an empirical margin, or learn when to stop calling the model. Surveys~ firoozi2024foundation,xu2024foundationmodels discuss the latency, cost, and hallucination risks that motivate our design. Combining LLMs with Learning Eureka~ ma2024eureka has an LLM write reward functions that RL optimizes; RL-GPT~ liu2024rlgpt lets an LLM decide what to code and what to learn; Voyager~ wang2023voyager keeps a growing library of LLM-written skills retrieved by embedding. SCBT shares the library with Voyager and the LLM/optimizer division of labor with Eureka, but the stored artifacts are BT subtrees, admission is gated by simulated invariants and an empirical margin, and the stated end state is a system with no model running. Multi-Robot Coordination and Verification Classical MRTA~ gerkey2004taxonomy,kuhn1955hungarian,gerkey2002sold,nunes2015tessi requires pre-defined tasks with comparable costs. LLM coordination~ mandi2024roco,chen2024scalable describes robots by textual capability profiles; we adopt that idea as a capability manifest that gates which leaves a patch may use and declares substitutions across vehicle classes. Prior verification of generated control checks syntax and simulated execution~ izzo2024btgenbot ; we add invariant monitors, a landing-reserve constraint, and a required margin over the unpatched tree. Problem Formulation sec:problem Behavior Trees A BT is a rooted tree whose internal nodes are control-flow nodes (Sequence, Fallback, Parallel, decorators) and whose leaves are actions and conditions~ colledanchise2018bt . It is ticked at a fixed rate; each node returns Success, Failure, or Running. We use py trees~ pytrees with an XML dialect that mirrors BehaviorTree.CPP: Sequence/Fallback with memory, Reactive variants that re-evaluate all children every tick, Parallel, Inverter, ForceSuccess/Failure, Retry, Repeat. Leaves declare typed ports; numeric ports may carry bounds, and bounded ports are tunable. We write for a vector of tunable port values. Vehicles and Capability Manifests Each vehicle has a class with a manifest : the leaf types the class may execute, with port signatures and one-line descriptions, plus substitutions (e.g.\ a camera-less class substitutes RequestScout for InspectRegion). Classes differ physically (frame mass, speed cap enforced by the leaves, battery drain). Missions and Success A mission plan is a base tree plus required and optional goals; goal leaves record completion on the blackboard. A mission succeeds if all required goals are reached and the vehicle lands. Mission value weights required goals 1 and optional goals 0.5. An abort to the hand-coded safe branch after the required goals are met is not a failure; an abort before them is. This definition matters: a recovery that merely returns to launch scores zero when a required goal is outstanding, which is what makes the battery curriculum (Sec.~ sec:curriculum ) a prioritization problem rather than a trivial one. Failure Events [Failure event] A failure event on a vehicle is where is the deepest leaf that returned Failure in the tick in which the mission-critical subtree failed, and with a textual context, the telemetry snapshot, the class, the last status changes in the enclosing subtree, and the XML of the enclosing subtree with marked. In the headless setting is generated from telemetry (failed node type, leaf feedback, altitude, speed, wind, battery, GPS and link status); on a rendering host it is a VLM description. The vehicle class is deliberately excluded from so that retrieval surfaces cross-class candidates. Objective Over a sequence of failure events the learning phase maximizes where is mission success after event , indicates an LLM call, (s) and ( battery) are the time and energy from the event to the end of the episode, and weight cost, time and energy. The deployment objective is that the crystallized tree matches learning-phase success with no LLM, optimizer, or bandit running. The SCBT Framework sec:framework Fig.~ fig:arch shows the components and the boundary between what is deployed and what only runs during learning. Failure Interception A MissionCritical decorator wraps the mission subtree. When its child returns Failure and patching is enabled, it returns Running for that tick and raises a flag; the runner pauses the simulator,

title: BiDex-100: A Comprehensive Benchmark for Bimanual Dexterous Manipulation Across 100+ Simulation Tasks
summary: Bimanual manipulation with dexterous hands has attracted growing attention in research on robotic action models. However, few studies have developed benchmarks specifically tailored for dexterous manipulation, leaving the dexterous manipulation capabilities of existing models insufficiently characterized. In this paper, we present BiDex-100, a simulation benchmark for bimanual dexterous manipulation that combines broad task coverage, multi-dimensional evaluation, and high-DoF hand embodiments. Concretely, the benchmark comprises 106 tasks organized along five capability axes: generalization, instruction following, limited demonstrations, long horizon, and memory. Each task is paired with an out-of-domain variant featuring controlled visual and spatial changes, allowing systematic assessment of robustness. In addition, the benchmark supports two embodiments and provides 8,080 success-validated teleoperated demonstrations, totaling 6.25 million frames. We evaluate seven recent Vision-Language-Action models under a unified protocol, establishing baselines for capability-specific performance, robustness, and data efficiency. The website is available at https://BiDex-100.github.io/BiDex-100/.
full_text: \\[ ] Overview of . The benchmark provides 106 declarative task specifications across five capability axes, 8,080 success-validated teleoperated demonstrations on two bimanual embodiments equipped with dexterous hands, and employs progress-based scoring under matched In-Domain and Out-of-Domain protocols. Five representative tasks, one per capability axis, each with a real demonstration and its language instruction, cover Memory, Long-Horizon, Instruction-Following, Limited-Demonstrations, and Generalization. ~ fig:overview Bimanual manipulation with dexterous hands has attracted growing attention in research on robotic action models. However, few studies have developed benchmarks specifically tailored for dexterous manipulation, leaving the dexterous manipulation capabilities of existing models insufficiently characterized. In this paper, we present BiDex-100, a simulation benchmark for bimanual dexterous manipulation that combines broad task coverage, multi-dimensional evaluation, and high-DoF hand embodiments. Concretely, the benchmark comprises 106 tasks organized along five capability axes: generalization, instruction following, limited demonstrations, long horizon, and memory. Each task is paired with an out-of-domain variant featuring controlled visual and spatial changes, allowing systematic assessment of robustness. In addition, the benchmark supports two embodiments and provides 8,080 success-validated teleoperated demonstrations, totaling 6.25 million frames. We evaluate seven recent Vision-Language-Action models under a unified protocol, establishing baselines for capability-specific performance, robustness, and data efficiency. The website is available at . INTRODUCTION sec:intro Bimanual dexterous manipulation, the coordinated control of two multi-fingered hands acting on a shared workspace, is widely regarded as a prerequisite for general-purpose household and industrial robots. The past two years have brought this capability within reach: VLA models~ brohan2023rt2,kim2024openvla,black2024pi0,intelligence2025pi05,bjorck2025gr00tn1 now absorb large-scale demonstrations and generalize across scenes, objects, and instructions. What has not kept pace is our ability to measure where such policies actually fail. As training corpora grow, average success on narrow pick-and-place suites saturates, and the discriminating power of a benchmark shifts away from task coverage toward capability edges: remembering scene state, sustaining long horizons, obeying instructions that change mid-episode, learning from few demonstrations, and degrading gracefully under visual and geometric shift. A 58-DoF bimanual dexterous system amplifies every one of these edges relative to the 7-DoF gripper platforms that dominate current evaluation. Its action space is high-dimensional and redundant, its success hinges on contact-rich finger coordination, and its failure modes are invisible to a binary success rate. Existing manipulation benchmarks leave this gap open in three distinct ways. First, the widely used suites, among them Meta-World~ yu2020meta , RLBench~ james2020rlbench , LIBERO~ liu2023libero , CALVIN~ mees2022calvin , RoboCasa~ nasiriany2024robocasa , and ManiSkill~ gu2023maniskill2 , are built around single arms terminated by parallel-jaw grippers, so the entire dexterity dimension is abstracted away. Second, dexterous-hand benchmarks such as Bi-DexHands~ chen2022bidexhands and DexMV~ qin2022dexmv target reinforcement learning from scratch on small task sets, without language grounding, large-scale demonstrations, or automated compositional scoring. Third, even recent large-scale efforts, such as RoboTwin~ mu2025robotwin,chen2025robotwin and RoboDojo~ chen2026robodojo , evaluate bimanual gripper platforms and report largely binary success, while the community has converged on the need for capability-targeted diagnosis of memory, long-horizon competence, and instruction fidelity that binary scores cannot provide. In short, the field lacks a benchmark that simultaneously offers bimanual dexterous hands, a capability-organized task suite with progress-based predicate scoring, matched In-Domain and Out-of-Domain evaluation, and a large teleoperated demonstration dataset released alongside the benchmark. To address this gap, we introduce BiDex-100, a MuJoCo benchmark of 106 bimanual dexterous manipulation tasks spanning five capability axes. BiDex-100 is built on a simple premise: as average task success improves, evaluation should reveal not only whether a policy succeeds, but also what it can do reliably and where it fails. Our contributions are: [leftmargin=*] A capability-based benchmark for bimanual dexterity. The 106 tasks measure Generalization, Instruction-Following, Limited Demonstrations, Long Horizon, and Memory. These axes expose distinct limitations of VLA policies. Results therefore form a capability profile rather than a single aggregate score. Matched In-Domain (ID) and Out-of-Domain (OOD) evaluation. Each task has a reproducible OOD counterpart with controlled changes to appearance, scene layout, distractors, object scale, and left-right configuration. This design makes in-domain performance and robustness directly comparable. A large-scale dataset and reference study. We provide 8,080 success-validated teleoperation episodes, covering 6.25M frames of data across the 106 released tasks. We also evaluate 7 recent VLA models under a unified protocol, establishing baselines for capability-specific performance, robustness, and data efficiency. RELATED WORK sec:related Manipulation benchmarks. The field's standard suites measure gripper-based manipulation. Meta-World~ yu2020meta and RLBench~ james2020rlbench offer 50--100 tasks for meta-RL and few-shot learning. LIBERO~ liu2023libero studies lifelong transfer across 130 tasks. CALVIN~ mees2022calvin targets language-conditioned long-horizon chains. RoboCasa~ nasiriany2024robocasa and BEHAVIOR-1K~ li2023behavior scale scene and activity diversity. ManiSkill2~ gu2023maniskill2 and VLABench~ zhang2025vlabench emphasize generalizable skills and language grounding. SimplerEnv~ li2024evaluating aligns simulation with real-world policy rankings. All of these terminate the arm in a parallel-jaw gripper and score success binarily. RoboTwin~ mu2025robotwin and RoboTwin~2.0~ chen2025robotwin move to bimanual grippers with generative digital twins and strong domain randomization, and RoboDojo~ chen2026robodojo organizes 60 gripper tasks along capability dimensions with a unified sim-and-real protocol, but neither exercises multi-fingered dexterity, and their scoring remains predominantly binary. DexJoCo~ wang2026dexjoco is a bimanual dexterous benchmark with teleoperated demonstrations and matched ID/OOD variants, but only 11 tasks, binary scoring. BiDex-100 extends the design to 106 capability-organized tasks with progress-based predicate scoring. BiDex-100 occupies the vacant corner of this design space (Table~ tab:benchmarks ): bimanual 22-DoF dexterous hands, five capability axes, progress-based predicate scoring, and matched ID/OOD evaluation. Dexterous manipulation and teleoperation. Dexterous-hand benchmarks historically trade breadth for fidelity: early Shadow-Hand suites~ rajeswaran2017learning cover a handful of canonical tasks; Bi-DexHands~ chen2022bidexhands provides RL environments for two Shadow hands without demonstrations or language; DexMV~ qin2022dexmv retargets human videos but offers no standardized compositional scoring. Demonstrations for such systems depend on teleoperation: DexPilot~ handa2020dexpilot and AnyTeleop~ qin2023anyteleop retarget visual hand tracking, TeleMoMa~ dass2024telemoma composes input modalities, Open-TeleVision~ cheng2024opentelevision streams immersive head-mounted video, and FACTR~ liu2025factr adds low-cost force-aware exoskeleton. BiDex-100 adopts the last two modalities and unifies them through a single optimization-based retargeting stack (Section~ sec:teleop ). Vision-language-action models. VLAs fine-tune web-scale vision-language backbones into action policies~ brohan2023rt2,kim2024openvla,octo2024 , with recent designs adding flow-matching or diffusion action experts for high-frequency dexterous control~ black2024pi0,intelligence2025pi05,bjorck2025gr00tn1 . Their published evaluations concentrate on gripper embodiments, and cross-model comparisons are complicated by per-paper protocols, action spaces, and data mixtures. BiDex-100 supplies the missing controlled substrate for this model class on dexterous bimanual tasks: a fixed 58-DoF joint-space interface, a shared demonstration corpus, and a stratified, automated scoring protocol, which we use to benchmark seven contemporary VLAs. THE BiDex-100 BENCHMARK sec:benchmark Design Principles sec:principles Three principles guide BiDex-100. (1) Dexterity is the object of study. Tasks require dexterous hands for skills beyond conventional grippers, such as hammering nails and watering. (2) Diagnose capabilities, not tasks. Tasks are organized by the capability they stress, namely visual and geometric generalization, instruction fidelity, data efficiency, horizon depth, and latent-state memory, rather than by scene or object type. A leaderboard position therefore decomposes into an interpretable capability profile. (3) Scores must be reproducible and comparable. Machine-checkable predicate conjunctions, deterministic seeded evaluation, progress-based subtask credit, and matched ID/OOD variants replace human raters and per-paper protocols. Embodiments and Interfaces sec:embodiments BiDex-100 supports two robot embodiments with the same dexterous hand design (Fig.~ fig:overview ). The dual Franka platform consists of two 7-DoF Franka Research 3 arms~ franka2023fr3 mounted on a shared base, each equipped with a 22-DoF Dexterous hand~ sharpa2024wave . It has a 58-DoF action space and executes 96 of the 106 task specifications. The remaining 10 Generalization tasks execute on the Astribot S1 humanoid~ astribot2024s1 , which shares the same hands on two 7-DoF arms. Every task is evaluated on its designated embodiment under the unified protocol; consequently, the Generalization column in Tables~ tab:results_id -- tab:results_ood aggregates 30 dual-Franka and 10 Astribot tasks. Observations include synchronized RGB-D images from head, left-wrist, and right-wrist cameras at resolution and 25\,Hz, together with proprioceptive states. The latter include arm and hand joint positions and velocities, as well as absolute end-effector poses. Actions are 58-dimensional joint targets, , executed by position-controlled actuators. End-effector control is also available and is converted to joint targets through inverse kinematics. Simulation runs in MuJoCo~ todorov2012mujoco at 500\,Hz, with control at 25\,Hz. The dexterous hands are central to BiDex-100. Fig.~ fig:replay visualizes the Memory task pour ice into cups by overlaying solid hand and object snapshots with time-gradient fingertip trajectories and markers that terminate at the pour instant. The right hand lifts and tilts the source cup above the recipient to transfer the ice ball while both hands coordinate within centimeters and reconfigure among open-palm transport, precision pinch, and power grasp. Fig.~ fig:dexterity (a) shows that the end effectors partition but substantially overlap a shared workspace, and Fig.~ fig:dexterity (b) shows substantial motion across every finger. Fig.~ fig:dexsynergy reveals that the bimanual posture follows a low-dimensional manifold: eight principal components capture 80 of postural variance, indicating a compact set of reusable grasp synergies. title: S3D-Mosaic: Subgradient-Guided Cross-Band Structure Transfer for Spectral Demosaicing
summary: Multispectral filter array (MSFA) imaging enables snapshot spectral acquisition, but its per-band sparse sampling causes severe spatial aliasing. Although missing spatial structures can be inferred across bands, wavelength-dependent contrast variations make direct cross-band transfer unreliable. Existing model-based methods lack explicit magnitude-invariant mechanisms, and learning-based methods require layout-specific training or per-image tuning, limiting generalization. To address these issues, we propose S3D-Mosaic, a model-based spectral demosaicing method built upon a subgradient-guided cross-band structure transfer framework. We first establish a subgradient-guided regularization framework with a generalized cosine-similarity interpretation, providing a convex mechanism for magnitude-invariant information transfer. Then we design a compact Directional Sparse Equivariant Difference Convolution (DSE-DConv) for band-level extraction of orientation-selective, high-frequency structure features at low computational cost. Instantiating the framework with DSE-DConv on spectrally adjacent bands yields a cross-band self-structure similarity regularizer for spectral demosaicing, which we optimize via a dual-scan ADMM algorithm that decouples the bidirectional dependency while propagating magnitude-robust structural information across bands. With DSE-DConv's two parameters trained once via self-supervision, S3D-Mosaic outperforms state-of-the-art unsupervised methods on CAVE and NTIRE 2022, and generalizes robustly to varying MSFA layouts, pan-mosaic fusion, and real-world UAV data with fixed reconstruction hyperparameters. The source code is available at \url{https://github.com/bestwishes43/S3D-Mosaic}.
full_text: S3D-Mosaic: Subgradient-Guided Cross-Band Structure Transfer for Spectral Demosaicing Weiqiang~Zhao , Xian~Li ,~ Yuzhe~Gui , Tianzhu~Liu ,~ Yanfeng~Gu ,~ Zhao : S3D-Mosaic Spectral Demosaicing Multispectral filter array (MSFA) imaging enables snapshot spectral acquisition, but its per-band sparse sampling causes severe spatial aliasing. Although missing spatial structures can be inferred across bands, wavelength-dependent contrast variations make direct cross-band transfer unreliable. Existing model-based methods lack explicit magnitude-invariant mechanisms, and learning-based methods require layout-specific training or per-image tuning, limiting generalization. To address these issues, we propose S3D-Mosaic, a model-based spectral demosaicing method built upon a subgradient-guided cross-band structure transfer framework. We first establish a subgradient-guided regularization framework with a generalized cosine-similarity interpretation, providing a convex mechanism for magnitude-invariant information transfer. Then we design a compact Directional Sparse Equivariant Difference Convolution (DSE-DConv) for band-level extraction of orientation-selective, high-frequency structure features at low computational cost. Instantiating the framework with DSE-DConv on spectrally adjacent bands yields a cross-band self-structure similarity regularizer for spectral demosaicing, which we optimize via a dual-scan ADMM algorithm that decouples the bidirectional dependency while propagating magnitude-robust structural information across bands. With DSE-DConv's two parameters trained once via self-supervision, S3D-Mosaic outperforms state-of-the-art unsupervised methods on CAVE and NTIRE 2022, and generalizes robustly to varying MSFA layouts, pan-mosaic fusion, and real-world UAV data with fixed reconstruction hyperparameters. The source code is available at . Spectral demosaicing, subgradient guidance, self-similarity, structural feature extraction. Introduction napshot spectral imaging provides an effective way to capture three-dimensional spatio-spectral information in a single exposure. Among various hardware realizations, multispectral filter array (MSFA) cameras overlay a spatially repeating spectral filter on a conventional sensor, achieving a compact, cost-effective form factor suited to applications including material identification~ lin_underdetermined_2026 , biophysical parameter retrieval~ cao_improved_2025 , and 3D reconstruction~ wang_robust_2023, wang_adaptive_2024 . However, this design trades spatial resolution for spectral diversity: each band is observed only at a sparse set of positions, causing high-frequency spatial components to alias into lower frequencies. These artifacts are hard to remove in scenes with sharp boundaries or fine textures, because the lost high-frequency information cannot be uniquely recovered from a single band. A key observation is that spatial discontinuities, such as object boundaries, shadows, and surface geometry, are shared across most spectral bands, and the MSFA's sampling means details lost in one band are often preserved in others. This suggests that missing high-frequency structures can be inferred across bands. Yet cross-band transfer is not straightforward: corresponding edges often exhibit markedly different contrast across wavelengths, so directly matching intensities or gradients may distort spectral information. Existing model-based methods exploit global spectral correlations via sparsity~ elad_image_2006 or low-rankness~ candes_exact_2009,qin_lowrank_2022 , or encourage cross-band similarity by minimizing intensity/gradient differences~ mizutani_multispectral_2014 . While interpretable, they may transfer spectral contrast rather than spatial structure, and their priors often provide insufficient constraints for heavily aliased high-frequency content. Learning-based methods, including supervised networks~ feng_mosaic_2021,wu_mosaic_2025 and unsupervised approaches~ feng_unsupervised_2024,chen_unsupervised_2025 , learn expressive models from data. However, their performance can depend on the training data distribution, the MSFA layout used during training, or per-image hyperparameter tuning~ chen_unsupervised_2025 . This is especially problematic for spectral demosaicing, given the diversity of MSFA layouts and the cost of paired training data. To this end, we propose S3D-Mosaic, a model-based method that realizes magnitude-robust cross-band structure transfer through subgradient guidance. Instead of matching magnitudes, it aligns feature directions through the subgradient of a norm-based regularizer, giving a convex, magnitude-invariant mechanism with a generalized cosine-similarity interpretation. To instantiate the framework, we further design Directional Sparse Equivariant Difference Convolution (DSE-DConv), a compact two-parameter linear operator that extracts orientation-selective high-frequency structural features with transformation consistency. Using DSE-DConv, we construct a cross-band self-structure similarity prior between adjacent spectral bands and solve the resulting problem through a dual-scan ADMM algorithm. Fig.~ fig:illustration overviews the pipeline. The main contributions are summarized as follows: We establish a subgradient-guided feature-direction transfer framework with a generalized cosine-similarity interpretation, which provides a principled mechanism for magnitude-invariant information transfer. We design DSE-DConv, a two-parameter \(D_4\)-equivariant zero-sum operator, to extract transformation-consistent directional high-frequency structures for demosaicing. We instantiate the framework with DSE-DConv as a cross-band self-structure similarity prior and develop a dual-scan ADMM solver to decouple bidirectional spectral dependencies. The resulting method generalizes to diverse MSFA layouts and real captures with fixed hyperparameters. The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Section~ sec:related reviews related work; Section~ sec:model formulates the problem; Sections~ sec:theory -- sec:algorithm present the proposed framework, DSE-DConv operator, and optimization algorithm; Section~ sec:experiments reports experiments; and Section~ sec:conclusion concludes the paper. Related Work sec:related The proposed S3D-Mosaic is related to spectral demosaicing, cross-band self-similarity priors, and low-level structural feature extraction. We review these three aspects below. Spectral demosaicing Existing methods can be broadly divided into model-based and learning-based approaches. model-based methods solve the reconstruction problem with explicit image priors. Early methods relied on spatial coherence in a single band, including bilinear interpolation~ brauers_color_2006 , edge-sensing interpolation~ miao_binary_2006 , and diffraction-limited interpolation~ yasuma_generalized_2010 . Although efficient, local interpolation is often insufficient for removing structured aliasing caused by severe high-frequency undersampling. Later methods, such as SD~ brauers_color_2006 and ItSD~ mizutani_multispectral_2014 , exploit spectral correlation among bands, while PPID~ mihoubi_multispectral_2015,mihoubi_multispectral_2017 constructs a pseudo-panchromatic image to provide stronger structural guidance. Later studies formulated spectral demosaicing as a regularized inverse problem using dictionary sparsity~ degraux_generalized_2015 , spectral low-rankness~ tsagkatakis_graph_2019,bian_generalized_2021 , spatial smoothness, or hybrid priors~ zhuang_hydemosaicing_2022,abbas_locallyrankonebased_2024 . Recently, Li et al.~ li_efficient_2025 proposed a convex formulation that combines spectral low-rankness and spatial smoothness and shows robustness to different MSFA layouts. Although interpretable and requiring little or no training data, they do not explicitly address the key difficulty of transferring aliasing-corrupted structures across bands when corresponding edges have wavelength-dependent magnitudes or contrasts. Learning-based methods learn either the reconstruction mapping or the image prior from data. Supervised networks, including attention-based modules~ feng_mosaic_2021 , spatial-frequency representation networks~ wu_mosaic_2025,wu_joint_2025,xu_waveformer_2025 , and multi-stage restoration networks~ xiong_multistage_2025 , rely on paired data for training. Unsupervised methods reduce the data dependence; USD~ feng_unsupervised_2024 leverages an equivariant imaging prior for unsupervised reconstruction network training, while UnNull~ chen_unsupervised_2025 performs reconstruction via Deep Image Prior (DIP)~ lempitsky_deep_2018 . Despite their strong performance, these methods may be sensitive to training distributions, MSFA layouts, or per-scene optimization settings. In contrast, S3D-Mosaic maintains an explicit reconstruction model and uses learning only to calibrate a compact structural feature operator. Cross-Band Self-Similarity Priors Self-similarity is a fundamental image prior. Classical non-local methods, such as NL-means~ buades_nonlocal_2005 and BM3D~ dabov_image_2007 , exploit repeated patches within an image, while BM4D~ maggioni_nonlocal_2013 and non-local low-rank models~ chang_hyperlaplacian_2017,he_nonlocal_2022 extend this idea to volumetric or spectral data. However, these methods usually measure similarity at the intensity or patch level and do not explicitly separate structural direction from feature magnitude. For spectral images, cross-band consistency provides another important form of self-similarity. Spectral-spatial TV variants penalize local spatial-spectral variations~ yuan_hyperspectral_2012,chen_hyperspectral_2023,zhao_spatialspectral_2026 , while low-rank priors encourage global spectral coherence~ tsagkatakis_graph_2019,bian_generalized_2021,he_nonlocal_2022 . Explicit structural guidance can also be constructed from the spectral data itself, such as pseudo-panchromatic images~ mihoubi_multispectral_2015,mihoubi_multispectral_2017 or estimated green channels~ guo_joint_2021,kong_image_2025 . These strategies demonstrate the value of cross-band guidance, but the guidance is commonly imposed through intensity or gradient consistency, making it sensitive to wavelength-dependent contrast variations. Recent deep models also inject self-similarity implicitly or explicitly. Non-local networks~ wang_nonlocal_2018,liu_nonlocal_2018 , Vision Transformers~ dosovitskiy_image_2021 , and state-space models~ liu_vmamba_2024 can learn long-range or cross-channel dependencies from data, while Wu et al.~ wu_mosaic_2025 exploit self-similarity through spatial-spectral attention and PPI guidance, and UnNull~ chen_unsupervised_2025 combines an online DIP with spectral-smoothness regularization. However, these deep-learning methods typically learn the cross-band relationship implicitly from training data, without enforcing an explicit structural alignment mechanism. In contrast, S3D-Mosaic formulates cross-band self-similarity using a convex subgradient-guided transfer mechanism: it transfers the feature direction via a dual subgradient, providing a principled way to propagate structural information robust to intensity variations across bands. Low-Level Structure Extraction Classical filters such as Gabor, log-Gabor, and steerable filters explicitly encode oriented, localized, and band-pass responses. The relevance of such responses to efficient visual representation is supported by sparse-coding studies of natural images~ olshausen_emergence_1996 , but these filters often require large filter banks and careful parameter selection. Learnable convolutions have been developed to incorporate useful inductive biases into neural operators. Difference-based convolutions, including Local Binary Patterns~ liu_extended_2012,liu_median_2016 , Central Difference Convolution~ yu_searching_2020,yu_nasfas_2021 , and Pixel Difference Convolution~ su_lightweight_2023 , enhance high-frequency and edge-sensi

title: AQUAACT: A Joystick-Level Underwater Teleoperation Dataset and Closed-Loop Benchmark
summary: Underwater robots support a growing range of work, from inspecting offshore structures and pipelines to surveying reefs and accompanying divers. Most of these tasks, however, are still flown by hand by a pilot, which raises the question of whether they can be carried out autonomously instead. On land, vision-language-action (VLA) models already let robots carry out tasks autonomously from language instructions, which makes them a natural candidate for taking the pilot's place. Underwater, however, there is little data to train such models. We take inspiration from how these tasks are flown today: the pilot watches the camera image and steers with a joystick, whose commands the flight controller turns into motion. We therefore record the pilots and introduce AQUAACT, to our knowledge the first publicly available language-annotated underwater dataset pairing camera images with human joystick commands. It comprises 1.9 hours of real-world and 17.9 hours of simulated demonstrations, both flown by human pilots, together with the vehicle's inertial measurements. Experiments with AQUAACT show that its simulated demonstrations transfer to real data and greatly reduce the real demonstrations a policy needs. A closed-loop benchmark of seven policies in simulation, from imitation-learning baselines to VLA models, each trained with its default recipe, shows that these tasks remain far from solved: no policy completes more than a fifth of the episodes. Pretraining on land data gives large VLA models no advantage over small policies trained from scratch, a gap that land-trained models have yet to close underwater.

Pretraining on land data gives large VLA models no advantage over small policies trained from scratch, a gap that land-trained models have yet to close underwater. Introduction sec:intro Underwater inspection, monitoring, and surveying are essential for maintaining marine infrastructure and studying ocean environments: subsea pipelines, offshore wind foundations, and aquaculture facilities require regular inspections, while reef monitoring, shipwreck exploration, and diver assistance demand operations in diverse and often challenging environments~ auv_inspection_review,offshore_inspection_review,netpen_visual_servo,oystersim,dream_uwmonitor,caddy . These environments often exceed the depth, bottom time, and risk that human divers can safely accept~ osha_diving , so underwater robots increasingly take over this work~ petillot2019 . However, most of these operations still rely on remotely operated vehicles (ROVs) flown by human pilots through onboard camera feedback, so pilot workload limits the scale and duration of these missions~ offshore_inspection_review,sharc,subsea_hmi_review . Reducing this dependence on human pilots requires autonomous systems that interpret underwater scenes, follow high-level instructions, and act accordingly. Conventional underwater autonomy builds a perception--planning--control pipeline for each task and sensor setup~ hover2012hull,ridao_iauv,netpen_visual_servo , which must be adapted for every new environment or task~ uw_full_autonomy_review . Vision-language-action (VLA) models offer an alternative: they learn to predict robot actions from visual observations and language instructions~ rt2,openvla,octo,pi0,pi05,gr00t,smolvla and, trained on large demonstration datasets such as Open X-Embodiment~ oxe and BridgeData V2~ bridgev2 , have shown that skills transfer across tasks and robots~ octo,robot_vla_survey . Despite these advances, underwater robotics lacks comparable demonstration data for training general-purpose policies. Collecting real underwater demonstrations requires deploying a vehicle and a skilled pilot, making large-scale data acquisition costly and difficult. For an underwater vehicle, the natural action for such data is the pilot's joystick command. It is what the pilot actually issues in response to the onboard camera view. It also leaves stabilization to the vehicle's flight controller, which holds attitude and depth in a control loop far faster than a policy can run. The policy then only decides where the vehicle should go, much as VLA models on land output end-effector targets and leave joint control to the robot's own controllers. Existing underwater learning datasets provide only parts of this. The closest vehicle-level effort relies entirely on simulation, with demonstrations generated by scripted experts and actions given as thruster commands~ usim_u0 . Real-world imitation learning with recorded operator commands has primarily focused on manipulation tasks in controlled pools or tanks~ uw_aquabot,uw_biaqua,uw_uloha , while underwater navigation datasets have relied on retrospectively annotated actions rather than the actual commands issued by human pilots~ uw_nav2goal,uw_uivnav . Consequently, to our knowledge, no publicly available language-annotated dataset provides synchronized onboard observations and pilot-issued joystick commands for learning real-world underwater vehicle action. We therefore collect such data by recording the pilots themselves, on the real vehicle and in simulation. Recording the onboard camera view together with the pilot's joystick commands yields paired observations and actions directly, without manual action labeling, and we annotate each task with a language instruction that states its goal, such as ``Scan the deck from left to right'' or ``Follow the pipeline''. Because the control chain, from the joystick through the ground-control software to the flight-controller firmware, can be reproduced in simulation, pilots can record further demonstrations there, at sites a real vehicle reaches only rarely. Building on this approach, we introduce , comprising 2.0 hours of real-world underwater demonstrations (Fig.~ fig:teaser ) and 17.9 hours of simulated demonstrations (Fig.~ fig:system ), with the simulator calibrated against real-world runs. This combination allows us to investigate whether pretraining on underwater demonstrations collected from our simulation pipeline improves learning from limited real-world data. We further evaluate how existing general-purpose robot policies perform when learning to control underwater vehicles through joystick commands: we train seven policies, from imitation-learning baselines to VLA models, on the simulated part with their default recipes and run each for 50 closed-loop episodes in the same simulation pipeline, where a program scores the success and completion of every episode from the ground-truth state and a human reviewer checks each score. Our contributions are: Underwater Dataset: We introduce , a language-annotated dataset of real and simulated ROV demonstrations with synchronized visual, inertial, and joystick data (Sec.~ sec:dataset ). Simulation Data Collection: We develop a real-world-calibrated, firmware-in-the-loop simulation pipeline for collecting human demonstrations through the same control chain as the real ROV (Sec.~ sec:sim , sec:fidelity ). Sim-to-Real Evaluation: We show that pretraining using data from our simulation pipeline reduces real-world data requirements for policy learning (Sec.~ sec:exp_real ). Policy Benchmark: We benchmark seven policies, from imitation-learning baselines to VLA models, in closed-loop simulation and analyze where they fail, revealing a clear gap in transferring land-trained models underwater (Sec.~ sec:exp_sim ). Related Work sec:related Classical Underwater Autonomy Autonomous underwater inspection has traditionally been built as a modular perception--planning--control pipeline engineered around one task, such as ship-hull inspection~ hover2012hull , subsea cable tracking~ xiang2016cable , net-pen inspection~ netpen_visual_servo and intervention~ ridao_iauv . Learning has entered these stacks mainly as better components, such as detectors or controllers~ uw_ai_review . These systems are reliable within their design envelope, but each new task or site calls for new modules and new tuning~ uw_full_autonomy_review . Learning from Demonstrations and VLA Models Learning from demonstrations removes the need to engineer a pipeline for each task: a policy maps observations to actions directly, and a new task calls for new data rather than new modules. Imitation-learning policies such as action-chunking transformers (ACT)~ act and diffusion policies~ diffusionpolicy map images and proprioception to short action sequences and learn fine-grained skills from a modest number of demonstrations, but each is typically trained for a narrow task family. Generality has come from data: large corpora such as BridgeData~V2~ bridgev2 and Open X-Embodiment~ oxe pool demonstrations across tasks, scenes and robots, and VLA models build on them by attaching an action output to a pretrained vision-language backbone, so that one model follows language instructions across tasks. RT-2~ rt2 emits actions as tokens, OpenVLA~ openvla and Octo~ octo are open, fine-tunable generalist policies, ~ pi0 and ~ pi05 add a flow-matching action expert, GR00T~N1~ gr00t targets humanoids, SmolVLA~ smolvla shows that a compact model can be competitive, and MemoryVLA~ memoryvla adds a memory of past observations. Vision-language navigation models~ navid,uninavid,omninav also follow instructions through space, but they output waypoints or motion primitives for a lower layer to execute rather than the continuous commands a pilot issues. All of these models, however, are trained on terrestrial data; none of their corpora contains underwater demonstrations or uses an operator's joystick as the action space. Underwater Robot Learning and Simulation Underwater, learning from demonstrations is still small in scale. AquaBot~ uw_aquabot records a pilot's gamepad commands with video for about a thousand manipulation demonstrations in a pool, without language, and imitation learning for underwater arms has likewise been shown in pools and tanks~ uw_biaqua,uw_uloha , including a VLA evaluated on real underwater manipulation~ uw_uloha . For navigation, real-world learning has used camera footage whose actions were labeled afterwards~ uw_nav2goal,uw_uivnav , and Khanmeh et~al.~ uw_rovtether_scidata released BlueROV2 pilot inputs without camera images. Simulation is the standard way to scale beyond this. MarineGym~ marinegym adds hydrodynamics to GPU physics for reinforcement learning, and USIM~ usim_u0 , the closest vehicle-level effort toward underwater VLA, generates 20 navigation and manipulation tasks in simulation with hand-crafted experts that use ground-truth state and fine-tunes U0 from GR00T~N1.5 to map images, language and sensor readings to per-thruster commands and arm joint angles, without real-world deployment. Thus real-world work records a human operator's commands only for manipulation in pools or tanks; no existing dataset pairs open-water observations with pilot commands for vehicle-level tasks, in reality or in simulation. Filling this gap in simulation, where demonstrations are cheap, adds a further requirement: simulated demonstrations help if the simulated vehicle moves like the real one, which depends on the hydrodynamic model~ fossen and on the controller in the loop, and looks like it, which depends on how water attenuates and scatters light~ akkaynak2018,seathru . Taken together, these lines of work point to four needs that guide our collection pipeline and dataset: (i) real underwater observations paired with the joystick commands a human pilot actually sent; (ii) simulated demonstrations recorded through the same control chain, from the pilot's joystick through the ground-control software to the flight-controller firmware; (iii) a simulator whose dynamics and appearance are calibrated against the real vehicle; and (iv) an evaluation of how current policies, developed for other action spaces, learn from the pilot's commands.
