title: Vector-Quantized World Model: Latent Feedback Motion Planning for Robot Manipulation
summary: Visual world models have shown strong potential for robot planning, yet long-horizon manipulation remains challenging due to compounding prediction errors, large search complexity, and latent plans that the low-level controller cannot reliably reach. In this work, we introduce Vector-Quantized World Model (VQ-WM), a latent feedback motion planning framework that integrates discrete long-horizon search with continuous visual feedback control: a discrete latent predictor models transitions between vector-quantized latent states, allowing the planner to look far ahead and find a shortest path to the goal through discrete search and a continuous learned controller sequentially reaches the planned states through visual feedback, correcting deviations to mitigate compounding errors. Whereas most vector quantization uses Euclidean distance, we use a novel estimator of the first-passage-time as a quasi-metric, which aligns the planning abstraction with the controller's capabilities. We evaluate on the physical robot manipulation of the Tower of Hanoi puzzle: whereas existing state-of-the-art foundation models (VLAs, WAMs) only succeed when the solution trace in their training dataset, our method achieves 100\% success rate with only short-play data, demonstrate its ability to compose long-horizon solutions beyond the short demonstrated trajectories and execute them reliably. Our solution also outperforms strongest world-models by 13.3--85.3 percentage points on simulation benchmarks spanning manipulation and locomotion, demonstrating consistent progress and new capabilities.

In this work, we introduce Vector-Quantized World Model (VQ-WM), a latent feedback motion planning framework that integrates discrete long-horizon search with continuous visual feedback control: a discrete latent predictor models transitions between vector-quantized latent states, allowing the planner to look far ahead and find a shortest path to the goal through discrete search and a continuous learned controller sequentially reaches the planned states through visual feedback, correcting deviations to mitigate compounding errors. Our solution also outperforms strongest world-models by 13.3--85.3 percentage points on simulation benchmarks spanning manipulation and locomotion, demonstrating consistent progress and new capabilities. Introduction Visual world models combine latent representations with predictive dynamics, enabling planners to evaluate action sequences directly from visual inputs and select those that lead toward a desired long-term outcome before acting in the environment. Recent advances in model architectures and training methods allow these models to learn from reward-free offline trajectories and perform zero-shot planning from visual observations~ dino-wm,lewm . However, long-horizon manipulation tasks requiring multi-stage decision making and precise sequential execution remain challenging. Existing world-model planners typically optimize action sequences through autoregressive rollouts in continuous latent space. As the planning horizon grows, prediction errors can accumulate across rollout steps, while longer action sequences become harder to optimize. These limitations constrain the effective planning horizon and can cause failure even when the dynamics model is accurate over short horizons. Recent work has improved long-horizon world-model planning by addressing these limitations. Hierarchical approaches such as H-JEPA learn multiple levels of latent abstraction to support coarse-to-fine planning~ hjepa . Discrete latent representations have also been explored for hierarchical planning and control~ director,thick , while Hi-LeWM investigates vector-quantized macro-actions for high-level prediction and planning~ hilewm . Hydra~ hydra uses vector-quantized multimodal intents for sampling-based navigation planning. Other approaches improve the geometry of the latent planning space by encouraging locally straighter latent trajectories~ temporal . Despite these advances, plans formed in latent space may still be difficult to execute reliably. Replanning can correct deviations, but does not by itself ensure that proposed targets are compatible with the controller's capabilities. The planning abstraction should reflect which states the controller can reliably reach and stabilize, a principle central to classical feedback motion planning~ sequential_composition,funnels . The LQR-Trees framework makes this connection explicit by associating each trajectory with a feedback controller and a region of attraction, characterizing the states from which the controller can recover deviations and steer the system toward the goal~ lqrtrees . Motivated by these limitations and the principle of coupling planning and control, we propose Vector-Quantized World Model (VQ-WM), a latent feedback motion planning framework for long-horizon robotic manipulation. As illustrated in Fig.~ fig:motivation , VQ-WM uses vector quantization to construct a discrete planning space whose vector-quantized states serve as targets for visual feedback control. The planner runs discrete search on the resulting graph to find a path to the goal, and the controller runs tracking control between consecutive vector-quantized states on the path. The central design choice is to define vector quantization through the controller’s ability to reach these targets, aligning the planning abstraction with the controller’s capabilities. In particular, we use the first-passage time, which is the number of controller calls until a trajectory driven by the controller first enters a neighborhood of its target. We estimate this quantity through closed-loop controller rollouts in a latent world model learned from offline data, and use it to construct the state codebook and assign continuous latent states to vector-quantized states. Our main contributions are: We introduce VQ-WM, a latent feedback motion planning framework that uses vector quantization to integrate discrete long-horizon search with continuous visual feedback control. We propose first-passage time as a measure of controller reachability for state vector quantization and estimate it through closed-loop controller rollouts in a learned latent world model. The first-passage time from one state to another is the number of controller calls until the closed-loop trajectory first reaches it. This aligns the planning abstraction with the controller’s capabilities and supports effective planning with compact state codebooks. We validate VQ-WM in hardware and simulation. Learning from short play data without full-task demonstrations, it solves the physical Tower of Hanoi puzzle with 100 task progress, outperforming the competitive industrial baselines by at least 95 percentage points. In simulation, it surpasses the strongest world-model planner, H-JEPA, by 13.3--34.6 percentage points on challenging long-horizon manipulation tasks, and adding proprioceptive inputs to the controller raises Walker success from 22.0 to 97.3 . Related Work World Models for Visual Planning World models learn predictive dynamics from observations to support action selection. Early approaches combine visual representations with latent dynamics for control~ e2c,planet , or predict future images for goal-directed manipulation~ visualforesight . Universal Planning Networks jointly learn representations and differentiable action planning~ upn , while Dreamer learns behavior through latent imagination~ dreamer and TD-MPC methods combine short-horizon latent planning with value estimation~ tdmpc,tdmpc2 . More recent methods support image-goal planning from pretrained visual features or reward-free offline trajectories~ dino-wm,lewm,pldm,vjepa2 . Planning efficiency is improved through alternative rollout mechanisms~ fast-lewm . However, continuous action-sequence planning becomes increasingly challenging over long horizons as search complexity grows rapidly and prediction errors can accumulate during autoregressive rollouts. VQ-WM instead performs discrete search over vector-quantized states without optimizing the full sequence of low-level actions. Abstractions for Long-Horizon Planning Temporal hierarchies decompose extended tasks into shorter planning problems ~ director . HWM learns world models at multiple temporal scales and demonstrates hierarchical planning for real-world pick-and-place from a single goal image ~ hwm . H-JEPA combines multiple prediction horizons with latent spaces at different abstraction levels~ hjepa . However, predicted subgoals can still be difficult for the execution mechanism to realize~ mindthegap . Vector quantization provides a compact state space for efficient discrete search, but the resulting state assignments must also reflect controller reachability. Graph-based methods incorporate reachability into planning through learned goal-conditioned control. SoRB searches over replay-buffer states using distances learned through goal-conditioned reinforcement learning~ sorb , while L3P learns latent landmarks and graph edges from reachability estimates distilled from value functions~ l3p . VQ-WM vector-quantizes states based on first-passage times estimated through closed-loop controller rollouts in a learned world model, then learns vector-quantized transitions from offline trajectories for discrete search. This couples the planning abstraction to the controller’s ability to reach the assigned targets. Feedback Motion Planning and Goal-Conditioned Control Feedback motion planning accounts for feedback control during planning to avoid trajectories that are difficult or costly to stabilize~ lqrtrees . Classical approaches compose local controllers so that each brings the system into a region where the next can succeed, using domains of attraction or trajectory funnels to characterize these regions~ sequential_composition,lqrtrees,funnels . Goal-conditioned methods learn reusable behaviors from play~ play_lmp or generate goal-directed action sequences through inverse dynamics models~ glamor . Composing such behaviors into long-horizon plans requires accounting for the states from which each target can be reached. VQ-WM applies this composition principle to a learned goal-conditioned controller in visual latent space. Instead of formally verifying funnels, it estimates controller reachability using first-passage times from closed-loop rollouts in a learned world model. These estimates guide the composition of local behaviors into long-horizon plans, which the controller executes using continuous visual feedback. We demonstrate reliable long-horizon manipulation on real hardware using this latent feedback motion planning framework. Problem Definition and Background sec:problem Our work follows a vision-based control framework, which models the environment as a controlled Markov process , where is the observation space and is the physical action space. At each time step , the robot receives an observation and applies an action . The transition distribution describes how the robot’s observation changes in response to its action. Given a pre-collected, reward-free offline dataset of observation–action trajectories with respective episode lengths , our goal at test time is to steer the system from an initial observation to a state specified by a goal image . title: HumanSkill-4D: Training-Free Language Querying of Animatable Gaussian Avatars in Space and Time
comment: 29 pages, 14 figures, 16 tables. Project page: https://jjunsss.github.io/HumanSkill-4D/
summary: We introduce avatar referring segmentation, which selects regions of animatable Gaussian avatars from language queries. A query can also specify a pose or motion to select matching intervals. This lets users interact with avatars for local editing and motion inspection. However, making these selections with existing language Gaussian splatting methods poses two challenges: adjacent parts and garments are hard to separate and may be referred to indirectly (region ambiguity), while fine-grained motions can look alike in RGB (motion ambiguity). We address these challenges with HumanSkill-4D, a training-free framework that shares a multimodal large language model (MLLM) and geometric operators across avatars. For each avatar, a semantic memory links body-part and garment categories to persistent Gaussian regions and appearance descriptions. The MLLM uses category names and descriptions to select categories by appearance, relation, or function. To find matching intervals, it composes operators into programs that check query conditions on driving joint trajectories stored in a motion memory. These category choices and operator outputs make selections traceable, while composing or adding operators supports new motion conditions. To evaluate this task, we introduce three human-annotated benchmarks and show that HumanSkill-4D outperforms the baselines in part segmentation and 3D and 4D referring segmentation, with compact memories and only minutes of setup per avatar.

A query can also specify a pose or motion to select matching intervals. This lets users interact with avatars for local editing and motion inspection. However, making these selections with existing language Gaussian splatting methods poses two challenges: adjacent parts and garments are hard to separate and may be referred to indirectly (region ambiguity), while fine-grained motions can look alike in RGB (motion ambiguity). For each avatar, a semantic memory links body-part and garment categories to persistent Gaussian regions and appearance descriptions. The MLLM uses category names and descriptions to select categories by appearance, relation, or function. To find matching intervals, it composes operators into programs that check query conditions on driving joint trajectories stored in a motion memory. These category choices and operator outputs make selections traceable, while composing or adding operators supports new motion conditions. To evaluate this task, we introduce three human-annotated benchmarks and show that outperforms the baselines in part segmentation and 3D and 4D referring segmentation, with compact memories and only minutes of setup per avatar. Introduction sec:intro Gaussian avatars reconstruct a person's geometry and appearance and animate the result using a driving pose sequence~ qian2024gsavatar,kocabas2024hugs . In applications such as AR/VR and sports~ hu2024gauhuman,jiang2025dnfavatar , users may need to edit an avatar's appearance or inspect its motion. Clothing transfer and appearance editing~ lin2024layga,ho2023locallyeditable , for example, require selecting the body part or garment to modify ( Where ). Inspecting that region during a particular pose or motion also requires finding the intervals in which that pose or motion occurs ( When ). A language query can describe both, but the avatar has no part or garment labels on its Gaussians and no motion labels on its frames. We therefore introduce avatar referring segmentation: a 3D query selects the described region (Fig.~ fig:queries (a)), while a 4D query also selects the intervals that match the specified pose or motion (Fig.~ fig:queries (b)). In reconstructed scenes, language Gaussian splatting already selects regions and relevant time intervals. In 3D, these methods attach image-language features to Gaussians and select regions whose features match a query~ qiu2024featuresplatting . These features are learned per scene as a language field in LangSplat~ qin2024langsplat or registered directly in Dr.~Splat~ kim2025drsplat , whereas ReferSplat~ he2025refersplat learns per-scene referring features from annotated expressions. To also determine when a query is relevant, 4-LEGS~ fiebelman2025_4legs grounds video-text features in dynamic Gaussians, while 4D LangSplat~ li2025_4dlangsplat learns a temporal language field from captions generated by a multimodal large language model (MLLM). For humans, OpenHuman3D~ suzuki2025openvocab3dhuman segments body parts and garments with a CLIP image encoder fine-tuned on human parsing data, and OpenHuman4D~ suzuki2025openhuman4d tracks part masks over time. Despite these advances, enabling language querying on Gaussian avatars presents two challenges. The first is region ambiguity. Human parts and garments lie close together and often overlap. As the pose or viewpoint changes, different boundaries become visible. Feature-matching methods~ qin2024langsplat rely on class-agnostic SAM masks~ kirillov2023sam , which do not necessarily follow these boundaries, and on generic CLIP~ radford2021clip features, which poorly distinguish body parts and garments~ suzuki2025openvocab3dhuman . Replacing the SAM masks with human-parser masks improves the overall accuracy of LangSplat and Dr.~Splat, but leaves their CLIP-based matching unchanged. Queries may also refer to a part or garment indirectly, through its relation to another region or its function, and CLIP-based matching remains unreliable for such references in our evaluation (Tab.~ tab:static3d ). The second is motion ambiguity. Even after the target region is identified, locating the intervals of a fine-grained pose or motion remains difficult (e.g., ``Select the upper clothing while both upper arms lift outward until they are parallel to the ground'' in Fig.~ fig:queries (b)). Mask tracking~ suzuki2025openhuman4d keeps the clothing selected over time but does not determine when the arms meet this condition. RGB-based methods can localize intervals~ fiebelman2025_4legs,li2025_4dlangsplat , but different motions can look alike in RGB frames while differing in their dynamics~ yang2026movie , and even video MLLMs struggle with fine-grained motion understanding~ hong2025motionbench . Gaussian avatars, however, already provide structure suited to both challenges. Each Gaussian is defined in a canonical space and deformed to every pose~ qian2024gsavatar , so it keeps its identity as the avatar moves. The driving pose sequence also provides joint trajectories. Building on this structure, we introduce , which organizes avatar-specific knowledge and shared procedures into an agent skill~ tang2026wikiskill for a frozen MLLM. The skill's knowledge lies in per-avatar memories of the Gaussians in each part or garment and of joint trajectories. Its procedures are geometric operators that check pose and motion conditions and are shared across avatars. Specifically, to address region ambiguity, we accumulate labels from a 2D human parser~ khirodkar2026sapiens2 across views and poses into category scores that link body parts and garments to the avatar's Gaussians. A semantic memory combines these scores with category names and MLLM-generated appearance descriptions. Given a query, the MLLM uses the names and descriptions to select categories by appearance, relation, or function, rather than matching the query to CLIP features, and the Gaussians linked to these categories form the selected region. For motion ambiguity, we store the driving joint trajectories in a motion memory and check query conditions on them rather than on RGB frames. The checks use geometric operators adapted from PoseScript~ delmas2022posescript , which describes poses by relations between joints, and MotionScript~ yazdian2025motionscript , which extends these relations to motion. Given a 4D query, the MLLM composes these operators into a program by linking them with temporal relations, and running it on the trajectories gives the matching intervals. In Fig.~ fig:queries (b), for example, the program keeps the outward movements of both upper arms that end parallel to the ground. Because the MLLM chooses categories and operators rather than regions or intervals, each selection can be traced to these choices, and new motion conditions only require composing existing operators and relations or adding new ones. To evaluate this task, we introduce three human-annotated benchmarks for selecting regions and pose or motion intervals. performs best in part segmentation and 3D and 4D referring segmentation. We make four contributions: (1)~we introduce avatar referring segmentation and , a training-free framework that gives the structure of Gaussian avatars to a frozen MLLM as a skill, making its decisions traceable; (2)~to address region ambiguity, we build a semantic memory that also supports part segmentation; (3)~to address motion ambiguity, we localize motions on joint trajectories with MLLM-composed programs, extensible by composing or adding operators and relations; and (4)~to evaluate this task, we introduce three benchmarks and show that is the most accurate on all three, with compact memories and only minutes of setup per avatar. Related Work sec:related 3D language Gaussian splatting. Most language Gaussian methods select regions by matching a query to CLIP features that are learned per scene~ qin2024langsplat,shi2024legaussians,wu2024opengaussian or registered without per-scene optimization~ kim2025drsplat,ding2026extrinsplat . Beyond object names, ReferSplat~ he2025refersplat learns per-scene referring features from annotated expressions, and ReLaGS~ xie2026relags adds relation-guided retrieval. Open-vocabulary part segmentation likewise matches text to language-aligned features of 3D shapes~ ma2025find3d and humans~ suzuki2025openvocab3dhuman . Whereas these methods match queries to language features, uses an MLLM to interpret region queries through a semantic memory of avatar parts and garments, supporting both referring and part segmentation. 4D language Gaussian splatting. Recent work extends language Gaussian splatting to dynamic scenes, where a query specifies a region and when it is relevant. 4D LangSplat~ li2025_4dlangsplat and 4-LEGS~ fiebelman2025_4legs learn temporal language features from MLLM-generated captions and video-text features, respectively, and ST4R-Splat~ meng2026st4rsplat extends referring segmentation to 4D Gaussians. For humans, OpenHuman4D~ suzuki2025openhuman4d and 4D-DRESS~ wang20244d parse human parts over time. However, these methods mainly rely on RGB evidence, in which different motions can look alike~ yang2026movie and fine-grained motion remains hard to capture~ hong2025motionbench . instead measures pose and motion conditions on the driving joint trajectories, so it can distinguish subtle differences, such as the direction and extent of a movement, and return the queried region with its matching intervals using a compact memory. Agent skills and executable procedures. Large language models increasingly solve complex or fine-grained tasks through supplied procedures rather than task-specific training. Some compose predefined actions or handlers~ khot2023decomposed,pan2025chainofaction , whereas others generate code over visual tools~ gupta2023visprog,suris2023vipergpt . More recently, agent skills compile experience into reusable knowledge and procedures that accompany the query~ wang2024voyager,tang2026wikiskill , and this paradigm now extends to 3D spatial and 4D spatiotemporal reasoning~ li2026skill3d,sohn2026r4 . Building on this paradigm, gives an MLLM per-avatar memories as knowledge and shared geometric operators and temporal relations as procedures, so a new avatar needs only its memories, and a new motion condition requires only composing existing procedures or adding new ones. Preliminaries sec:preliminaries Gaussian avatars and motion. 3DGS-Avatar~ qian2024gsavatar represents an avatar as a fixed set of Gaussians with position, shape, opacity, and color. These Gaussians are defined in a canonical space corresponding to the reference pose of SMPL~ loper2015smpl , a body model parameterized by shape and joint rotations. A driving pose sequence of frames specifies the joint rotations and root translation at each frame, which determine the 3D joint positions. Animation deforms the Gaussians with the body into each target pose, so is the same Gaussian across frames. Rendering. Rendering projects the Gaussians posed at frame into camera view and blends their colors at pixel from front to back~ kerbl2023gaussian . The rendering contribution of to pixel , the coefficient of its color in the blended pixel, is where the product is the transmittance through the Gaussians in front of . title: O-SCD++: Replay-Free Online Scene Change Detection via Recursive Evidence Fusion
summary: Online scene change detection requires an agent to detect what has changed in a previously mapped environment while it is still on site, observing from unconstrained viewpoints and without access to future observations. This causal setting is strictly harder than its offline counterpart, and online methods have consistently trailed offline accuracy. O-SCD closed that gap by treating change as a persistent property of a 3D Gaussian splatting map of the reference scene, surpassing the strongest offline methods in change detection accuracy while operating at over 10 frames per second. O-SCD optimizes a change field over the Gaussians of the reference map, refitting it to all past cue maps at every frame, a step that consumes more than half of the per-frame budget and forces accuracy to be traded against speed. We present a replay-free formulation that eliminates this trade-off. Because the reference map stays fixed, rendering the change field is a linear operation. Each new observation can therefore be carried onto the map's Gaussians directly, by a single backward pass of the renderer, which reduces multi-view fusion to an exact two-scalar recursion per Gaussian. Past observations are never stored or revisited. The self-supervised objective that O-SCD minimizes by descent also determines the decision threshold exactly, by sorting, yielding a label-free per-frame cutoff whose margin provides a selective-prediction signal. On PASLCD, our method improves mean intersection over union from 0.489 to 0.575 and throughput from 11.8 to 25.6 frames per second, even exceeding O-SCD's offline result while remaining strictly causal.

Online Scene Change Detection, 3D Gaussian Splatting. Introduction sec:intro n autonomous agent that revisits a previously mapped environment -- an inspection robot returning to an electrical substation or a construction site, a service robot re-entering a room it mapped the day before -- must work out what has changed since its last visit, and must do so while suppressing nuisance variation such as shadows, reflections, or illumination shifts. The answer is only actionable if it arrives while the agent is still on site: a change report delivered after the deployment has ended cannot trigger a closer inspection, a re-planned route, or an intervention. Multi-view scene change detection (SCD) has accordingly developed along two regimes. In the offline regime, complete pre- and post-change captures are available and change is inferred with full hindsight. Work in this regime has matured rapidly, moving from image pairs at near-identical viewpoints~ sakurada_change_2015,alcantarilla2018street,daudt2018fully,cyws2d to pose-agnostic, label-free formulations that reason inside a photorealistic 3D representation of the reference scene~ galappaththige2025multi,lu20253dgs,galappaththige2026pixels,jiang2025gaussian,zhou2026d . In the online regime, the agent must emit a decision for every frame as it arrives, from a partial and incrementally growing stream, with no access to the future. This is the regime that matters for acting on site, and it is strictly harder than the offline counterpart. This online regime has received very little attention compared to the offline counterpart. Early work~ park2021changesim in the online regime lagged far behind the offline regime in detection accuracy. The conference version of our work, O -SCD~ galappaththige2025changes , closed that gap. Its central idea is that change could be held as a persistent property of the scene representation rather than predicted per image individually. O -SCD attaches a scalar change attribute to every primitive of a 3D Gaussian splatting (3DGS)~ kerbl20233d map of the pre-change scene representing a change field; incoming images are registered against that map, image-space cues are extracted against a rendered reference view, and those cues are fused into the per-primitive attributes. Because the attributes are shared across viewpoints, consistent evidence reinforces while view-dependent nuisance does not, so multi-view consistency is obtained without annotation and without any assumption on the revisit trajectory. O -SCD~ galappaththige2025changes was the first online method to be simultaneously pose-agnostic, label-free, multi-view, and operate at over 10\, FPS while even surpassing offline baselines. However, that result comes at a structural cost: the fusion step of O -SCD~ galappaththige2025changes is an iterative optimization. At every frame, it performs a budget of gradient steps on the change attributes, each step rendering the change field at a frame sampled from a growing buffer of previously observed frames and backpropagating a self-supervised objective against that frame's stored cue map. We refer to this re-use of stored past observations as replay. The procedure accounts for more than half of O-SCD's per-frame runtime, and the iteration budget is the only quantity available to reduce it: fewer steps buy throughput and leave the change field less converged. O -SCD's accuracy and speed therefore trade off directly ( ). In this paper, we replace the iterative fusion and the fixed decision cutoff of O -SCD with direct computations. Each observation is fused into the change field in closed form, without replay, and the decision threshold of every frame is derived exactly from the self-supervised objective that O -SCD imposes as a loss during its iterative optimization. The exact threshold also gives every pixel a decision margin. The resulting method is more accurate than O -SCD and more than twice as fast. Three insights make this possible. forward model is already known. For a fixed camera and fixed primitive geometry and opacity, alpha compositing is linear in the per-primitive attribute being rendered~ kerbl20233d,galappaththige2026predictive . Carrying an image-space signal back onto the primitives that produced it is therefore a transpose rather than a fit, as exploited by training-free lifting of 2D features onto Gaussians~ marrie2025ludvig,joseph2025gradient . The differentiable rasterizer already computes that transpose in a single backward pass. For change detection, one probe render and one backward call give each primitive the contribution-weighted mean of the cue over its footprint, with no iteration budget to choose. can be avoided. What remains is combining the per-view estimates across observed viewpoints. Replay combines them implicitly by refitting the field to every stored observation, so past observations must be kept and the estimate re-derived at each frame. We make the combination explicit: the support-weighted mean of the per-view estimates satisfies an exact two-scalar recursion, so the aggregate is reached by processing each observation once. Persistent state is two scalars per primitive, independent of sequence length. decision can be reduced to a sort. In O -SCD, descent on its self-supervised objective drives the change field towards a near-binary state, so a fixed midpoint cutoff suffices. A field computed in closed form is not driven there, and the label-free setting provides no annotation to tune a threshold against. For every frame, we instead choose the threshold whose mask minimizes that same objective. Evaluated over threshold masks rather than over a continuous field, that objective depends on a mask only through the number of pixels it selects and the cue those pixels carry. The resulting one-dimensional problem is discretely convex, and one sort and one prefix scan return its exact minimizer for every frame, without descent. Because the cutoff is explicit, the distance of a pixel's score to it is a well-defined decision margin, and we find it strongly predictive of correctness: withholding the of pixels closest to the boundary raises intersection over union on the retained region from to . The margin therefore ranks pixels by how reliably the mask labels them, without an auxiliary uncertainty model or held-out calibration data. This study extends our CVPR~2026 work. The resulting method, O -SCD++, sets a new state of the art in online SCD, improving change detection accuracy and throughput simultaneously. We believe it moves online SCD a step closer to real-time use, where accuracy no longer has to be traded for speed. In summary, we make the following contributions: Replay-free fusion. We show that the iterative, replay-based fusion of O -SCD can be replaced by a direct, closed-form estimator. Each observation is transferred onto the Gaussians through the adjoint of the renderer, weighted by reference coverage ( ). The transfers are combined as a support-weighted mean that a two-scalar recursion maintains exactly ( ). The persistent state is two scalars per Gaussian regardless of sequence length, and the estimator eliminates the per-frame iteration budget behind the accuracy--speed trade-off ( ). Exact label-free decision. We derive each frame's decision threshold exactly from the self-supervised objective of O -SCD, without labels or iterative optimization. Evaluated over threshold masks of the fused score, the objective reduces to a one-dimensional, discretely convex problem in the number of selected pixels and the cue they carry ( ), whose exact minimizer one sort and one prefix scan find ( ). The distance of each pixel's score from the threshold gives, at no extra cost, a decision margin that ranks pixels by confidence ( ). Extended evaluation and analysis. We extend the evaluation of the conference version to CL-Splats and ChangeSim and to recent baselines. We further analyse retrospective inference, showing that the final fused state is independent of frame order. We also analyse the proposed decision margins in detail, showing that they strongly predict decision errors. Used upstream to attenuate cues, predictive photometric uncertainty~ galappaththige2026predictive improves both methods on all three datasets. On PASLCD, O -SCD++ improves mIoU by 18 at the throughput of O -SCD, and exceeds the offline result of O -SCD while remaining causal ( ). Related Work sec:related Change Detection from Image Pairs SCD was classically posed as a bitemporal, pairwise learning problem: given two images of the same place captured at different times from identical~ sakurada_change_2015,alcantarilla2018street,daudt2018fully,varghese2018changenet or closely aligned~ cyws2d,sakurada2020weakly,lin2025robust viewpoints, predict the pixels that differ for a relevant reason, as a segmentation or less commonly as bounding boxes~ cyws2d,cyws3d . These methods are trained on human annotations, fully~ alcantarilla2018street,daudt2018fully,cyws2d,varghese2018changenet or partially~ sakurada2020weakly,lee2024semi , to separate the change signal from nuisance variation such as illumination shifts, shadows, or slight viewpoint discrepancies. This paradigm has proven effective for street-view change detection. Scene-level change detection by an autonomous agent revisiting an environment is a different use case, and there the paradigm carries two major limitations. First, an autonomous agent under an unconstrained revisit rarely reoccupies an exact earlier viewpoint, so the near-identical-viewpoint assumption often fails, and methods trained under it degrade sharply when it is violated~ galappaththige2025multi . title: SteerAct: Unlocking Action Models through Few-Shot Temporal Steering
summary: Improving pretrained robot action models at test time from only a few rollouts remains challenging. Activation steering offers a lightweight approach by modifying feature activations while keeping model weights fixed. However, effective steering requires identifying which features to modify and determining the timing and strength of modification. We introduce SteerAct, a few-shot temporal steering framework that uses a shared temporal descriptor of sparse-feature dynamics for offline feature selection and online control. A pretrained sparse autoencoder provides candidate features, and our temporal descriptor summarizes the distribution of local activation-order patterns for each feature, enabling comparisons across rollouts without requiring timestep alignment. Before steering begins (offline), we use successful and failed reference rollouts to select a single task-specific feature whose temporal descriptors best distinguish the two outcomes and construct its reference banks. During each new execution (online), we compare the feature's evolving temporal descriptor with these references to determine when to intervene and how strongly to increase or decrease its activation via a steering coefficient. Using only 24 outcome-labeled rollouts per task, SteerAct improves task success by approximately 10% relative to unsteered models in evaluations spanning $π_{0.5}$, Fast-WAM, RoboTwin 2.0, DexJoCo, and real-world manipulation, without updating action-model weights. Code and demos are available at: https://steeract.github.io/.
full_text: Methodology sec:method is a few-shot temporal steering framework that uses a shared representation of feature dynamics for offline feature selection and online intervention (Figure~ fig:method ). A pretrained SAE decomposes the action model's hidden activations into sparse features, each associated with a decoder direction for intervention. A temporal descriptor summarizes each feature's activation history, placing complete reference histories, observed execution prefixes, and candidate-edited histories in the same representation space. Before steering begins (offline), differences between successful and failed references identify task-specific steering features. During execution (online), comparisons in this space determine whether intervention is warranted and guide the steering coefficient. The SAE is shared across tasks, and both its weights and the action model's weights remain frozen throughout. The complete procedure is summarized in Algorithm~ alg:steeract in the appendix. Problem Setting We consider a frozen robot action model with access to its hidden activations at a fixed intervention site. title: Revealing and Bridging the Physical Executability Gap in Vision-Language Navigation
summary: Continuous vision-and-language navigation (VLN) is typically evaluated by goal-reaching success, assuming it reflects an agent's ability to execute language-grounded behavior. We show that this assumption can fail: permissive contact models in current simulators may mask physically infeasible actions, creating a physical executability gap between semantic competence and embodied realization. To bridge this gap, we introduce Visual-Semantic Traversability Alignment (VeSTA), a framework that aligns VLN policies with physically executable futures. We define visual-semantic traversability as the ability to predict instruction-conditioned trajectories that are semantically valid, geometrically feasible, and physically robust. VeSTA addresses this misalignment through two complementary mechanisms: improving executable support in trajectory generation and risk-aware selection among multimodal futures. Specifically, Trajectory Relative Group Policy Optimization uses strict-contact feedback to reshape the candidate distribution toward executable regions, while the Traversability Risk Critic learns a risk-adjusted scalar utility for candidate-wise future selection. Experiments on R2R and RxR reveal substantial dependence of existing VLN agents on simulator contact semantics. Under strict-contact evaluation, VeSTA substantially reduces collision-induced failures while preserving or improving goal-reaching performance, and controlled real-world robot experiments provide evidence that the learned preference transfers beyond simulation.

We show that this assumption can fail: permissive contact models in current simulators may mask physically infeasible actions, creating a physical executability gap between semantic competence and embodied realization. To bridge this gap, we introduce Visual-Semantic Traversability Alignment (VeSTA), a framework that aligns VLN policies with physically executable futures. We define visual-semantic traversability as the ability to predict instruction-conditioned trajectories that are semantically valid, geometrically feasible, and physically robust. VeSTA addresses this misalignment through two complementary mechanisms: improving executable support in trajectory generation and risk-aware selection among multimodal futures. Specifically, Trajectory Relative Group Policy Optimization uses strict-contact feedback to reshape the candidate distribution toward executable regions, while the Traversability Risk Critic learns a risk-adjusted scalar utility for candidate-wise future selection. Experiments on R2R and RxR reveal substantial dependence of existing VLN agents on simulator contact semantics. Under strict-contact evaluation, VeSTA substantially reduces collision-induced failures while preserving or improving goal-reaching performance, and controlled real-world robot experiments provide evidence that the learned preference transfers beyond simulation. Introduction Vision-and-language navigation (VLN) maps natural-language instructions and visual observations to goal-directed behavior. Whereas R2R formulates navigation over discrete graphs anderson2018vision , continuous VLN must further realize semantic decisions through low-level motion in 3D environments krantz2020beyond,savva2019habitat . Navigation success therefore depends on two related but distinct capabilities: identifying a semantically appropriate goal and converting that intention into motion that can be executed under local geometric and physical constraints. Permissive contact resolution can obscure this distinction: an obstacle-directed command may be projected into tangential displacement, yielding apparent progress without a realizable local motion, a simulator behavior previously shown to distort sim-to-real navigation comparisons kadian2020sim2real . We call the discrepancy between semantic intent and executable behavior the physical executability gap. We define visual-semantic traversability as predicting instruction-conditioned trajectories that are semantically valid, geometrically feasible, and robust to persistent contact or immobilization; it is not a claim of general safety. We diagnose this gap by changing only contact semantics. Strict contact blocks obstacle-directed motion rather than repairing it through tangential progress. With policies and episode specifications fixed, the resulting performance change measures system-level sensitivity, not the pointwise causal effect of a collision. This intervention separates two questions that goal-reaching metrics conflate: whether the agent chooses an instruction-consistent direction and whether its local motion can actually realize that choice. We formulate local execution alignment through two complementary mechanisms: trajectory distribution bias, which governs executable support in the candidate distribution, and multimodal future selection uncertainty, which governs utility-based choice among incompatible candidates. The former determines which futures are proposed; the latter determines which future is executed. VeSTA augments a dual-system VLN agent dualvln2025 while keeping its high-level planner fixed. TR-GRPO uses strict-contact feedback and a local action-marginal surrogate to shape executable candidate support; TRiC learns a scalar utility from multi-factor trajectory preferences to select an individual future. We evaluate this design through contact intervention, R2R/RxR benchmarks, ablations, and controlled robot trials. Our contributions are fourfold. First, we expose contact-semantics sensitivity as a diagnostic of the physical executability gap. Second, we formalize visual-semantic traversability through complementary alignment of candidate generation and multimodal selection. Third, VeSTA combines TR-GRPO for executable-support formation with TRiC for candidate-level utility. Finally, strict-contact benchmarks, component ablations, and robot trials show substantially lower collision burden without reducing reported goal-reaching performance. Related Work Continuous VLN. Continuous VLN extends graph-based instruction following to embodied control in 3D environments anderson2018vision,krantz2020beyond,savva2019habitat . Language-conditioned waypoint, topology, map, and world-model representations include Topological Planning with Transformers, Waypoint Models, discrete-to-continuous transfer, CM2, BEVBert, GridMM, DREAMWALKER, and NavMorph pashevich2021topological,krantz2021waypoint,hong2022bridging,georgakis2022crossmodal,an2023bevbert,wang2023gridmm,wang2023dreamwalker,ghaus2025navmorph . Recent video/VLM systems include NaVid, NaVILA, Uni-NaVid, StreamVLN, JanusVLN, AwareVLN, and EvoNav zhang2024navid,cheng2024navila,zhang2024uninavid,streamvln2025,janusvln2025,guo2026awarevln,dai2026evonav . Complementary work scales synthetic VLN training or introduces explicit map- and LLM-guided planning, including ScaleVLN, MapGPT, and NavGPT-2 wang2023scalevln,chen2024mapgpt,zhou2024navgpt2 . These methods improve semantic reasoning, memory, data coverage, or local motion proposals; our complementary question is whether the selected intention remains executable when contact-prone commands are no longer repaired. Multimodal trajectory futures. Candidate-based forecasting preserves distinct futures instead of collapsing them into a single regression target. DESIRE samples, ranks, and refines diverse trajectories, while MultiPath represents multiple modes through learned anchor trajectories lee2017desire,chai2020multipath . Although developed for dynamic-scene forecasting rather than instruction following, they motivate VeSTA's candidate-wise treatment of incompatible local futures; TRiC differs by scoring instruction-conditioned robot trajectories using strict-contact execution feedback. General visual navigation policies. Beyond VLN, ViNT learns a reusable visual navigation backbone across robots and environments, while NoMaD uses goal-masked diffusion for navigation and exploration shah2023vint,sridhar2024nomad . Diffusion Policy similarly demonstrates multimodal visuomotor action generation through denoising chi2023diffusion . These systems are not substitutes for language grounding, but they motivate RGB-conditioned, multimodal local policies; VeSTA focuses on aligning such local futures with an instruction-derived subgoal and strict-contact executability. Collision-aware execution. Classical planners optimize feasible velocities or short-horizon trajectories under geometry fox1997dynamic,rosmann2013efficient . Safety-aware or execution-aware VLN may instead add LiDAR fallback, repulsive collision estimation, language-model-assisted correction, or an obstacle-avoiding controller yue2023safevln,kim2025care,jeong2024vlncm,an2025etpnav . Many specialized systems therefore use extra range sensing or an external correction stage, although this is not universal. VeSTA augments a general-purpose VLN policy with RGB-only inference and no added LiDAR/depth or external local planner. This comparison distinguishes sensing assumptions and design scope rather than claiming superiority over methods targeting broader notions of safety. Recent physically grounded VLN evaluation further documents collisions, falls, observation shifts, and embodiment-dependent locomotion constraints that are absent from idealized point-agent evaluation wang2025embodiedgap . Hierarchical RL. DualVLN separates semantic planning from trajectory generation dualvln2025 , allowing us to hold planning fixed and isolate local execution. This modularity is important experimentally: changing only S1 avoids attributing improved contact behavior to a stronger language planner. TR-GRPO builds on flow matching lipman2023flow , flow-policy fine-tuning lyu2025fpo , and group-relative optimization shao2024deepseekmath,li2026navgrpo . NavGRPO uses group-relative learning to promote robust and diverse instruction-following trajectories, but evaluates graph-based VLN; our objective instead uses strict-contact feedback for continuous local execution. Candidates share a visual-language state, and a collapsed action marginal provides a tractable local ratio that acts directly on the VLN policy rather than through an external recovery controller. Instead, it favors trajectories whose intended progress remains realizable when environment-side correction is absent. title: Vehicle-State-Aware Confidence Estimation for Direct Wind Sensing on a Multirotor
summary: Direct wind sensing from a multi-rotor UAV enables localized atmospheric measurements, but the reliability of the anemometer depends on vehicle motion. This work presents a vehicle-state-aware confidence method that uses horizontal and vertical vehicle speed to quantify the acquisition of each wind observation. The resulting confidence score is used to adapt measurement influence to a two-dimensional vector estimator. Experiments were conducted during horizontal translation, vertical motion, and held-out autonomous waypoint flight. The proposed two-feature formulation achieved an ROC-AUC of 0.995, with 98.84% of translation observations identified as unreliable. The confidence-aware adaptation reduced median estimator gain during translation from 0.207 to 0.064 while retaining median gain of 0.151 during hover. The results show that vehicle state provides useful proprioceptive context for regulating the influence of direct airborne wind observations.
full_text: Direct wind sensing from a multi-rotor UAV enables localized atmospheric measurements, but the reliability of the anemometer depends on vehicle motion. This work presents a vehicle-state-aware confidence method that uses horizontal and vertical vehicle speed to quantify the acquisition of each wind observation. The resulting confidence score is used to adapt measurement influence to a two-dimensional vector estimator. Experiments were conducted during horizontal translation, vertical motion, and held-out autonomous waypoint flight. The proposed two-feature formulation achieved an ROC--AUC of 0.995, with 98.84 of translation observations identified as unreliable. The confidence-aware adaptation reduced median estimator gain during translation from 0.207 to 0.064 while retaining median gain of 0.151 during hover. The results show that vehicle state provides useful proprioceptive context for regulating the influence of direct airborne wind observations. Introduction Unmanned aerial vehicles provide flexible platforms for localized atmospheric observation as they can hover at required locations and perform vertical hovers and traverse short trajectories in the atmospheric boundary layer ~ palomaki2017wind,wetz2021distributed . Multirotor platforms are suitable for in-situ wind, sensing as a lightweight sonic anemometer can be carried to locations difficult to instrument using fixed towers ~ thielicke2021accurate,ghirardelli2025samurai . Direct airborne wind sensing introduces a coupling between environmental observation and the motion of the sensing platform, as the anemometer is exposed not only to atmospheric flow but also to changes in relative airflow associated with vehicle translation and the local aerodynamic environment generated by the propulsion system. Sensor elevation can reduce these effects but does not eliminate them ~ thielicke2021accurate, yang2025correction,ghirardelli2025samurai . Additionally, the calibration of the anemometer alone does not imply that every airborne wind observation is under favorable sensing conditions. The vehicle motion itself provides information about the acquisition condition. Previous work has used attitude, internal measurements, motor information and learned dynamic models to estimate wind without a dedicated sensor ~ neumann2015realtime,gonzalezrocha2019sensing, wetz2021distributed,zimmerman2022wind,chen2026wind . These approaches show the relationship between wind and multirotor dynamics. However, vehicle state is primarily used for reconstructing wind fields. This work takes the approach where rather than estimating ambient wind directly from vehicle dynamics, we use the instantaneous vehicle state to quantify vehicle conditions associated with direct onboard wind observation. Horizontal and absolute vertical speeds are compared with an empirically determined stable hover reference to obtain a continuous wind observation confidence score. The score is used to adapt the measurement covariance of a navigation-frame wind-vector estimator, reducing the influence of observations obtained during strong departure from stable sensing while preserving measurement streams. The contributions of this work are: A proprioceptive confidence model that uses multirotor motion state to assign sample-level confidence to direct wind observations, enabling motion-aware adaptation of measurement uncertainty in downstream state estimation without discarding observations or requiring a vehicle dynamic model. A confidence-aware vector wind estimator that propagates calibrated wind-speed and direction uncertainty into a sample-dependent measurement covariance and continuously adapts measurement influence using the vehicle-state confidence score. Experimental validation across development, independent vertical-motion, and held-out autonomous waypoint flights, including feature ablation and estimator sensitivity analyses, demonstrates that the frozen confidence models transfer across distinct flight regimes and selectively reduce the influence of wind observation acquired under motion-disturbed sensing conditions. Related Work UAV-Based Atmospheric Wind Sensing Multirotor UAVs are increasingly used for atmospheric wind observation. Palomaki et al. demonstrated direct wind sensing using a sonic anemometer above a hexacopter and indirect estimation using vehicle attitude ~ palomaki2017wind . Wetz et al. demonstrated distributed atmospheric boundary layer measurement using multiple quadrotors and a dynamic-based wind estimator method ~ wetz2021distributed . Recently, sonic anemometer systems have been developed for high-fidelity atmospheric measurements, including rigidly mounted configurations~ thielicke2021accurate and suspended sensor systems designed to further separate instrument from propulsion-induced flow~ ghirardelli2025samurai . These studies establish that multi-rotors are useful platforms and cannot be treated as aerodynamically independent measurements. Direct Wind Measurement and Vehicle-Induced Disturbance Sensor placement and vehicle-induced flow are important considerations. Palomaki et al. stated that measured wind speed increases for a sonic anemometer mounted above a hovering multi-rotor ~ palomaki2017wind . Thielicke et al. showed that the accurate multi-rotor wind measurement is dependent on anemometer separation from the propellers, with appropriate treatment for propeller-induced flow ~ thielicke2021accurate . Yang et al. developed a correction that accounts for rotor-induced airflow and changes in flight attitude during three-dimensional rotary UAV wind measurements ~ yang2025correction . While these approaches seek to reduce or correct the aerodynamic disturbance, in the present work elevated mounting and calibration are retained but no aerodynamic correction is assumed. Instead the vehicle state is used to describe how far instantaneous acquisition condition departs from stable-hover phase. Vehicle-State-Based Wind Estimation and Sensing Confidence Other methods estimate wind from the vehicle itself. Neumann and Bartholmai estimated wind data using an onboard inertial measurement unit~ neumann2015realtime , González-Rocha et al. evaluated kinematic and dynamic motion models to estimate wind from quadrotor motion~ gonzalezrocha2019sensing , while Wetz et al. estimated based on aerodynamic-force-based formulation for atmospheric measurement ~ wetz2021distributed . Data-driven alternatives have also been investigated. Zimmermanet al. used machine-learning models using multirotor dynamic and motor information ~ zimmerman2022wind . Work by Chen et al. shows that the relationship between UAV attitude and wind depends on relative wind direction and platform configuration ~ chen2026wind . The anemometer observation remains the wind measurement while the vehicle state supplies proprioceptive context describing the acquisition condition. This allows a sample-level confidence score to be assigned for direct observation and subsequently used to adapt its influence in the wind-vector estimator. Unlike dynamics-base approaches that reconstruct wind from vehicle response, the proposed method retains the anemometer as the primary wind sensor and uses proprioceptive vehicle state to assign confidence to each observation based on its acquisition condition. This addresses a complementary robotics problem: how the robot's own motion state can inform when an environmental measurement should be trusted and how strongly it should influence downstream estimation. Multirotor Sensing Platform and Characterization sec:platform Representative D6 Sensing Platform The platform used in this work is a DJI F550 hexacopter frame equipped with Pixhawk 6C flight controller and a Raspberry Pi 4B as the companion computer. The MeteoNode payload has a BME280 environmental sensor and a HY-WDC2E ultrasonic anemometer to observe wind speed and direction measurements. The anemometer is mounted in the center of the frame on an elevated mast to reduce the effects of propeller wash. Although the placement reduces direct aerodynamic interference from propeller wash, it does not fully isolate the sensor from vehicle-induced flow. Onboard Wind and Vehicle-State Acquisition The Raspberry Pi acquires the wind measurement, applies sensor-specific calibration and publishes the resulting observation through ROS~2. Vehicle position, attitude, and linear velocity are obtained from the Pixhawk through the onboard MAVLink interface. The wind and vehicle state are recorded together for synchronized processing. Direct wind observations are associated with the nearest state sample within a temporal tolerance; unmatched observations are treated as unavailable. The wind condition wind-speed variability used to parameterize the nominal measurement covariance was . Wind direction performance was also evaluated at eight different orientations, from to in increments. The maximum absolute directional error was around , with circular variability of approximately -- across the orientations. The directional repeatability of was used in the nominal covariance model. The FROM direction of the anemometer is relative to the vehicle body frame, where the sensor axis aligns with the vehicle forward direction. Vehicle-Induced Flow Characterization A controlled propulsion experiment was conducted to determine whether the elevated sensor positioning isolates the anemometer from vehicle-induced flow. The propulsion-induced change in measured wind speed was defined as: Across the evaluated propulsion and flow conditions, ranged approximately from to . The slope was not linear with the propulsion level, showing that mounting alone does not guarantee undisturbed airborne wind observation. This observation motivates the vehicle-state-dependent confidence introduced in section IV. Vehicle-State-Aware Wind Confidence Estimation sec:method Measurement Association and Availability The wind and odometry measurements are synchronized, as the data are acquired asynchronously. Each observation is associated with the nearest vehicle-state sample. The association uses a defined temporal matching tolerance, and observations that are missing or invalid/clipped for the state are considered unavailable, whereas Unreliable observations remain usable measurements acquired when the vehicle state departs from stable hover. where indicates a usable synchronized observation. Vehicle-State Reconstruction The vehicle state is represented using the horizontal and absolute vertical speeds. The horizontal speed provides a measure of vehicle translation, while represents the magnitude of vertical motion irrespective of ascending or descending. Both quantities are obtained from synchronized vehicle odometry. The linear-velocity odometry components were verified to be expressed in the local NED frame. where the horizontal vehicle speed and the absolute vertical speed are defined as These two quantities constitute the vehicle-state features used in the confidence formulation. Both features capture complementary modes of vehicle motion which influences the condition under which the wind observations are acquired. The horizontal speed characterizes translational motion in the horizontal plane, which affects the relative airflow experienced in the anemometer. The absolute vertical speed represents departure from stable hover while treating ascents and descents symmetrically. title: ReDOA: Real-World Distillation via Observation Alignment for Image-Based Manipulation Policy Learning
summary: Data-driven learning for general-purpose robotic manipulation presents a fundamental trade-off between data-collection cost and adaptability to real-world environments. Imitation learning (IL) requires costly human demonstrations, whereas simulation-based learning is vulnerable to sim-to-real gaps in dynamics and sensor observations. We propose ReDOA (Real-World Distillation via Observation Alignment), a framework that decouples control learning from perception learning to learn image-based policies in the real world. A state-based teacher policy trained in simulation is executed on a real robot, and its control knowledge is distilled into an image-based student policy using the collected trajectories. Observation Alignment resolves observation mismatches between data collection and deployment. This framework collects successful, efficiently executed trajectories paired with real-world visual observations, without requiring demonstrations from human experts. In real-robot experiments on three non-prehensile manipulation tasks, including bimanual manipulation, our method achieves better overall performance when jointly considering task success and execution efficiency than both IL based on human demonstrations and policy distillation in simulation. https://isri-aist.github.io/redoa-project-page/
full_text: Data-driven learning for general-purpose robotic manipulation presents a fundamental trade-off between data-collection cost and adaptability to real-world environments. Imitation learning (IL) requires costly human demonstrations, whereas simulation-based learning is vulnerable to sim-to-real gaps in dynamics and sensor observations. We propose ReDOA (Real-World Distillation via Observation Alignment), a framework that decouples control learning from perception learning to learn image-based policies in the real world. A state-based teacher policy trained in simulation is executed on a real robot, and its control knowledge is distilled into an image-based student policy using the collected trajectories. Observation Alignment resolves observation mismatches between data collection and deployment. This framework collects successful, efficiently executed trajectories paired with real-world visual observations, without requiring demonstrations from human experts. In real-robot experiments on three non-prehensile manipulation tasks, including bimanual manipulation, our method achieves better overall performance when jointly considering task success and execution efficiency than both IL based on human demonstrations and policy distillation in simulation. https://isri-aist.github.io/redoa-project-page/ Introduction Although demand for automating manipulation tasks in unstructured environments, such as homes and industrial workplaces, continues to grow, successful real-world deployments remain limited. Data-driven learning has therefore attracted considerable attention as a promising solution. However, learning both robust control under complex dynamics and reliable perception across diverse real-world environments remains challenging while keeping the costs of collecting demonstrations and setting up environments low. Existing data-driven approaches face an inherent difficulty in balancing data collection cost and real-world adaptability. Imitation learning (IL) based on human demonstrations can naturally adapt to real-world visual observations and contact dynamics, but teaching complex dual-arm manipulation through teleoperation requires operator skill and teleoperation interface setup. Moreover, because vision-based IL is sensitive even to minor appearance variations such as lighting or background shifts, adapting to new environments requires collecting demonstrations again, repeatedly imposing substantial labor and time on human demonstrators. In contrast, simulation-based methods (sim-to-real approaches) enable training on large datasets at low cost, but gaps in dynamics and sensor observations tend to degrade real-world performance. However, recent work has shown that separating control learning in simulation from perception learning in the real world can bypass the sim-to-real gap in observations. For example, PTLD~ Chen:PTLD:2026 uses real-world policy distillation to bypass the sim-to-real gap of tactile sensors. We propose ReDOA (Real-World Distillation via Observation Alignment), which applies distillation across observation spaces in the real world to image-based manipulation policy learning. Figure~ fig:concept illustrates the concept of our method. The pipeline proceeds as follows. First, we roll out the teacher policy while estimating the object state using temporarily installed trackers, collecting demonstrations for distillation. The trackers appear in the collected images; using these images directly to train the student policy creates an observation mismatch when the trackers are removed at deployment. We therefore perform Observation Alignment to resolve this mismatch and train the student policy using the aligned observations and collected actions. These stages form a sim-to-real-to-real pipeline. The framework reduces the burden of human demonstration and bypasses the visual sim-to-real gap by learning perception from images collected in the real world. We evaluate the proposed method on three non-prehensile manipulation tasks using a real robot. Non-prehensile manipulation requires continuous visual perception to maintain precise robot--object--environment contact, making it a suitable benchmark. Prior sim-to-real studies have attempted to limit the performance degradation of vision-based policies by using visual domain randomization~ Josh:VisualDomainRandomization:IROS2017 , green-screening, or texture projection~ Xuanlin:EvalRealinSim:PMLR2025 . However, these methods suffer from training instability caused by randomization~ Josip:AnalysisRandomization:IROS2022 and require substantial effort to set up the environment. Our method uses images collected in the real environment to train the student policy, eliminating the need to render its training images in simulation. Observation Alignment then mitigates the appearance mismatch caused by trackers introduced for real-world data collection. Unlike conventional IL based on human demonstrations, our method collects data using a consistent policy without relying on human experts or being affected by human fatigue or individual operating habits. Because the state-based teacher does not depend on visual appearance, it can also autonomously collect new real-world demonstrations without retraining when lighting or backgrounds change. In summary, our contributions are as follows: A real-world distillation framework for bypassing the visual sim-to-real gap through Observation Alignment that resolves observation mismatches between demonstration collection and deployment. Automated generation of high-quality demonstration data without expert teleoperation, reducing human labor costs. Real-world validation on three non-prehensile tasks, demonstrating the simultaneous achievement of high success rates and high motion efficiency. Related Work Challenges in IL and Demonstration Data Collection subsec:ILDemoData Recent advances in IL, including ACT~ Zhao:ACT:RSS2023 and Diffusion Policy~ Chi:DP:RSS2023 , have led to significant success in approaches that generate robot actions directly from visual observations. However, the performance of these data-driven methods depends strongly on the quality and quantity of demonstration data collected from human experts~ Mandlekar:RoboMimic:2021,Kase:MotorBabbling:JRM2021 . In particular, the non-prehensile manipulation tasks considered in this study require controlling continuous contact dynamics among the object, the environment, and the robot~ Fabio:NonprehensileSurvey:RAL2018 . Prior work has proposed RL-based approaches focused primarily on control, including maintaining contact modes during whole-arm manipulation~ Kawarai:WholeArmManipulation:JRM2010 , integrating tactile sensors into the end effectors of a dual-arm robot~ Yijiong:Bi-Touch:RAL2023 , and combining optimization-based demonstration generation with RL~ Shirai:Pivoting:NeurIPS2025 . These studies show that non-prehensile manipulation requires continuous state observation and sequential action correction to handle delicate physical interactions. Consequently, collecting a large-scale, high-quality, and consistent real-world dataset for IL through teleoperation is costly. To address the cost of collecting human demonstrations, RLDG uses reinforcement learning directly on real robots to collect demonstrations containing real-world RGB images and fine-tunes a generalist model on these data~ Xu:RLDG:RSS2025 . By autonomously generating high-quality trajectories through reward maximization, this approach has been shown to outperform fine-tuning on human demonstrations. In contrast, this study focuses on training task-specific image-based policies from scratch. Policy Distillation across Observation Spaces subsec:related_distill_obs Deploying a state-based policy in the real world requires continuously providing the policy with task-relevant state information, such as object poses. Such state information can be obtained using planar fiducial markers attached to objects~ Cong:SelfAdaptingPushing:IROS2020 or marker-based motion capture~ Sueoka:RealWorldCooperativeTransport:JRM2025 . However, in settings where many objects of the same type are handled in sequence, attaching markers to each object in advance is impractical. Image-based policies avoid explicit object-state measurement~ Lerrel:AsymmetricActorCritic:RSS2018,Yarats:DrQ-v2:ICLR2022 . However, end-to-end policy learning from high-dimensional visual observations requires learning of visual representations and control simultaneously, which tends to reduce sample efficiency and training stability. In addition, repeatedly rendering visual observations in simulation also increases computational resource requirements and training time. Policy distillation across observation spaces is used to address these sample-efficiency and computational-cost issues. A teacher policy is first trained in simulation using privileged observations, and its control knowledge is then distilled, also in simulation, into a student policy that uses observations available at deployment, such as RGB images~ Singh:DextrAH-RGB:2024,He:VIRAL:CVPR2026,Sorokin:Sidewalk:RAL2022 , depth images~ Lum:DextrAH-G:ACRL2024 , or point clouds~ Yamada:Combo-Grasp:PMLR2025,Chen:ClutterDexGrasp:CoRL2025 . PTLD~ Chen:PTLD:2026 also performs policy distillation in the real world. It bypasses the sim-to-real gap of tactile sensors by using real-world data to learn to estimate latent representations based on privileged information from tactile and proprioceptive observations. Our method likewise performs distillation in the real world, using Observation Alignment to resolve the image-observation mismatch caused by the presence of trackers during data collection and their absence at deployment, thereby enabling real-world distillation into an image-based policy. Visual Sim-to-Real Gap subsec:related_sim2real_data In sim-to-real transfer, the visual gap associated with RGB images is a serious problem and degrades real-robot deployment performance~ Acar:Single-CameraDistill:RAL2024,Liu:FetchBot:2025 . Real-to-sim-to-real methods such as Re Sim~ Han:Re3Sim:2025 reduce the visual sim-to-real gap by reconstructing real-world 3D geometry and appearance in photorealistic simulation environments. Whereas their training data are generated entirely in simulation, our method executes the teacher policy on a real robot to generate demonstrations that directly reflect real-world visual observations and contact dynamics. Moreover, Re Sim considers only rigid objects, and its applicability to articulated-object manipulation, as studied here, remains unverified. By training the student policy using real-world images, our method eliminates the need to transfer from simulated images to real images. Observation Alignment further mitigates the observation mismatch caused by tracker artifacts in the real data.
