title: VLA-Rolling: Fewer Denoising Steps, Better Control via Adaptive Action Reuse
summary: Flow-matching vision-language-action (VLA) models generate an action chunk by iteratively denoising Gaussian noise, but typically execute only a short prefix before replanning with updated observations. Under this receding-horizon paradigm, the unexecuted remainder---the action tail---is discarded, and the next chunk is regenerated from fresh noise. We show that this discarded tail retains transferable denoising progress: action-tail initialization can match or outperform a native 10-step Gaussian baseline using fewer denoising steps. However, the optimal denoising budget varies substantially across samples, indicating that tail reuse should be adapted to the updated environment. Based on this observation, we introduce VLA-Rolling, a lightweight inference framework that reuses action tails through three stages: action-tail inheritance, per-action confidence estimation, and confidence-guided refinement through renoising and denoising budget allocation, while the underlying VLA remains frozen. Across $π_{0.5}$, SmolVLA, X-VLA, and MolmoAct2 on LIBERO, MetaWorld, LIBERO-Plus, and RoboTwin 2.0, VLA-Rolling reduces action-chunk inference cost in all 16 model--benchmark pairs, achieving up to a $1.48\times$ speedup, while improving success rate in 14 pairs by up to $15.08$ percentage points. These results show that action tails are not merely discarded predictions, but reusable intermediate states that enable more efficient and accurate VLA inference. These results demonstrate that the action tail can support the generation of better actions with fewer denoising steps. Our project is available at https://chenbao123ww.github.io/VLA-Rolling/.
full_text: Introduction sec:introduction Flow-matching vision-language-action (VLA) models generate future robot actions from visual observations and language instructions~ black2024pi_0, intelligence2025pi_, shukor2025smolvla, zheng2026x, lee2025molmoact, bjorck2025gr00t, cai2026xiaomi . Their architectures differ, but they share a flow-matching action generator that iteratively transforms Gaussian noise into a sequence of future actions, called action chunk~ jing2025mixture, liang2026adaptive,xu2026knowing, wang2026vla, lu2026faster . In models such as ~ intelligence2025pi_ and SmolVLA~ shukor2025smolvla , this generator is implemented as a dedicated Transformer module called the action expert, conditioned on features from a vision-language model (VLM). Thanks to this , the robot can plan and execute several coherent steps without calling the model after every action. Yet the whole chunk is predicted from one observation, so environmental changes can make later actions inaccurate. To limit this error accumulation, receding-horizon execution runs only a short prefix, then observes and replans~ zhao2023learning,jing2025mixture,liang2026adaptive . The price of this feedback is a fresh start: the unexecuted remainder, or action tail~ huang2026chainvla , is discarded, and the next chunk starts again from Gaussian noise. A fresh start may waste completed computation. The action tail has already undergone denoising and overlaps in time with the actions needed in the next inference round, so it may be a better starting point than fresh Gaussian noise. Yet the tail was generated from an earlier observation and may have become stale. It is neither a ready-to-execute plan nor fresh noise: its value as a starting point depends on how much the environment has changed. This tension raises a compelling question: We probe this possibility on and SmolVLA ( ). On LIBERO and MetaWorld, tail initialization matches or improves the action error of a 10-step Gaussian baseline in four denoising steps for and six for SmolVLA ( ). Yet no fixed short budget suits every sample: the sample-wise optimal step counts span the full range from 1 to 10 for both models ( ). The question is therefore not simply whether to reuse the tail, but how much to trust it under each new observation. To adapt reuse to each new observation, we introduce VLA-Rolling, a three-stage inference framework ( ). First, action-tail inheritance aligns unexecuted actions with the next planning window, using completed denoising work as the starting point for a new prediction. Second, a lightweight action confidence estimator predicts the reuse value of each inherited action from the new observation and state change. We train it offline on temporally adjacent demonstrations: smaller error between an inherited action and its aligned demonstrated action yields a higher confidence target, while the loss penalizes overestimated confidence more heavily. Third, confidence-guided refinement injects more noise into low-confidence actions and assigns more denoising steps when the chunk contains an unreliable action. The underlying VLA remains frozen. To summarize, our main contributions are: [itemsep=1.5pt, topsep=1.5pt, leftmargin=20pt] Action-Tail Reuse Potential ( ): We reveal that discarded tails retain transferable denoising progress: four steps for and six for SmolVLA match a 10-step Gaussian baseline. Yet the sample-wise optimal budgets span 1--10 steps, exposing both the opportunity for reuse and the need to adapt it to each new observation. Confidence-Guided Rolling Reuse ( ): We propose VLA-Rolling, a lightweight inference framework that learns per-action reuse confidence from temporally adjacent demonstrations. This confidence jointly controls how much of each inherited action to retain and how many denoising steps to allocate, preserving useful motion while correcting stale predictions without retraining the base VLA. Extensive Experiments and Analysis ( ): On , SmolVLA, X-VLA, and MolmoAct2 across LIBERO, MetaWorld, LIBERO-Plus, and RoboTwin 2.0, VLA-Rolling reduces action-chunk inference time in all 16 pairs, achieving up to a speedup (32.52 lower cost), and improves success in 14 pairs by up to 15.08 percentage points. Ablations expose the risk of naive reuse, while real-world target changes trigger additional refinement. Probing the Feasibility of Action Tail Reuse sec:motivating_observations Flow-matching VLA jointly predicts an -step action chunk from a single environment state . However, during the execution of the action chunk, the latest observations from the environment are not used to update the action, causing all subsequent actions to be based on the state observed before execution began. Errors in early actions cause a deviation between the actual state of the robot and the environment and the state expected by the remaining predicted actions, and this state mismatch propagates to subsequent actions, gradually accumulating throughout the execution scope. Receding-horizon execution mitigates such error accumulation by periodically closing the perception--action loop. Instead of executing all predicted actions, the robot only the first actions (where ), then obtains the updated observations and generates a new action block. This execution paradigm consumes more inference iterations in exchange for the ability to use new observations to update actions more frequently. This execution strategy also leaves part of every generated action chunk unused. After executing the first actions, the remaining actions are which we refer to as the action tail. Under conventional receding-horizon execution, this tail is discarded once the observation is refreshed. However, our statistics show that under the execution horizon of common VLA models, the environment does not change significantly. VLA-Rolling is a inference paradigm that uses the action tail of each round as prior knowledge for the next inference round, as shown in . title: Scene-Adaptive VLA: Efficient Autonomous Driving via Dynamic Layer Routing
summary: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models offer a promising paradigm for autonomous driving. However, the massive parameter scale of VLAs strains onboard computational resources during real-time inference. This directly increases energy consumption and limits vehicle battery range, making it critical to minimize computational overhead without compromising driving capability and explainability. Current research on efficient VLA-based driving focuses on sequential adaptation (\textit{e.g.}, Chain-of-Thought and token adjustment), leaving structural adaptation underexplored despite parameter redundancy across dynamic driving scenes. To address this gap, we propose Scene-Adaptive VLA, an efficient framework leveraging dynamic layer routing to adjust active parameters based on real-time scenes. Inspired by the temporal continuity of scenes and model predictive uncertainty, our approach characterizes model-perceived scene complexity via frame-level temporal scene variations and decision deviations. To uncover latent scene-to-parameter correspondences, we encode this characterization into scene-aware tokens, alongside two specialized queries. A budget-conditioned layer routing mechanism evaluates these refined queries to allocate a budget that determines the active parameter ratio and subsequently selects appropriate layer combinations. The entire framework is optimized end-to-end. Extensive evaluations on the Bench2Drive benchmark show that when adapted to a state-of-the-art VLA model, our approach significantly reduces inference-time computational overhead by 53.5\% with negligible degradation in driving and language capabilities. Code is available at https:github.com/yang-luvu/Scene-Adaptive-VLA.

Introduction sec:introduction Built on Vision-Language Models (VLMs), Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have emerged as a dominant paradigm in autonomous driving, unifying visual perception, linguistic reasoning, and action prediction within a cohesive framework xu2025drivegpt4,sima2024drivelm,renz2025simlingo,fu2025orion . However, the massive parameter scale of VLA models creates severe onboard computational resource pressure for real-time inference, directly increasing energy consumption and reducing vehicle battery range. Consequently, minimizing computational overhead without compromising driving capability and explainability has become a paramount objective in VLA-based autonomous driving research zhou2025autovla,yang2025drivemoe . Currently, efforts to improve inference efficiency in VLMs can be broadly categorized into two directions: sequential adaptation, which dynamically adjusts the number of input or output tokens based on the task shang2025llava,liu2026global,zhang2025continue,zhang2025adaptthink , and structural adaptation, which selectively activates model parameters during inference to adapt to the task xu2025learning . In the domain of VLA-based autonomous driving, existing efficient inference strategies predominantly focus on sequential adaptation, such as adjusting the length of Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning zhou2025autovla or modulating input token counts based on the scene yang2025drivemoe . Conversely, structural adaptation remains largely underexplored. As illustrated in Fig.~ fig:introduction (a), the ratio of parameters required for successful driving varies significantly across scenes of varying complexity. Structural adaptation thus holds substantial potential to enable dynamic, task-aware adjustment of active parameters, thereby facilitating efficient autonomous driving. Furthermore, varying the active parameter ratio and combination yields distinctly different performance within identical scenes as shown in Fig.~ fig:introduction (b) and (c). Therefore, we aim to design a VLA framework that dynamically determines the optimal parameter ratio and combination for each driving frame. However, establishing this scene-to-parameter mapping is non-trivial due to the considerable diversity of driving scenes and the abstract nature of model capabilities. Specifically, determining the scene-to-parameter ratio is challenging because perceiving scene complexity and translating it into a measure of required model capacity is a highly implicit process. Furthermore, optimizing the scene-to-parameter combination is complex. Accurately selecting optimal active parameters for a specific driving scene is complicated by the entangled black-box nature of neural networks and the high variance of driving scenarios. To address these challenges, we propose Scene-Adaptive VLA, an efficient VLA-based autonomous driving framework leveraging dynamic layer routing. Inspired by the temporal continuity of driving scenes and model predictive uncertainty theory ovadia2019can,lakshminarayanan2017simple,cao2024pasco , Scene-Adaptive VLA characterizes model-perceived scene complexity via frame-level temporal scene variations and decision deviations. To uncover latent scene-to-parameter correspondences, we formulate scene-aware tokens that encode the aforementioned scene characterization, alongside two specialized queries: a budget token for determining parameter ratios and a routing token for selecting layer combinations. After processing these tokens through shallow layers of the Large Language Model (LLM) to capture their complex interdependencies, we introduce a budget-conditioned layer routing mechanism. This mechanism evaluates the refined queries to first determine the active parameter ratio and subsequently route inputs to the optimal layer combinations. Finally, the entire framework is optimized via two-stage fine-tuning supervised by both driving performance and resource consumption, effectively establishing an efficient scene-to-parameter mapping. Theoretically, our framework can be integrated into prevailing VLA architectures that employ dense backbones. To validate its effectiveness under hardware constraints, we adapt our framework to SimLingo renz2025simlingo , which achieves optimal performance with minimal parameter scale in VLA-based driving models. The main contributions of this work are summarized as follows: 1. A novel formulation for the characterization of model-perceived scene complexity. Leveraging temporal continuity of driving scenes and model predictive uncertainty theory, it effectively characterizes scene complexity via temporal frame-level driving scene variations and decision deviations, encoding them into scene-aware tokens. 2. A lightweight, budget-conditioned routing mechanism for efficient dynamic parameter activation. Utilizing two queries alongside the extracted scene-aware tokens and the LLM's shallow layers, this mechanism dynamically allocates a real-time inference budget to determine the active parameter ratio and selects the optimal parameter combination via layer routing, all optimized end-to-end. 3. Exceptional closed-loop performance on the Bench2Drive benchmark. When adapted to the state-of-the-art (SOTA) VLA-based driving model, our framework achieves a 53.5 reduction in inference-time computational overhead with negligible degradation in driving proficiency and language capabilities, as demonstrated by extensive evaluations on the Bench2Drive benchmark and language tasks. Related Work VLA-based End-to-end Autonomous Driving. End-to-end autonomous driving has witnessed rapid advancements in recent years. These frameworks integrate perception and planning within unified architectures to enhance driving efficacy hu2023planning,jiang2023vad . To address complex long-tail scenarios, recent approaches integrate VLMs either for language-centric scenario understanding park2024vlaad, sima2024drivelm or for guiding downstream driving models pan2024vlp, jiang2024senna . However, these decoupled paradigms lack direct end-to-end optimization grounded in continuous actions. Consequently, VLA architectures have emerged to directly couple VLMs with action generation. While Drivegpt4-v2 xu2025drivegpt4 maps multimodal inputs to control signals and EMMA hwang2024emma unifies tasks via plain text representations, a critical modality gap remains. To bridge this gap between semantic reasoning and numerical control, ORION fu2025orion incorporates a generative planner alongside a query-based temporal module, enabling unified optimization for scenario reasoning and trajectory prediction. Concurrently, SimLingo renz2025simlingo enforces strict language-action alignment via an auxiliary task trained on synthetic instruction-action pairs, yielding superior performance in closed-loop evaluation. Efficient VLA-based Model Inference in Autonomous Driving. Despite their formidable capabilities, the immense parameter scale of VLA models imposes a prohibitive computational burden on vehicular hardware. To address this, recent studies have explored efficient inference strategies. For instance, AutoVLA zhou2025autovla reduces reasoning overhead by introducing a fast-and-slow thinking mechanism that dynamically adjusts CoT lengths via Group Relative Policy Optimization shao2024deepseekmath (GRPO). Similarly, DriveMoE yang2025drivemoe alleviates the cost of long vision sequences by employing a Mixture-of-Experts architecture with on-demand vision token filtering. While effective, these methods largely overlook active parameter redundancy during inference. Structural Adaptation in VLMs. Structural adaptation optimizes the performance-efficiency trade-off by dynamically allocating active parameters based on task demands. For Vision Transformers and LLMs, this is typically achieved by selectively dropping computational modules or employing adaptive early-exit mechanisms zhu2025ea, meng2020ar, rotem2023finding . Extending these paradigms to VLMs, AdaLLaVA xu2025learning introduces a framework that selectively disables entire Transformer layers using binary switches under an inference latency constraint. For structural adaptation in VLA-based autonomous driving, it is essential to determine the optimal parameter activation ratio and enable flexible parameter combinations conditioned on driving scenes. Thus, we adopt a similar paradigm to achieve active-ratio-aware layer selection for VLA models. Scene-Adaptive VLA sec:Scene-Adaptive-VLA To validate our method under hardware constraints, we adapt it to SimLingo renz2025simlingo , a VLA driving model that achieves optimal performance with minimal parameters. As illustrated in Fig.~ fig:method , our approach enables scene-adaptive parameter activation through two core components. First, Model-Perceived Complexity Characterization encodes scene complexity into scene-aware tokens by quantifying temporal visual variations and inter-frame decision deviations. Second, Budget-Conditioned Layer Routing dynamically allocates a real-time computational budget to dictate the active parameter ratio and layer combinations. These decisions are governed by budget and layer routing queries, which are processed in the shallow layers of the LLM alongside scene-aware tokens to capture scene-parameter correlations. The training proceeds in two stages. Stage 1 employs SFT with randomized budgets to initialize scene and routing representations. Stage 2 leverages GRPO shao2024deepseekmath for end-to-end optimization, utilizing a composite reward derived from driving proficiency and computational overhead. Framework Base VLA Model. The backbone is InternVL2-1B gao2024mini , comprising the InternViT-300M vision encoder and the Qwen2-0.5B-Instruct yang2407qwen2 LLM. To ensure lightweight and efficient execution, we partition the language model into shallow prefix layers and subsequent routable layers. We augment this architecture with two compact multi-layer perceptron (MLP) schedulers. Operating on intermediate features extracted by the prefix layers, these schedulers leverage the infused scene-aware tokens and specialized queries to dynamically determine the routing plan for the remaining layers without introducing substantial computational overhead. title: TrajWAM: An Efficient Trajectory-Guided World Action Model for Dynamic Robotic Manipulation
summary: Dynamic object manipulation requires robots to anticipate target motion while replanning fast enough to avoid executing outdated actions. Existing approaches either rely on fast reactive control without an explicit future target state or encode anticipated motion only implicitly. World Action Models (WAMs) offer a promising alternative by coupling future visual prediction with action generation, but scene-level video objectives may underrepresent target dynamics that are critical for manipulation, while iterative video-action denoising introduces substantial latency. We present TrajWAM, a trajectory-guided world action model for efficient dynamic robotic manipulation. Our key insight is to explicitly ground future visual imagination in predicted target-object motion and use the resulting future representation to condition action generation, while preserving this anticipation pathway after acceleration. Given a short history of object masks, a history-conditioned motion predictor forecasts future masks encoding the target object's trajectory. A lightweight Trajectory ControlNet then steers a pretrained video model toward trajectory-consistent futures. The resulting future representation conditions an action expert to predict executable action chunks. To enable one-step inference without breaking this interface, we introduce a decoupled distillation scheme that combines distribution matching for the video backbone, Trajectory ControlNet realignment, and action rollout distillation to support accurate one-step action prediction conditioned on the compressed future representation. Comprehensive evaluations in simulation and the real world show that TrajWAM achieves state-of-the-art performance on dynamic object manipulation tasks while enabling efficient one-step video-action inference. Project page: https://kevingeng3.github.io/TrajWAM/.

Introduction sec:introduction Dynamic object manipulation is essential for robots operating in human environments, factories, and warehouses, where task-relevant objects may continue moving while the robot perceives and acts~ 10948321, c2rope, sope . Unlike static manipulation, in which the target state is approximately fixed between observation and execution, dynamic manipulation couples perception, prediction, and control in a continuously changing scene. An action that is appropriate for the current observation may therefore become outdated before execution, and even a small delay may lead to a missed grasp or inaccurate contact. Successful dynamic manipulation consequently requires both anticipation of the target object's motion and sufficiently fast closed-loop replanning. World Action Models (WAMs) have recently emerged as a promising alternative to vision-language-action policies by coupling future visual prediction with action generation ~ bi2025motusunifiedlatentaction, ye2026worldactionmodelszeroshot, li2026causalworldmodelingrobot . By modeling how observations evolve under interaction, WAMs provide an additional physical prior for control and are particularly appealing for dynamic manipulation. However, as illustrated in Fig.~ fig:teaser , existing WAMs predict scene evolution at the full-frame level, where robot-induced changes can dominate the imagined future. In dynamic manipulation, task success may instead depend critically on target motion that evolves independently of the robot's actions. A scene-level forecast entangles robot motion, background dynamics, and target-object motion, making the task-relevant trajectory only indirectly represented and difficult to control explicitly during generation. Extending WAMs to dynamic object manipulation thus calls for an object-centric future representation that specifies the anticipated spatial trajectory of the target while remaining coupled to action prediction. Moreover, most existing WAMs synthesize future videos and actions through iterative denoising, introducing latency that can make the resulting prediction stale before execution. Recent methods reduce this cost either by skipping future imagination during inference~ yuan2026fastwamworldactionmodels, ye2026gigaworldpolicyefficientactioncenteredworldaction or by compressing the denoising process~ li2026efficientwam1bparameterworldactionmodel, akbari2026flashwammodalityawaredistillationworld, cai2026ahawamasynchronoushorizonadaptiveworldactionmodeling . However, the former sacrifices an explicit predictive pathway for anticipating target motion, while the latter leaves open whether a spatially explicit motion condition can remain effective after aggressive denoising compression. To address these challenges, we propose TrajWAM, a trajectory-guided world action model for efficient dynamic robotic manipulation. Our key insight is to explicitly incorporate predicted target-object motion into future visual imagination and propagate its influence to action generation through the resulting video representation. Starting from a short observation history, TrajWAM predicts how the task-relevant object will evolve and represents this motion as a sequence of future object masks. These predicted masks provide an explicit spatial guide for future generation, steering the world model toward futures that are consistent with the anticipated target motion. The resulting imagined future then conditions action prediction, allowing the robot to act not only on what is currently observed, but also on where the target is expected to be. The remaining challenge is to make this anticipation pathway fast enough for dynamic control. Simply bypassing future imagination would remove the mechanism through which predicted target motion influences the action, while naively compressing the generative process can degrade both trajectory controllability and downstream action prediction. We therefore introduce a decoupled one-step distillation strategy that accelerates the video and action generation processes according to their different requirements. The video pathway is distilled while explicitly preserving its response to trajectory guidance, whereas the action pathway is distilled to retain accurate predictions under the compressed future representation. In this way, TrajWAM substantially reduces inference latency without discarding the trajectory-guided future imagination that enables anticipatory control. We evaluate TrajWAM on dynamic manipulation tasks in both simulated and real-world settings, covering diverse object categories, motion patterns, and task types. On DOMINO, as shown in Fig.~ fig:teaser (b), TrajWAM achieves state-of-the-art performance with a success rate of 43.54 , outperforming the strongest evaluated baseline by 14.24 percentage points at an inference latency of 108.5\, ms. In real-world experiments, TrajWAM achieves success rates of 77.9 on conveyor-belt grasping and 70.4 on rotating-disc grasping, consistently outperforming the evaluated baselines. Our contributions are summarized as follows: We introduce TrajWAM, a trajectory-guided world action model that explicitly incorporates predicted target-object motion into future visual imagination and propagates this anticipation to downstream action prediction. We develop a decoupled one-step distillation strategy that accelerates video and action generation while preserving trajectory controllability and accurate future-conditioned action prediction. Extensive experiments in simulation and on real robots establish state-of-the-art dynamic manipulation performance while demonstrating efficient one-step inference and the effectiveness of trajectory-guided anticipation. Related Work World Action Models and Dynamic Robotic Manipulation Vision-language-action models have made substantial progress in robot manipulation by directly mapping visual observations and language instructions to actions~ kim2024openvlaopensourcevisionlanguageactionmodel,black2026pi0visionlanguageactionflowmodel . World-action models (WAMs) extend this paradigm by jointly modeling future observations and executable actions, using visual dynamics prediction as an additional physical prior for control. Recent WAMs have studied different ways to balance future imagination and action execution. Fast-WAM~ yuan2026fastwamworldactionmodels shows that explicit future generation can be skipped at inference, while AHA-WAM~ cai2026ahawamasynchronoushorizonadaptiveworldactionmodeling and HarmoWAM~ feng2026harmowamharmonizinggeneralizableprecise further improve the temporal coordination between world prediction and action generation. Dynamic manipulation requires anticipating the motion of objects that move independently of the robot. DOMINO~ fang2026generalizableroboticmanipulationdynamic exposes the resulting performance degradation, while DynamicVLA~ xie2026dynamicvlavisionlanguageactionmodeldynamic and PUMA~ fang2026generalizableroboticmanipulationdynamic address it through low-latency inference and implicit object-motion prediction, respectively. DynamicWAM~ lou2026dynamicwamdualpathmotionconditioning incorporates recent motion into WAMs through dual-path flow conditioning, whereas TrajWAM predicts future target-object mask trajectories to guide future imagination for action prediction. Trajectory-Controllable Video Generation Trajectory-controllable video generation aims to synthesize videos that follow explicit spatial motion conditions, complementing text- or image-conditioned generation where object motion is often under-specified. Existing methods use point tracks or trajectories for fine-grained motion control~ zhang2025toratrajectoryorienteddiffusiontransformer , bounding boxes or tracklets to guide object locations~ wang2024boximatorgeneratingrichcontrollable and interactions~ li2024trackdiffusiontrackletconditionedvideogeneration , and 3D or depth-aware trajectories to reduce ambiguity in object motion~ wang2025levitor3dtrajectoryoriented . More recently, MagicMotion~ li2025magicmotioncontrollablevideogeneration proposes dense-to-sparse trajectory guidance with masks, boxes, and sparse boxes, improving trajectory adherence and object consistency. We build on this idea of explicit motion conditioning, but use it as a future-imagination mechanism inside WAMs: future object masks are predicted from observation history and injected into the video branch to support downstream dynamic manipulation. Distillation for Diffusion-Based Models Dynamic manipulation requires low-latency inference, since the policy must continuously update actions while objects move. This is challenging for diffusion-based WAMs, where both future imagination and action generation rely on iterative denoising. Diffusion distillation provides a common way to reduce sampling steps~ salimans2022progressivedistillationfastsampling,song2023consistencymodels,luo2023latentconsistencymodelssynthesizing , and has been extended to efficient video generation~ wang2023videolcmvideolatentconsistency,li2024t2vturbobreakingqualitybottleneck and trajectory-controllable generation~ li2026flashmotionfewstepcontrollablevideo . Recent WAMs also explore this direction: Flash-WAM~ akbari2026flashwammodalityawaredistillationworld proposes modality-aware step distillation for joint video-action diffusion, while AHA-WAM-Flash~ cai2026ahawamasynchronoushorizonadaptiveworldactionmodeling applies ODE distillation to compress its action sampler from multi-step denoising to few-step inference. While these works primarily improve the efficiency of existing WAM inference pipelines, preserving trajectory controllability and action accuracy under compression remains underexplored. title: Long-Horizon Multi-Object Rearrangement via Distilled Tree Search over Continuous Actions
comment: Accepted at CoRL 2026 (Oral). Project page: https://distilled-search.github.io
summary: Despite recent advances in policy learning, long-horizon manipulation remains difficult because learned policies must avoid compounding errors while preserving future feasibility. While search-based planning can explicitly reason over such future consequences, it quickly becomes expensive in high-dimensional continuous action spaces. This raises a central question: how can long-horizon reasoning from search be transferred into policies in continuous action spaces? To this end, we propose DISCO: Distilled Tree Search over Continuous Actions. DISCO uses progressive-widening MCTS in physics simulation to generate long-horizon plans. During search, a learned policy proposes continuous actions, while a learned value function scores actions by their expected progress toward task completion. Using GPU-parallelized simulation, DISCO periodically distills MCTS-generated plans into the policy-value model, improving the action proposals and value estimates used in subsequent searches. Finally, the learned policy-value model can be directly deployed without the need for simulator-based search at test time. Across simulated and real-world rearrangement tasks, DISCO outperforms behavior cloning, reinforcement learning, and search-based baselines.
full_text: Long-Horizon Multi-Object Rearrangement via Distilled Tree Search over Continuous Actions Kallol Saha , \ Yining Hong , \ Amber Li , \ Yejin Choi , \\[5px] \ Maxim Likhachev , \ David Held \\[5px] Robotics Institute, Carnegie Mellon University \ \ \ \ \ \ Stanford University \\[7px] Despite recent advances in policy learning, long-horizon manipulation remains difficult because learned policies must avoid compounding errors while preserving future feasibility. While search-based planning can explicitly reason over such future consequences, it quickly becomes expensive in high-dimensional continuous action spaces. This raises a central question: how can long-horizon reasoning from search be transferred into policies in continuous action spaces? To this end, we propose DISCO: Distilled Tree Search over Continuous Actions. DISCO uses progressive-widening MCTS in physics simulation to generate long-horizon plans. During search, a learned policy proposes continuous actions, while a learned value function scores actions by their expected progress toward task completion. Using GPU-parallelized simulation, DISCO periodically distills MCTS-generated plans into the policy-value model, improving the action proposals and value estimates used in subsequent searches. Finally, the learned policy-value model can be directly deployed without the need for simulator-based search at test time. Across simulated and real-world rearrangement tasks, DISCO outperforms behavior cloning, reinforcement learning, and search-based baselines. Website: Introduction sec:intro Robot learning has advanced rapidly in recent years, enabling neural network policies to acquire complex behaviors across a wide range of tasks in robot manipulation~ 3dfa,3dda,peract,rvt,bridgevla,zhou2023hacman,jiang2024hacmanpp . Despite their strong performance on short-horizon behaviors, these methods still struggle with long-horizon manipulation tasks such as multi-object rearrangement~ stilman2007mamo, saha2025spot, huang2024points2plans, wang2022efficient, kee2023sdf, kulshrestha2023structural, wu2022transporters . Such tasks require reasoning over many sequential decisions, where each action must be locally feasible while preserving future task feasibility. This makes behavior-cloned policies brittle: errors compound over long sequences~ simchowitz2025pitfalls, ross2011dagger , and short-horizon supervision does not capture how early actions affect later success~ learning2search, learningtrialserrorsreflective, sailor . For example, shelf packing requires fine-grained pick-and-place actions that are feasible and preserve space for later objects (Figure~ fig:teaser ). Meanwhile, search-based planning~ m4m_icra2023, em4m_icaps2023, improvedm4m_icra2024, cuTAMP, forwardsearchplanning provides a natural mechanism for reasoning over future consequences of an action, by evaluating whether it leads to successful downstream configurations. Building on this, the integration of learning with tree search has been powerful in solving long-horizon decision-making problems like Go, chess, and Atari. Most notably, AlphaGo~ alphago, alphago-zero, muzero, anthony2017exit combines Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS)~ banditmcts,mctssurvey with learned policy and value networks to achieve strong sequential reasoning capabilities. In these systems, search explores the future consequences of actions, while learned policies and value functions guide exploration toward promising regions of the decision space. However, these domains are highly structured, with discrete actions and exact transition dynamics. In contrast, robots see noisy, partially-occluded observations such as point clouds and operate in continuous action spaces. As a result, naively applying tree search quickly becomes computationally expensive. This raises a question: how can the long-horizon reasoning of search be transferred into learned policies for robot manipulation in continuous state-action spaces? In this work, we take a step toward bridging this gap with DISCO, a framework for DIstilled tree Search over COntinuous actions. DISCO combines a learned manipulation policy with MCTS using progressive widening to efficiently search over continuous action spaces~ chaslot2008progressive,continuous-uct,mcts-optimization . The policy proposes continuous grasp-and-place actions conditioned on point clouds, while a learned value function estimates long-term task completion to guide search towards promising regions. To efficiently explore the space of feasible long-horizon plans, we leverage GPU-parallelized simulation for batched node expansion and rollout evaluation~ huang2022parallel,cuTAMP . Similar to AlphaGo, DISCO distills MCTS-generated plans back into both the policy and the value function, allowing search to progressively discover long-horizon plans. The distillation process also enables DISCO to directly execute long-horizon behaviors during execution (Figure~ fig:teaser ). Search and simulation are used only during training: DISCO trains one shared policy-value model per task on randomized simulated instances, and at test time this model acts directly from point clouds on unseen instances, without search or a simulator. In this way, DISCO incorporates long-horizon reasoning capabilities into manipulation policies through iterative search-based self-improvement. We evaluate DISCO on several challenging multi-object rearrangement tasks in simulation and in the real world. We observe that DISCO achieves stronger long-horizon success than behavior cloning, reinforcement learning, sampling-based optimization, and alternative search-based planners. We also show that DISCO benefits from both policy-guided expansion and progressive widening, scales with task complexity, and transfers to real-world manipulation tasks. Our main contributions are:\\[3px] (1) We show that long-horizon behavior can be bootstrapped purely from short-horizon data (e.g., single-object pick-and-place) by using MCTS with progressive widening to search over continuous state-action spaces. This removes the need for expensive long-horizon demonstrations.\\[3px] (2) We show that DISCO self-improves both the policy and the value function through iterative distillation rounds, enabling search to progressively generate more long-horizon plans for supervision. \\[3px] (3) We show that the distilled point-cloud-conditioned policy-value model executes long-horizon tasks by direct rollout, without search or a simulator at test time, scales better than baselines as the number of objects increases, and transfers to held-out simulation tasks and a real robot. Related Work sec:related-work Combined Learning and Planning. Recent Task and Motion Planning (TAMP) methods~ tamp,pddlstream,cuTAMP incorporate learning for continuous samplers~ skillcomposing,silver2023neurosymbolicskills,chitnis2016guidedsearch,kim2019scorespace , symbolic abstractions and operators~ silver2021symbolicoperators,silver2023neurosymbolicskills,silver2023predicateinvention,curtis2022abstractions,IVNTR , skill and parameter models~ liang2022skillmodels,kumar2024practice , and search heuristics~ valuefunctiontamp,yang2023piginet,khodeir2023lazysearch,forwardsearchplanning . These methods rely on symbolic representations, whereas DISCO operates directly on point-cloud observations and predicts continuous actions. Skill-chaining methods~ skilldiscovery,lee2022adversarialskillchaining,genskillchaining,mosaic,logicskillprogramming,planning-with-diffusion compose temporally extended skills or options~ options,option-critic for long-horizon planning. Rather than learning a skill graph or composing separate skill models, DISCO distills plans into a policy-value model. World-model-based planning methods learn transition models for imagined rollouts or model-predictive control~ ha2018worldmodels, dino-wm, hafner2019planet,hafner2020dreamer,hansen2022tdmpc,li2025worldmodelrobotplanning,khorrambakht2025worldplanner . In contrast, DISCO does not learn a transition model, and uses physics simulation only during training to generate long-horizon supervision. Other approaches plan from point clouds using object-centric transformations~ saha2025spot , relational abstractions~ huang2024points2plans, huang2023erdtransformer,pairwiserd , or neural object descriptors~ simeonov2021long,cheng2024nodtamp . DISCO instead learns a closed-loop policy-value model and executes without explicit tree search at inference.\\[3px] Plan Distillation and Policy Learning. Prior work has distilled planning pipelines into neural policies, including TAMP imitation~ dalal2023optimus and neural motion-planner distillation~ mpd,saha2024edmp,dalal2024neuralmp,drp . Related learning-to-search methods~ learning2search,sailor train policies to reduce compounding errors from imitation learning~ ross2011dagger . In contrast, DISCO iterates between planning and learning: generated long-horizon plans update the policy-value model, which then guides subsequent plan generation. Recent 3D visuomotor policies map point clouds~ 3dfa,3dda,zhou2023hacman,jiang2024hacmanpp , voxel grids~ peract , or multi-view features~ rvt,bridgevla,manipgen directly to robot actions, but are typically trained from fixed-horizon demonstrations. DISCO instead self-generates long-horizon plans to train a closed-loop model for execution. \\[3px] Monte-Carlo Tree Search. For continuous high dimensional action spaces, prior work extends MCTS using progressive widening~ chaslot2008progressive,continuous-uct,mcts-optimization , learned action sampling~ kim2017guidingsearchcontinuousstateaction , policy priors~ pa-mcts,sampledmuzero , state abstraction~ iterativelyrefiningmcts , or prioritized branching~ improvedpomdptreesearch,monte-carlo-pomdp,onlinePOMDP . In robotics, MCTS has been used for nonprehensile rearrangement~ song2020multi , clutter retrieval~ huang2022visual,huang2022interleaving , batched long-horizon planning~ huang2022parallel , contact planning~ zhu2023efficient , confined-space rearrangement and occluded-object grasping~ ren2024multistage,kang2022grasp , multi-goal task planning~ pfeiffer2023monte , and world-model-based planning~ khorrambakht2025worldplanner,huang2025forgetree . AlphaGo-style systems further show that MCTS can be coupled with policy-value learning in a self-improving loop~ alphago,alphago-zero,muzero,anthony2017exit , and dual policy iteration~ sun2018dpi alternates between a planning policy and a learned reactive policy. Neural Tree Expansion~ riviere2021nte guides MCTS with learned policy-value models for continuous multi-robot planning, but runs MCTS online at test time, whereas DISCO runs MCTS only during training. DISCO extends progressive-widening MCTS over continuous actions into robot manipulation problems, using a point-cloud conditioned policy-value model that is iteratively improved during search. Problem Statement and Assumptions sec:problem We consider a distribution over long-horizon, multi-object robot manipulation task instances . Each instance consists of a discrete set of objects. The state is represented by a 6D pose for each object. The initial state varies across task instances. A goal state should satisfy , where checks whether the object poses complete the task instance, such as being placed in a shelf or stacked correctly. At test time, we only have access to a point cloud , with each point assigned a segmentation label for an object. We operate in a continuous action space , where an action is represented by target end-effector poses. We use motion planning~ curobo to convert the poses into a trajectory. During training, but not during inference, we assume access to a simulator ~ maniskill that executes an action to induce the next state . We define a valid plan as a sequence of states and actions, , satisfying the goal condition and the simulator transition constraint . title: AeroIntent: A Synchronized Multimodal Benchmark for UAV Mission Intent Recognition
summary: Reliable recognition of mission-level UAV intent from multimodal observations is essential for low-altitude airspace surveillance and security. Existing multimodal UAV datasets primarily support detection, tracking, and localization, leaving limited support for evaluating mission-intent recognition across held-out trajectory programs and incomplete radar histories. We introduce AeroIntent, a simulation-based benchmark comprising 990 synchronized multimodal sequences generated by 22 trajectory programs across five mission intents. The benchmark provides radar, RGB, infrared, and depth observations, together with program-disjoint, radar-gap, and observation-prefix evaluation protocols. Building on this benchmark, we propose AeroMIR, a structured Multimodal Intent Reasoner that integrates radar trajectories, derived behavioral features, selected visual evidence, and task knowledge for candidate-based UAV intent recognition. Under a strict program-disjoint protocol evaluating unseen tactical realizations, AeroMIR achieves a mean accuracy of 71.56% and a mean Macro-F1 of 69.84% across three seeds, outperforming the strongest trajectory-only baseline by 7.79 Macro-F1 points and a conventional radar-RGB late-fusion baseline by 19.32 points. AeroMIR also demonstrates strong performance under controlled radar gaps and early intent recognition settings. AeroIntent and AeroMIR provide a reproducible foundation for multimodal UAV intent recognition. The benchmark is available at: https://anonymous.4open.science/r/AeroIntent
full_text: Experiments sec:experiments Experimental Setup We evaluate three questions on the frozen tests in Sec.~ sec:dataset-protocol : intent recognition under unseen tactical realizations, with contiguous radar gaps, and early intent recognition. We report Accuracy and Macro-F1 as percentages, with population standard deviation across seeds 42/43/44. . Six trajectory models use the same 30-slot input: MLP, LSTM, GRU, Attention-TCN-BiGRU~ teng2021tcn , BLAC cross-attention BiLSTM~ niu2025blac , and Behavior-to-Language~ li2024behavior . The latter three are benchmark adaptations of the cited designs. A radar--RGB late-fusion control combines a two-layer bidirectional GRU with a compact, from-scratch CNN and an MLP classifier, using the same selected RGB frame as AeroMIR. The Lei-style zero-shot reference follows the prompt organization in~ lei2026towards , replacing its backbone with Qwen3-VL-2B-Instruct and supplying ground-truth payload in place of YOLO output. These comparisons cover motion encoders, conventional multimodal fusion, and a language-based architectural reference. AeroMIR additionally receives timestamps, frame-gap/validity information, and confidence in its structured evidence; the six-dimensional trajectory baselines do not receive separate time or mask channels. The comparisons therefore assess the complete input representations and models, rather than isolating the effect of multimodal fusion under identical temporal metadata. and evaluation. Classical models use train-only feature standardization, class-balanced loss, up to 80 epochs, and validation early stopping with patience 12. Late fusion uses RGB, batch size 24, learning rate , weight decay , and dropout 0.2. AeroMIR uses AdamW, learning rate , zero weight decay, 3 warmup, batch size one, and eight-step gradient accumulation. It trains for 20 epochs with the candidate objective; the checkpoint with highest validation Macro-F1 among epochs 10--20 is selected, breaking ties by Accuracy and then later epoch. Gap and Early require inference only, without condition-specific tuning. Generalization to Unseen Tactical Realizations sec:main-results Table~ tab:main reports the main results. AeroMIR achieves Accuracy and Macro-F1. Attention-TCN-BiGRU is the strongest trajectory baseline, at 67.85 Accuracy and 62.05 Macro-F1. AeroMIR improves these means by 3.71 and 7.79 points, respectively, and exceeds radar--RGB late fusion by 19.32 Macro-F1 points. Figure~ fig:confusion-comparison further resolves the recognition patterns of individual intent classes. The gains in transit, probe, and strike come at the cost of lower reconnaissance recall (71.9 versus 99.3 for Attention-TCN-BiGRU). AeroMIR improves transit recall from 75.56 to 94.07 and probe recall from 2.96 to 24.44 relative to Attention-TCN-BiGRU, while strike recall rises from 88.89 to 94.07 . The Lei-style zero-shot reference reaches 13.64 Macro-F1 with the same backbone and ground-truth payload. Together with the supervised comparisons, this shows that access to a general-purpose MLLM and perception summaries alone does not solve the benchmark. The full improvement combines structured representation, pretraining, and supervised candidate adaptation. . On the split generated with seed 42, we train six candidate-CE variants using the same backbone, optimization settings, and frame-selection rule. a, b, and c use radar (R), derived behavior (B), and RGB (V) individually, whereas d, e, and f use R+B, R+V, and R+B+V, respectively. Their Macro-F1 values are 64.86, 46.53, 39.35, 65.93, 67.51, and , respectively, as shown in Fig.~ fig:evidence-ablation . Adding behavior to radar gives 1.07 points, while adding it when RGB is present gives 8.16 points. Adding RGB gives 2.65 points over radar alone and 9.74 points over radar plus behavior. Thus, on this matched split, the largest benefit occurs when explicit motion descriptors and visual evidence are interpreted together. Neither behavior-only nor RGB-only reproduces the full model's result. -choice sensitivity. We compare gap-guided selection with random, midpoint, terminal, and highest-visibility frame selection on the complete program-disjoint test sets. Each of the three seeds (42/43/44) includes 225 test sequences, with 45 sequences per intent class. We keep the non-image evidence fixed, varying only the selected RGB frame. We report the unweighted mean of the three seed-wise Macro-F1: 69.84/68.10/68.67/68.46/67.95 , respectively. The results show that the gap-guided rule provides a modest advantage over alternative frame-selection strategies, although the improvement is limited. This suggests that temporal frame selection is beneficial, but should be regarded as a practical evidence-selection choice rather than a major independent source of performance gains. Controlled Radar-Gap Recognition sec:gap We evaluate recognition under contiguous radar outages using the same program-disjoint test splits as the main experiment. For each sample, we remove one contiguous interval from the original Echo sequence, resample the remaining target states to 30 slots, and recompute velocities and behavioral descriptors. Gap levels 0/10/20/30/40 specify the removed interval's duration as a percentage of the full recording. A sample-specific random anchor, fixed for reproducibility, defines nested intervals across gap levels. All methods share the same radar deletions, while RGB observations remain uncorrupted. At each nonzero gap level, AeroMIR and Radar--RGB Late Fusion reselect their RGB frames using the same gap-guided rule applied to the remaining radar observations. The Lei-style zero-shot reference consistently uses the first RGB frame of the full recording. All models remain frozen throughout the evaluation. As shown in Fig.~ fig:gap , AeroMIR achieves the highest mean Macro-F1 across all five gap levels. With an interval covering 40 of the recording duration removed, it achieves 59.50 Macro-F1, exceeding the strongest trajectory baseline, Attention-TCN-BiGRU, by 6.30 percentage points (53.20 ). It also outperforms radar--RGB late fusion by 14.08 points (45.42 ), showing that the benefit extends beyond simply providing both sensing modalities. Across the tested gap range, AeroMIR achieves a normalized Macro-F1 AUC of 63.08, compared with 57.67 for Attention-TCN-BiGRU (Table~ tab:temporal ). Its mean Macro-F1 decreases from 69.84 at Gap0 to 59.50 at Gap40 and remains the highest among the compared methods at all tested gap levels. These results support the effectiveness of structured multimodal evidence integration for intent recognition when contiguous portions of the radar history are unavailable. Early Recognition sec:early We next evaluate how recognition performance evolves as observations accumulate on the held-out programs. Figure~ fig:early reports results at 25 , 50 , 75 , and 100 coverage of the ordered 30-slot radar history, corresponding to prefixes of 8, 15, 23, and 30 slots. Each partial prefix is resampled to 30 slots, after which velocities and behavioral descriptors are recomputed. For RGB selection, AeroMIR and Radar-RGB Late Fusion apply gap-guided RGB selection using only radar observations and RGB frames available up to the corresponding prefix endpoint. The Lei-style zero-shot reference consistently uses the first RGB frame of each recording. Coverage is defined over observation slots rather than elapsed flight time. Each method uses its frozen full-data checkpoint throughout the evaluation. AeroMIR demonstrates strong early intent recognition once sufficient partial evidence becomes available. At P25, it achieves 44.42 Macro-F1, trailing Attention-TCN-BiGRU by 2.90 points. However, AeroMIR leads all compared methods from P50 onward, reaching 58.54 Macro-F1 at P50 and 66.97 at P75, with gains of 5.72 and 9.88 percentage points over Attention-TCN-BiGRU, respectively. Notably, with only 75 of the radar observation slots, AeroMIR exceeds the strongest baseline's full-observation Macro-F1 by 4.92 points and falls just 2.87 points below its own full-observation performance. These results show that AeroMIR can recognize task-level intent effectively before the complete trajectory is observed. Table~ tab:temporal summarizes performance using normalized trapezoidal AUC over P25/P50/P75/P100. AeroMIR achieves an Early AUC of 60.88, outperforming Attention-TCN-BiGRU by 6.01 points and supporting its overall advantage under partial observations.

title: Beyond Geometric Closure: Measuring and Diagnosing Mechanical Consistency in Visual Dynamics
comment: 34 pages, including supplementary material; 16 figures and 38 tables
summary: Visual accuracy leaves open whether predicted motion obeys dynamics. We introduce a framework for measuring and diagnosing mechanical consistency in visual dynamics. An independent SI audit of rigid closed chains separates geometric admissibility, reaction-free actuator effort, and work--energy balance. Continuous scoring measures progress against fixed engineering targets, while reference replay quantifies measurement error. With three seeds per setting, we evaluate KeyCLD and CON across 343 planar assemblies at 64/256 pixels and V-JEPA + AC and LingBot-VA on 100 shared spatial test assemblies. CON reduces image MSE by 37.6%/37.2% relative to persistence, yet neither planar model attains valid native geometry. At 256 pixels, calibrated RGB replay places forecast errors far above measurement error. With exact states, KeyCLD preserves geometry and RK4 training raises its score from 52.65 to 64.30. In both spatial pathways, CAD/IK reconstruction restores geometry while mean actuator residuals exceed five times the engineering targets. The interventions distinguish gains in visual prediction and geometric admissibility from remaining force and energy errors.

Introduction sec:intro Picking objects, folding garments, and opening doors require predictions that support physical interaction. We study mechanical consistency: agreement between predicted motion and independently specified geometry, forces, and work in SI units. Evaluating these relations connects visual prediction to the actuator demands of physical interaction. Rigid closed chains make these relations concrete. Their closure constraints define admissible configurations, while speed and acceleration along the same path determine different actuator demands. A prediction can therefore trace a valid shape and still require the wrong torque, providing a controlled setting for diagnosing mechanical consistency. Our independent SI audit first checks the predicted configuration, then eliminates unknown joint reactions to evaluate actuator effort and work--energy balance ( ). Reference replay and targeted interventions locate errors in coordinate readout, numerical integration, and the learned force model. We apply the audit to constrained Lagrangian dynamics (KeyCLD)~ daems2024keycld and latent coupled oscillators (CON)~ stolzle2024con at two planar image resolutions, then to predictive features (V-JEPA 2.1 + AC)~ murlabadia2026vjepa2_1,assran2025vjepa2 and generative video--action modeling (LingBot-VA)~ li2026causal on Stewart and Delta mechanisms. Resolution and measurement controls test whether physical failures persist as visual information and localization accuracy improve. We contribute (1) a six-criterion framework for mechanical consistency and tracking, with continuous SI tolerance scoring; (2) reference calibration and interventions that separate observation, integration, and constitutive effects; and (3) a 343-assembly planar benchmark at two resolutions and a 100-test-assembly spatial study, spanning four modeling paradigms. title: Vision-Language-Delta-Action: Learning Compact Deltas as Actionable Transition Interfaces for Robotic Manipulation
summary: Robotic manipulation is not merely observation-to-action generation, but the realization of task-specified state changes in the physical world. Existing vision-language-action (VLA) methods directly learn observation-to-action mappings, imposing a substantial learning burden due to the gap between semantic understanding and action execution. Although world-action models (WAMs) improve control through future prediction, modeling complete future states wastes capacity on static appearance and action-irrelevant changes. We propose Vision-Language-Delta-Action (VLDA), a paradigm that reformulates full future prediction as compact actionable transition modeling. Its core is a compact Delta variable that captures latent world-state changes, serving as an interface between vision-language understanding and action generation. VLDA learns Delta through a unified objective composed of the Local Transition Filter (LT-Filter) and Global Transition Anchor (GT-Anchor). LT-Filter captures task-relevant manipulation-centric changes while suppressing static reconstruction biases. GT-Anchor provides coarse future-level regularization to preserve the overall direction of state changes. Delta-Driven Action Refinement (DDAR) further grounds Delta in the action manifold and injects it as a structured seed to guide action denoising. We implement VLDA within LoongForge, an open-source training framework for large-scale foundation and embodied models, using its modular and distributed infrastructure for unified two-stage optimization. Experiments show that VLDA improves long-horizon consistency, robustness, and generalization, validating actionable Delta as an alternative to direct action prediction and full future-state modeling.

As shown in Fig.~ fig:intro (top), conditioned on visual observations, a robot must not only recognize the current scene and interpret the task-relevant physical context around it~ oft, pi05 , but also determine which part of the scene should change and how such change can be realized through continuous action execution~ souvcek2024genhowto, alayrac2017joint . This requirement fundamentally distinguishes robotic manipulation from generic vision-language understanding, as the critical decision variable is not the complete visual state itself, but the task-relevant transition that drives the current state toward the desired physical outcome. r 0.48 fig:intro However, existing VLA and WAM paradigms share a common limitation in lacking a dedicated, action-grounded representation of task-relevant physical transitions. Most VLA models still follow an observation-to-action formulation that entangles task-relevant object identification~ openvla, pi0, yuan2026qwen, zheng2025x , desired physical state-change inference, and executable action-chunk generation within a single policy. Without dedicated modeling of task-relevant state changes, the policy must implicitly infer the intended physical transition from action supervision alone, leaving a substantial representational gap between semantic understanding and action execution. A straightforward way to bridge semantic understanding and action execution is future modeling, as illustrated in Fig.~ fig:intro (a) and (b). WAMs predict future observations~ cotvla, cen2025worldvla, yuan2026fast , visual latents~ sun2026vlajepa, lu2024manigaussian , or action-conditioned dynamics~ vjepa2, jiang2025enerverse to provide temporal cues beyond the current observation. However, they typically represent the future as another complete state, causing task-relevant transition cues to remain entangled with static scene content and action-irrelevant variations. Moreover, future prediction is often used only as an auxiliary objective, without providing a structured intermediate variable that can directly guide action generation. Robotic manipulation instead requires a compact transition variable that captures task-relevant manipulation-centric changes, remains consistent with the overall direction of future evolution, and is directly grounded in executable actions. Taken together, these limitations motivate a transition interface that is selective, predictive, and actionable. It should isolate task-relevant manipulation-centric changes, remain consistent with future evolution, and be directly consumable by the action generator. To this end, we propose , a new paradigm that models actionable transitions through a low-dimensional Delta interface rather than predicting the complete future state. Specifically, VLDA instantiates the transition interface as a compact low-dimensional that captures the task-relevant transition implied by the task. Together, these constraints reconcile local transition selectivity with global predictive consistency, yielding a compact and future-grounded representation of task-relevant physical change. To make Delta directly actionable, VLDA further introduces , which grounds Delta in the action manifold through Delta-action alignment and injects it into the action flow as a structured transition seed. The action expert then refines this transition-informed seed into executable action chunks conditioned on the predicted transition. Rather than treating future prediction as auxiliary supervision, VLDA therefore establishes a closed , where vision-language representations interpret the task context, Delta specifies the required state transition, and DDAR realizes that transition through continuous action generation. We evaluate VLDA on standard robotic manipulation benchmarks and challenging long-horizon tasks. Experimental results show that VLDA improves long-horizon consistency, robustness under distribution shifts, and generalization to complex manipulation scenarios. These results demonstrate that modeling actionable Delta provides a more effective alternative to both direct observation-to-action learning and full future-state prediction. Related Work sec:related Observation-to-Action Learning in VLA Models. Existing VLA models primarily employ action-token prediction, implemented either autoregressively or in parallel~ Rt-2, openvla, oft, hu2026ar, shao2025large, li2026consisvla , and continuous action experts based on diffusion or flow matching~ diff, pi0, pi05, wen2025dexvla, li2026unimpa, hu2026abstraction, li2026global . This creates a substantial gap between high-level semantic observations and low-level executable actions. VLDA bridges this gap with a compact Delta that explicitly mediates what should change and how that change is executed. Predictive World-Action Modeling. Recent WAMs couple future modeling with robot control through cascaded future-to-action generation~ tian2024predictive, li2026causal, zhu2026h , joint world-action prediction~ guo2024prediction, cen2025worldvla, yuan2026fast, zhu2026learning , and predictive latent dynamics~ hu2024video, huang2025ladi, miao2026jepavla . VLDA instead reparameterizes the prediction-control connection through a compact Delta, whose control role is explicitly defined by transition learning and Delta-driven action refinement. Discrete approaches tokenize visually inferred motion patterns for scalable VLA pretraining~ ye2024latent, univla, chen2025villa , while continuous formulations learn smooth latent control variables that can be mapped to embodiment-specific actions with limited supervision~ liang2025clam, tharwat2025latent . title: Spectral-Aware Proposal Enhancement for Diffusion-Based Multispectral UAV Multi-Object Tracking
comment: Accepted for publication in IEEE Geoscience and Remote Sensing Letters. 5 pages, 4 figures, 3 tables. Author accepted version
summary: Multispectral UAV multi-object tracking (MOT) with oriented bounding boxes remains challenging due to small targets, cluttered backgrounds, and unstable inter-frame associations. Although diffusion-based MOT provides an effective iterative proposal refinement paradigm, existing diffusion-based trackers lack dedicated designs for exploiting multispectral cues in proposal initialization and confidence calibration, limiting tracking robustness in complex UAV scenarios. This letter proposes DSATrack, a diffusion-guided spectral-aware tracking framework for multispectral UAV MOT. Specifically, a lightweight spectral encoder injects multispectral information into the RPN branch through feature fusion, enabling the RPN head to generate high-quality object-aware proposals. These proposals are then injected into the initial proposal set to provide reliable spatial priors for diffusion refinement. Furthermore, a spectral-saliency confidence modulation strategy recalibrates refined tracking confidence according to local multispectral saliency contrast before score thresholding, enhancing spectrally reliable candidates while suppressing unreliable ones. Without modifying the original diffusion refinement head, DSATrack improves both proposal quality and post-refinement candidate selection. Experiments on the MMOT benchmark demonstrate that DSATrack outperforms the adapted DiffusionTrack baseline by 4.6 HOTA, 9.0 MOTA, and 7.7 IDF1 points, showing its effectiveness for multispectral UAV MOT.

Diffusion model, multispectral imaging, multi-object tracking, proposal enhancement, unmanned aerial vehicle. Introduction ultispectral unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) imagery provides complementary spectral information beyond conventional RGB images~ lsa_spectral_dl,lsa_bess,lsa_hsi_rs , improving target--background separability under degraded appearance conditions, and compact computational spectral imagers make such data increasingly practical to acquire on airborne platforms~ elight_spectropol,lam_spectrometer,elight_meta_imaging . This is particularly valuable for UAV-view multi-object tracking (MOT), where small, dense, arbitrarily oriented targets, camera motion, weak appearance cues, and cluttered backgrounds cause inaccurate localization, missed detections, and unstable identity association~ lss_tracking . Reliable multispectral UAV MOT therefore requires both accurate oriented-box localization and robust inter-frame association. Existing MOT methods fall into tracking-by-detection~ sort,bytetrack,ocsort,botsort , query-based tracking~ motr,motrv2,memotr,motip , and diffusion-based proposal refinement. The first detects objects per frame and then associates them, so it depends heavily on detector quality and association rules and is sensitive to missed or unreliable detections in small-target UAV scenes; in the second, the query-object correspondence becomes unstable when targets are small, dense, or weakly distinguishable. Diffusion-based detection instead formulates localization as an iterative denoising process that refines noisy proposals into target boxes~ diffusiondet , and DiffusionTrack extends this paradigm to MOT by refining paired proposals for joint localization and association~ diffusiontrack . Such refinement suits UAV-view tracking because it maintains multiple hypotheses and gradually corrects imperfect initialization. Related efforts improve detection or tracking under specific sensing conditions by strengthening per-frame features or association cues, such as visible--infrared fusion~ vi_tracking , disparity-guided multiscale fusion~ dmf , inter-domain adaptive detection~ wasserstein_da , roadside vehicle tracking~ isn_roadside , and SAR or sonar target tracking~ tfst,yoloshiptracker,sonar_mot . None of them acts on the two stages that are specific to diffusion-based trackers: the initial proposal set is still built from tracklets and random noise without image-conditioned priors, and refined candidates are selected purely by learned scores without verification. To address this gap, this letter proposes DSATrack, a diffusion-guided spectral-aware framework for multispectral UAV MOT. Unlike DiffusionTrack, which initializes proposals from tracklets and noise and trusts refined scores directly, DSATrack introduces spectral cues before and after iterative refinement without redesigning the refinement head: a lightweight spectral encoder with residual-style gated fusion is incorporated into the RPN branch to generate multispectral-enhanced proposals that are injected into the diffusion proposal set as spatial priors, and a spectral-saliency confidence modulation recalibrates refined tracking confidence before score thresholding. The main contributions of this letter are summarized as follows: We propose DSATrack, which improves proposal initialization and post-refinement candidate selection for multispectral UAV MOT without modifying the diffusion refinement head. We introduce a spectral-aware proposal generation and injection strategy that feeds multispectral information into the RPN branch, providing more reliable object-aware proposals for diffusion refinement. We design a spectral-saliency confidence modulation strategy that recalibrates tracking confidence before score thresholding, improving candidate selection in cluttered UAV scenes. Methodology sec:methodology Overview subsec:overview The overall framework of DSATrack is illustrated in Fig.~ fig:framework . Given a pair of frames from a multispectral UAV video, the backbone extracts multi-scale pyramid features from both frames; during training the pair is the current frame and a reference frame randomly sampled within a temporal window of frames, and during inference it is the previous and the current frame. Meanwhile, a lightweight spectral encoder extracts spectral-spatial representations from the multispectral input, which are fused with the pyramid features and fed into an RPN branch~ fasterrcnn to generate object-aware proposals. Tracklet, RPN, and random proposals are then assembled into the initial proposal set (Sec.~ subsec:rpn_injection ), the diffusion head progressively updates it to predict oriented bounding boxes with classification and association scores, and the refined scores are recalibrated using multispectral saliency before score thresholding. Spectral-Aware Proposal Generation subsec:spectral_rpn Injected RPN proposals provide the image-conditioned spatial priors of the initial proposal set, but a standard RPN relies on backbone features that may not preserve discriminative spectral-spatial responses in multispectral UAV imagery~ essfnet . DSATrack therefore fuses compact spectral-spatial representations with the pyramid features before the RPN head. Given an 8-channel multispectral image , the spectral encoder performs band mixing with a convolution, extracts lightweight spatial responses with a depthwise separable block (a depthwise convolution followed by a pointwise convolution), recalibrates spectral-channel responses with a channel gate to emphasize informative bands, and builds a multi-scale spectral pyramid with progressive stride-2 convolutions. Let and denote the FPN feature and the corresponding spectral feature at the -th pyramid level. Before fusion, is spatially aligned with and projected to the same channel dimension through a convolution. A gated fusion module is then adopted at each pyramid level to adaptively inject spectral information into the proposal branch: where denotes channel-wise concatenation, denotes the level-specific convolutional block at the -th pyramid level, and denotes the sigmoid function. The fused feature is computed as where denotes element-wise multiplication and the coefficients and are learnable weights made non-negative by the Softplus function, so that the fusion strength is learned at each pyramid level. The fused pyramid features are fed into a standard RPN head~ fasterrcnn that predicts objectness scores and box offsets. Since the branch only provides coarse spatial priors, it predicts horizontal proposals for efficiency; after decoding and post-processing, the retained proposals are converted into five-dimensional oriented proposals by assigning the same constant initial angle to all of them, and their orientation is re-estimated by the refinement head. RPN-Guided Proposal Injection subsec:rpn_injection In the original diffusion tracking pipeline, active trajectories from previous frames are propagated as tracklet proposals, which serve as temporal priors for continuing targets but are unavailable for newly appearing or missed ones. DSATrack therefore complements them with spectral-aware RPN proposals that provide image-conditioned spatial priors, while random proposals preserve diversity; the three sources form a fixed-size initial proposal set. For pairwise tracking, proposals with the same index in two frames are treated by the refinement head as the same target hypothesis. To avoid index mismatch caused by independently generated RPN proposals, we generate RPN proposals from the previous frame and reuse them for the current-frame proposal set, which provides index-aligned initial proposals rather than assuming static targets; inter-frame motion, scale variation, and rotation are handled by iterative refinement. During training, ground-truth boxes take the place of tracklet proposals as supervised references, while RPN and random proposals are retained; this is the only difference between the training and inference proposal sets. Spectral-Saliency Confidence Modulation subsec:spectral_confidence_modulation After refinement, the model outputs a fixed number of oriented boxes with classification and association confidence scores. Since these scores are predicted from deep features, background-like candidates may still obtain high confidence when local multispectral evidence is weak, so DSATrack recalibrates them using local spectral saliency before score thresholding. To avoid an additional trainable verification branch, a single-channel spectral saliency map is computed by aggregating multi-scale Gaussian difference responses over all spectral channels: where denotes Gaussian filtering and min-max normalization over the whole frame, with the scale set . Given the classification and association confidences and of the -th refined proposal, the original tracking confidence is For each refined box, the mean foreground saliency is computed inside the box and the background statistics and from the ring between the box and its enlarged box with the same orientation, giving the spectral confidence The constant avoids division by zero. Finally, the tracking confidence is recalibrated as where controls the modulation strength. It is applied to the candidates that pass the original score threshold, keeping at most the 500 highest-scoring ones, and is thresholded again before class-wise rotated non-maximum suppression (NMS), so that proposals with stronger local spectral support are preferentially retained.
