title: PaceVLA: Adaptive Temporal Action Quantization in Vision-Language-Action Models
comment: 25 pages, 7 figures, 10 tables. Project page: https://pacevla.github.io/
summary: Fast and reliable manipulation is crucial for practical robot deployment. Although Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have recently shown remarkable progress as generalist robot policies, their execution often remains temporally inefficient. A key source of this inefficiency is that policies learn fine-grained temporal patterns from teleoperated demonstrations, requiring many low-level action steps. Temporal action quantization offers a simple way to accelerate execution by aggregating consecutive low-level actions into temporally coarser actions. However, applying action quantization without considering when fine-grained control is required introduces a speed-accuracy trade-off: accelerated actions may efficiently reduce redundant steps in some phases, while discarding critical motion details in precision-sensitive interactions. To address this, we propose PaceVLA, a unified framework for adaptive temporal execution in VLAs that integrates two coupled components: (1) mode-specific action decoders built on a shared action expert, supporting multiple temporal granularities and prediction horizons, and (2) a quantizability-guided mode selection scheme which decides whether coarse execution is appropriate, and a context-conditioned router that selects an execution mode at each inference step. Experiments across three multi-task simulation benchmarks and six real-world tasks show that PaceVLA improves execution efficiency while maintaining task success rate across multiple embodiments, including long-horizon and dexterous manipulation.
full_text: 0.51 1pt 1pt 1pt 0pc 3.1ex plus4pt minus3pt 5pt 0pc 2.58ex plus3pt minus2pt 2pt Introduction Vision-Language-Action models (VLAs)~ zitkovich2023rt, kim2024openvla, intelligence2025pi_, pertsch2025fast, nvidia2025gr00t have emerged as a promising framework for generalist robot policies, achieving strong performance through imitation learning from diverse robot demonstrations~ walke2023bridgedata, o2024open, khazatsky2024droid , many of which are collected through human teleoperation~ zhao2023learning,wu2024gello . However, teleoperated demonstrations often exhibit conservative behavior: human-in-the-loop control is typically performed through limited-rate interfaces, and human operators adopt cautious motions to avoid failures during data collection~ mandlekar2018roboturk, mandlekar2021matters . Since imitation learning trains policies to reproduce the demonstrated trajectories, VLAs inherit these patterns and execute tasks through many slow action steps even in phases where faster motion is physically feasible. Recent works have explored accelerating robot policies beyond demonstration speed, addressing two complementary questions: where to accelerate and how coarsely to execute actions. DemoSpeedup~ guo2025demospeedup segments per-frame action entropy with a proxy policy and trains a policy on the resulting accelerated trajectories. SAIL~ arachchige2025sail combines high-fidelity tracking with switching between preset slow and fast speeds based on motion complexity and gripper events. A particularly simple mechanism is temporal action quantization~ figure2025helixlogistics, tang2025vlash , which merges consecutive actions into coarser ones. It fits naturally with chunk-based VLAs since each predicted action chunk can be executed at a chosen granularity. Despite their promise, these approaches have two limitations. First, the acceleration decision is either fixed into the training data, using the action entropy of a fine-tuned proxy policy as an implicit indicator~ guo2025demospeedup , or applied at execution time to the output of a policy trained at demonstration speed, switching between preset speeds according to kinematic cues~ arachchige2025sail . Both signals are statistics of the actions, yet how much precision a phase demands is determined by the robot's interaction with the scene rather than by the motion itself. Second, existing temporal action quantization applies a fixed granularity across the entire trajectory, inducing a speed--accuracy trade-off: coarse actions suffice during free-space motion but discard trajectory details required in precision-critical phases such as grasping and contact-rich interaction. Moreover, granularity is closely coupled with the prediction horizon: phases that tolerate coarse execution can commit to longer predictions, whereas precision-critical phases benefit from shorter horizons with more frequent re-planning. We argue that both the temporal granularity and the prediction horizon of action execution should be treated as a policy decision, adapted to the precision each phase requires. To this end, we propose , a unified framework for adaptive temporal action execution in VLAs. equips a shared action expert with mode-specific action decoders that support different temporal granularities and prediction horizons. At each inference step, a quantization judge and a router jointly select an execution mode from the visual and language context. Each execution mode is defined by a temporal action quantization level and a prediction horizon, allowing the policy to choose both the granularity of its commands and the temporal extent of its action predictions. To validate the effectiveness of , we conduct extensive experiments across Robocasa-Kitchen~ nasiriany2024robocasa , LIBERO~ Liu2023libero , and DexJoCo~ wang2026dexjoco simulated robotic benchmarks and six real-world manipulation tasks including long-horizon, dexterous tasks covered on three robot platforms: Franka Research arm with gripper, OpenArm robot arm with two 6-DoF dexterous hands, and humanoid ALLEX robot with two 15-DoF dexterous hands. Compared with the baselines, achieves up to 1.8 faster than the base VLA, and 1.75 throughput on the conveyor package-handling task with the humanoid ALLEX, while maintaining task success rates. Our contributions are: [leftmargin=*,itemsep=0mm] We highlight the tendency of VLA policies to inherit fine-grained execution patterns from teleoperated demonstrations as a key source of temporal inefficiency. We propose , a lightweight architecture that models execution modes with different temporal quantization levels and action horizons using mode-specific action decoders, a quantization judge and a context-conditioned router. We demonstrate consistent gains on simulation benchmarks and real-world tasks, achieving a stronger balance between task success and execution efficiency than the base VLA and fixed temporal quantization baselines. Related Work sec:related Vision-Language-Action models (VLAs). VLAs have recently shown great promise in robotic policy learning by leveraging large-scale robot datasets. One line of VLA models~ kim2024openvla, pertsch2025fast, driess2023palm discretizes the continuous action space and predicts actions as tokens, showing that pre-trained VLMs~ beyer2024paligemma, chen2026eagle, bai2025qwen3, chen2023pali can be effectively adapted to low-level action prediction. In contrast, a growing body of studies~ intelligence2025pi_, li2024cogact attaches action experts that generate continuous action chunks via diffusion or flow-matching, enabling more accurate predictions. For example, GR00T N1.5~ nvidia2025gr00t and RLDX-1~ kim2026rldx condition a flow-matching head on VLM features to produce action chunks. In this work, we build on a flow-matching action expert for action generation. While most diffusion-based VLAs predict action chunks at a single, fixed temporal granularity set by the data collection frequency, this single granularity is not equally suited to all phases of a task. Motivated by this observation, we explore whether jointly learning actions at multiple temporal granularities and adapting the action granularity to the current context can lead to faster and more accurate task execution. Faster-than-Demonstration Execution. The execution speed of imitation-learned policies is bounded by the pace of their demonstrations, and several lines of work have aimed to exceed it. Reinforcement-learning-based fine-tuning adjusts the policy using task-level rewards to encourage faster and more decisive behaviors~ yuan2025speedtuning , but tends to push the policy toward uniformly faster execution. Another direction modifies the temporal structure of actions, as explored in DemoSpeedup~ guo2025demospeedup and SAIL~ arachchige2025sail . While these approaches improve execution speed, they determine the degree of acceleration either at implicit action entropy signals or through kinematic cues for switching between preset speeds, both derived from action statistics, rather than letting the policy itself decide how much to accelerate from the scene it perceives at inference time. Router-Based Expert Selection. Conditional computation employs a lightweight router that selects which sub-network to apply to each input, and has been widely adopted to scale capacity without proportional cost. In most designs the candidates are structurally identical and differ only in learned weights, whether FFN experts~ fedus2022switch or attention heads~ jin2024moh , so a routing decision carries no predefined meaning. Within VLAs, MoLe-VLA~ zhang2026mole routes over backbone layers to reduce the cost of each forward pass, leaving the action output unchanged. Mixture of Horizons~ jing2025mixture is the closest to our setting, as it constructs action heads at several chunk lengths, but it fuses their outputs through a gate, so each action is still emitted at a single fixed temporal granularity. None of these, however, treat the temporal granularity of the action as the routing target, where a router selects one decoder per state from a set of decoders that differ in temporal resolution and horizon. In a nutshell, leverages a shared action expert with multiple action decoders that support different temporal granularities and prediction horizons. At each inference step, a learned quantization judge determines whether to use fine-grained or quantized decoding, and a router selects a mode within the chosen group. title: From Views to Worlds: Active Exploration over 3D Worlds for Vision-Language Models
summary: Vision-language models (VLMs) have achieved remarkable progress in 2D visual understanding tasks, yet the passive view-centric perception paradigm limits their capacity for 3D spatial reasoning. Such reasoning often requires actively acquiring spatial evidence beyond the currently visible views, such as camera poses and cross-view spatial relationships, to infer 3D relationships that are not explicitly represented in 2D images. However, existing methods either lack active exploration or merely provide additional views during inference, without explicitly acquiring such spatial evidence beyond 2D images. In this paper, we propose View-to-World (V2W), an active exploration framework that enables VLMs to actively explore 3D worlds and lifts VLMs from passive view-centric perception to active world-centric spatial reasoning. Given a spatial reasoning task with multi-view images, V2W first reconstructs an explicit 3D world with geometry, camera poses, and language-grounded semantics, and exposes it to VLMs through visual and linguistic interfaces. Through multi-turn interaction with these interfaces, VLMs iteratively acquire spatial evidence from the constructed 3D world, enabling active world-centric spatial reasoning. V2W can be integrated with existing VLMs in a training-free manner and can be further enhanced by optimizing the exploration policy via reinforcement learning. Experiments on spatial mental modeling benchmarks demonstrate that V2W substantially improves VLM baselines in the training-free setting and achieves state-of-the-art performance with the learned exploration policy, highlighting the importance of active exploration for spatial intelligence. Project page: \url{https://fangzhou2000.github.io/projects/v2w}.

Introduction sec:intro Recent advances in vision-language models (VLMs) have demonstrated remarkable capabilities in 2D visual understanding tasks, including image captioning~ personalizing, caparena , visual question answering~ blip, instructblip, mmmu , and visual grounding~ kosmos2, qwen2.5vl, qwen3vl . Building on their strong image-level perception and reasoning capabilities, recent works~ spatialvlm, spatialrgpt have begun to explore the potential of VLMs for 3D spatial reasoning. However, 2D images are inherently partial observations of the 3D world from specific viewpoints, making view-centric perception fundamentally limited for understanding 3D space. This limitation stems from two key factors. First, critical spatial evidence may be occluded or absent from the currently visible views, which requires active viewpoint changes beyond fixed-view inputs. Second, even with more viewpoints, 2D images alone fail to explicitly represent the cross-view 3D information, such as relative camera poses, cross-view entity correspondences, and object-level 3D spatial relations. Addressing these limitations requires models to actively acquire evidence over a coherent 3D world representation that integrates geometric, visual, and semantic information. However, most existing methods still rely on passively perceiving 2D inputs for spatial reasoning. Some methods attempt to incorporate geometric priors into VLMs, including encoding 3D geometry into the representation space~ llava3d,leovl,video3dllm,gpt4scene,spatialmllm,map2thought , fusing implicit 3D information at the feature level~ vlm3r,vgllm,geothinker,gapmllm , and introducing 3D priors through distillation~ 3drs,ross3d,seeingthroughimagination or latent reasoning~ machinementalimagery,lvr,3dthinker . Although these methods provide VLMs with additional 3D priors, they mainly improve the internal representation capability rather than provide VLMs with an explicitly interactive and actively explorable 3D world, and therefore still belong to the passive perception from fixed-view input. More recent methods~ think3d, mindjourney, spatialdreamer have further explored active perception by providing VLMs with additional 2D observations. Nevertheless, these methods remain largely view-centric, as additional observations are still presented as 2D views and lack cross-view 3D information needed for spatial reasoning. Such 3D information is not explicitly represented in 2D views, but is grounded in the underlying 3D world. We refer to reasoning over such information as world-centric spatial reasoning. Therefore, advancing VLMs toward 3D spatial reasoning requires moving from passive view-centric perception to active world-centric spatial reasoning, as shown in Fig.~ fig: teaser . In this paper, we propose View-to-World (V2W), a model-agnostic framework that enables VLMs to actively explore over an explicit 3D world representation. Given multi-view images, V2W first recovers scene geometry and camera poses with off-the-shelf 3D foundation models and incorporates language-grounded semantics to build a geometrically consistent, semantically aligned, and language-queryable 3D world. We denote it as a VLM-compatible 3D world, since the geometry, camera poses, and semantic evidence are exposed to VLMs through images and natural language rather than raw 3D representations. We design two interfaces to achieve the exposure: a visual interface that provides 2D observations from newly explored viewpoints and a linguistic interface that converts geometric and semantic information from the 3D world into explicit natural-language cues. V2W enables VLMs to actively explore the constructed 3D world through visual and linguistic interfaces and progressively acquire and integrate spatial evidence via multi-turn interaction, thereby performing spatial reasoning in an active world-centric manner. Experiments on spatial mental modeling benchmarks show that V2W improves existing VLMs in a training-free manner, revealing their inherent capability for active exploration. However, we also find that smaller VLMs often struggle to perform effective active exploration, exhibiting insufficient or uninformative exploration. To this end, we further propose to train the exploration policy through reinforcement learning, thereby improving the active exploration capability. With the learned exploration policy, V2W achieves state-of-the-art performance, substantially outperforming both baseline methods and proprietary commercial models (e.g., surpassing GPT-4o by 48.5 percentage points on MindCube-Tiny), demonstrating the importance of active exploration capability for spatial reasoning. Our contributions are summarized as follows: We construct a VLM-compatible 3D world representation that is geometrically consistent, semantically aligned, and language-queryable, providing a 3D environment that lifts VLMs from view-centric perception to world-centric spatial reasoning. We propose V2W, an active exploration framework that enables VLMs to interact with the constructed 3D world through visual and linguistic interfaces and progressively acquire world-grounded evidence via multi-turn exploration. We introduce reinforcement learning to train the exploration policy of V2W, enabling more effective evidence acquisition from the constructed 3D world. Experiments on spatial mental modeling benchmarks demonstrate that V2W substantially improves VLM baselines in the training-free setting and achieves state-of-the-art performance with the learned exploration policy. Related Work Vision-Language Models for Spatial Reasoning Spatial reasoning is essential for intelligent perception and interaction. It allows agents to represent, organize, and transform objects and their spatial relationships in 3D environments~ mentalmodelsincognitivescience, mental, spatialreasoning, exemplar2vqa . However, recent studies show that existing VLMs still struggle with spatial reasoning~ scanrefer, scanqa, scan2cap, multi3drefer, 3dbench, sat, vsibench, beacon3d, spar, spatialbench, mindcube . Prior efforts have attempted to improve the capability of VLMs mainly in two ways. The first line of work injects 3D priors into VLM representations. These methods encode 3D geometry into the representation space~ llava3d, leovl, video3dllm, gpt4scene, spatialmllm, map2thought , fuse implicit 3D information at the feature level~ vlm3r,vgllm, geothinker, gapmllm , or introduce 3D knowledge through distillation~ 3drs, ross3d, seeingthroughimagination or latent reasoning~ machinementalimagery, lvr, 3dthinker . While effective, they often require large-scale aligned data and costly training, and they do not provide explicit geometric constraints. The second line of work provides 3D information externally in the VLM context~ pyspatial, mssr, gca, think3d, pigeon , which offers a more direct and model-agnostic way to improve 3D spatial awareness. However, a key challenge is how to help VLMs understand and use this external 3D information effectively. In this work, we also provide 3D information externally, but we construct a VLM-compatible 3D world that supports active exploration, allowing VLMs to make better use of 3D information. 3D Foundation Models and Scene Understanding Recent feed-forward reconstruction models~ dust3r, mast3r, drivingforward, vggt, da3, pi3 have made rapid progress in 3D modeling. These models can recover 3D geometry from multi-view images and accurately estimate camera parameters and other 3D information. Their strong generalization ability further positions them as 3D foundation models. In parallel, visual foundation models, such as the SAM series~ sam, sam2, sam3 , have demonstrated strong capabilities in scene parsing and understanding. Recent studies~ iggt, ff3r, uniforward, fleg, groupforward further integrate 3D and visual foundation models to support semantic 3D scene understanding. While the above work mainly focuses on 3D representation and perception-oriented tasks, our work investigates how VLMs can benefit from such foundation models to improve spatial reasoning capability. Vision-Language Models with Active Interaction Recent VLMs have advanced from direct reasoning over given inputs to interactive reasoning~ react, mmreact, chameleon . Representative methods allow models to interact with external resources during inference through multi-turn reasoning, including tool-augmented VLMs~ hugginggpt, deepeyes, vtoolr1, vilasr, openthinkimg and visual programming methods~ visprog, vipergpt, vadar, pyspatial . Such interaction reflects the active exploration capability of VLMs~ activeo3, actiview, sieve . This capability is particularly important for spatial reasoning, since understanding 3D space often requires integrating observations from different viewpoints and reasoning about regions beyond the current field of view. Recent works have introduced active exploration into spatial reasoning through novel-view rendering~ think3d or generation~ mindjourney, spatialdreamer . However, these methods mainly provide additional 2D views to VLMs and therefore remain view-centric, without explicitly exposing 3D information beyond 2D images. Another work~ pyspatial performs active exploration through code generation, but this paradigm restricts multi-turn exploration and relies heavily on the code-generation ability of VLMs. In contrast, V2W constructs a VLM-compatible 3D world with visual and linguistic interfaces, enabling VLMs to gather spatial evidence through multi-turn interaction and shift from passive view-centric perception to active world-centric exploration. sec:related Methods sec:methods Overview Given multi-view images and a spatial reasoning question , V2W aims to produce the answer by enabling a VLM to actively explore an explicit 3D world. title: FR-VLA: Implicit Force Reasoning VLA for Contact-Rich Manipulation
summary: Integrating force awareness into Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models involves not merely encoding wrench measurements as an additional modality, but determining when and how strongly physical interaction should influence robot action generation. Existing VLAs that use force typically inject it through a fixed pathway, without explicitly determining when it is relevant to the current action. This calls for an intermediate force relevance mechanism inside the VLA, in which visual-language context estimates the relevance of physical feedback to the current task before force enters the action pathway. FR-VLA addresses this gap with a Vision-Language Force-Reasoning Model that uses learnable force query tokens to derive a force admission signal grounded in visual-language context, and uses this signal to modulate an external tokenized force pathway for action generation. In real-world experiments on five contact-rich tasks across two robotic platforms, FR-VLA achieves the highest mean success rate over six evaluated stages, and trajectory visualizations show that its force admission varies with the interaction phase.

Existing VLAs that use force typically inject it through a fixed pathway, without explicitly determining when it is relevant to the current action. This calls for an intermediate force relevance mechanism inside the VLA, in which visual-language context estimates the relevance of physical feedback to the current task before force enters the action pathway. FR-VLA addresses this gap with a Vision-Language Force-Reasoning Model that uses learnable force query tokens to derive a force admission signal grounded in visual-language context, and uses this signal to modulate an external tokenized force pathway for action generation. In real-world experiments on five contact-rich tasks across two robotic platforms, FR-VLA achieves the highest mean success rate over six evaluated stages, and trajectory visualizations show that its force admission varies with the interaction phase. Introduction Modern VLAs have become effective generalist policies by grounding robot action generation in visual observations and language instructions through pretrained VLM backbones~ kim2024openvla,black2024pi_0,brohan2023rt2,pi2025pi05 . However, contact-rich manipulation exposes a limitation of this visual-language foundation: interaction states in insertion, assembly, wiping, and pressing are often only partially observable from images, making force feedback essential for precision-oriented tasks~ leesense2019,gao2022seehearfeel,gelfusion2025,huang2024vitac,huang2025vtrefine . The importance of force feedback for action generation varies across task phases, depending on the intended interaction and the evolving contact state~ foar2024,forcematched2024,zhang2021impedanceirl . This motivates policies that use visual-language context to determine when and to what extent force feedback should influence action generation. Consequently, force integration is not merely a problem of sensing or encoding wrench measurements, but one of dynamically grounding physical feedback in visual-language task context~ hao2025tla . Existing force-aware VLA architectures mainly differ in the point at which force is injected, as illustrated in Figure~ fig:teaser (a). Injecting low-dimensional wrench signals into the VLM token stream risks diluting force information within high-dimensional visual-language representations~ forcevla2_2026,fdvla2026,tactilevla2025,vlatouch2025 . Relocating force conditioning to the action expert avoids this representational imbalance, but bypasses the VLM state where task progress and interaction phase are inferred~ forcevla2025,zhang2025tavla,favla2026,forcepolicy2026 . Both choices therefore provide force exposure rather than force grounding: the policy can react to measured wrench changes, but it is not explicitly supervised to decide when force should affect action generation under a task-dependent contact phase. We frame force-aware VLA as a modality grounding problem, where grounding denotes estimating the task-conditioned admissibility of physical feedback from the VLA's visual-language state before measured force is allowed to affect action generation. Recent advances in multimodal foundation models have shown that heterogeneous inputs can be grounded in pretrained backbones through intermediate interfaces such as latent queries, resamplers, and gated attention~ jaegle2021perceiverio,alayrac2022flamingo,li2023blip2 . These interfaces transfer information into VLM representation spaces without requiring raw non-visual signals to be inserted as ordinary input tokens. For force-aware VLA, such an interface can use visual-language context to assess when physical feedback should influence action generation, taking task progress and contact phase into account. This perspective motivates separating the estimation of force relevance from the encoding of force measurements. Such a separation calls for a mechanism that uses the VLA's visual-language task state to modulate the contribution of measured wrench histories to action generation. FR-VLA instantiates this mechanism with force query states that infer a force admission signal from visual-language context, while measured wrench histories remain in a separate action-side force pathway. The resulting admission behavior varies with task progress rather than simply with wrench availability, as illustrated in Figure~ fig:teaser (b). Real-world evaluations on two robotic platforms and five contact-rich tasks show improved performance and robustness over vision-only and directly force-conditioned VLA baselines. Our contributions are summarized as follows: (i) Force-aware VLA is formulated as a modality grounding problem for low-dimensional physical feedback, where force relevance is inferred from visual-language task context rather than assumed from sensor availability. (ii) FR-VLA introduces a force admission architecture in which visual-language states determine when force can influence action generation, while measured wrench histories are encoded separately for action-side control. (iii) A detailed analysis of grounded force admission shows that the learned admission behavior follows task phase interaction regimes rather than instantaneous force magnitude. Related Work sec:related_work Force-Aware Policy Learning and Contact Control. Classical contact control provides model-based approaches to compliant manipulation. Hybrid position/force control assigns position and force objectives to complementary directions in a task-related coordinate frame~ raibert1981hybrid . Impedance control specifies the dynamic relationship between motion and interaction force, shaping the robot's mechanical response to its environment~ hogan1985impedance . Force feedback has been studied in both policy learning and contact control~ zhu2019flexure,zhu2022weightimprinting,xue2025rdp,ranjbar2021residual,zhang2023admittance . ForceMimic combines force-aware demonstration collection with imitation learning of force--motion commands and hybrid force-position control~ liu2025forcemimic . Force Policy separates vision-guided global behavior from a local force feedback policy that estimates an interaction frame for hybrid force-position control~ forcepolicy2026 . Learning variable impedance provides another approach to adapting robot behavior under contact uncertainty~ bogdanovic2019variableimpedance,martin2019vices . Beyond control design, effective multimodal learning requires preventing policies from neglecting force feedback. FACTR addresses this issue through a curriculum that progressively reduces visual corruption, encouraging the policy to use force information rather than overfit to vision~ factr2025 . CRAFT similarly addresses modality imbalance in VLAs, using a variational information bottleneck to regulate visual-language representations during curriculum fine-tuning~ craft2026 . FR-VLA addresses force utilization through an explicit architectural separation between context-dependent force admission and wrench history representation. Force-Aware VLAs and Contact-Dependent Fusion. Recent approaches incorporate physical feedback into VLAs through different interfaces~ tactilevla2025,favla2026,zhang2025vtla,cheng2025omnivtla . ForceVLA introduces a force-aware mixture of experts for action generation, while ForceVLA2 combines force-based prompts in the VLM with cross-scale fusion in the action expert for hybrid force-position control~ forcevla2025,forcevla2_2026 . Other approaches exploit physical information during training while reducing deployment-time sensing requirements: FD-VLA distills force information into latent tokens, and HapticVLA transfers tactile-aware behavior to a student that operates without inference-time tactile sensing~ fdvla2026,hapticvla2026 . Prediction-based designs anticipate future interaction: FoAR uses future contact prediction to guide visual--force fusion and dynamically adjust force use across contact and non-contact phases~ foar2024 , and 3D world model policies forecast future scene states to guide action generation~ wang2026dream . In FR-VLA, force query states infer interaction phases from visual-language context, and the resulting admission signal biases action-side attention to a separately represented wrench history. This phase-supervised interface connects task context to force utilization while keeping measured wrench inputs in a dedicated action-side pathway. Cross-Modal Interfaces and Grounding. Latent queries and gated interfaces offer useful building blocks for connecting heterogeneous modalities. Perceiver IO uses latent arrays to process structured inputs, Flamingo introduces gated cross-attention between visual features and a language model, and BLIP-2 uses a query-based interface between frozen visual and language models~ jaegle2021perceiverio,alayrac2022flamingo,li2023blip2 . FR-VLA adopts a task-specific query interface: its force query states receive motion phase supervision to ground force admission in visual-language context. Measured wrench histories remain outside the VLM token stream and condition the action model through a separate force pathway. This design distinguishes the inference of force relevance from the representation of measured physical feedback. Force often becomes informative over temporal regimes in which wrench dynamics evolve before and during contact changes, not only at instants of large measured transients. This ambiguity is evident in precision insertion, where a large contact force may indicate constraint or misalignment, while a subsequent reduction in force during corrective motion remains decision relevant because it indicates that the adjustment is releasing the constraint. A useful policy should therefore maintain force eligibility across such regimes, allowing the action model to observe evolving force patterns rather than react only to magnitude peaks, as shown in Figure~ fig:force_admission . title: Self-Supervised Inertial Odometry
summary: Learning inertial odometry for a new platform usually requires ground-truth trajectories. We show that an inertial odometry model can instead be trained from scratch by a myopic teacher that integrates the IMU over each short window independently, a scheme we call integration self-supervision.Interestingly, although supervised only by short-window velocity changes, the student learns to directly predict velocity, and does so more accurately than its integration teacher. Pose graph distillation then refines the model with sequence-consistent targets from a pose graph over many windows. Training on a new platform therefore no longer requires collecting ground-truth trajectories, but only calibrating the IMU and recording data during normal operation. Across six datasets spanning pedestrians, drones, quadrupeds, and a humanoid, the same recipe with no velocity or position labels trains models that come within $0.07$~m/s average velocity error of a same-architecture supervised baseline.
full_text: Self-Supervised Inertial Odometry sec:method We train an inertial odometry model for a target platform using only its unlabeled onboard measurements ( ). The foundation of our method is integration self-supervision: the IMU measurements inside each sampled window are integrated into a body-frame velocity change between its endpoints, and the network is trained so that the difference of its predicted velocities at those endpoints matches this integrated change. A regularization loss on IMU-detected stops suppresses the drift that integration noise and bias induce where the measurements carry no excitation. Once the network provides reliable velocity estimates, PGD can refine it with velocities optimized jointly over many windows in a pose graph. Every network is trained from random initialization on unlabeled training sequences, without ground-truth velocity or position as training targets (the initial state of each PGD graph is described in ), and evaluated on a held-out test split. Motion network. At deployment the student sees only the IMU, with no label and no guaranteed onboard attitude filter, so it must infer velocity from the raw measurements alone. We therefore build on AirIO~ qiu2025airio and remove its attitude encoder, denoting the modified network ( ). Given the raw accelerometer and gyroscope measurements in a window of samples ending at sample , the network predicts the body-frame velocity where are the network weights and the superscript denotes the IMU body frame at the corresponding timestamp. Following the observability insight of AirIO, we keep both the input and the predicted velocity in the body frame. Raw body-frame measurements retain the gravity direction, which a global-frame, gravity-removed input discards, so the network can infer tilt from the IMU history itself. The body frame also suits self-supervision, because the teacher's preintegrated velocity change is expressed in the body frame at the window start and can be compared with body-frame predictions through the relative rotation alone, without any global heading. Removing the attitude encoder costs the supervised at most ~m/s AVE relative to AirIO ( ). Before integration, we subtract constant accelerometer and gyroscope biases estimated from stationary samples in each sequence. A constant bias is the simplest correction that stationary samples can estimate without labels, and shows that bias, not noise, is the error the teacher cannot average away. The teacher requires an estimate of gravity direction and relative rotation; the attitude source used in our experiments is stated in . We match this prediction to the integrated increment with The sum runs over sampled training windows. Stationary Regularization sec:stationary At rest, residual noise and bias produce small nonzero integration targets that the network would otherwise reproduce as spurious motion. Stationary samples supply a label-free zero-velocity constraint, and detecting them from the raw IMU is the most straightforward signal available on every platform, so we adopt it as the regularizer. We detect stationary intervals from low variation in accelerometer and gyroscope magnitudes, a small mean angular rate, and an acceleration magnitude close to gravity. On these samples, penalizes the mean squared predicted speed and is added to the integration loss with a weighting coefficient. The same samples provide the teacher's constant bias estimates by averaging deviations from zero angular velocity and the expected gravity reading. Pose Graph Distillation sec:m2 -2 1 A single-window target carries one window of teacher noise and no consistency across windows. Chaining many windows in a pose graph averages that noise and yields a velocity posterior with a longer effective horizon than any single window, a sharper target from the same teacher. PGD starts from an integration-self-supervised network because the graph also consumes network velocity predictions. Because the graph adds no independent measurement, repeating the round copies the student's own drift back into the target ( ), so we optimize each training graph once and fine-tune the network on the resulting targets, unlike the repeated alternation of imperative learning~ wang2024imperative . The graph jointly optimizes orientation and body-frame velocity at its keyframes, with the first keyframe held fixed to remove the gauge freedom of the graph. Integration factors enforce consistency with the teacher's relative rotations and velocity changes, while network factors keep velocities close to the student's predictions. We weight integration factors by their propagated uncertainty and use a fixed isotropic weight for network factors, since self-supervision does not train the predicted covariance. Position is omitted because it provides no additional velocity constraint. We solve this weighted least-squares problem with Gauss--Newton, using the sparse solver of . We forward-integrate corrected IMU between the optimized keyframes to obtain dense velocity targets at every sample. PGD minimizes so the network learns the longer-horizon velocity that the graph recovers from the same integration teacher. Proprioceptive Input sec:proprio_input The proprioceptive variant, reported as + Proprio when trained with labels and Ours + Proprio when self-supervised, extends the same network to read the articulated sensing available on legged platforms. The student also encodes joint positions, velocities, and torques, together with auxiliary IMUs when available. On MIPO~ yang2023mipo , these include four calf-mounted IMUs in addition to the base IMU. The additional inputs require no annotation and expose embodiment context such as gait phase and contact. title: OmniInteract: Towards Unified Whole-Body Interaction Control for Dual Humanoids
comment: 30 pages including appendix, 11 figures. Project page: https://calvinyhli.github.io/omniinteract.github.io/
summary: Physical interaction is a key capability for humanoid collaboration, requiring coordinated whole-body motion and precise contact. However, learning diverse dual-humanoid interactions faces two major challenges: (1) human-robot morphological differences disrupt contact interfaces and spatial relationships during retargeting, and (2) jointly learning motor skills and partner coordination makes it difficult to retain control fidelity as interaction diversity grows. In this paper, we propose OmniInteract to address these challenges through surface-aware modeling and scalable residual policy learning. First, we introduce Surface Contact-Aware Retargeting, which leverages dense human-robot surface correspondences to jointly retarget both humanoids, preserving explicit interaction contact interfaces and their near-field geometric context. Second, we propose a Scalable Flow-based Interaction Policy for partner-conditioned residual generation. It factorizes dual-humanoid control into a reusable motor foundation and interaction-specific adaptations: partner-aware experts learn corrections over a frozen whole-body motion prior, while conditional flow matching unifies them in a shared residual action space. This enables scalable skill consolidation while retaining pretrained motor capabilities. Extensive experiments demonstrate that OmniInteract improves retargeting fidelity and dual-humanoid coordination while better retaining interaction performance as skill diversity grows. Real-world deployment further demonstrates successful contact establishment, stable whole-body coordination, and recovery from external perturbations.

Second, we propose a Scalable Flow-based Interaction Policy for partner-conditioned residual generation. It factorizes dual-humanoid control into a reusable motor foundation and interaction-specific adaptations: partner-aware experts learn corrections over a frozen whole-body motion prior, while conditional flow matching unifies them in a shared residual action space. Extensive experiments demonstrate that OmniInteract improves retargeting fidelity and dual-humanoid coordination while better retaining interaction performance as skill diversity grows. Real-world deployment further demonstrates successful contact establishment, stable whole-body coordination, and recovery from external perturbations. page: Introduction Advances in whole-body control and motion imitation have equipped humanoid robots with increasingly versatile motor capabilities ben2025homie,fu2024humanplus,he2024omniho . Most existing systems, however, focus on single-humanoid skills chen2025gmt,jiang2026wholebodyvla,he2025asap,li2026bfm , whereas many real-world tasks require collaboration and physical interaction between agents shaoul2025collaborative, doshi2026chorus . Human-human interaction demonstrations offer a rich source of such behaviors. Transferring them to dual humanoids requires preserving the intended relationships between the bodies across embodiments and maintaining coordinated motion and contact under coupled dynamics. The first challenge is Morphological differences in body proportions and surface shape can disrupt contact interfaces despite plausible individual poses reda2023physics,yin2025dexteritygen . Although recent interaction-aware approaches have begun to explicitly model relative geometries between bodies, sparse body representations remain insufficient for capturing fine-grained surface-level interactions chen2026rhythm . Explicit contact relationships constrain where two bodies should interact, but they do not fully determine how surrounding limbs and body regions should be arranged liu2025takes . Conversely, preserving neighborhood-level geometric structures may maintain overall spatial consistency while hiding local contact deviations. Therefore, High-fidelity retargeting requires preserving both where the bodies meet and how nearby regions are arranged. The second challenge is Independent motion trackers lack the partner feedback needed to correct deviations under coupled dynamics. Training from scratch instead requires learning individual tracking, whole-body balance, and partner coordination together. More importantly, different interactions exhibit substantially different contact patterns and coordination requirements. As interaction diversity increases, jointly training multiple interaction behaviors within a unified policy can introduce severe gradient interference, making it increasingly difficult to maintain high-fidelity interaction performance. Motivated by this analysis, we propose OmniInteract, a unified framework for learning diverse dual-humanoid interactions from human demonstrations via surface-aware retargeting and scalable residual policy learning, as illustrated in Fig.~ fig:o1 . To overcome the retargeting bottleneck, we introduce Surface Contact-Aware Retargeting (SCAR), which leverages dense human–robot surface correspondences to construct a contact-aware surface interaction graph between humanoid. It preserves interaction geometry through complementary surface constraints: explicit bilateral contact edges maintain the contact interface, while near-field Laplacian relationships preserve the surrounding spatial structures. SCAR jointly optimizes both humanoids under kinematic constraints, generating synchronized interaction motion references for downstream control. To overcome the interaction control bottleneck, we propose a Scalable Flow-based Interaction Policy that consolidates partner-dependent corrections from task-specific dual-humanoid experts into a unified generative residual controller through flow matching. This design decouples stable single-humanoid motion priors from interaction control learning, leveraging high-capacity generative policies to expand interaction representation capability while avoiding severe interference multi-interaction behaviors reinforcement learning. Extensive experiments demonstrate that OmniInteract improves retargeting fidelity and dual-humanoid coordination, together with stronger generalization to unseen motions and better performance retention as interaction diversity grows. Deployment on two Unitree G1 robots further demonstrates successful contact establishment, stable whole-body coordination, and recovery from external pushes. Our contributions are summarized as follows: [leftmargin=*] We present OmniInteract, a unified framework for learning dual-humanoid interactions from human demonstrations, integrating interaction-preserving retargeting with scalable coordination. We introduce a surface contact-aware retargeting (SCAR) method that leverages dense human--robot surface correspondences to preserve bilateral contact interfaces and surrounding interaction geometry for generating synchronized dual-humanoid references. We propose a scalable flow-based interaction policy that distills partner-aware corrections into a unified residual action space, enabling diverse coordination control while retaining a stable whole-body motion prior. Related Works Motion Retargeting for Humanoid. Retargeting human motions to humanoid robots is a fundamental step for transforming large-scale human demonstrations into robot-executable references park2025demodiffusion,luo2023perpetual . Early approaches typically rely on manually designed correspondences between human and robot joints or body parts, followed by optimization under kinematic constraints araujo2025retargeting,qin2022one . Recent studies have improved retargeting quality by incorporating whole-body geometric structures, interaction constraints, and physical feasibility yang2025omniretarget,pan2025spider . However, existing representations often rely on sparse body configurations or predefined correspondences, which is insufficient to capture fine-grained surface interactions between multiple humanoids chen2026rhythm,liu2025takes . Recent dense correspondence-based approaches represent humanoid bodies through surface-level geometric correspondence cao2026unified , enabling more scalable motion transfer across embodiments. Our work builds upon this direction and extends surface-based retargeting toward dual-humanoid interaction by explicitly modeling bilateral contact interfaces and surrounding interaction geometry. Whole-body Control for Humanoid Robots. Learning robust whole-body control policies for humanoid robots has recently advanced through motion imitation ji2024exbody2,xie2026kungfubot,han2025kungfubot2 , reinforcement learning li2026w1, peng2018deepmimic,zhang2025falcon , and generative policy learning li2026language, liu2025commanding, shao2025langwbc . Prior works have demonstrated impressive capabilities in single-humanoid locomotion, manipulation gu2026humanoid, he2026viral , and dynamic motion tracking wang2026omnixtreme . Extending these abilities to dual-humanoid interaction introduces additional challenges, as the policy must simultaneously maintain individual motion stability and adapt to partner-dependent coordination requirements. Existing dual-humanoid control approaches typically learn interaction policies directly through reinforcement learning or task-specific optimization, which can become difficult to scale as interaction diversity increases liu2025takes,chen2026rhythm . In contrast, our approach leverages pretrained single-humanoid motion priors and learns interaction-specific residual adaptations, followed by specialist-to-unified policy consolidation, enabling scalable learning of diverse dual-humanoid interactions while preserving stable individual motion capabilities. title: Directionally Factorized Illumination with Spherical Harmonic Rotation
summary: Many real-world capture scenarios involve an active light source rigidly attached to the camera: camera flashes for dark-environment imaging, underwater vehicle lights, and endoscopic/laparoscopic medical procedures. As the camera moves, the co-mounted light moves with it, causing the illumination direction at each surface point to change across views. Neural rendering methods (NeRF, Gaussian Splatting) encode this pose-dependent illumination as surface coloration, producing appearance inconsistencies and making it harder to recover the underlying scene. We present \textbf{DaFISH}, which can be plugged into any novel-view synthesis (NVS) pipeline such as NeRF. It factorizes per-point emitted color into surface albedo and a spherical harmonic (SH)-represented illumination factor. During training, the SH illumination is evaluated directly, enabling stable joint optimization of albedo, lighting, and geometry. \textbf{DaFISH} provides analytical generalization of illumination to arbitrary camera poses without retraining. Building on the closed-form SH-to-irradiance conversion, the training pipeline is fully differentiable from SH evaluation through volume rendering. Averaged over the held-out frames of the five scenes, \textbf{DaFISH} attains the best mean PSNR (38.91\,dB), SSIM (0.9613), and LPIPS (0.0582) among all compared methods. It improves over the strongest splatting baseline as well as the closest NeRF-based baseline, while recovering the scene consistently across views compared to prior methods.

Introduction sec:intro Neural radiance fields (NeRF)~ nerf, mipnerf360 and Gaussian Splatting (GS)~ tdgs,tdgs2d have transformed novel view synthesis (NVS) and 3D scene reconstruction. However, both assume a static scene under static illumination, where the radiance emitted from a surface point is modeled as a fixed function of position and viewing direction. The incident illumination is treated as a fixed function of world coordinates, independent of camera pose or acquisition time. Under active illumination, the image-capture scenario violates this assumption. Whenever the light is attached to the camera, or the object moves relative to a stationary camera and light, the illumination is fixed in the camera frame, so in the scene's frame the light moves with every pose. In direct lighting capture, the light source is rigidly attached to the camera for imaging in dark, underwater, or enclosed spaces~ tranzatto2022cerberus,darkgs,sunfaded,relillum . We call this the co-located (or co-moving~ sunfaded,relillum ) lighting configuration. Standard neural rendering lacks a mechanism to distinguish variation in local appearance due to change in illumination. This becomes a problem under a co-located light source, in which bright and dark regions occur together, as shown in Fig.~ fig:1 . In such cases, as the camera repositions, the irradiance it produces on the scene shifts with every camera motion, while its angular emission profile is constant in the camera frame. As a result, each image exhibits strong, spatially localized appearance variations due to the light's pose relative to the scene surface, and the same 3D point may display entirely different colors in different views due to illumination changes. This breaks the multi-view photometric consistency that standard neural rendering relies on, leading to reconstruction artifacts. Recent work has proposed solutions to this NVS problem. Many of these approaches construct explicit lighting or model constraints~ darkgs,lightneus,prendo,reimnerf . Other methods, like~ nighttime3dgs , make strong physical assumptions about camera or light behavior. Luminance-GS~ luminancegs uses global per-view tone curves to handle challenging lighting conditions but cannot model spatially varying illumination across an image plane. Gaussian in the Dark~ gaussindark resolves cross-view brightness inconsistency in dark captures but attributes it to the camera imaging characteristics. In contrast to these approaches, we propose a formulation (DaFISH) that exploits the known rigid coupling between camera and light. As illustrated in Fig.~ fig:overview , we decompose the rendered color into an intrinsic albedo and an illumination field with irradiance, and we parameterize the irradiance in low-order spherical harmonics (SH), an orthonormal basis for functions on the sphere. The key insight, established by~ ramaho_rel,ramaho_env , is that the irradiance of a Lambertian surface is a smooth, low-order function of the normal and is well approximated by a small number of coefficients. Also, rotating a function on the sphere acts linearly and band-wise on its SH coefficients via the Wigner-D matrices~ rose1995elementary,sloan2008stupid . So, the irradiance for a given normal is obtained by an analytic Wigner-D rotation of the coefficients rather than by re-integrating over the hemisphere. This is general, only assuming a co-located lighting function, instead of a specific lighting geometry and target scene, and further does not require a well-lit reference frame. Like~ relillum,hong2026spotlessgs , it requires no calibration target and no separate calibration capture. Our main contributions can be summarized as follows: (1) We formulate an NVS rendering method for the co-located light setting as a factorization of color into albedo and a illumination field with directional SH irradiance carried across frames by an analytic Wigner-D rotation of the known camera motion. (2) We present experiments on synthetic and real co-located captures that demonstrate better novel view reconstruction quality. (3) The formulation requires no calibration target and no separate calibration capture, making it applicable to captures already collected in the field. Related Work sec:related View-Dependent Appearance Most NVS methods assume world-fixed illumination. NeRF~ nerf and Mip-NeRF~360~ mipnerf360 model view-dependent color directly, and 3D/2D Gaussian Splatting~ tdgs,tdgs2d do so with explicit primitives. Ref-NeRF~ refnerf structures the view-dependent term around the reflection direction but still bakes lighting as a scene property. NeRF-W~ martin2021nerf handles illumination with a per-image appearance embedding, and GS-W~ gsw refines this with per-Gaussian dynamic features sampled from an encoding of each reference image. Both infer each frame's lighting independently and ignore any known relationship between frames. In our setting, this relationship is known, and we exploit it analytically. Illumination Modeling Illumination modeling has been extended to the NVS domain, often for low-light or challenging illumination scenarios. RawNeRF~ mildenhall2022rawnerf trains directly on linear raw measurements, recovering noisy and near-dark scenes. Gaussian in the Dark~ gaussindark handles brightness inconsistency in the dark via a learned camera response module. Luminance-GS~ luminancegs applies view-adaptive color-curve adjustments, and RobustSplat++~ robustsplatpp decouples illumination from geometry and dynamics in the in-the-wild setting. In both, each view's lighting is fitted independently of camera pose. We derive the frame-to-frame lighting transform within a single capture, where the known rigid camera extrinsics make the transform analytic rather than something to be solved for. Co-located Lighting Several methods target capture where the light is co-located with the camera: dark-scene robot exploration~ darkgs,sunfaded , endoscopy~ lightneus,prendo,reimnerf , and underwater imaging~ relillum . In endoscopy, LightNeuS~ lightneus builds inverse-square decline into the renderer, PR-ENDO~ prendo utilizes a physically based model, and ~ reimnerf conditions the radiance field on light position. DarkGS~ darkgs additionally requires a calibration profile of the light. SpotlessGS~ hong2026spotlessgs removes the calibration step by jointly optimizing the light parameters, and uses SH to model an ambient residual. SunFaded~ sunfaded predicts per-tile lighting maps in image space from depth and light direction. We instead assume only co-located coupling with no calibration capture. Relative Illumination Fields (relative-illumination)~ relillum and SunFaded~ sunfaded factorize pixel color into albedo times an illumination factor. We adopt the same factorization but structure the illumination term such that its directional component is an SH irradiance field transported analytically via the known camera movement, rather than being learned in full. Irradiance and SH Rotation The closed-form radiance/irradiance relationship for Lambertian surfaces can be expressed using low-order SH expansions~ ramaho_rel,ramaho_env . Wigner-D matrices are the standard tool for rotating SH signals in physics and computer graphics~ rose1995elementary,sloan2008stupid . Wang and Ramamoorthi derive analytic SH coefficients for polygonal area lights via zonal-harmonic rotation~ wang2018analytic . In neural rendering, NeRF-OSR~ nerfosr embeds an SH lighting model in a NeRF, but fits it as a world-frame environment independently for each image. In contrast, we apply the analytic Wigner-D transport of the known capture motion to the irradiance coefficients, yielding a nearly zero-overhead, per-frame lighting transform inside a neural radiance field. title: Robotic Photography System based on Vision-Language-Action Model
summary: Modern robotic photography requires understanding photographic intent, planning camera motions, and producing aesthetically pleasing images in complex environments. We present RoboPhoto-VLA, a unified Vision-Language-Action framework that jointly models perception, reasoning, and camera control for autonomous robotic photography. RoboPhoto-VLA incorporates PhotoCoT for structured action planning and Aesthetic Direct Preference Optimization (ADPO) to align camera behaviors with human aesthetic preferences. To facilitate training and evaluation, we construct OpenPhotography, a robotic photography dataset with language-guided demonstrations. Extensive real-world experiments demonstrate that RoboPhoto-VLA produces photographs better aligned with human aesthetic preferences while generalizing effectively to unseen subjects, viewpoints, poses, and complex photographic instructions.
full_text: RoboPhoto-VLA: Robotic Photography System based on Vision-Language-Action Model Song-Li Wu , Chubin Zhang , Wenbo Ding , Yansong Tang Shenzhen International Graduate School, Tsinghua University \ wsl24, zcb24\ @mails.tsinghua.edu.cn \ ding.wenbo, tang.yansong\ @sz.tsinghua.edu.cn This work was supported by the National Natural Science Foundation of China under Grant No.~U25A20537. Corresponding author. Modern robotic photography requires understanding photographic intent, planning camera motions, and producing aesthetically pleasing images in complex environments. We present RoboPhoto-VLA, a unified Vision-Language-Action framework that jointly models perception, reasoning, and camera control for autonomous robotic photography. RoboPhoto-VLA incorporates PhotoCoT for structured action planning and Aesthetic Direct Preference Optimization (ADPO) to align camera behaviors with human aesthetic preferences. To facilitate training and evaluation, we construct OpenPhotography, a robotic photography dataset with language-guided demonstrations. Extensive real-world experiments demonstrate that RoboPhoto-VLA produces photographs better aligned with human aesthetic preferences while generalizing effectively to unseen subjects, viewpoints, poses, and complex photographic instructions. Introduction Robotic photography is emerging as an important embodied AI application in creative production, event recording, and commercial media, where robots are expected to autonomously execute camera movements according to high-level user instructions~ ma2024survey,lu2023thinkbot,zhang2026clap . Unlike conventional robotic manipulation~ lu2025vla,lu2025gwm,guo2026vla , whose objective is successful task execution, robotic photography requires balancing two complementary objectives: accurately understanding the semantic intent of the user while producing photographs that satisfy human aesthetic preferences. Achieving this objective demands not only precise camera control, but also reasoning about abstract photographic concepts such as composition, viewpoint, framing, and subject interaction. Developing robots capable of jointly perceiving scenes, interpreting photographic intent, and generating aesthetically pleasing camera behaviors therefore remains a fundamental challenge~ luo2026stare,lu2024manigaussian,wu2026activemem . Existing robotic photography systems have explored reference-guided camera control, semantic event photography, and interactive computational photography~ limoyo2024photobot,rivkin2023ansel,choi2024snapbot . However, these methods are typically built upon modular pipelines that decouple perception, language understanding, and camera control~ kawaharazuka2025vision,lin2025showui,adilkhanov2025survey , limiting their ability to reason over abstract photographic intent and adapt to open-ended instructions, unseen subjects, and dynamic shooting environments. Recent Vision--Language--Action (VLA) models address this limitation by unifying perception, reasoning, and action within a single policy~ nair2022r3muniversalvisualrepresentation,karamcheti2023languagedrivenrepresentationlearningrobotics,stone2023open,wu2026dpamixersr,wang2024autonomousbehaviorplanninghumanoid,wang2024hypermotion . Nevertheless, existing VLAs are primarily optimized for task completion rather than photographic quality, lacking both photography-oriented reasoning and explicit optimization toward human aesthetic preferences. Moreover, the scarcity of embodied robotic photography datasets further limits their applicability to autonomous photography. To address these challenges, we formulate robotic photography as an aesthetic-aware Vision--Language--Action learning problem and propose RoboPhoto-VLA, a unified framework that jointly models perception, reasoning, and embodied camera control. Specifically, we introduce PhotoCoT, a photography-oriented reasoning strategy that grounds abstract photographic intent into structured camera operations, including viewpoint selection, framing adjustment, and camera motion planning. To further optimize photographic quality, we propose Aesthetical Direct Preference Optimization (ADPO), which explicitly aligns camera behaviors with human aesthetic preferences through preference learning rather than conventional task-success supervision. To facilitate training and evaluation, we further construct OpenPhotography, the first open-ended robotic photography dataset containing language-guided demonstrations together with aesthetic preference pairs. Extensive real-world experiments demonstrate that RoboPhoto-VLA consistently produces photographs that better align with human aesthetic preferences while generalizing effectively across unseen subjects, viewpoints, poses, and diverse photographic scenarios. Our contributions are threefold: we propose RoboPhoto-VLA for aesthetic-aware robotic photography, introduce PhotoCoT and ADPO for structured reasoning and aesthetic alignment, and construct OpenPhotography for real-world evaluation under diverse unseen settings. Related Works Recent Vision--Language Models (VLMs) have achieved remarkable progress in multimodal understanding by combining pretrained vision encoders with large language models, enabling strong performance on visual reasoning, captioning, and question answering tasks~ hudson2019gqa,singh2019towards,li2023blip,laurenccon2024obelics,zhang2024vision,wu2026capedit . Building upon these advances, Vision--Language--Action (VLA) models integrate perception, language, and robot control into a unified policy, allowing pretrained VLMs to directly predict robot actions for embodied manipulation and long-horizon planning~ stone2023open,wang2026grpo,padalkar2023open,li2023vision,wu2026codeskill,karamcheti2024prismatic,kim2024openvla . Representative models such as RT-2-X and OpenVLA demonstrate impressive generalization across robotic manipulation tasks but are primarily designed for task execution rather than photography-oriented reasoning and aesthetic decision-making. Robotic photography has traditionally focused on camera control, viewpoint selection, framing, and target tracking through rule-based or modular pipelines~ limoyo2024photobot,rivkin2023ansel,choi2024snapbot . Although recent systems incorporate language understanding and scene perception, they generally lack unified reasoning over visual observations and abstract photographic intent, as well as explicit optimization toward human aesthetic preferences. In contrast, our work formulates robotic photography as an aesthetic-aware Vision--Language--Action problem. Built upon a unified VLA framework, RoboPhoto-VLA introduces photography-oriented reasoning and preference optimization to bridge abstract photographic intent with executable camera actions, enabling aesthetically aligned robotic photography. 1 Method We formulate robotic photography as an embodied vision--language--action (VLA) learning problem. Given an RGB observation , a natural-language photography instruction , and a camera action trajectory , the objective is to learn a policy , that not only executes feasible camera motions but also produces photographs aligned with human aesthetic preferences. To this end, we propose RoboPhoto-VLA, which extends a general-purpose VLA policy with photography-oriented reasoning and preference optimization. The overall framework consists of three components: an OpenVLA backbone for end-to-end policy learning, PhotoCoT for structured photographic reasoning, and Aesthetical Direct Preference Optimization (ADPO) for aesthetic alignment. OpenVLA-based Policy We adopt OpenVLA-7B as the backbone policy due to its strong embodied reasoning capability. Following OpenVLA, the policy consists of a dual visual encoder, a lightweight projector, and a large language model (LLM). Given an observation image, visual features are extracted by SigLIP and DINOv2, , while the language instruction is encoded as . The projected visual tokens and language tokens are concatenated and processed by the LLM to obtain a joint representation , from which the policy autoregressively predicts the camera trajectory . Following OpenVLA, each continuous action dimension is independently discretized into 256 bins according to the 1 and 99 quantiles of the training distribution and represented as language tokens, allowing robot control to be optimized using the standard next-token prediction objective. Unlike OpenVLA, RoboPhoto-VLA explicitly introduces photography-oriented reasoning and aesthetic preference learning, enabling the policy to optimize photographic quality rather than only task completion. Photography-Oriented Chain-of-Thought General-purpose VLA models directly predict actions from observations, making it difficult to interpret abstract photographic instructions. We therefore introduce PhotoCoT, which decomposes policy learning into photographic grounding and camera planning. Given an observation and instruction, PhotoCoT first generates a grounding representation , where , , , and denote the target subject, viewpoint, composition, and scene constraints, respectively. Instead of directly producing actions, the policy first predicts an intermediate reasoning sequence , which explicitly describes the multi-step camera adjustment process. The final camera trajectory is then generated as . Aesthetic Direct Preference Optimization Although supervised fine-tuning enables reliable camera control, it does not explicitly optimize photographic aesthetics. We therefore formulate aesthetic alignment as a trajectory-level preference learning problem. For each observation--instruction pair , multiple candidate camera trajectories are executed to capture corresponding images. These images are evaluated using a multimodal aesthetic assessment model, and the trajectories with higher and lower aesthetic scores are used to construct preference pairs . We initialize preference optimization from the PhotoCoT-supervised policy. The reference policy is a frozen copy of this policy, while denotes the policy optimized during preference learning. Following DPO, the preference margin is defined as where controls the strength of deviation from the reference policy. The standard DPO objective is Standard DPO treats all preference pairs equally, although their reliability may vary. We therefore introduce an adaptive confidence weight where denotes the aesthetic-score difference between the images produced by and , and denotes their LPIPS perceptual distance. The coefficients and control the contributions of aesthetic confidence and perceptual variation, respectively. Consequently, preference pairs with a clear aesthetic margin receive larger weights, whereas pairs with large perceptual differences are down-weighted to reduce the influence of unrelated visual-content changes. We first perform supervised fine-tuning with PhotoCoT reasoning traces to learn photography-oriented grounding and camera planning. The resulting policy is subsequently optimized using ADPO to align camera trajectories with human aesthetic preferences. The overall objective is where balances supervised policy learning and preference optimization. During inference, RoboPhoto-VLA directly predicts an executable camera trajectory from an RGB observation and a natural-language instruction through a single forward pass. title: SwitchSplat: Learning Discrete Object States from Casually Captured Scenes
comment: SIGGRAPH Asia 2026 (Conference Papers). 19 pages, 15 figures, 8 tables. Project page: https://switchsplat.github.io
summary: 3D Gaussian Splatting has made high-fidelity 3D reconstruction fast and accessible, yet existing representations assume a static world. This assumption breaks down in casual captures, where a user naturally interacts with the environment -- opening doors, toggling switches, or moving objects -- introducing discrete state changes that no current framework can model. Time-conditioned dynamic methods such as 4DGS conflate when a state was observed with what state the scene is in, limiting them to replaying seen sequences rather than composing arbitrary object configurations. We present SwitchSplat, the first 3DGS representation to address this gap via a base+slot decomposition: a shared static base captures the invariant scene, while each slot independently holds the two binary states (on/off) of one interactable object. Because the assignment of Gaussians to slots is fully differentiable, the model discovers the geometry of each state directly from video, without manual annotation. At inference, the user can freely combine slot states and render the resulting scene from any viewpoint. We validate SwitchSplat on a new casual-capture dataset and show that it outperforms static and dynamic baselines in novel-view synthesis quality, while uniquely supporting rendering of state combinations never seen during capture. Project page: https://switchsplat.github.io
