Its combination of fast training and efficient rendering has driven broad adoption across academia as well as industry, from Matterport's digital twins and Niantic Scaniverse's mobile reconstruction to Meta's Hyperscape . While early 3DGS pipelines required meticulous data acquisition~(fixed exposure and white balance, controlled lighting, and a perfectly static scene), recent works like 3DGRT~ 3dgrt and FullCircle~ fullcircle have unlocked casual capture: viewpoints need not be carefully curated -- made possible by cameras held in a single hand -- and the capturer's pixels are automatically masked out to satisfy the static-scene assumption. This freedom naturally invites users to interact with the environment during capture -- opening doors, toggling switches, or repositioning objects -- turning the operator into both an active agent and a dynamic distractor within the scene. Yet no existing reconstruction framework is equipped to handle these interactions. Many contemporary 3D representations enforce a strict static-world assumption: when an operator triggers a discrete state change -- opening a door, flipping a switch, relocating an object -- the model has no mechanism to account for the resulting geometric variation. As a result, even state-of-the-art pipelines can only represent a single, frozen scene configuration, and capturing multiple stable states requires re-recording the scene from scratch. One could argue that the natural candidate to address this limitation is the family of 4D Gaussian Splatting methods~ 4dgs , which extend 3DGS to dynamic scenes by conditioning the scene representation on time. However, this design choice fundamentally conflates when a state was observed with what state the scene is in: the model learns to replay a specific sequence of observations, not to understand independent object configurations. As a result, 4D methods are largely limited to novel-viewpoint synthesis of seen sequences; composing an unseen combination of object states---e.g., door open and light on---is not directly supported, since no single timestamp in the training data corresponds to that configuration. What is needed instead is a representation that de-correlates scene state from time, allowing the user to freely specify both the viewpoint and the desired configuration of each object independently. To address these challenges, we propose SwitchSplat, a method that learns ``state-aware'' representations from casual captures featuring human-object interactions; see . SwitchSplat organizes the scene into a static base -- the parts that never change throughout the capture -- and a set of slots, one per interactable object. Each slot holds two 3D representations corresponding to the binary states of that object (``on'' and ``off''). For example, if a room was captured while a closet door was closed for part of the recording and open for another, a single slot would hold both the ``off'' state (door closed, interior hidden) and the ``on'' state (door open, interior visible), while the walls, floor, and furniture -- unchanged throughout -- are handled by the static base. To assign each Gaussian primitive to the right part of the scene, we attach a small learnable score vector that controls how strongly the primitive belongs to the base, or to either state of each slot. This decomposition avoids data redundancy: without a shared static base, one would need to duplicate the full scene geometry for every slot, with no reusable structure across states. Instead, SwitchSplat shares the base across all configurations and only stores the geometry that actually differs per state. Because the full pipeline is differentiable end-to-end, the model learns simultaneously which Gaussians belong to which slot and when each slot is active -- directly from the input video, without any manual annotation. At inference, the user can query any combination of slot states independently -- e.g., closet door open and desk lamp on -- and render the resulting scene from any viewpoint. To summarize our contributions: (1) We \- in the 3DGS literature: existing representations cannot model scenes with discrete, user-triggered state changes (e.g., objects that can be opened, switched, or moved), and we show that na\" i vely applying dynamic methods such as 4DGS fails to address this. (2) We propose SwitchSplat, the first 3DGS representation to address this problem via a , where a shared static base captures the invariant scene and each slot independently models the binary states of one interactable object. (3) We demonstrate on a that SwitchSplat improves novel-view synthesis quality over static and dynamic baselines, and uniquely supports rendering arbitrary combinations of object states from unseen viewpoints. Related Work sec:related 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS)~ 3dgs has become the dominant representation for novel-view synthesis, optimizing a set of anisotropic Gaussian primitives that render at real-time rates. Extensions beyond the standard perspective-camera model are particularly relevant to our setting: 3DGRT~ 3dgrt reformulates rendering via ray tracing, and 3DGUT~ 3dgut adds support for highly distorted cameras and secondary rays, enabling casual capture with wide field-of-view sensors. FullCircle~ fullcircle further shows that raw dual-fisheye video suffices for high-quality reconstruction, automatically masking the camera operator. Despite these advances, all of these pipelines represent the scene as a single, fixed configuration. When multiple object states are present in the capture---a door open in some frames and closed in others---the model either conflates them into averaged geometry and ghosting artifacts, or learns to discard the minority state as a distractor~ sabour2024sls . Either way, only one configuration survives in the final model; there is no mechanism to retain, switch between, or compose multiple stable states at inference time. A large family of methods extends 3DGS to dynamic scenes by conditioning the representation on time. Dynamic 3D Gaussians~ dynamic tracks persistent primitives across frames, while Deformable 3D Gaussians~ deformable and 4DGS~ 4dgaussiansplatting deform a canonical scene over time, with 4DGS using a learned space-time encoding. Spacetime Gaussians~ spacetime further augments primitives with temporal opacity and parametric motion. Subsequent work improves efficiency, temporal consistency, or geometric accuracy via depth priors~ 4dgs,3dgstream,4drotorgs,st4dgs,modgs . Differently from our method, all of these methods are parameterized by time, not by object state: recovering a specific scene configuration requires locating the right moment in the recording, and rendering a novel combination of states---e.g., two objects in configurations never co-observed---is not supported. More recent dynamic Gaussian methods, such as SDD-4DGS~ sdd , observe that applying deformation models to the entire scene is often inefficient, since most real-world scenes are largely static. This motivates methods that decompose scenes into static and dynamic components: GauFRe~ gaufre combines a static Gaussian component with deformable dynamic Gaussians, while Swift4D~ swift4d improves efficiency by passing only dynamic Gaussians through the deformation model. DeGauss~ degauss further uses dynamic-static decomposition to improve robustness to transient distractors. This observation is closely aligned with our setting, since object interactions usually affect only a small part of a environment. In contrast to our method, existing decomposition methods still treat the dynamic component as a temporally varying foreground: they separate dynamic regions from a static background, but provide no mechanism to independently switch or compose object states at inference time. A parallel line of work studies controllable and articulated 3D representations. Pre-Gaussian methods such as Watch It Move~ watchitmove discover articulated structure from object motion; PARIS~ paris goes further by decoupling static and movable parts from two multi-view captures of the same scene. Gaussian-based approaches extend this to photorealistic settings: SC-GS~ scgs enables motion editing via sparse control points, Template-free Articulated Gaussian Splatting~ template supports re-posing with super-points, and RigGS~ riggs adds rig-based editing and interpolation. ArtGS~ artgs and ArticulatedGS~ articulatedgs further focus on part-level modeling of individual objects. Crucially, all of these methods aim to encode object motion or articulation---they model how parts move, rather than discarding motion entirely to focus on the discrete stable configurations of the scene. In contrast, our method treats object interactions as a nuisance to be factored out, retaining only the clean on/off states and ignoring the transient motion between them. Closest to our setting are methods that reconstruct scenes across discrete object states. IGFuse~ igfuse and RecurGS~ recurgs address this by using semantic cues to detect state changes and aligning them via rigid transformations. GaussianCut~ gaussiancut and DecoupledGaussian~ decoupledgaussian contribute related tools for object segmentation and scene decomposition. However, all of these methods assume that state changes can be described as rigid motions of segmented object entities---an assumption that breaks down for casual capture, where interaction boundaries are fuzzy and deformations are non-rigid. In contrast, SwitchSplat learns which Gaussians belong to each state directly from photometric supervision, without requiring object masks, or rigid-body assumptions. Method SwitchSplat learns a state-aware 3D representation from casual captures by decomposing the scene into controllable, state-conditioned component

title: ALIGN: Aligning Condition Estimation and Expression in Advantage-Conditioned Behavior Cloning
summary: Human-collected robot manipulation data often mix successful behavior with retries, pauses, recoveries, and failures. Advantage-Conditioned Behavior Cloning (AC-BC) can exploit such mixed-quality data, but only if the conditioning signal is both accurately constructed from offline trajectories and effectively incorporated into the policy's action-vector-field prediction. Existing pipelines can weaken this signal by thresholding estimator-derived advantage scores into noisy conditions, and by routing conditions through prompts that weakly affect the action vector field. We introduce ALIGN, a condition-aligned AC-BC framework for vision-language-action policies. ALIGN directly predicts categorical pairwise conditions in the policy-facing label space and injects them into a DiT action expert through AdaRMS modulation fused with flow time. We evaluate ALIGN on deliberately mixed real-robot datasets for ARX X5 bowl stacking and Franka key hanging, each combining standard demonstrations with retry-heavy trajectories. ALIGN improves condition fidelity, strengthens conditional vector-field separability, and achieves 90.0% and 56.7% closed-loop success, compared with 56.7% and 33.3% for the strongest AC-BC baseline. These results indicate that aligning conditions from estimation to action prediction is an effective way to extract robust manipulation policies from data in which success, recovery and error coexist.
full_text: Human-collected robot manipulation data often mix successful behavior with retries, pauses, recoveries, and failures. Advantage-Conditioned Behavior Cloning (AC-BC) can exploit such mixed-quality data, but only if the conditioning signal is both accurately constructed from offline trajectories and effectively incorporated into the policy's action-vector-field prediction. Existing pipelines can weaken this signal by thresholding estimator-derived advantage scores into noisy conditions, and by routing conditions through prompts that weakly affect the action vector field. We introduce ALIGN, a condition-aligned AC-BC framework for vision-language-action policies. ALIGN directly predicts categorical pairwise conditions in the policy-facing label space and injects them into a DiT action expert through AdaRMS modulation fused with flow time. We evaluate ALIGN on deliberately mixed real-robot datasets for ARX X5 bowl stacking and Franka key hanging, each combining standard demonstrations with retry-heavy trajectories. ALIGN improves condition fidelity, strengthens conditional vector-field separability, and achieves 90.0 and 56.7 closed-loop success, compared with 56.7 and 33.3 for the strongest AC-BC baseline. These results indicate that aligning conditions from estimation to action prediction is an effective way to extract robust manipulation policies from data in which success, recovery and error coexist. Introduction Robot manipulation datasets collected from human teleoperation are rarely clean: besides successful execution, they contain pauses, retries, recoveries, and erroneous actions. This heterogeneity is important when adapting vision-language-action (VLA) models, which have emerged as strong robot policy backbones~ zitkovich2023rt,kim2024openvla,intelligence2025pi_,team2025gemini,team2025gemini15 , including diffusion- and flow-based variants for multimodal action distributions~ chi2025diffusion,black2024pi_0 . Advantage-Conditioned Behavior Cloning (AC-BC) offers a natural way to extract useful behavior from such mixed-quality offline data~ peng2019advantage,ashvin2020accelerating,intelligence2025pi06vlalearnsexperience : it estimates behavior quality, converts it into a policy-facing condition, trains imitation conditioned on that label, and deploys the policy under the desired high-quality condition. In principle, conditioning can retain useful recovery behavior while learning from both positive- and negative-conditioned examples. Filtering with the same classifier can also retain recovery frames predicted as positive; the distinction is that filtering discards predicted-negative examples. In practice, its benefit depends on whether the condition is both correctly constructed from data and strongly expressed by the policy. We argue that existing VLA-based AC-BC pipelines can lose this conditioning signal at both stages. First, the condition is often constructed indirectly: a continuous value, progress, or reward score is evaluated at two frames, differenced, thresholded, and then mapped to a discrete positive/negative label~ intelligence2025pi06vlalearnsexperience,yu2026chi_,chen2025sarm . This indirect conversion is fragile: continuous value/progress estimates are imperfect predictions, differencing can amplify local prediction noise, and thresholding turns near-boundary errors into discrete condition flips. Our temporal-gap supervision likewise represents local task progress, rather than independently annotated action quality or calibrated advantage. We study how this progress-based signal is converted into the condition consumed by AC-BC. The supervision used to define this signal is a separate design axis from estimator parameterization and condition expression. Second, even a correct condition may be weakly expressed. Prompt-based conditioning is convenient for VLA policies, but the condition must pass through the language or vision-language context before reaching the flow-based action expert. If changing the condition barely changes the predicted action vector field, the learned policy has little ability to act differently under different conditions. We introduce ALIGN, an AC-BC framework that aligns the policy-facing condition from estimation to action prediction. For condition construction, ALIGN replaces post-hoc thresholding of scalar value/progress differences with a direct categorical pairwise estimator, , trained to predict the same discrete condition consumed by the policy. For condition expression, ALIGN fuses the categorical condition with the flow-time embedding and injects it into the DiT action expert through AdaRMS modulation, giving the condition a direct and repeated influence on vector-field computation rather than relying only on prompt-level conditioning. Figure~ fig:architecture summarizes this estimation-to-expression pipeline. We evaluate ALIGN using standard and retry-heavy successful real-robot demonstrations for policy training; failed trajectories are used only for held-out condition evaluation. Our contributions are threefold: [leftmargin=*, itemsep=1pt, topsep=2pt, parsep=0pt] We formulate AC-BC for mixed-quality robot data as two coupled problems: condition construction and condition expression, diagnosed by AC-BC Condition Fidelity (ACF) and Conditional Vector-Field Separability (CVFS). We propose a direct categorical pairwise condition estimator that predicts the policy-facing AC-BC condition directly, reducing conversion error relative to value/progress thresholding. We introduce AdaRMS action-expert injection for flow-based VLA policies and validate ALIGN across two real-robot embodiments under controlled standard and retry-heavy training mixtures, showing improved condition fidelity, stronger condition-dependent vector-field separation, and higher closed-loop success. Related Work -language-action models for robot control. Modern robot policies increasingly use vision-language-action (VLA) backbones that combine perception, language, robot state, and action prediction, spanning embodied multimodal models, scalable transformer policies, cross-embodiment data, open-source generalists, and foundation-model-coordinated visuomotor policies~ driess2023palm,brohan2022rt,zitkovich2023rt,o2024open,team2024octo,kim2024openvla,shukor2025smolvla,cai2026xiaomi,bjorck2025gr00t,he2025falcon,team2025gemini,team2025gemini15 . Diffusion- and flow-based variants further model actions through generative dynamics~ chi2025diffusion,liu2025rdt,black2024pi_0,zhang2025spatial,hu2026bagelvla . These backbones improve action modeling but leave open how mixed-quality segments should be selected or conditioned during imitation. -conditioned imitation and policy extraction. Offline RL and policy extraction use learned returns, values, rewards, or advantages to bias imitation, including AWR/AWAC, CRR/IQL, and return- or goal-conditioned sequence models~ peng2019advantage,ashvin2020accelerating,wang2020critic,kostrikov2021offline,chen2021decision,emmons2021rvs . Robot variants learn rewards or progress for data selection, online RL, policy steering, and evaluation~ wagenmaker2025steering,liang2026robometer,ma2022vip,ma2023liv,sontakke2023roboclip,ayalew2025progressor,tan2025robo,chen2026topreward,chen2025sarm ; ReWiND improves policies with language-guided rewards without new demonstrations~ zhang2025rewind , and GR-RL filters progress-positive transitions before VLA specialization~ li2025gr . Other work exploits imperfect or mixed-quality data by self-supervised failure scoring, segment selection, value-guided retrials, or human recovery/correction trajectories~ wu2025learning,chen2025towards,du2024err,hu2025rac . Closest to our setting, \( ^*_ 0.6 \) converts learned score differences into positive/negative VLA conditions~ intelligence2025pi06vlalearnsexperience ; \( _0\) predicts a stage-conditioned pairwise advantage before thresholding it into a binary optimality label~ yu2026chi_ . ARM also uses pairwise supervision, but for advantage reward modeling rather than the local condition consumed by AC-BC~ mao2026arm . ALIGN is complementary: instead of treating value, progress, reward, or advantage as a continuous score for filtering, reweighting, or later thresholding, we directly predict the categorical AC-BC condition and study how it enters the action expert. interfaces for generative action policies. Condition estimation is distinct from condition expression. VLA policies can express advantage through prompts or special tokens~ intelligence2025pi06vlalearnsexperience , while generative policies provide lower-level conditioning through timestep modulation, feature-wise affine transforms, or conditional vector-field guidance~ peebles2023scalable,perez2018film,ho2022classifier . We compare action-expert condition-injection interfaces using downstream success and CVFS; among the tested mechanisms, AdaRMS gives the strongest vector-field separation and closed-loop performance. Method sec:method -Mediated Decomposition. We formulate AC-BC as a condition-mediated policy extraction process with two coupled stages: \[ c_t &= g_ ( _ ), && ,\\ v_t &= v_ (x_t,t,o_t,c_t), && . \] Here, \( _ \) denotes mixed-quality offline trajectories, \(c_t\) is the policy-facing AC-BC condition, and \(v_ \) is the vector field predicted by the flow-matching action expert. This decomposition makes explicit two places where the conditioning signal can be weakened. The first is condition construction: whether mixed trajectory evidence, including retries, pauses, recoveries, and failures, is mapped to the correct discrete condition consumed by the policy. The second is condition expression: whether changing this condition produces a meaningful change in the features and vector field that determine action prediction. Under this view, successful AC-BC requires not only estimating behavior quality, but also preserving the resulting condition as an effective control variable inside the policy. ALIGN instantiates this principle by directly estimating categorical pairwise conditions in the policy-facing label space and injecting them into the DiT action expert through AdaRMS modulation fused with flow time. Section~ sec:experiments evaluates these two stages using held-out condition fidelity, vector-field diagnostics, and downstream robot success. title: SPAR: Structural Pruning and Action Recovery for Vision-Language-Action Models
summary: The limited onboard computing resources of robots make the inference demands of vision-language-action (VLA) models costly to accommodate. Reducing these demands through aggressive compression, however, can degrade manipulation performance beyond what supervised fine-tuning alone recovers. We present SPAR (Structural Pruning and Action Recovery), which simultaneously prunes the hidden and feed-forward intermediate dimensions of the large language model (LLM) backbone through pruning-aware tuning, then applies reinforcement learning (RL) to recover policy performance. Applied to $π_{0.5}$, SPAR reduces the language backbone from 2.34B to 0.09B parameters and the full model from 3.37B to 1.12B, removing approximately 96% and 67% of their parameters, respectively. At this compression level, RL raises average success across the four LIBERO suites from 84.55% to 93.45%, an 8.90-percentage-point gain. The compressed policy achieves a $1.98\times$ full-policy inference speedup over the unpruned model. These results identify substantial intermediate-dimension redundancy and show that post-pruning RL can recover manipulation performance in compact policies.
full_text: Experiments Tasks and Training Protocol We train one policy per configuration across all 40 tasks in LIBERO's Spatial, Object, Goal, and Long (LIBERO-10) suites~ NEURIPS2023_8c3c6668 , covering spatial, object, goal, and long-horizon variation. Using OpenPI's PyTorch implementation~ physicalintelligence2025openpi with a Gemma 2B backbone, we vary retention targets for the hidden and intermediate dimensions and report suite success rates and their mean. Baselines We compare with unpruned before and after RL and published results for NORA~ hung2025norasmallopensourcedgeneralist , NORA-1.5~ hung2025nora15 , SmolVLA~ shukor2025smolvlavisionlanguageactionmodelaffordable , GraspVLA~ deng2025graspvla , and EcoVLA~ huang2026ecovla . SPAR's parameter-pruning ratios are relative to the unpruned full model (3.37B) and LLM (2.34B), with pruning percentages rounded to integers. EcoVLA's labels denote its reported channel/head pruning settings. Implementation Details SFT uses a batch size of 256 for 30,000 steps: 6,000 for PAT mask learning and 24,000 for post-pruning fine-tuning. Training and RL use NVIDIA A800 GPUs. We deploy on NVIDIA Jetson AGX Orin and measure median full-policy inference latency using TensorRT. PPO Configuration PPO uses eight NVIDIA A800 GPUs on one node, with 128 training and 80 evaluation environments across all four suites. The actor global batch size is 2,048, with a per-rank micro-batch size of 128 and two gradient-accumulation steps. The runner allows up to 200 RL epochs. title: Learning Geometry-Aware Planning Representations for Monocular Flight with Cross-Modal Supervision
summary: Existing high-speed navigation systems for micro aerial vehicles (MAVs) commonly rely on depth cameras, stereo vision, or LiDAR to obtain explicit geometric information, while monocular cameras offer a lighter and lower-cost alternative. However, monocular flight remains challenging because RGB images offer no direct metric cues and visual appearance varies considerably across environments. We propose a geometry-aware monocular visual planning framework that predicts trajectories from two image frames, their relative pose, and the MAV state. Without explicitly reconstructing depth, the proposed method complements the downstream planning objective with feature-level geometric supervision by transferring the planning-relevant representation learned by a privileged depth expert to the RGB planner through cross-modal distillation. The framework first trains a depth-based geometric expert, then distills its planning features into a monocular branch using paired RGB-D observations, and finally adapts the planner to the downstream trajectory planning objective. This design encourages the policy to learn planning-relevant geometric features, enabling collision avoidance. We further use a 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) simulator to render visual observations for data collection, paired RGB-D supervision, and simulation evaluation. The planner trained in simulation is then deployed in real-world environments without real-world fine-tuning, achieving obstacle avoidance at speeds of up to 6.5 m/s.

Perception and autonomy, collision avoidance, integrated planning and learning, aerial systems. Introduction Achieving agile autonomous flight in highly cluttered environments remains a long-standing challenge for MAVs. Most existing autonomous navigation systems rely on sensors that provide explicit metric geometry, such as LiDARs and depth cameras, to perceive the surrounding environment, followed by well-established mapping-and-planning pipelines or end-to-end policy networks to generate collision-aware trajectories r4,r8,r9 . While these approaches have demonstrated impressive performance, their reliance on dedicated geometric sensors constrains the compactness and design flexibility of miniature aerial platforms. In contrast, monocular RGB planning requires only a lightweight commodity camera, offering greater flexibility under stringent payload and energy budgets. Biological vision demonstrates that agile flight does not necessarily rely on explicit geometric perception. Small flying animals such as bees and forest-dwelling birds can rapidly navigate through densely cluttered environments using only two-dimensional visual cues, such as object scale changes and scene contours, without explicitly reconstructing the surrounding geometry r6,r7 . Likewise, experienced first-person-view (FPV) pilots can execute aggressive maneuvers and traverse narrow gaps using only a monocular video stream r5 . These observations indicate that monocular images contain sufficient information to support agile autonomous flight, making monocular cameras an attractive sensing modality for MAVs. Compared with LiDARs and depth cameras, monocular cameras are lightweight, inexpensive, easy to integrate, and naturally compatible with wide field-of-view optics such as fisheye lenses. Moreover, they provide rich texture and contextual information that is unavailable to purely geometric sensors. Despite these advantages, learning agile navigation policies directly from these images remains fundamentally challenging. Most existing navigation methods employ imitation learning or reinforcement learning to train RGB policies directly using downstream task objectives r11,r12 , without explicitly constraining their internal representations to preserve planning-relevant geometry. As a result, they often suffer from appearance overfitting and poor cross-scene generalization. Unlike depth sensors, monocular cameras provide no explicit metric distance information, making it difficult to infer the traversable spatial structure required for motion planning. Furthermore, these images are highly sensitive to illumination, textures, and object appearance, forcing the navigation policy to distinguish geometry relevant to obstacle avoidance from appearance variations that are irrelevant to planning. To alleviate these issues, some approaches introduce explicit geometric intermediate representations, such as depth r16,r19 or optical flow r14,r17 , to extract geometry-aware cues from observations, while others exploit privileged depth supervision or ground-truth geometric information during training to guide policy learning r15,r18 . However, explicit geometric intermediate representations incur additional computational overhead and inference latency. Directly trained RGB policies, on the other hand, rely primarily on downstream task supervision, without explicitly encouraging the learned representations to preserve planning-relevant geometric information. Consequently, these representations may remain sensitive to appearance variations and may not reliably capture the geometric structure required for collision avoidance. To address these limitations, we propose a geometry-aware monocular navigation framework that takes two consecutive RGB images, their relative pose, and the MAV state as input. It should be noted that the primary objective of monocular navigation is not to recover pixel-wise accurate depth, but to learn geometry-aware representations that preserve planning-relevant structural information. Guided by this insight, the framework narrows the geometric gap between a privileged depth expert and a monocular planner by transferring planning-oriented geometric representations through feature-level distillation. During training, the depth expert learns geometry-aware planning features under privileged supervision, while the student network reproduces these structured representations via feature alignment. To further encourage the learned representations to preserve planning-relevant geometry and reduce their dependence on appearance cues, we introduce a lightweight coarse-depth prediction branch with an auxiliary training objective. This auxiliary task provides additional geometric regularization for the distilled representations. Furthermore, we develop a scalable simulation pipeline based on 3DGS, which provides photorealistic images, corresponding geometric supervision, and map-based trajectory cost labels for data generation and training. During deployment, the planner operates solely on two consecutive monocular images and MAV states, without requiring any depth estimation module or additional geometric sensors. The main contributions of this work are summarized as follows: We propose a framework that transfers planning-oriented geometric representations from a privileged depth expert to the student planner, aided by a lightweight coarse-depth branch that reinforces geometric structure. We develop a monocular planner that plans trajectories from sequential images, relative pose, and MAV states, and performs online evaluation to enable agile, collision-aware flight. We establish a 3DGS-based data pipeline that provides aligned RGB observations, privileged geometry, vehicle states, and trajectory-cost labels for training and evaluation. Related Work Navigation with Explicit Geometric Perception Most autonomous navigation systems rely on depth cameras or LiDAR to obtain explicit geometric information. Classical pipelines construct ESDF maps from depth observations and combine path search with trajectory optimization r21, r25 , whereas methods based on safe flight corridors (SFCs) optimize trajectories within convex collision-free corridors r20 . Ren et al. jointly optimized trajectory safety and efficiency using LiDAR, enabling high speed autonomous flight r9 . Learning-based planners further reduce latency by directly mapping sensor observations to trajectories or controls. Loquercio et al. used imitation learning to predict planning outputs from depth images and MAV states r8 . Without expert demonstrations, Lu et al.'s Guidance Learning trains a polynomial-trajectory predictor by back-propagating gradients of the trajectory objective r2,r33 . Zhang et al. combined differentiable physics with reinforcement learning to train a GRU policy from depth observations and vehicle states for agile multi-MAV flight r24 . Xu et al. fused LiDAR range images with temporal point-flow features in an RL policy that directly generates obstacle-avoidance controls r22 . Monocular Vision-based Navigation Monocular cameras are lightweight and power-efficient, making them suitable for resource-constrained MAVs. Early methods directly mapped RGB images to navigation commands using CNN r11, r12 . However, their lack of explicit geometric supervision may limit policy reliability and generalization. Other approaches recover geometric cues as intermediate representations. MonoNav estimates depth and reconstructs local geometry before planning r16 , whereas Hu et al. use optical flow to represent scene depth and structure for robust and agile navigation r14 . Sim-to-real transfer remains another challenge for monocular navigation. CAD2RL combines deep reinforcement learning with domain randomization to transfer policies to real MAVs r13 . More recently, 3DGS has enabled rapid, high-fidelity reconstruction of real scenes for robotic simulation r28 . Compared with manually constructed game-engine environments, it provides realistic visual observations with less scene-building effort. Low et al.'s SOUS VIDE uses 3DGS to collect data for end-to-end policies deployed on real MAVs r29 . Huang et al. further combine 3DGS environments with domain adaptation and randomization to improve real-world generalization r15 . Method Problem Formulation sec:problem We study monocular visual trajectory planning for a quadrotor. At each planning step, the planner maps the visual and state observation to a single smooth polynomial trajectory that drives the robot toward a goal. The planner receives two types of inputs. (i) A pair of temporal images and their relative camera pose, represented by a unit quaternion and a metric translation , which together provide geometric cues for scene understanding. (ii) A body-frame state observation , comprising the current velocity, acceleration, and goal vector. Following the one-stage planning paradigm~ r2 , the network simultaneously predicts candidate motion primitives. For each primitive it outputs an end state , a selection score , and a predicted collision cost . We first use only to shortlist a top- candidate set, and then select within it the primitive that minimizes a trajectory cost combining the predicted collision cost with the closed-form dynamics terms evaluated online. The same cost structure is also used as the training objective, ensuring that online selection follows the same optimality criterion as training. The candidate primitives are associated with anchors on a polar lattice spanning the camera field of view. Each primitive is realized by a single-segment quintic polynomial that matches the current state and the predicted end state . The polynomial coefficients admit a closed-form solution in for fixed and ; trajectory costs such as the jerk integrals are therefore differentiable in the end state and are reused both as training objectives and as the closed-form selection cost at inference. title: ReInsVLN: Revisiting Historical Evidence for Training-Free Vision-and-Language Navigation
summary: Vision-and-language navigation (VLN) relies on retaining and using relevant observations. Yet growing histories introduce redundancy, and retained information may remain underused. We introduce ReInsBench, a diagnostic benchmark that examines history utilization through controlled continuation trials. Its results show that history-review reinstruction can recover navigation failures using the existing task context. Motivated by this finding, we propose ReInsVLN, a training-free framework supporting memory construction and utilization in frozen navigators. Coverage- and Instruction-Aware Compression constructs compact visual context through temporal redundancy reduction, coverage-aware protection, and instruction-guided token selection. Forgetting-Inspired History Reminders guide navigators to revisit retained observations according to a predefined schedule, without additional model calls. On R2R Val-Unseen, ReInsVLN improves success rates by 8.48 and 3.37 percentage points over the native StreamVLN and InternVLA-N1, reaching 64.27% and 64.44%, respectively. Visual compression largely preserves navigation performance while reducing prefill latency and KV cache memory by up to 21.77% and 32.25%, respectively, on matched observation workloads. Real-world trials on humanoid and quadruped robots further support the applicability of ReInsVLN to sequential instruction following and ordinal navigation.

Real-world trials on humanoid and quadruped robots further support the applicability of ReInsVLN to sequential instruction following and ordinal navigation. Introduction Vision-and-language navigation (VLN) requires an agent to follow natural-language instructions using a sequence of visual observations~ anderson2018r2r, krantz2020vlnce . Partial observability makes decisions depend on previously encountered landmarks~ hong2021vlnbert . As illustrated in Fig.~ fig:motivation , following the instruction ``Pass the armchair beside the blue cabinet, then stop at the next armchair'' requires the navigator to use the previously observed relation between the cabinet and the first armchair to identify the next armchair as the stopping point. Such dependencies make memory essential for retaining information from past observations and using it to guide subsequent actions~ chen2021hamt . Effective navigation memory involves two complementary capabilities: memory construction and memory utilization. Here, memory construction selects and organizes past observations into available context, while memory utilization uses that context to guide decisions. Spatial maps offer one way to organize navigation history~ chen2022duet . As navigation proceeds, repeated views introduce redundancy into the growing observation history, increasing the cost of processing it~ zhang2024navid, wei2026streamvln, internnav2025, wei2026ground . This requires retaining useful historical information within limited context and computation budgets, while preserving cues for later decisions. However, retained information does not guarantee effective use, even in long-context language models~ liu2024lostmiddle . In the example in Fig. 1, the cabinet observation may remain in the navigator's history without guiding it to stop at the correct armchair. This raises a central question: even when relevant historical information is retained, can the navigator use it effectively? To examine this question, we introduce ReInsBench, a diagnostic benchmark constructed from selected R2R~ anderson2018r2r navigation episodes. At selected decision points, a frozen navigator continues under different prompts from the same observation history and environment state. The benchmark assesses whether directing the navigator to revisit its existing history improves subsequent navigation, using neutral reminders to control for the effect of generic prompting. In a controlled subset of 198 instances, history review yields 64 successful continuations, compared with 53 for neutral reminders and 40 without an additional prompt. These findings suggest that navigators do not always make effective use of the historical information already available to them. Building on this diagnosis, we aim to improve memory construction and utilization within existing navigators. A compact visual context must preserve cues whose relevance may emerge only later~ lu2026stepnav, wang2026historypruning . Once retained, these cues need to inform subsequent decisions at appropriate moments, requiring guidance that encourages their use while limiting interference with otherwise correct navigation. To this end, we propose ReInsVLN, a training-free framework that combines visual context compression and history-review reminders within the existing context mechanisms of navigators. For memory construction, we adopt a two-stage visual compression strategy consisting of pre-LLM compression and in-LLM compression. The pre-LLM stage reduces temporal redundancy before visual tokens enter the language model, combining causal token reduction with dynamic-token protection to prioritize content poorly covered by previously retained tokens. The in-LLM stage builds a query from the original instruction and expands it with high-scoring visual seeds. It then combines semantic relevance with positional information to select a compact subset of visual tokens, restoring their original order after selection. For memory utilization, short reminders guide the navigator to revisit retained observations in relation to the original instruction. A predefined, forgetting-inspired schedule uses the number of decision calls elapsed since the previous reminder as a temporal prior for determining when to introduce history review. The prompts are inserted at existing decision calls, preserving the native action-execution pipeline. Experiments on R2R Val-Unseen evaluate ReInsVLN with StreamVLN and InternVLA-N1, representing streaming and non-streaming inference, respectively. With Coverage- and Instruction-Aware Compression and Forgetting-Inspired History Reminders applied together, ReInsVLN improves success rates by 8.48 and 3.37 points over the corresponding native navigators. These improvements exceed the sum of individual gains on both navigators, suggesting synergy between two components. Visual compression also reduces prefill latency and KV cache usage. Physical deployment is another focus of legged-robot VLN~ cheng2025navila . The main contributions are summarized as follows: We introduce ReInsBench to diagnose history utilization through controlled prompting comparisons, showing that history-review reinstruction can recover navigation failures using the existing task context. We develop Coverage- and Instruction-Aware Compression for memory construction in ReInsVLN, combining temporal redundancy reduction with instruction-guided visual token selection. We introduce Forgetting-Inspired History Reminders to support memory utilization by guiding frozen navigators to revisit retained observations according to a predefined schedule, without additional model calls. Simulation experiments show navigation gains on both navigators, together with reduced prefill latency and KV cache storage. Real-world trials on humanoid and quadruped robots further support the training-free generalization of ReInsVLN to challenging tasks requiring sequential landmark tracking. Related Work History Modeling in VLN History modeling connects current observations with previously encountered landmarks. Explicit visual-language maps~ wen2025ovlmap organize observations spatially, while NaVid incorporates historical observations into action prediction. StreamVLN separates recent interactions from slowly updated visual memory and reuses cached states across decisions. ReInsBench complements these approaches by assessing history utilization through controlled prompting. ReInsVLN builds on existing context mechanisms, combining visual compression and history-review reminders to reduce redundancy and improve history utilization. Visual Token Compression Visual token compression accelerates MLLM inference by shortening visual token sequences, either in a single step or progressively across multiple stages~ wu2026data,yin2026bifocal,zheng2026geogr . LLaVA-PruMerge~ shang2025llava prunes and merges tokens before the LLM. FastV~ chen2024fastv prunes at a selected LLM layer, while PyramidDrop~ xing2024pyramiddrop and HiDrop~ wu2026hidrop prune progressively across layers. For streaming video, StreamForest~ zeng2026streamforest uses hierarchical event-level merging, and ViCoStream~ tan2026vicostream uses chunk-level temporal token dropping. In VLN, STEP-Nav~ lu2026stepnav and history-conditioned pruning~ wang2026historypruning reduce spatial and temporal redundancy. While prior compression work primarily targets inference efficiency, ReInsVLN couples two-stage compression with history-review reminders to improve the utilization of retained visual context. Memory Utilization and Reactivation Memory utilization connects retained information with current decisions. CMMR-VLN~ li2026cmmrvln retrieves prior navigation cases as rules, while Memoir~ xu2026memoir queries observation and behavioral histories using predicted states. MemVR~ zou2025memvr reinjects visual evidence into intermediate layers under uncertainty, and VisRef~ ghosal2026visref reintroduces selected visual tokens during reasoning. MemoryBank~ zhong2024memorybank and DART-VLN~ zhang2026dartvln incorporate temporal priors into memory retention and readout, respectively. ReInsVLN provides reactivation at the input level through scheduled history-review prompts, guiding frozen navigators to revisit existing observations without additional retrieval or model calls. ReInsBench: Diagnosing History Utilization sec:diagnostic Retaining history does not guarantee its effective use. ReInsBench is a diagnostic benchmark that examines this gap through matched R2R continuation trials. A frozen navigator resumes from the same observation history and environment state under different prompting conditions. Paired outcomes quantify navigation recovery and disruption. Benchmark Construction ReInsBench is constructed from R2R Val-Unseen in continuous environments, using recorded rollouts of StreamVLN, InternVLA-N1, and AwareVLN. As illustrated in Fig.~ fig:reinsbench_construction , episodes are retained only when exactly one navigator succeeds. The successful rollout demonstrates episode-level solvability, while the two unsuccessful rollouts provide diagnostic instances. This yields 812 model-specific instances from 406 episodes, spanning 296 scene--trajectory pairs across 11 scenes. For each unsuccessful rollout, the first disagreement between recorded and reference actions defines an offline checkpoint. The recorded prefix is replayed to restore the simulator state, with the checkpoint registered before the disagreeing action is executed. The collection contains 451 checkpoints after navigation begins and 361 initial checkpoints, allowing separate analyses of navigation with prior history and initial instruction grounding. Intervention and Evaluation Protocol Controlled continuation ( ) adds no text and controls for renewed inference. Neutral prompting ( ) requests careful continuation. History-review reinstruction ( ) asks the navigator to revisit available history and realign subgoals with the original instruction. The intervention combines a review request with task restatement. For 794 template reminders, reference sequence length determines a coarse starting clause and the repeated instruction suffix; 18 pilot reminders use fixed semantic restatements. Reference information informs offline construction, but no new reference action sequence is supplied to the navigator. At each checkpoint, the frozen navigator resumes from the same replayed state under different prompting conditions. We evaluate whether each continuation reaches the goal and compare the resulting successes and failures. title: HAF-VLA: Hierarchical Action Flow Framework for Humanoid Vision-Language-Action Control
summary: Humanoid robots hold great promise as general-purpose agents in human-centered environments, yet adapting generalist vision-language-action (VLA) policies to real-world humanoid loco-manipulation remains challenging. Unlike fixed-base or wheeled manipulators, humanoids must coordinate locomotion, posture, gaze, and dual-arm manipulation over a high-dimensional whole-body action space, where inaccurate base or waist motions can easily induce unstable and aggressive upper-body compensation. We propose HAF-VLA, a hierarchical action-flow framework for humanoid VLA control. Built upon a pretrained flow-matching VLA, HAF-VLA inherits the vision-language prefix encoder and action expert weights, and adapts them to humanoid whole-body loco-manipulation with learnable stage embeddings and cross-stage KV-cache conditioning. Instead of generating the full action chunk in a single pass, HAF-VLA progressively denoises a shared whole-body action space: first locomotion and head commands, then waist refinement, and finally full-body manipulation. To preserve structural dependencies across stages, we introduce a cross-stage KV cache conditioning mechanism, enabling subsequent action generation stages to refine and augment their outputs based on the action representations from preceding stages. Experimental results across six real-world tasks demonstrate that our framework significantly enhances the performance of existing models in humanoid loco-manipulation tasks, demonstrating an effective pathway for adapting strong mobile-manipulation VLAs to humanoid whole-body loco-manipulation.

Introduction Humanoid robots hold the promise of becoming general-purpose agents capable of operating in human-centered environments. Unlike fixed-base or wheeled robots, humanoids must coordinate locomotion, waist motion, gaze, and dual-arm manipulation to navigate large spaces, adjust posture, maintain balance, and physically interact with the environment~ homie,falcon,softa,almi,exbody2,liao2025beyondmimicmotiontrackingversatile,ze2025generalizable,jiang2026wholebodyvla . This whole-body nature makes humanoid loco-manipulation fundamentally different from conventional manipulation: inaccurate base or waist motions can force the upper body to produce compensatory movements, degrading precision, stability, and energy efficiency. Recent vision-language-action models and world-action models have achieved strong results on fixed-base, dual-arm, and wheeled mobile manipulators~ pi0, intelligence2025pi05visionlanguageactionmodelopenworld, gr00tn1_2025, kim2026cosmos, openvlaoft, fan2025xr . However, most of them are not explicitly designed for the structured action space and unstable bipedal dynamics of humanoids. Directly applying a single-stage action generator to humanoid loco-manipulation may entangle locomotion, posture, and manipulation in an unstructured manner, making the policy prone to unstable base motions or aggressive upper-body compensation~ exbody2, liao2025beyondmimicmotiontrackingversatile,omnih2o,r2s2 . Therefore, humanoid VLA control requires an action-generation structure that respects the kinematic dependencies among the legs, waist, head, and arms while preserving the semantic reasoning ability of pretrained VLA models. To this end, we propose HAF-VLA, a hierarchical action-flow framework for humanoid vision-language-action control. Built upon a pretrained flow-matching VLA~ intelligence2025pi05visionlanguageactionmodelopenworld , HAF-VLA reuses its vision-language prefix encoder~ beyer2024paligemmaversatile3bvlm and action expert weights, and adapts them to humanoid whole-body loco-manipulation through progressive action generation. Instead of synthesizing the full action chunk in a single pass, HAF-VLA first generates locomotion and head commands, then incorporates waist refinement, and finally produces full-body manipulation actions. This design encourages locomotion-related motions to be planned before manipulation, reducing the tendency of the upper body to compensate for inaccurate base or waist movements~ chen2025acdit, jiang2025behaviorrobotsuitestreamlining . We further introduce cross-stage KV-cache~ liang2025mixtureoftransformerssparsescalablearchitecture conditioning to propagate structured action information across the hierarchy (see (b)). After each non-final stage completes flow denoising~ yaron2023flowmatching , its clean action prediction is re-encoded by the shared action expert to form an action KV cache, which conditions the following stage. In this way, later stages refine and augment their actions based on earlier motion plans, while all stages remain grounded in the same visual-language prefix representation. We evaluate HAF-VLA on two full-sized humanoid platforms, Tian Gong 3.0 and Tian Gong 2.0, across six real-world loco-manipulation tasks spanning household and industrial scenarios (see (a)). HAF-VLA consistently improves normalized task scores over imitation-learning, VLA, and world-model baselines (see (c)), especially on tasks requiring long-distance locomotion, precise body positioning, and coordinated whole-body manipulation. Our contributions are: (i) a hierarchical action-flow formulation for humanoid VLA loco-manipulation over a shared whole-body action space; (ii) a cross-stage KV-cache conditioning mechanism for progressive whole-body action generation; and (iii) real-world validation showing that this structure effectively adapts pretrained mobile-manipulation VLAs to humanoid loco-manipulation. Related Work Vision-language-action models. Vision-language-action models (VLAs) aim to map visual observations and language instructions directly to robot actions~ rdt, kim2025openvla, zheng2026xvla, univla . Representative works such as RT-2~ zitkovich2023rt2 and OpenVLA~ kim2025openvla show that vision-language pretraining can be effectively transferred to robotic manipulation, while and further move toward continuous generative action modeling with flow matching~ pi0, intelligence2025pi05visionlanguageactionmodelopenworld . However, most existing VLAs still focus on tabletop tasks or mobile manipulators, leaving high-dimensional humanoid whole-body action generation underexplored. Humanoid VLAs. Recent works have begun to extend VLAs to humanoid robots~ shao2025langwbclanguagedirectedhumanoidwholebody, xue2025leverb, humanoidvla, bai2026hexhumanoidalignedexpertscrossembodiment . GR00T N1.7~ gr00tn1_2025 studies general-purpose humanoid action generation from vision-language inputs, while WholeBodyVLA~ jiang2026wholebodyvla explores latent VLA learning for large-space humanoid mobile manipulation. Recently, ~ wei2026psi0openfoundationmodel introduced an open humanoid foundation model pretrained from egocentric human videos. In contrast to methods that rely on latent skills, cross-embodiment transfer, or learning from human videos, our method is directly built upon a pretrained generalist VLA and improves its performance on humanoid by generating structured whole-body actions grounded in the humanoid forward-kinematic chain, sparing the computational cost of training a new model. Whole-body manipulation. title: MultiAltitudeSR: Multi-Altitude Agricultural UAV Image Super-Resolution via Physical Ground Sampling Distance Conditioning
summary: Unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) enable high-throughput platforms for crop monitoring but face a fundamental trade-off between flight altitude and image spatial resolution. Many existing super-resolution (SR) methods for UAV imagery rely on oversimplified synthetic degradation models and are restricted to fixed integer upsampling scales, limiting their ability to handle real-world degradations and varying flight altitudes. This study proposes MultiAltitudeSR, a framework that conditions feature modulation and reconstruction on source and target ground sampling distances (GSDs). MultiAltitudeSR trained jointly on real UAV images at altitudes of 10 to 70 m above ground level supports all 21 source-to-target altitude pairs without pair-specific fine-tuning, covering scale factors ranging from 1.18$\times$ to 6.03$\times$. The framework can be extended to additional source-target GSD combinations by incorporating corresponding image pairs into training. On the 20-to-10 m pair, the model achieved competitive perceptual performance compared with pair-specific baselines, with LPIPS of 0.2236, DISTS of 0.2431, and NIQE of 8.9020. Experiments using the same architecture demonstrated the value of acquiring real-world multi-altitude UAV image pairs for SR training, with real-pair training achieving better average reconstruction performance across the 21 altitude pairs than training with the tested synthetic degradation pipeline. Downstream zero-shot segmentation case studies illustrated task-dependent benefits of super-resolved imagery for crop monitoring, suggesting potential UAV flight-time savings through image acquisition at higher altitudes.

UAV Super Resolution Real-world Image Degradation Multi-altitude UAV Imagery Ground Sampling Distance Plant Phenotyping Introduction Unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) have become one of the most promising high-throughput platforms for plant phenotyping and vegetation monitoring at field to regional scales. A major bottleneck of high-throughput UAV monitoring is the trade-off between flight heights and time. While low-altitude high-resolution (HR) UAV images capture fine plant structures and features essential to downstream tasks, their limited ground coverage constrains comprehensive crop monitoring and is thus impractical for breeding population selection. For example, a 2-ha breeding trial takes hours of flight time at 10 m, but only minutes at 70 m. Moreover, UAV acquisition should fall within a narrow window of stable conditions, since image quality depends on weather, solar angle, and various other field factors gao2021weather . A multi-hour low-altitude flight cannot yield radiometrically consistent imagery across a single trial. High-altitude UAV low-resolution (LR) images are more practical for real-world production, providing higher throughput but less accurate phenotyping characteristics MAO2023110698 . Such trade-offs between throughput and accuracy have become a crucial barrier in plant phenotyping and precision agriculture towards the next green revolution yang2020crop . As a potential solution to this trade-off, deep learning-based super-resolution (SR) in UAV crop imagery has started to draw more attention in recent years lu2024effective, zhang2025phenosr . Existing SR methods learn from paired LR and HR images wang2020deep, liu2022blind , and usually comprise three components: a degrader that synthesizes LR inputs from HR references zhang2021designing, wang2021real , a generator that restores high-frequency details wang2018esrgan , and an up-sampler that projects features to the target resolution shi2016real . Unlike compression-induced degradations in general computer vision, changes in UAV flight altitude introduce physical degradations that are difficult to characterize and quantify with no explicit function expression luo2022learning, liu2025real . Owing to the limited availability of real-world multi-altitude UAV imagery, existing UAV SR studies often rely on synthetic datasets to learn simplified degradation patterns, in which LR images are generated from HR references under simplified degradation assumptions. These assumptions fail to reproduce the altitude-dependent degradation of real UAV imagery, which combines ground sampling distance (GSD) variation, altitude-specific optical blur, and various altitude-related effects such as wind-induced motion blur. Due to this domain gap, models trained on synthetic datasets exhibit degraded performance when transferred to real-world applications. Aside from degradation assumptions, SR models in agricultural applications are commonly formulated for predefined integer scales, such as 2 , 3 , and 4 lu2024effective, zhang2025phenosr . These fixed integer scales do not fully reflect the physical resolution characteristics of UAV imagery, which are determined by physical acquisition parameters, including flight altitude and imaging configuration shi2016unmanned, chakhvashvili2024crop . Different plant phenotyping tasks require imagery at different physical resolutions velumani2021estimates, hu2021coupling . Consequently, predefined scale factors cannot flexibly represent the diverse source-target GSD mappings encountered in practical UAV phenotyping. Furthermore, the same upsampling factor can still correspond to different source and target GSDs, which are indistinguishable when resolution changes are represented solely by scale factors. These characteristics motivate an SR formulation that explicitly accounts for the physical source and target resolutions of UAV imagery. Collectively, these limitations restrict the translation of conventional SR methods to practical UAV-based plant phenotyping and other image-based agricultural crop-monitoring applications, which require handling both real-world UAV image degradations and flexible resolution mappings. To address these gaps, this study proposes MultiAltitudeSR, a GSD-conditioned multi-scale SR model learning altitude-dependent real-world degradation patterns in UAV crop imagery. By explicitly conditioning the reconstruction process on source and target GSDs, MultiAltitudeSR jointly handles 21 source-target GSD mappings within a single unified model, covering all low-to-high GSD combinations acquired at altitudes from 10 m to 70 m AGL in 10 m increments. Beyond these 21 pairs, MultiAltitudeSR can be readily extended to additional resolution mappings without requiring separate scale-specific models. The main contributions of this work are as follows: (1) A real-world multi-altitude UAV image dataset constructed across multiple crop types and growth stages, enabling SR to learn practical degradation patterns directly from paired imagery acquired at different flight altitudes. (2) A GSD-conditioned multi-scale SR framework, MultiAltitudeSR, that jointly handles 21 source-target GSD mappings within a unified model, providing flexibility beyond conventional fixed integer-scale SR. The study interprets the learned SR patterns via advanced visualization techniques and ablation experiments for validation. (3) The effects of real-world and synthetic SR datasets are compared under the same SR architecture. Reconstruction of different GSDs and crops is analyzed and interpreted through ablation experiments and visualization. (4) The potential benefits of SR for downstream crop monitoring are illustrated through zero-shot segmentation case studies spanning different tasks, crop scenes, and source-target GSD mappings. Methodology Multi-altitude Crop SR Dataset The multi-altitude UAV RGB dataset was acquired using a DJI Mavic 3 Multispectral UAV (SZ DJI Technology Co., Shenzhen, China) with a visible RGB camera (4/3 CMOS, 20MP). RGB imagery was radiometrically corrected together with the multispectral bands using a Sentera Calibrated Reflectance Panel (Sentera LLC, St. Paul, USA) and measurements from the UAV’s onboard sunlight sensor. The dataset includes seven flight altitudes ranging from 10 m to 70 m above ground level (AGL) in 10-meter increments. Orthomosaic maps were reconstructed using Agisoft Metashape (Agisoft LLC., Calgary, Canada), followed by georeferencing, preprocessing and manual validation of image pairing quality. All the flights were conducted with 75 frontal overlap and 80 side overlap. Despite identical flight and reconstruction settings used throughout the dataset, minor variations in the actual GSDs occurred among reconstructed orthomosaics due to changes in actual acquisition conditions, including local terrain elevation and flight dynamics, as well as in the photogrammetric reconstruction process. Representative GSDs derived from the reconstructed orthomosaics were assigned to each acquisition altitude and used as the conditioning variables. For flight altitudes of 10, 20, 30, 40, 50, 60, and 70 m AGL, the assigned GSDs were 3.3, 5.5, 8.4, 11.3, 14.0, 16.8, and 19.9 mm/pixel, respectively. This discretization enables GSD-aware routing in the proposed framework, with minor inter-flight and reconstruction-induced GSD variations absorbed into the altitude-level representation rather than explicitly calibrated on a per-flight basis. Representative samples from the multi-altitude UAV dataset are shown in Fig.~ fig: Dataset_overview . This dataset covers multiple crops, including common bean, soybean, strawberry, canola, chickpea, and various weeds. To illustrate altitude-dependent changes in fine spatial details and image degradation under field conditions, common bean and chickpea were selected as examples of crops with relatively large and small leaves, respectively. Fig.~ fig: Chickpea_Common_Bean presents local image details and their corresponding intensity luminance surfaces across flight altitudes. The luma values were computed as , where , , and denote the gamma-encoded RGB channel values series2011studio . The dataset was split into training, validation, and test sets at an approximately 8:1:1 ratio, comprising 8,673, 1,050, and 1,029 images, respectively. The three subsets have approximately consistent crop proportions. Synthetic HR-LR Pairs Due to practical challenges in acquiring paired UAV imagery of different GSDs, existing SR methods commonly rely on synthetic HR-LR pairs generated through predefined degradation processes tian2025lightweight, li2024lswinsr, aslahishahri2021spatial . However, real UAV image degradation arises from complex and interacting factors, including optical effects, platform motion, sensor noise, environmental variations, and subsequent image processing leem2025practical, sieberth2016automatic, ludwig2020quality . Consequently, accurately reproducing real-world UAV image degradation through synthetic modeling remains challenging. To validate the necessity of acquiring a real-world multi-altitude dataset, an on-the-fly (OTF) high-order degradation was applied, which is similar to the degradation used in Real-ESRGAN wang2021real . A random high-order degradation was generated for every sample at every epoch, as illustrated in Figure~ fig: Synthetic_on-the-fly (a). To imitate the conditions in which real-world datasets are unavailable, the real-world intermediate altitudes from 20 m to 70 m were also hidden from the model during training and validation.
