title: FineSplat: Fine Patches, Local Groups, Detailed Splats
summary: Feed-forward 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) promises instant scene reconstruction with high-quality novel-view synthesis. Yet, fine-grained geometry and appearance remain difficult to recover, motivating us to revisit how feed-forward models represent, aggregate, and refine detailed visual information. We introduce FineSplat, a feed-forward 3DGS framework built around fine-grained image patches. Since global multi-view attention becomes prohibitively expensive at such high token resolutions, we develop a dual-grouping strategy that combines two complementary forms of locality: view-wise grouping enables efficient interaction among neighboring views, while 3D spatial grouping reconnects geometrically related tokens that may never have interacted under view-wise grouping by lifting them into the 3D scene space. We further leverage reconstruction error as direct feedback, providing an explicit rendering-based signal to recover fine-grained structures and appearance, thereby overcoming the limitations of one-pass feed-forward prediction. Finally, a compact Gaussian generation scheme preserves the benefits of fine-grained features without unnecessarily increasing the number of primitives. Together, these designs enable FineSplat to recover richer geometry and appearance while remaining efficient and compact, achieving state-of-the-art results by a substantial margin, under the same or smaller Gaussian budgets than existing methods.
full_text: https://hyebinny.github.io/FineSplat/ Feed-forward 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) promises instant scene reconstruction with high-quality novel-view synthesis. Yet, fine-grained geometry and appearance remain difficult to recover, motivating us to revisit how feed-forward models represent, aggregate, and refine detailed visual information. We introduce FineSplat, a feed-forward 3DGS framework built around fine-grained image patches. Since global multi-view attention becomes prohibitively expensive at such high token resolutions, we develop a dual-grouping strategy that combines two complementary forms of locality: view-wise grouping enables efficient interaction among neighboring views, while 3D spatial grouping reconnects geometrically related tokens that may never have interacted under view-wise grouping by lifting them into the 3D scene space. We further leverage reconstruction error as direct feedback, providing an explicit rendering-based signal to recover fine-grained structures and appearance, thereby overcoming the limitations of one-pass feed-forward prediction. Finally, a compact Gaussian generation scheme preserves the benefits of fine-grained features without unnecessarily increasing the number of primitives. Together, these designs enable FineSplat to recover richer geometry and appearance while remaining efficient and compact, achieving state-of-the-art results by a substantial margin, under the same or smaller Gaussian budgets than existing methods. Introduction 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS)~ kerbl20233dgs, yu2024mip, ye2025gsplat has emerged as a powerful representation for high-quality and real-time novel view synthesis, combining an explicit 3D scene representation with efficient differentiable rasterization. Since conventional 3DGS relies on iterative per-scene optimization to achieve high reconstruction quality, it typically requires substantial computational resources for every new scene, limiting its scalability and applicability. To overcome these limitations, recent works have explored feed-forward 3DGS, where a single network forward pass directly predicts Gaussian representations from a set of input images. These approaches have rapidly advanced in both posed~ charatan2024pixelsplat, chen2024mvsplat, ziwen2025longlrm, kang2026ilrm, kang2026mvp and pose-free~ zhang2025flare, ye2025noposplat, ye2026yonosplat, an2025c3g settings, enabling fast reconstruction with promising generalization. However, replacing iterative per-scene refinement with a single feed-forward prediction places a much greater burden on the network, requiring it to resolve complex multi-view ambiguities and recover fine-grained scene details all at once. As a result, existing feed-forward approaches still exhibit a considerable reconstruction-quality gap compared with per-scene optimization methods, particularly in recovering fine-grained geometry and appearance details. Many recent feed-forward 3DGS methods build upon powerful 3D foundation models, benefiting from their strong geometric priors and multi-view reasoning capabilities. However, these models commonly inherit the relatively coarse patch resolution of their geometry backbones, typically using or image patches~ wang2025vggt, lin2026da3, wang2026pi3 . Such large patches provide broader spatial context that supports large-scale geometric reasoning and helps disambiguate cross-view correspondences, particularly when fine patches contain insufficiently distinctive local visual cues. However, compressing a broad image region into a single token can discard the high-frequency cues needed to reconstruct thin structures, sharp boundaries, textures, and other fine-grained details. Moreover, attention between coarse tokens operates at a limited spatial resolution, which can make it more difficult to precisely localize corresponding image regions across views. Finer patch tokens, particularly with attention between them, may therefore offer a promising avenue for preserving richer local visual cues and enabling more spatially precise cross-view interactions. Yet, finer tokenization introduces a fundamental computational challenge. Most multi-view transformers rely on global self-attention across tokens from multiple input images, whose quadratic complexity quickly becomes prohibitive as the number of views, image resolution, and token density increase. A practical alternative is to restrict the attention scope. For example, MVP~ kang2026mvp partitions input views into small groups and performs fine-grained multi-view attention only within each group, substantially improving the efficiency of high-resolution multi-view reconstruction while maintaining strong accuracy. Such view-wise grouping is particularly effective when the inputs are sequentially captured and nearby views are likely to observe overlapping scene regions. However, the restriction is ultimately imposed in view space rather than scene space: tokens corresponding to the same 3D surface may fall into different view groups and therefore never directly interact. Consequently, any fixed view grouping inevitably creates blind spots, excluding potentially relevant correspondences simply because they lie across group boundaries. In this work, we propose FineSplat, which addresses this challenge through a dual-grouping strategy that exploits two complementary forms of locality. First, we perform fine-grained multi-view interaction within small groups of neighboring views, enabling efficient attention over high-resolution tokens. We then lift the resulting tokens into 3D space using their predicted scene locations and regroup them according to 3D spatial proximity. This allows tokens from different, potentially distant view groups to interact when they correspond to nearby regions of the underlying 3D scene, recovering geometric relationships missed by view-wise grouping alone. By combining view-wise locality with 3D spatial locality, FineSplat enables rich interactions among fine-grained tokens without the prohibitive cost of global multi-view attention. A faithful 3D reconstruction should reproduce the input images when rendered from their viewpoints, which provides a natural signal for assessing its quality. Conventional per-scene optimization repeatedly exploits this signal, comparing rendered and observed images to identify residual errors and progressively correct the scene representation. A one-pass feed-forward model, in contrast, typically produces its reconstruction without an opportunity to inspect and correct its own errors. Motivated by this observation and recent work~ xu2026resplat , we explicitly leverage this readily available feedback as a direct signal in the second stage of our proposed framework. This provides the network with a second chance to recover structures and fine details that were missed in the first stage, without resorting to costly iterative optimization. We further introduce a compact Gaussian generation scheme that predicts only a small number of Gaussians from each patch token, rather than densely generating pixel-aligned Gaussians. This design allows the model to retain the benefits of fine-grained image features without increasing the number of Gaussian primitives. Together, the fine-grained representation, dual-grouping strategy, reconstruction error-driven correction, and compact Gaussian generation enable substantially improved reconstruction quality while maintaining an efficient and compact 3D representation. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our method achieves state-of-the-art rendering quality by a substantial margin in both posed and pose-free settings, while using the same or fewer Gaussians than existing methods. Related Works sec:related Feed-forward 3DGS and compact Gaussian representation. Feed-forward 3DGS methods amortize per-scene optimization~ kerbl20233dgs by directly predicting Gaussians from input images in a single forward pass. One common design is pixel-aligned prediction, where each pixel is unprojected along its camera ray into one Gaussian, using epipolar attention~ charatan2024pixelsplat , cost volumes~ chen2024mvsplat,xu2025depthsplat , or large transformers~ zhang2024gslrm,ziwen2025longlrm,kang2026mvp,wang2026tttlrm . This keeps the geometry well-conditioned and helps preserve fine appearance, but the number of Gaussians grows linearly with resolution and view count, often producing many redundant primitives in overlapping regions~ park2025ecosplat,kim2026f4splat,RoSplat . In contrast, non-pixel-aligned methods predict a compact set of Gaussians from learnable tokens, clustered scene features, 3D anchors, or voxels~ ren2026tokengs,an2025c3g,veicht2026zipsplat, wang2026volsplat,moreau2026offthegrid,zhang2026anchorsplat,itkin2026globalsplat,zhang2026sparsesplat,wang2026zpressor , but lose the explicit pixel-ray correspondence, which tends to hurt fine detail and makes optimization harder. Between these extremes, patch-aligned methods predict Gaussians at a reduced spatial resolution~ kang2026ilrm,xu2026resplat . In our framework, we extend this patch-aligned approach by generating only a small number of Gaussians along the rays of each sub-patch, and further compact the representation by pruning Gaussians according to their rendering contribution to the context views. Pose-free feed-forward 3DGS and geometry foundation models. Geometry foundation models~ wang2024dust3r,leroy2024mast3r,wang2025vggt,wang2026pi3,lin2026da3 estimate camera poses and dense geometry directly from unposed images. Building on such models, pose-free methods jointly predict camera poses and Gaussians~ ye2025noposplat,zhang2025flare,jiang2025anysplat,ye2026yonosplat,kang2025selfsplat , mostly in a pixel-aligned manner on top of the geometry backbone. However, these backbones operate on relatively coarse image tokens, which are well suited for global geometric reasoning but may discard local appearance cues important for fine-grained Gaussian reconstruction. To compensate, existing methods often fine-tune the backbone end-to-end so that its pretrained features adapt to appearance reconstruction. This adaptation is computationally expensive, and the model still relies on representations shaped by the coarse tokenization, which may limit its ability to recover fine-grained appearance. Recent works instead decouple geometry estimation from appearance modeling~ zhang2025flare,jeong2026twoxplat . We follow this decoupled design for pose-free reconstruction, using a 3D foundation model, such as DA3~ lin2026da3 , to predict the camera poses while FineSplat performs fine-grained Gaussian prediction. Combining image-space and 3D locality. Many useful cues for 3D reconstruction, such as dense image features and rendering errors, are naturally defined in image space, where they are grouped by proximity in the image plane rather than in the underlying scene. Several works therefore bring such image-space cues into 3D and process them according to 3D spatial locality. ODIN~ jain2024odin alternates 2D within-view layers with 3D cross-view attention over unprojected features, and DITR~ knaebel2026ditr projects DINOv2~ oquab2023dinov2 features onto 3D points and injects them into a Point Transformer V3~ wu2024ptv3 backbone. MoGe-3~ kong2026moge lifts monocular geometry into a sparse voxel volume guided by image features to recover sharp details near depth boundaries. In feed-forward 3DGS, ATSplat~ cho2026atsplat unprojects patch features into sparse 3D anchors that gather context from their 3D neighbors, and expands them where rendering errors are predicted to be high. Our second stage lifts fine tokens from all views into 3D and applies serialized attention over their 3D neighborhoods, so that tokens separated by view grouping can interact. Iterative refinement. title: RoboValue: A Fine-Grained Sim-and-Real Benchmark for Unified Evaluation of Robotic Value Models
summary: Robotic value models assess task execution from visual observations and instructions, providing feedback for policy learning and execution monitoring. However, existing evaluations cover only selected aspects of execution understanding, leaving the reliability of value feedback insufficiently tested. We introduce RoboValue, a fine-grained sim-and-real benchmark for unified evaluation of robotic value models. Its framework evaluates four complementary capability dimensions through shared interfaces: task-state understanding, temporal progress monitoring, failure and recovery reasoning, and value consistency. Diagnostic trajectories and instruction variations test whether value judgments accurately reflect task requirements and changes throughout execution. RoboValue-Dataset covers 15 simulation and 20 real-world manipulation tasks, providing expert demonstrations for training and annotated trajectories for fine-grained evaluation. We evaluate representative robotic value models in zero-shot and one-shot settings under standard conditions and separate shifts in robot embodiment and environment. Our results reveal errors in fine-grained instruction grounding, history-dependent progress tracking, and recovery assessment, even in models with strong outcome and forward-progress scores. The same semantic subtask can also receive substantially different value gains across valid execution orders. These findings identify concrete targets for value supervision, while the dataset and public leaderboard support continued assessment of feedback reliability. The website is available at https://robovalue-benchmark.github.io/.

Introduction sec:introduction General-purpose robotic value models assess task execution from visual observations and task instructions~ alakuijala2024video , providing learned feedback that reduces reliance on task-specific reward design~ mu2024drs,kim2025subtask . Their predictions support training data selection and reweighting~ budzianowski2025opengvl,liang2026robometer,ma2025vision,yu2026warp and supply reward or advantage signals for policy improvement~ tan2025robo,huang2026rynnvalue,tsao2026learning,intelligence2025pi,fei2026srpo,liu2026taco,yong2026generalizable . At inference time, value estimates guide planning over predicted future states~ ma2023liv,kim2026cosmospolicy , while action-conditioned evaluators rank and refine candidate actions~ dai2025rover . They also enable execution monitoring and failure detection~ liang2026robometer,tan2025interactive,ye2025robofac,park2026hide,zhai2025vision and process-level policy diagnosis~ ji2026prm,liu2026prm15 . These assessments influence which behaviors are selected, reinforced, or corrected, so their errors can propagate into both policy learning and execution. Systematic evaluation is therefore essential to determine when value feedback accurately reflects task execution and can reliably guide downstream policies. R 0.46 fig:teaser Existing evaluations assess task completion and trajectory preferences~ lee2026roboreward,liang2026robometer , as well as process understanding through diagnostic questions and progress comparisons~ xia2026roboprocessbench,ji2026prm,liu2026prm15 . These tests capture important aspects of execution, but strong outcome accuracy or forward-progress correlation can still conceal errors in intermediate value judgments. Differences in model interfaces and value semantics further hinder consistent diagnosis across models~ zhang2026progress . Such blind spots matter for policy learning: optimizing imperfect feedback can increase predicted reward while degrading actual task performance~ pan2022effects . Recent evidence in robotics likewise shows that embodied reward models can over-reward poor execution and shortcut behaviors, motivating broader coverage of negative behavior in training and evaluation~ tian2026badbehavior . Figure~ fig:teaser illustrates values rising during reverse playback, rebounding after unsuccessful recovery, or failing to reflect accumulated progress when similar states recur. If used as learning signals, such errors could reinforce unproductive continuation, ineffective correction, or omission of required subtasks. These cases motivate joint assessment of whether value changes correspond to changes in task attainment across diverse execution conditions. We introduce RoboValue, a fine-grained sim-and-real benchmark for unified evaluation of robotic value models. RoboValue is organized around a central principle: value feedback should accurately reflect how well task requirements are being fulfilled throughout execution. This requires grounding assessments in the specified goal, tracking advancement and regression using relevant history, and distinguishing unresolved errors from successful recovery. Reliability also depends on stable, informative feedback within trajectories and consistent subtask credit across valid solutions. As illustrated in Figure~ fig:overview , these requirements motivate four complementary capability dimensions: task-state understanding, temporal progress monitoring, failure and recovery reasoning, and value consistency. We make these requirements testable through diagnostic trajectories and instruction variations that probe specific ambiguities in execution assessment. Counterfactual instructions hold the observed execution fixed while changing the requested goal, and recurring visual states require history to disambiguate accumulated progress. Contrasting error continuations with effective and ineffective recoveries tests whether models distinguish corrective activity from its outcome. Alternative valid subtask orders test whether the same semantic subtask receives consistent value gains across solutions. RoboValue-Dataset covers 15 simulation and 20 real-world manipulation tasks (Section~ sec:construction ). Simulation provides diverse object assets and varied scene configurations under controlled conditions, while real-world data captures visual sensing and contact dynamics in complex physical environments. Shared interfaces and model-specific adapters enable comparison across heterogeneous models while preserving their native value semantics (Section~ sec:robovaluebenchmark ). We evaluate representative robotic value models in zero-shot and one-shot settings under standard conditions and separate shifts in robot embodiment and environment (Sections~ sec:leaderboard and~ sec:experiment ). Our analyses reveal uneven capability profiles across model scales and input designs, as well as broader degradation under the tested environment shifts than embodiment shifts. These findings motivate supervision that captures task semantics, relevant execution history, and recovery outcomes (Section~ sec:analysis ). Our main contributions are: We construct RoboValue-Dataset, with expert training demonstrations and annotated test trajectories in simulation and the real world. Contrasts in task instructions, execution history, recovery outcomes, and valid subtask orders expose unreliable value judgments, while separate embodiment and environment shifts test generalization. We introduce RoboValue-Benchmark, a unified framework for evaluating robotic value models across four complementary capability dimensions. Joint assessment under a shared protocol reveals limitations that outcome discrimination and forward-progress correlation alone can overlook. We establish RoboValue-Leaderboard with overall rankings and capability profiles for each evaluation track. Our analyses distinguish instruction insensitivity from incorrect semantic grounding and reveal weaknesses in history awareness, recovery reasoning, and subtask credit, informing value supervision for policy learning, action planning, and execution monitoring. Related Work sec:related_work Value Models for Robotic Manipulation Robotic value models differ in both the meaning of their predictions and the evidence used to produce them. Some derive scores from ordinal completion ratings or the likelihood of a completion response~ lee2026roboreward,chen2026topreward , while others estimate absolute task progress~ ma2025vision,zhang2025rewind,yan2026progressvla . Stage-aware models further structure progress around procedures and subtasks~ feng2026procvlm,chen2026sarm,chen2026sarm2,hung2025victor . Other methods estimate temporal distances between observations or to task completion~ huang2026rynnvalue,liu2025timerewarder , or predict relative progress and local advantages between states~ tan2025robo,zhai2025vision,mao2026arm,liu2026steam . Large Reward Models expose progress, completion, and temporal-comparison interfaces within a single framework for robot policy refinement~ wu2026largereward . Recent work also expands supervision and temporal context to address imperfect execution. RoboMeter combines frame-level progress and trajectory-preference supervision~ liang2026robometer ; ReTVL models degradation and recovery around retries~ qin2026beyond , and DenseReward incorporates synthesized physical failures~ fang2026densereward . ViVa and World Value Models draw on video-generation priors for value estimation~ lv2026viva,wang2026world , while Robo-Dopamine~2.0 explicitly addresses execution history and out-of-distribution states~ xu2026robo . These developments motivate evaluation that tests shared behavioral requirements while respecting differences in value semantics. Evaluation of Robotic Value Models Fine-grained policy evaluation calls for assessing execution behavior alongside task outcomes, as exemplified by RoboEval's structured behavioral measures~ wang2025roboeval . StepEval proposes using VLMs to automate assessment of intermediate subgoal outcomes~ elmallah2025score . Using learned models as evaluators requires checking whether their judgments faithfully reflect task execution. Eval-Actions addresses this need by comparing predicted execution-quality scores with expert grading and ranking annotations~ liu2026evalactions . Value-model evaluations examine complementary aspects of feedback quality. title: Robot Learning with Vision-Language-Action Models for Agricultural Manipulation
summary: Robotic manipulation in agricultural environments remains challenging due to variations in plant geometry, occlusion, and camera viewpoints. Pretrained vision-language-action (VLA) and generalist robot policies offer a promising approach to addressing these challenges by learning manipulation behaviors from multimodal observations and language instructions. However, adapting these policies to agricultural tasks requires domain-specific demonstrations, which are costly and time-consuming to collect on physical robots. In this work, we develop a simulation-to-real robot-learning framework for agricultural reaching and grasping that integrates task-specific demonstration collection and pretrained policy adaptation. A MuJoCo-based agricultural environment is developed with diverse tomato plant structures to support demonstration collection and controlled evaluation. Expert demonstrations are collected through joystick teleoperation, with a low-level controller used to execute robot actions. Two pretrained generalist robot policies, Octo and $π_{0.5}$, are adapted using simulated demonstrations, followed by further fine-tuning on a physical Franka Research 3 manipulator using real-robot demonstrations. The adapted policies are evaluated under in-distribution, viewpoint/spatial-shift, and out-of-distribution conditions in simulation, followed by physical-robot experiments. The influence of proprioceptive information on policy performance is also investigated. Results show that $π_{0.5}$ achieves higher task-performance scores than Octo and exhibits less degradation under distribution shifts. These findings demonstrate the potential of integrating pretrained generalist policies with task-specific demonstration learning for agricultural manipulation.

Pretrained vision-language-action (VLA) and generalist robot policies offer a promising approach to addressing these challenges by learning manipulation behaviors from multimodal observations and language instructions. However, adapting these policies to agricultural tasks requires domain-specific demonstrations, which are costly and time-consuming to collect on physical robots. Expert demonstrations are collected through joystick teleoperation using a low-level controller that executes the learned policy actions. Two pretrained generalist robot policies, Octo and , are adapted using simulated demonstrations, followed by further fine-tuning on a physical Franka Research 3 manipulator using real-robot demonstrations. The adapted policies are evaluated under in-distribution, viewpoint/spatial-shift, and out-of-distribution conditions in simulation, followed by physical-robot experiments. The influence of proprioceptive information on policy performance is also investigated. Robot Learning; Vision Language Action; Agricultural Tasks; Learning from Demonstration. INTRODUCTION Many agricultural operations remain labor-intensive and physically demanding, making them a compelling domain for robotic automation. Robotic manipulators are increasingly being explored for tasks such as harvesting, planting, monitoring, weeding, and spraying in greenhouses, open fields, and orchards jin2024robotic,jo2025review . However, agricultural environments are substantially less structured than typical industrial settings. Crops exhibit significant variations in geometry, orientation, and height, while leaves, branches, and other plant structures can occlude targets and constrain manipulator access rong2025decoupled,zhao2026improved . These characteristics make target localization, motion planning, and reliable robotic manipulation complicated. Conventional agricultural manipulation systems commonly employ a modular architecture in which perception, planning, and control are implemented as separate components jin2024robotic . On the perception side, the literature commonly relies on vision or multi-sensor processing to detect crops and estimate 3D target locations, often requiring careful camera placement, calibration, and coordinate-frame alignment to achieve reliable target estimates under occlusion and clutter liu2026deep,gursoy2023towards . For example, in miao2023efficient , a tomato-harvesting system combines YOLOv5 with image processing and depth information to recognize tomato clusters and localize stems, transforming image-based estimates into spatial coordinates for robot motion. Similarly, in gursoy2023towards , a dual-arm fruit-harvesting framework combines YOLOv5 and object tracking with RGB-D measurements to estimate fruit positions, while image processing identifies the tree trunk. In these systems, learning-based perception serves as a front-end component that provides geometric targets and information about the surrounding scene for downstream motion generation. Using these target estimates and a representation of the workspace, the planning module generates feasible motions that account for the robot's kinematics, reachability, and surrounding obstacles. In agricultural applications, rong2025decoupled combines manipulator placement optimization with an improved RRT* planner to generate collision-free trajectories for tomato harvesting. Other fruit-picking systems modify the RRT* sampling strategy to improve path generation in cluttered environments containing branches and leaves zhao2026improved . During motion execution, feedback control can improve positioning accuracy and interaction safety. In shi2023lightweight , visual feedback is used to refine the end-effector position, while estimated contact forces are monitored to prevent unsafe interaction with workers or plants. In wang2023biologically , localized fruit positions are used by a neural control framework to generate coordinated reaching and cutting motions while accounting for robot constraints. These studies illustrate how conventional agricultural manipulation systems integrate perception, planning, and control through a modular architecture. Although such modular approaches benefit from mature robotics tools and explicit handling of constraints, their performance depends on the accuracy and completeness of the information exchanged between components. Errors in target localization or incomplete representations of surrounding plant structures can affect motion generation and execution. Reported challenges include occluded targets, unmodeled branches, and fruit displacement during interaction gursoy2023towards . Changes in lighting and crop arrangement may also require adjustments to perception and target-access strategies miao2023efficient . Moreover, many agricultural robotic systems are developed for specific crops, environments, and tasks, and adapting them to new agricultural settings may require additional development and validation jin2024robotic,jo2025review . These limitations motivate the investigation of learning-based approaches that map observations more directly to robot actions while retaining feedback and low-level control for execution. Robot learning provides a framework for acquiring manipulation behaviors from data and interaction rather than relying solely on manually designed models and controllers billard2016learning,calinon2019learning . Two major paradigms are reinforcement learning (RL), which learns behaviors through interaction and reward feedback kober2013reinforcement , and learning from demonstration (LfD), which learns from expert demonstrations billard2016learning . Recent advances in machine learning and the growing availability of large-scale robot datasets have significantly expanded both paradigms o2024open . In particular, pre-collected datasets have enabled offline RL, while large and diverse demonstration datasets have supported the development of generalist policies that can transfer across tasks, environments, and robot embodiments. While offline RL typically relies on reward information associated with collected trajectories, specifying appropriate reward functions for complex manipulation tasks can be challenging. In contrast, LfD enables policies to be learned directly from expert demonstrations without requiring explicit reward labels shafiullah2022behavior . Previous research has explored a wide range of LfD approaches for acquiring robot manipulation skills. One class of methods focuses on representing and generalizing demonstrations at the trajectory level (e.g., joint-space or end-effector motion) using structured movement representations such as probabilistic and neural network-based movement primitives calinon2007learning, saveriano2021dynamic, seker2019conditional, theofanidis2024safe, ravichandar2020recent, hafezi2026safe . A second class instead learns policies that directly map robot observations, such as RGB/depth images and proprioceptive states, to robot actions, including joint-space, end-effector, or gripper commands. Representative examples include implicit policies formulated as energy-based models florence2022implicit , diffusion-based visuomotor policies chi2025diffusion , and Transformer-based behavior cloning approaches such as the Behavior Transformer shafiullah2022behavior . Although these methods have demonstrated strong performance, many are developed for specific tasks and trained on datasets with limited diversity. More recently, large-scale multi-task robot datasets such as Open X-Embodiment o2024open have accelerated interest in generalist robot policies, which use large Transformer backbones to scale across tasks and embodiments. Some of these policies, such as RT-1 brohan2022rt and Octo team2024octo , are trained primarily on robot data with lightweight vision and language encoders. Others, referred to as vision-language-action (VLA) models, build on vision-language models pretrained on web-scale data and adapt them to predict robot actions; examples include RT-2 brohan2023rt , OpenVLA kim2024openvla , black2024pi_0 , and intelligence2025pi0 . Both families have demonstrated broad transfer and, in some settings, zero-shot or few-shot generalization to novel tasks. Recent studies have also investigated learning-based and vision-language models (VLMs) for agricultural robotics, including task-specific imitation learning for outdoor pepper harvesting kim2025autonomous , VLM-guided task planning for crop monitoring through navigation and active-vision tools cuaran2026visual , and scene-graph-grounded vision-language reasoning for greenhouse manipulation through predefined basic actions park2026scene . Despite these advances, adapting pretrained generalist policies to agricultural manipulation remains limited and challenging due to differences between pretraining and agricultural environments, while collecting task-specific demonstrations across diverse plant configurations on physical robots is costly and time-consuming. Moreover, understanding how these adapted policies perform under variations in plant structure, camera viewpoint, and robot configuration remains an important research question. To address these challenges, we develop a simulation-to-real robot-learning framework that integrates demonstration collection, pretrained policy adaptation, and low-level manipulator control. The framework includes a MuJoCo-based agricultural simulation environment for scalable demonstration collection and controlled evaluation, together with a joystick-based teleoperation system and a damped, null-space-based inverse-kinematics controller for demonstration collection and learned-policy execution. Two pretrained generalist robot policies, Octo and , are adapted to a tomato reaching-and-grasping task through fine-tuning on simulated demonstrations, followed by further fine-tuning using demonstrations collected on a physical Franka Research 3 (FR3) robot. We further evaluate the adapted policies under in-distribution, viewpoint/spatial-shift, and out-of-distribution conditions in simulation, followed by physical-robot experiments, while investigating the influence of proprioceptive information on policy performance. The overall learning and deployment workflow is illustrated in Fig.~ fig:general_structure . The main contributions of this work are as follows: A MuJoCo-based agricultural manipulation environment with diverse tomato plant structures, integrated with a joystick-based teleoperation and low-level inverse-kinematics control framework for demonstration collection and learned-policy execution. A simulation-to-real adaptation of two pretrained generalist robot policies, Octo and , for agricultural reaching and grasping, using simulated demonstrations followed by further fine-tuning with demonstrations collected on a physical Franka Research 3 (FR3) robot. A comparative evaluation of the adapted policies under in-distribution, viewpoint/spatial-shift, and out-of-distribution conditions in simulation, together with real-robot experiments investigating their performance and the influence of proprioceptive information. title: HandsOn: A Large-Scale Simulation Benchmark for Generalizable Dexterous Manipulation
summary: General-purpose manipulation requires reliable behavior across embodiments, objects, and task demands. We introduce HandsOn, a composable simulation platform and benchmark for cross-embodiment dexterous manipulation. It supports five robotic arms, six dexterous hands, and approximately 200 rigid, articulated, and deformable assets in randomized scenes. The benchmark pairs 18,000 curated human demonstrations with 66 human-verified tasks: Core-50 supports demonstration-based learning and execution tests, while Transfer-16 evaluates asset and relation transfer, skill composition, and deformable manipulation without target-task training demonstrations. Qualitative real-robot rollouts illustrate sim-to-real transfer. Across diffusion, vision-language-action, world-action, and prompted VLM-based methods, the best trained multi-task policy achieves 29.1% Core-50 success. Without benchmark finetuning, GPT-6 using move_eef for palm-and-finger control achieves 5.2% on Core-50 and 1.9% on Transfer-16 over 660 trials. Trained-policy stage diagnostics expose failures in contact establishment, action coordination, and maintaining achieved goals, with additional sequencing errors in composed tasks. HandsOn provides a shared basis for investigating manipulation generalization and the limits of reliable physical interaction.

title: Bio-inspired Thrust-Assisted Trotting on a legged-Aerial Robot via Real-Time QP-MPC
comment: To be published in IEEE/RSJ International Conference on Intelligent Robots and Systems (IROS 2026)
summary: This paper presents the hardware implementation of a quadratic program-based controller on Harpy: thruster-assisted bipedal robot to perform thruster-assisted trotting. This is inspired by wing-assisted locomotion observed in birds such as the chukar partridge, which employ thrust vectoring to manipulate the ground reaction force. The proposed controller formulates the thruster-assisted spring-loaded inverted pendulum dynamics as a condensed QP-based model predictive control problem, enabling simultaneous regulation of ground contact force and active thrust vectoring at 500 Hz. A decoupled control architecture is used, where the robot's sagittal dynamics are controlled using QP-MPC while the frontal dynamics is regulated using a cascade orientation stabilization controller. Two experiments were conducted with different forward reference velocities of 0 m/s and 0.1 m/s. While the instantaneous velocity oscillates, the mean velocities can track their respective reference. Additionally, joint tracking error remains within 1 deg while tracking the desired leg length given by the leg trajectory controller and desired swing trajectory given by Raibert's heuristic. The QP-MPC problem is consistently solved with 0.18ms, which is well within the 2ms computation budget while satisfying the GRF friction cone constraint.

The QP-MPC problem is consistently solved with 0.18ms, which is well within the 2ms computation budget while satisfying the GRF friction cone constraint. Introduction Birds are capable of using their wings to fly and also use their feet to walk on the ground, perch, and grabbing objects. Additionally, birds such as chukar’s wing-assisted incline running bundle_mechanics_2003 and widowbirds’ controlled flapping descent jackson_precocial_2009 can use their wings while walking over a steep slope or during a rapid descent to stabilize their upper body orientation and velocity. We aim to take inspiration from and mimic the biological counterparts by combining both ground and aerial locomotion modes to achieve a versatile legged-aerial multi-modal robot. There are several studies focused on multi-modal locomotion, specifically ground-aerial robots showing their versatility in traversing various terrains. Some of these studies focus more on transitioning between locomotion modes instead of using all available actuators at the same time. Some robot design requires transformation to switch mode of locomotion, such as sihite_multi-modal_2023,salagame_nmpc-based_2025 , which transitions between terrestrial and aerial locomotion by morphing its appendages, wang_dynamic_2025 is a quadrupedal robot with propellers attached to its knee-axis and can perform flight after transforming into a quadrotor configuration. On the other hand, some robot design with a fixed configuration such that they can perform ground and aerial locomotion without transforming, such as a jet powered bipedal robot capable performing large vertical jumps li_jet-hr2_2022 , pogo-stick mechanism with quadrotor dynamics zhu_pogodrone_2022 , a bipedal robot kim_bipedal_2021 and a quadrupedal robot krishnamurthy2025thruster with quadrotor style propulsion attached to its torso. A multi-modal robot can utilize both ground and aerial actuators at the same time if the design allows it, making it possible to augment a mode of locomotion or perform a gait that can't be done by using either ground or aerial actuator by themselves. This work explores the capability of our legged-aerial Harpy platform, shown in Fig.~ fig:-cover , in performing a trotting gait using both the legs and thrusters at the same time. Bipedal robot locomotion requires a regulation of ground reaction force (GRF) so that the foot does not slip. The addition of thruster forces during walking will impact the resulting GRF and must be regulated together with the walking gait. Simulation studies have laid a theoretical groundwork for using both legs and thrusters at the same time to augment the legged locomotion to perform difficult maneuvers, such as narrow path walking wang2025quadratic,krishnamurthy_narrow-path_2024 and steep incline walking krishnamurthy_enabling_2024,krishnamurthy_optimization_2024,krishnamurthy2025thruster,venkatesh_krishnamurthy_wair_2026,krishnamurthy_contact-implicit_2026 . Building on this foundation, the Harpy platform has also been validated in simulation across various locomotion tasks, such as jumping~ dangol_control_2021, sihite_posture_2024 , walking~ pitroda2024capture,pitroda_enhanced_2024,pitroda_conjugate_2025,wang_thruster-enhanced_2025 , and inclined slope walking~ pitroda_quadratic_2024 . However, unlike in simulations, the practical usage of the algorithm in a real-time controller requires an approach that can be solved quickly and efficiently. A common solution for GRF regulation for legged robot uses an optimization method, such as quadratic programming (QP) or nonlinear model predictive control (MPC), by modeling the robot's dynamics and implementing the foot no-slip condition (the friction cone constraint) as constraints in the optimization. The optimization problem needs to be solved quickly to be feasible for a real-time implementation, where a reduced order model (ROM) is often used to reduce the model complexity and computational time. The reduced-order modeling tool, such as the Linear inverted pendulum (LIP) and the spring-loaded inverted pendulum (SLIP) model, captures the essential dynamics of walking or running~ blickhan_spring-mass_1989,geyer_compliant_2006 . The SLIP model, first formalized by~ blickhan_spring-mass_1989 and validated through extensive biomechanical studies~ full_templates_1999,geyer_compliant_2006 , has emerged as the canonical template for understanding and controlling such dynamic gaits. The SLIP model's elegance lies in its simplicity: a point mass connected to a massless spring leg model, where the ground contact forces is applied alternatively between stance and flight phases. The reduced-order representation has proven remarkably effective in describing the locomotion of diverse running animals~ holmes_dynamics_2006 and has guided the development of numerous robotic systems, from Raibert's pioneering hopper~ raibert_experiments_1984 to modern dynamic bipeds~ poulakakis_spring_2009,hubicki_walking_2018,gong_feedback_2019,dadashzadeh_slip-based_2020,wang_fast_2022,sihite_locomotion_2026,wang_legged_2023,ramezani2021generative,salagame_letter_2022 . In this paper, we formulated an MPC optimization problem into a QP, and implemented it in our Harpy robot to satisfy ground constraints to perform a thruster-assisted trotting gait. The QP is formulated using a Thruster-SLIP (TSLIP) model, where thrusters are incorporated in the SLIP reduced order model, which then is implemented on hardware and solved in real-time using the qpSWIFT pandala_qpswift_2019 algorithm at 500 Hz control loop frequency. This controller is then tested on hardware during the thruster-assisted trotting gait, where the experimental results showed the controller's feasibility and performance. The contributions of this paper is listed as follows: 1) the derivation of the dynamic Thruster-SLIP model of a legged-aerial robot, 2) implementation of the QP-SLIP model on hardware, and 3) experimental validation of the controller performance showing the satisfaction of the GRF constraints in real-time. This paper is organized as follows: the robot design overview, followed by dynamic modeling, controller design and formulation, leg trajectory controller. Then, we present the experimental results, discussions, concluding remarks, and future work. Robot Overview Harpy~ pitroda_dynamic_2023,dangol_performance_2020,dangol_feedback_2020 is designed with three joints for each leg: hip frontal joint, hip sagittal joint, and knee joint. The lower leg forms a parallelogram linkage, where a shock absorber spring is attached to the rear lower linkage to reduce the impulsive force on leg touchdown. title: Physical Words: A Vocabulary for Structuring Latent Reasoning in Robot Manipulation
summary: Multimodal reasoning provides robotic foundation models with predictive context needed for reliable action generation. However, language-based reasoning captures task semantics but struggles to express fine-grained physical dynamics, while latent reasoning models future state evolution but offers limited structure for organizing these dynamics into reusable reasoning primitives. To bridge this gap, we introduce PhysWord, a reasoning-before-acting foundation model built on Physical Words, which use atomic action verbs as shared semantic anchors for continuous representations of physical dynamics. Specifically, PhysWord predicts upcoming atomic action words and directly aligns their contextual hidden states with latent targets derived from the corresponding future observations. Building on these primitives, we construct a temporally structured PhysWord space with visual and optional tactile variants of each action word. Autoregressively predicting Physical Words across future timesteps captures transitions between execution stages, providing structured multimodal context for action generation. PhysWord achieves state-of-the-art success rates of 90.3\% on visuotactile UniVTAC and 99.6\% on vision-based LIBERO-Long, and outperforms competing methods on real-world tasks using bimanual grippers and dexterous hands. Further evaluations demonstrate that our structured latent reasoning framework generalizes to unseen scenarios and enables long-horizon manipulation.

Introduction sec:introduction Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have emerged as a promising foundation for general-purpose robotic manipulation~ kim2024openvla,liu2025hybridvla , integrating the semantic knowledge of pretrained vision-language models (VLMs)~ karamcheti2024prismatic, bai2025qwen3, beyer2024paligemma with robot action learning. Reliable manipulation, however, requires anticipating how the physical environment evolves as the robot acts. This need has motivated reasoning-before-acting VLA approaches~ huang2025thinkact,liu2026last , which generate intermediate task plans or predictive context to guide action generation. World Action Models (WAMs) further integrate future world prediction with action generation, enabling policies to leverage dynamics knowledge learned from video and manipulation data. These advances highlight the value of multimodal reasoning in providing predictive context that aligns robot actions with evolving environments. Existing reasoning approaches differ in how they represent predictive context. On the one hand, some VLA models adopt the reasoning paradigm of pretrained VLMs, using language to decompose tasks and express task-level action semantics~ intelligence2025pi05visionlanguageactionmodelopenworld, lin2025onetwovla, zawalski2025roboticcontrolembodiedchainofthought . However, linguistic descriptions remain physically coarse, as a verb such as ``rotate'' identifies an operation without fully conveying its fine-grained dynamics. On the other hand, WAMs~ ye2026world, wang2026openwam and latent reasoning methods~ liu2026last, bi2025motus, tian2025interndata model future state evolution, providing rich predictive representations of interaction dynamics. Yet these approaches do not necessarily organize their representations around shared action semantics. Since the same manipulation skill can be applied across different objects and scenes, a useful reasoning representation should preserve shared semantics while capturing context-specific physical dynamics. This raises a central question: Can atomic action semantics organize physical latent representations into reusable reasoning primitives? To this end, we introduce PhysWord, a reasoning-before-acting foundation model built on Physical Words, which use atomic action verbs as semantic anchors for continuous latent dynamics. We assemble a vocabulary of atomic action verbs, such as “pick,” “rotate,” and “push,” based on the action taxonomy of prior work~ yuan2026qwen, chen2025rh20t . As shown in Figure~ fig:teaser (a), PhysWord predicts upcoming atomic action words from the current observation context and directly aligns their contextual hidden states with latent targets derived from the corresponding future observations. Joint semantic and latent supervision encourages these representations to capture shared action semantics while retaining action-related physical dynamics. To capture how these dynamics evolve during execution, we organize Physical Words at multiple future timesteps within the action-chunk horizon, forming a temporally structured PhysWord space. Within this space, we use separate visual and tactile variants of each action word to capture complementary motion and contact dynamics, including tactile variants only for tactile-enabled tasks. By autoregressively predicting these Physical Words, PhysWord captures changes in action semantics and physical dynamics across execution stages, providing structured multimodal predictive context for long-horizon manipulation. This token interface adapts to the available sensory modalities, bringing demonstrations with and without tactile observations into a unified training formulation. This flexibility enables us to jointly pretrain PhysWord on approximately 7,000 hours of real-robot and human-hand demonstrations. Across this corpus, we use a VLM~ openai2026gpt56 to automatically segment trajectories into atomic action stages and align the resulting atomic verbs with the corresponding observations. As shown in Figure~ fig:teaser (b), PhysWord achieves success rates of 90.3 on visuotactile UniVTAC and 99.6 on vision-only LIBERO-Long, outperforming prior SOTA methods. Real-world experiments on bimanual gripper and dexterous-hand platforms with visual and tactile sensing further demonstrate its effectiveness in contact-rich, precise, and long-horizon manipulation. To assess reusability, we evaluate both unseen scene configurations and extended task sequences absent from training. PhysWord outperforms competing methods under unseen backgrounds, object instances, and object positions on Powered Screw Driving and Pick A4 Paper, and successfully executes extended manipulation sequences, supporting reuse across both scenarios and task stages. To assess the predictive value of its tactile representations, we replace measured tactile inputs with predicted latents at inference. Remarkably, the resulting policies retain strong performance with only modest degradation, suggesting that semantic structuring preserves contact information needed for control and enables deployment without online tactile sensing. Our contributions: [nosep, leftmargin=*] We introduce PhysWord, a reasoning-before-acting foundation model built on Physical Words, which use atomic action verbs as semantic anchors for continuous physical dynamics by directly supervising their contextual hidden states with future latent targets. We construct a temporally structured PhysWord space with visual and tactile variants of atomic action words, capturing evolving motion and contact dynamics for action generation. PhysWord achieves 90.3 on UniVTAC and 99.6 on LIBERO-Long, outperforming prior SOTA methods. Experiments on real-world tasks demonstrate superior performance, stronger generalization, and long-horizon manipulation through sequential reuse of Physical Words. VLA models~ kim2024openvla, black2024pi_0, li2023manipllmembodiedmultimodallarge, bjorck2025gr00t, liu2025hybridvla, wen2025dexvla adapt pretrained VLMs to generate robot actions from visual observations and language instructions. Reasoning-before-acting VLAs introduce intermediate reasoning to anticipate task progression. Language-based approaches, including subtask prediction, embodied chain-of-thought (CoT), and motion descriptions~ intelligence2025pi05visionlanguageactionmodelopenworld, lin2025onetwovla, zawalski2025roboticcontrolembodiedchainofthought, belkhale2024rthactionhierarchiesusing , convey task semantics and subtask plans but struggle to express fine-grained dynamics. Beyond language, recent methods predict future visual observations~ wang2025unifiedvisionlanguageactionmodel, zhao2025cot, chen2025unifieddiffusionvlavisionlanguageaction, gao2025adaworld, bu2025agibot, zhang2025dreamvla or incorporate anticipated signals from multiple modalities~ liu2025mla, cen2025worldvla, gu2025manualvla . Latent Reasoning and World Action Models (WAMs). Latent CoT represents intermediate reasoning through continuous latent states in LLMs and VLMs~ hao2024training, deng2024explicit, yang2025machine, wang2025monet . ATLAS~ guo2026atlas further highlights the importance of LLMs' native language-based CoT for general reasoning tasks. In robotics, recent VLA models adopt latent reasoning to guide control using compact representations of future physical dynamics~ zhang2026atomicvla, huang2025thinkact, tan2025latent . Subsequent work incorporates reinforcement learning~ chen2026lastr1 and latent alignment between human and robot demonstrations~ liu2026lasthd . Related WAMs jointly model video and action sequences~ kim2026cosmos, agarwal2026cosmos, ye2026world, wang2026openwam . Several approaches condition action generation on latent representations of predicted future states~ hu2024video, yuan2026fast, luo2026being, wang2026tacdyn, chen2026uniwam . Although these approaches capture rich future dynamics, their latent representations are not structured around shared action semantics. PhysWord introduces this structure by anchoring future dynamics to atomic action verbs, forming reusable reasoning primitives that provide predictive context for action generation. title: ActTime: Action-Conditioned World Modeling for Time Series
summary: Time-series models increasingly condition on known future inputs. In controlled systems, some of these inputs are actions that can be changed, compared, and optimized before execution. A model must therefore do more than predict the realized future: it must predict how outcomes change under different actions from the same observed history and support reliable comparison of candidate plans. We introduce ActTime, an action-conditioned world model for time series. Over the observed history, ActTime updates variable-specific latent states through an action-conditioned transition and corrects them using observations. It then rolls the same transition forward under candidate actions to generate future trajectories. Training uses only factual trajectories, without paired alternative-action outcomes or planning supervision. We construct a simulator-grounded evaluation suite across building energy, traffic, greenhouse climate, and inventory management, covering factual prediction, intervention-effect prediction, offline decision making, and closed-loop planning. ActTime ranks first in 12 of 16 domain-task settings. Across eight methods, the mean pairwise model-ranking reversal rate is 17.8% between factual prediction and intervention fidelity, and rises to 28.4% between intervention fidelity and decision ranking. These results show that factual accuracy, intervention fidelity, and decision quality are related but not interchangeable.

Introduction sec:Introduction Modern time-series forecasting increasingly incorporates information beyond the target history. Models use multivariate observations, static attributes, exogenous covariates, and known-future inputs lim2021temporal,das2023longterm,wang2024timexer,li2026gcgnet,han2026unica . These advances broaden forecasting from history-only extrapolation to conditional prediction with rich contextual information yamaguchi2026citras,meyer2026t0timeseriesfoundationmodel . In controlled systems, however, some future inputs serve as decision variables rather than fixed context: they are actions selected by a decision maker and can be changed before execution, compared against alternatives, and optimized for downstream objectives. A forecasting model can in principle condition on an action sequence, but decision making requires more than predicting the future under one prescribed sequence. Given the same observed history, the model must predict how future outcomes vary across candidate action sequences, rather than only the outcome under the realized sequence, since these relative differences determine which actions should be preferred before execution. Figure~ fig:1 makes the resulting evaluation gaps explicit. Factual evaluation assesses the future generated by the action sequence that was actually executed, as in Fig.~ fig:1a . Accurate prediction of this trajectory does not directly test whether changing the future actions produces the correct change in the resulting trajectory. This gives the first gap: factual accuracy does not guarantee intervention fidelity. A model can fit the realized future well while still misestimating the effect of an alternative action sequence, as illustrated in Fig.~ fig:1b . A similar failure mode has been observed in recent action-conditioned world models, where performance on demonstrated actions can mask incorrect responses to valid alternative actions wang2026thermoforce,chen2026robotic . The second gap appears when these predictions are used to choose actions. A planner compares candidate action sequences according to their predicted outcomes, so the decision depends on their relative ordering, not only on the accuracy of each individual response. Prediction errors can therefore reverse the ordering of candidate actions even when their trajectory-level errors appear moderate donti2017task,elmachtoub2022smart . Thus, intervention fidelity does not by itself guarantee decision quality, as illustrated in Fig.~ fig:1c . Related work on world-model evaluation has similarly moved beyond predictive or visual fidelity toward direct assessment of policy rankings and closed-loop task performance quevedo2026worldgym,zhang2026world,yu2026should . Our experiments quantify both gaps across four controlled domains and eight methods: the average pairwise method-ordering reversal rate is from factual prediction to intervention fidelity and rises to from intervention fidelity to decision ranking. These gaps call for a model that represents controlled dynamics and can be rolled forward under alternative actions. This is the central role of a world model: learning action-conditioned dynamics that can be queried under candidate actions before they are executed hafner2019learning,hafner2020iclr-dream,hansen2024td . While this view is well established in model-based control and embodied agents, related ideas have also been explored in action-conditioned numerical dynamics and, more recently, in controlled and interventional time-series modeling shaj2021action,shaj2023multi,wang2026thermoforce,meng2026cedar, wu2026doflow . Yet a factual trajectory reveals only the action sequence that was executed and the future that followed it; matched outcomes under alternative actions are not observed. This leaves a practical question: can a time-series model learn action-conditioned dynamics from factual trajectories that remain reliable under alternative actions for intervention-effect prediction and decision making? We address this question with , an action-conditioned time-series world model built around a shared controlled transition. Over the observed history, variable-specific latent states are propagated under the executed actions and corrected using each new observation, allowing the transition to model action-conditioned evolution while the latent state remains grounded in the realized trajectory. At the history boundary, a lightweight residual prior from a frozen pretrained temporal backbone refines the terminal state. The same transition is then rolled forward under candidate future actions without access to future observations. Alternative-action predictions therefore arise directly from the action-conditioned dynamics learned on factual trajectories. To evaluate this capability, we construct simulator-grounded evaluation suites across four controlled systems. Training uses only factual trajectories, while same-history interventions, candidate-action comparisons, and closed-loop planning episodes are generated only for evaluation. This provides direct ground truth for the progression in Fig.~ fig:1 without paired alternative-action outcomes or planning supervision during training. Our main contributions are threefold: Decision-oriented formulation and evaluation gaps. We distinguish factual accuracy, intervention fidelity, and decision quality as three distinct evaluation criteria for action-conditioned time-series models, and show that model performance does not reliably transfer across adjacent criteria. Action-conditioned time-series world model. We introduce , which learns variable-specific latent states with a shared action-conditioned transition and observation-based correction. The same transition is used for observed-history modeling and open-loop rollout under candidate future actions, using factual supervision only. Simulator-grounded evaluation suite. We construct evaluation suites across four heterogeneous domains that cover factual prediction, same-history intervention fidelity, offline decision making, and closed-loop planning. The underlying simulators provide reference action effects and decision outcomes, enabling direct evaluation of whether action-conditioned models remain reliable when used for decision making. Related Work sec:Related_Works Time-Series Forecasting with Covariates Time-series forecasting has long incorporated information beyond target history, including static attributes, exogenous variables, and known-future inputs wen2017multi,rangapuram2018deep,salinas2020deepar . NBEATSx, TFT, and TiDE integrate such covariates through dedicated components or feature selection olivares2023neural,lim2021temporal,das2023longterm . More recent models focus on interactions between endogenous and exogenous series, including TimeXer, ExoTST, CrossLinear, and GCGNet wang2024timexer,tayal2024exotst,zhou2025crosslinear,li2026gcgnet . Covariate-aware forecasting has also reached TSFMs yamaguchi2026citras . Chronos-2 supports multivariate and covariate-informed forecasting ansari2025chronos , while UniCA adapts pretrained TSFMs to heterogeneous covariates han2026unica . These models show that contextual information can improve forecasting, but an action is not merely given context. It is changed, compared, and optimized. Factual accuracy therefore provides limited evidence about responses to alternative actions. Action-Conditioned Time-Series Modeling Several recent studies explicitly model actions or interventions in temporal systems. ThermoForce separates passive dynamics from control-induced responses and combines a frozen TSFM prior with a structured intervention model for HVAC control wang2026thermoforce . CEDAR learns action-conditioned demand dynamics for counterfactual simulation and budget planning meng2026cedar . DRIFT and NormWear-2 model physiological trajectories under treatment interventions liu2026drift,luo2026toward , while DoFlow unifies observational, interventional, and counterfactual time-series prediction in a causal generative framework wu2026doflow . Related work in longitudinal causal inference estimates outcomes under alternative treatment sequences using recurrent, representation-learning, and Transformer-based models lim2018forecasting,Bica2020Estimating,melnychuk2022causal,xiong2024g . These methods mainly target domain-specific intervention modeling or causal treatment-effect estimation. We instead study a common action-conditioned modeling framework across heterogeneous controlled systems and evaluate whether predictive accuracy translates into intervention fidelity and decision quality. World Models for Decision Making World models learn dynamics that can be rolled forward under candidate actions for planning and policy learning pmlr-v235-ma24i,pmlr-v267-zhou25t . PlaNet and Dreamer use latent imagined trajectories for decision making hafner2019learning,hafner2020iclr-dream,hafner2025mastering , while TD-MPC2 combines latent dynamics with trajectory optimization hansen2024td . AcRKN and MTS3 model action-conditioned transitions in numerical dynamical systems, including long-horizon prediction under control inputs shaj2021action,shaj2023multi . Another line studies reusable dynamics priors. APV pretrains from action-free videos before learning action-conditioned dynamics for control seo2022reinforcement , with related ideas explored in recent world-model pretraining pmlr-v267-gao25u,wan2026learning . Evaluation has also moved beyond predictive fidelity. WorldGym tests whether simulated rollouts preserve policy performance and rankings quevedo2026worldgym , World-In-World evaluates closed-loop task success zhang2026world , and recent work examines fidelity under alternative actions chen2026robotic . title: Map2Vid: Embodied Navigation Video Generation with Human-Friendly Motion Control
summary: Controllable video generation has recently achieved impressive visual quality, yet existing control paradigms remain poorly suited to embodied navigation. Text prompts are spatially ambiguous, while camera-trajectory control relies on low-level motion specifications that are unintuitive for human users and difficult to manipulate. In this work, we introduce Map2Vid, a novel task that reformulates embodied navigation video generation as a BEV-map-to-video synthesis problem, together with a large-scale benchmark for systematic evaluation. By using BEV maps, which provide a visual representation of global scene layout and intended navigation routes, Map2Vid enables human-friendly navigation video generation. To support this task, we construct a dedicated dataset with over 100K navigation sequences across 61 indoor scenes, each paired with egocentric videos, BEV maps, camera trajectories and language instructions. We further develop a unified framework that integrates multiple control signals, together with a curriculum training strategy that progressively weakens non-map inputs, enabling flexible inference under both full conditioning and map-only input. Extensive experiments across multiple foundation generation models demonstrate that controllable navigation video generation via BEV map is a viable and promising direction.

Existing methods rely on spatially ambiguous language (Top) or unintuitive camera trajectories (Middle). Map2Vid (Bottom) bridges this gap by conditioning on routed BEV map, combining human-friendly control with strong geometric control. fig:fig1 Controllable video generation has recently achieved impressive visual quality, yet existing control paradigms remain poorly suited to embodied navigation. Text prompts are spatially ambiguous, while camera-trajectory control relies on low-level motion specifications that are unintuitive for human users and difficult to manipulate. In this work, we introduce Map2Vid, a novel task that reformulates embodied navigation video generation as a BEV-map-to-video synthesis problem, together with a large-scale benchmark for systematic evaluation. By using BEV maps, which provide a visual representation of global scene layout and intended navigation routes, Map2Vid enables human-friendly navigation video generation. To support this task, we construct a dedicated dataset with over 100K navigation sequences across 61 indoor scenes, each paired with egocentric videos, BEV maps, camera trajectories and language instructions. We further develop a unified framework that integrates multiple control signals, together with a curriculum training strategy that progressively weakens non-map inputs, enabling flexible inference under both full conditioning and map-only input. Extensive experiments across multiple foundation generation models demonstrate that controllable navigation video generation via BEV map is a viable and promising direction. Controllable Video Generation, Diffusion Model, Egocentric Vision Introduction Embodied navigation~ anderson2018evaluation, anderson2018vision, Yu2025MossVLN requires an agent to perceive the world from an egocentric perspective and move through an environment under the geometric constraints imposed by scene layout. Beyond its importance to Embodied AI, this setting also exposes a distinctive challenge for controllable video generation: the synthesized video must remain temporally coherent~ Zhao2026LSTD under long-horizon ego-motion, while preserving scene geometry across turns, corridor traversals, and room transitions. Compared with generic text-to-video generation, navigation video synthesis therefore demands stronger spatial grounding, more reliable temporal consistency, and a control interface that can specify motion in an interpretable way. Recent progress in large-scale video generation has substantially improved visual quality and motion realism. Most state-of-the-art approaches~ wan2025wan, wu2025hunyuanvideo condition the generation on text prompts and an initial frame, where textual descriptions primarily emphasize the appearance of the scene and cannot provide spatial grounding. This makes it difficult to maintain trajectory consistency and geometric plausibility over long horizons. Several recent works~ he2024cameractrl, wang2025ati attempt to address this limitation by introducing explicit camera trajectory control. Although effective in certain scenarios, they still suffer from two fundamental limitations: First, they support only local, small-scale camera motions (modest translations and rotations). In contrast, embodied navigation involves large-scale cumulative pose changes, including frequent large-angle turns and long-range transitions across rooms, resulting in a substantial mismatch in motion scale. Second, trajectory-based control depends on low-level specifications such as camera transformation matrices. Such representations offer limited abstraction over the spatial structure of the environment, and are fundamentally misaligned with how humans naturally express navigation intent, making them difficult for non-expert use. These limitations motivate us to revisit the control signal itself. In natural navigation, humans rarely reason in terms of camera matrices; instead, they reason about the scene layout and the route through it .For this reason, we introduce Map2Vid, a new task that reformulates embodied navigation video generation as a BEV map. As shown in Fig.~ fig:fig1 , Map2Vid takes as input a BEV map depicting the scene layout together with an intended navigation route, and aims to generate an egocentric video consistent with the specified path. Compared to text prompt or camera trajectory, BEV map provides structurally grounded and globally consistent control signals, enabling a more human-friendly control interface for navigation video generation. To instantiate this task, we construct a large-scale dataset Map2Vid-100K. Specifically, we leverage high-fidelity indoor environments of Matterport3D~ ramakrishnan2021hm3d , and sample valid navigation trajectories from the R2R benchmark~ anderson2018vision . Each navigation episode is executed in the Habitat-Sim~ puig2023habitat3 simulator, during which we record the corresponding egocentric video together with aligned natural language instruction, camera trajectories and BEV map. The dataset covers 61 indoor scenes and contains 117.8K navigation sequences, with 94.2K used for training and 23.6K reserved for evaluation. While our benchmark is constructed in simulation, it provides precise geometric alignment across modalities, which is difficult to obtain in real-world settings. Building on this dataset, we adapt several representative video generation models to support map-conditioned navigation video synthesis. During training, models are provided with multiple control signals, including the BEV map, camera trajectories, text instruction, and initial frame. To prevent models from over-relying on expressive but less human-friendly controls, we propose a curriculum training strategy that gradually weakens non-map conditions, encouraging the model to internalize the spatial dynamics semantics encoded in the BEV map. This design enables flexible inference at test time, supporting either full control signals or the BEV map alone. Extensive experiments demonstrate that controllable navigation video generation via BEV map is viable and promising, while also highlighting the intrinsic difficulty of the task. In summary, our contributions are threefold: (1) We introduce Map2Vid, a novel task that reformulates embodied navigation video generation as a BEV map, providing a human-friendly control interface. (2) We construct Map2Vid-100K, a large-scale benchmark comprising over 117K synchronized multimodal navigation sequences (videos, BEV maps, trajectories, instructions) across 61 scenes, establishing a standardized dataset and dual-aspect evaluation protocol for this new task. (3) We provide a systematic empirical study across four state-of-the-art video foundation models and propose a unified baseline framework with a progressive curriculum training strategy, validating the feasibility of the task and laying a strong empirical foundation for future research. Related Work sec:related_work Controllable Video Generation. Recent advances in video generation have been significantly driven by scalable Diffusion Transformers (DiT)~ peebles2023scalable . Prominent examples of this architecture include flagship models such as HunyuanVideo~ wu2025hunyuanvideo, kong2024hunyuanvideo and Wan~ wan2025wan . Despite these successes, achieving fine-grained controllability in video generation remains challenging. Early approaches adapted image-based conditioning techniques, such as ControlNet~ zhang2023adding and T2I-Adapter~ mou2024t2i , to the temporal dimension for structural guidance~ guo2023animatediff, wang2023videocomposer, hu2024animate . While these methods effectively enforce spatial structures (e.g., Canny edges, depth maps, or pose skeletons), they often struggle to maintain long-horizon temporal coherence and 3D geometric consistency. To better control motion dynamics, subsequent works (e.g., MotionCtrl~ wang2024motionctrl , DragNUWA~ yin2023dragnuwa and CameraCtrl~ he2024cameractrl ) introduce explicit camera trajectory-based motion conditioning, with CameraCtrl~ he2024cameractrl standing out with its Plucker embeddings. Though these methods enable the geometry control of the video generation, the input form of accurate camera trajectories is too non-trivial for normal users. By contrast, in this paper, we for the first time introduce and explore the BEV map as a geometric condition. Embodied Video Understanding Synthesis. subsec:embodied_synthesis Advanced by large-scale egocentric datasets such as Ego4D~ grauman2022ego4d and Ego-Exo4D~ grauman2024ego , the field has expanded from passive video understanding to agent-centric embodied world models (e.g., GAIA-1~ hu2023gaia , UniSim~ yang2023unisim ). In the realm of embodied video synthesis, existing works primarily address geometric consistency through trajectory conditioning in structured driving domains~ gao2023magicdrive,wang2024drivedreamer or via cross-view synthesis from third-person observations~ liu2024exocentric . Distinct from these approaches, the potential of top-down BEV maps as a spatially grounded control signal remains largely underexplored. Embodied AI has increasingly shifted from passive perception toward agent-centric understanding, supported by large-scale egocentric datasets such as Ego4D~ grauman2022ego4d and Ego-Exo4D~ grauman2024ego . Beyond understanding, recent work has explored video generation as a foundation for embodied world models that simulate agent–environment interactions, exemplified by GAIA-1~ hu2023gaia and UniSim~ yang2023unisim . A central challenge in this line of research is generating egocentric video that remains consistent with agent motion and scene geometry over long horizons. Several studies address this challenge through trajectory-conditioned generation, particularly in structured domains such as autonomous driving, where motion patterns and scene layouts are relatively constrained (e.g., DriveDreamer~ wang2024drivedreamer , MagicDrive~ gao2023magicdrive ). Other works focus on alleviating the scarcity of egocentric data by synthesizing egocentric views from third-person observations (Exo2Ego), using multi-view and diffusion-based frameworks~ liu2024exocentric .
