title: EmbodiedWorld-200K: Toward Embodied World Agents via Embodied-Planning Dataset and Interactive World Models
summary: Building embodied agents that can perceive, reason, and act across diverse 3D worlds is a central research direction toward artificial general intelligence. Yet most existing work remains confined to specific tasks in a single scene and transfers poorly to new environments, leaving general embodied agents for open-world settings under-explored. We refer to such agents as Embodied World Agents (EWAs), whose defining property is the ability to understand diverse visual environments and execute general actions in open-world conditions. To advance EWA research, we study open-world embodied navigation-planning and release EmbodiedWorld-200K, a large-scale dataset of over 200K samples spanning diverse scenes. Each example is equipped with multi-level annotations, ranging from low-level camera-motion trajectories to high-level semantic instructions. The dataset also provides unified evaluation splits and task-specific metrics, supporting offline pretraining and fair evaluation of EWAs. Beyond offline supervision, a defining characteristic of an EWA is its interaction with the environment; training solely on offline data is therefore insufficient, especially for generalizing to scenes not covered in the training distribution. Building dedicated real interactive environments, however, is often prohibitively expensive. To address this, we propose a novel training scheme that employs a video world model as a low-cost environment proxy and performs interactive reinforcement-learning (RL) post-training of the EWA within it. Empirically, pretraining on EmbodiedWorld-200K substantially improves the open-world embodied planning ability of the EWA, and further RL post-training inside a world model yields clear gains on out-of-distribution scenes. The dataset, baseline checkpoints, and training and evaluation code are available at https://xiaokunfeng.github.io/EmbodiedWorld-200K/.
full_text: Building embodied agents that can perceive, reason, and act across diverse 3D worlds is a central research direction toward artificial general intelligence. Yet most existing work on embodied agents remains confined to specific tasks in a single scene and transfers poorly to new environments, leaving general embodied agents for open-world settings an important but under-explored direction. We refer to such agents as Embodied World Agents (EWAs), whose defining property is the ability to understand diverse visual environments and execute general actions in open-world conditions. To advance research on EWAs, we instantiate them on open-world embodied navigation-planning and release EmbodiedWorld-200K, a large-scale dataset of over 200K samples spanning diverse scenes. Each example is equipped with multi-level annotations, ranging from low-level camera-motion trajectories to high-level semantic instructions, and is accompanied by unified evaluation splits and task-specific metrics, providing a shared substrate for offline pretraining and fair evaluation of EWAs. Beyond offline supervision, a defining characteristic of an EWA is its interaction with the environment; training solely on offline data is therefore insufficient, especially for generalizing to scenes not covered in the training distribution. Building dedicated real interactive environments, however, is often prohibitively expensive. To address this, we propose a novel training scheme that employs a video world model as a low-cost environment proxy and performs interactive reinforcement-learning (RL) post-training of the EWA within it. Empirically, pretraining on EmbodiedWorld-200K substantially improves the open-world embodied planning ability of the EWA, and further RL post-training inside a world model yields clear gains on out-of-distribution scenes. The full dataset, baseline checkpoints, and the accompanying training and evaluation code for supporting future research on EWAs are publicly available at . Introduction sec:intro Vision--language large models (VLLMs) have demonstrated strong semantic understanding and multimodal reasoning capabilities~ hurst2024gpt,anthropic2024claude,comanici2025gemini,bai2025qwen3,wang2025internvl3 . However, VLLMs are trained almost exclusively on static, passively observed data, rather than through executing actions or reasoning about their consequences in real environments; the intelligence they acquire thus remains, at its core, disembodied and passive~ silver2025era,sima2 , and falls noticeably short on embodied tasks that require a closed perception--action loop~ majumdar2024openeqa,fung2025embodied . In response, building embodied agents that can perceive, reason, and autonomously act in diverse 3D worlds~ kim2024openvla,black2024pi0,rt2 has attracted growing attention, and is widely regarded as one of the key paths toward artificial general intelligence. Yet most existing work on embodied agents remains confined to specific tasks in a single scene---for example, navigation within a particular indoor simulator~ anderson2018vision,krantz2020beyond , manipulation on a particular robotic platform~ openxembodiment2023,kim2024openvla,black2024pi0,intelligence2504pi0 , or task execution within a single type of game~ fan2022minedojo,baker2022video,lifshitz2023steve,bytedance2025lumine,lee2022multi . By contrast, developing general-purpose embodied agents for broad open-world environments remains an important but under-explored direction. For ease of discussion, we refer to such agents as Embodied World Agents (EWAs): agents that aim to acquire both a general understanding of diverse visual environments in open worlds and a general ability to execute actions within them. While this vision is highly appealing, realizing it faces a fundamental infrastructure gap: the community currently lacks a large-scale, open-world dataset that can simultaneously support well-grounded training and unified evaluation, and a matching open-source baseline model together with a practical training recipe. Existing embodied-agent datasets, such as typical Vision-and-Language Navigation (VLN) benchmarks~ anderson2018evaluation,krantz2020beyond , are limited in scale, lack scene diversity, and offer only single-level annotations, preventing EWAs from learning robust, general-purpose priors through large-scale pretraining as VLLMs do. To fill this gap, we instantiate the EWA problem as open-world embodied navigation-planning, a task that jointly stresses perceiving a diverse visual scene, grounding a language goal within it, and executing an extended action sequence. We adopt this instantiation because translation and view rotation are the actions that remain universal across heterogeneous open worlds, and are also the action types that frontier video world models natively support~ bruce2024genie,gamecraft1,team2026advancing . Accordingly, we release EmbodiedWorld-200K, a large-scale public corpus for this task, comprising over 200K video clips collected from diverse open-world virtual game environments (as shown in Fig.~ fig:teaser ). Each sample is accompanied by multi-level annotations, ranging from low-level camera-motion/action trajectories to high-level semantic instructions that describe the underlying embodied navigation-planning task. Building on this large-scale corpus of instruction--action sequences, we pretrain an existing VLLM~ bai2025qwen3 in an offline manner, retaining its multimodal understanding while extending it into a Vision–Language–Action (VLA) model sapkota2025vision,kim2024openvla with open-world embodied navigation-planning capabilities. A defining property of EWAs is their interaction with open-world environments, where many required capabilities can only be acquired through closed-loop interaction. Consequently, training solely on EmbodiedWorld-200K in an offline manner is insufficient, particularly for generalization to unseen scenes. However, real-world interactive platforms, such as game engines, are limited in scalability across diverse environments. Fortunately, the rapid progress of video-generative world models (WMs)~ genie3,cosmos2025,matrixgame2025,pan2025,gamecraft1,gamecraft2,hyworld2025,team2026advancing opens a new avenue: modern WMs can already roll out future visual observations conditioned on actions, offering a flexible and scalable simulation substrate for open-world interaction across diverse scenes. Building on this capability, we propose a novel training paradigm that treats a video WM as an environment proxy and performs interactive reinforcement learning (RL) post-training of EWAs within it. Specifically, an offline-pretrained EWA generates trajectories inside a frontier WM. During rollout, a VLLM dynamically produces task instructions conditioned on the evolving environment semantics, while reward signals are derived by framing reward modeling as visual question answering (QA)~ rocamonde2024vlmrm,wang2024rlvlmf . Finally, we apply direct preference optimization (DPO)~ rafailov2023dpo on the collected trajectories, enabling the model to refine its policy from interactive feedback and improving embodied planning in unseen environments. Extensive experiments demonstrate that offline pretraining on EmbodiedWorld-200K significantly improves the open-world embodied planning ability of EWAs, and that subsequent interactive RL post-training within a video world model further enhances adaptation to out-of-distribution (OOD) scenes. Our main contributions are summarized as follows: [leftmargin=1em] We study general-purpose embodied agents for open-world environments, referred to as Embodied World Agents (EWAs), and position them as an important yet under-explored research direction. We further provide infrastructure support from both data and training perspectives. We release EmbodiedWorld-200K, a large-scale dataset for open-world embodied planning containing over 200K samples with multi-level annotations, together with a unified evaluation split and task-specific metrics, enabling standardized pretraining and fair evaluation of EWAs. We propose a two-stage training framework for EWAs and instantiate a corresponding baseline: offline pretraining on EmbodiedWorld-200K followed by interactive RL post-training using a video world model as a scalable environment proxy. Empirically, EmbodiedWorld-200K significantly improves embodied planning performance, while WM-based interactive post-training further enhances generalization to unseen scenes. We release the dataset, model weights, and code at the project page to support future research. Related Work sec:related Embodied agents. Building agents that perceive and act in 3D environments has been studied across multiple domains. In robotic manipulation, RT-2~ rt2 finetunes a vision–language model to directly output robotic actions, PaLM-E~ driess2023palme ingests multi-modal sensor streams into a large language model for embodied planning, SayCan~ saycan2022 grounds language plans through learned affordances, and OpenVLA~ kim2024openvla and ~ black2024pi0 scale open-source vision–language–action (VLA) policies with large robot datasets such as Open X-Embodiment~ openxembodiment2023 . In embodied navigation, the community has long relied on photo-realistic simulators with curated trajectories~ anderson2018vision,krantz2020beyond , yet these benchmarks remain limited to a few thousand paths in indoor scans. In open-world virtual environments, VPT~ baker2022video learns policies from unlabeled gameplay videos, MineDojo~ fan2022minedojo provides Internet-scale knowledge for open-ended agents, Voyager~ wang2023voyager demonstrates LLM-driven lifelong exploration, STEVE-1~ lifshitz2023steve trains a text-conditioned policy via latent goals, and SIMA~ sima1 shows instruction-following across multiple 3D games. Despite this progress, most efforts remain confined to a single task type, scene distribution, or platform. The prospect of general-purpose embodied agents operating across diverse open worlds---what we term Embodied World Agents (EWAs)---remains largely unexplored, primarily due to the absence of large-scale, multi-level annotated data and a matching training recipe. World (action) models. World models learn environment dynamics to support agent training or planning. Classic model-based RL methods such as DreamerV3~ hafner2023dreamerv3 learn compact latent dynamics for policy optimization, while IRIS~ micheli2023iris builds autoregressive world models with transformers. Recent video-generative world models move toward pixel-level fidelity: Genie~ bruce2024genie learns controllable interactive environments from unlabeled video, GameNGen~ valevski2024gamengen and DIAMOND~ alonso2024diamond simulate game engines with diffusion models, GAIA-1~ hu2023gaia1 generates driving scenarios, and Cosmos~ cosmos2025 provides a large-scale foundation world model for physical AI. UniSim~ yang2023learning further proposes learning interactive real-world simulators that unify visual, physical, and semantic signals. Connecting world models to downstream agents has been explored through several paradigms. Planning-based approaches use video generation as an imagination module for lookahead: Video Language Planning~ du2023videolanguageplanning leverages text-to-video models to synthesize visual plans, and RoboDreamer~ zhou2024robodreamer composes world models for robot imagination. Data-augmentation methods generate synthetic trajectories for offline policy improvement, as in UniPi~ du2023unipi , which casts policy learning as text-guided video generation, and GenRL~ mazzaglia2024genrl , which trains embodied policies inside a multimodal foundation world model. The paradigm closest to ours treats the world model as a closed-loop interactive environment for RL: UniSim~ yang2023learning trains reward and policy jointly within a learned simulator, and GR-2~ cheang2024gr2 uses generated video for a scalable robot post-training. title: Frechet Forcing: Training Long-Horizon Streaming World Models from Short Clips
summary: Streaming video world models generate the future chunk by chunk, conditioned on their own past and a stream of actions. Trained on short clips, they drift once a rollout exceeds the training horizon, as prediction errors re-enter the context and compound. A common remedy is to train the model on its own rollouts via distribution matching distillation (DMD). For action-conditioned world models, the teacher becomes a bottleneck: an external video model is agnostic to the actions, whereas the model's own pretrained network drifts in the same manner as the student. We observe that a long rollout need not match a teacher, provided it remains a realistic continuation of its own scene that follows the commanded actions. Realism and scene fidelity can be measured against real-data statistics, which remain valid at any horizon, while action following is preserved by the model's conditional generation loss. We propose Fréchet Forcing, which fine-tunes a world model together with its deployed multi-step sampler under three constraints. Generative anchoring applies the flow-matching loss after a self-generated history ending on real data. Context fidelity, a Fréchet distance (FD) on latent statistics of the free rollout centred on each clip's own ground truth, keeps every rollout faithful to its scene. Reality matching, an FD to real frames in a frozen perceptual space, keeps the generated frames realistic. Because all three targets are derived from short real clips without comparing a rollout against a long recorded future, training requires no teacher, no online critic and no long videos. Fine-tuning MiniWorld-1B, pretrained on 253-frame clips, for at most 36 GPU-hours on 381-frame clips yields rollouts that remain stable beyond 4,000 frames and continue to follow their actions in both robot manipulation and camera-controlled exploration.
full_text: Introduction World models that generate video in a streaming fashion, with each chunk conditioned on previously generated chunks and on an action, provide a natural substrate for interactive simulation, game engines and embodied agents~ ha2018worldmodels,bruce2024genie,alonso2024diamond,valevski2025gamengen,chen2024diffusionforcing,yin2025causvid,huang2025selfforcing . However, because they are trained on ground-truth history and deployed autoregressively on their own predictions~ bengio2015scheduled , small errors re-enter the context and compound over time. Rollouts therefore remain coherent for roughly the length of the training clips before drifting, fading to black or dissolving into texture (Fig.~ fig:teaser ). This long-horizon drift remains the central obstacle to sustained streaming generation~ huang2025selfforcing,cui2025selfforcingpp,yang2025longlive . The prevailing strategy to close this train-test gap is to train the model on its own rollouts. Because a self-generated rollout has no paired ground truth beyond the first few seconds, supervision must be distributional, and recent work has largely converged on distribution matching distillation (DMD)~ yin2024dmd,yin2024dmd2,yin2025causvid,huang2025selfforcing , where the difference between a frozen teacher's score and an online ``fake'' score of the student on noised student samples provides the training gradient. State-of-the-art systems reach minute-scale video by extending DMD to longer rollouts, rolling windows and chunk-wise scoring~ cui2025selfforcingpp,liu2025rolling,yang2025longlive,gao2026rmd . Teacher-free alternatives instead retain a per-sample regression target by conditioning the flow-matching or diffusion loss on a history corrupted by the model's own errors~ guo2025resampling,li2026svi,yang2026arforcing , or by reversing rollouts so that they end on or recover the ground-truth start~ po2026bagger,huang2026live . For action-conditioned world models, however, the teacher poses a fundamental dilemma. An effective teacher must simultaneously model the student's domain and action space while remaining more accurate than the student on the states the student visits. A large external video model violates the first requirement, as it is agnostic to the action signal and pulls rollouts towards a mismatched distribution. Conversely, the world model's own pretrained network satisfies the first requirement but violates the second: it is the very model whose rollouts drift, so on long-horizon states its score agrees with the student and provides no corrective signal. In our experiments, neither choice improved over the base model across a broad range of configurations. Per-sample teacher-free objectives avoid the teacher altogether, yet they supervise only states that can be paired with ground truth, where a degraded history is followed by its recorded continuation or a reversed rollout recovers its recorded start. Because the regression target always lies within a recorded clip, the states a rollout visits thousands of frames later are never supervised directly. We take a different view of the supervision required for long rollouts. Rather than matching a teacher or a paired recording, a rollout must remain a realistic continuation of its own scene while following the commanded actions. These properties call for complementary training signals. Visual realism and scene fidelity are distributional properties of the rollout that can be evaluated against real data at any horizon, because the distribution of real frames is fixed, compact to summarise and, unlike a learned score, equally valid one second or one minute into a rollout. Action following, by contrast, is a property of conditional generation that the model's pretraining loss already supervises. therefore fine-tunes free rollouts generated directly by the deployed sampler to minimise Fr\'echet distances (FD) to real-data statistics while retaining the conditional generation loss. Running moment estimates~ yang2026fdloss render the FD differentiable at a batch size of one per GPU, and truncated backpropagation through the final chunks keeps rollout training computationally tractable. Specifically, our objective combines three constraints, each targeting one essential property of a long rollout. Generative anchoring preserves action-conditioned generation by applying the flow-matching (FM) loss after a self-generated history ending on real data, exposing FM to the model's accumulated errors while keeping the regression target exact. Context fidelity keeps each rollout faithful to its initial scene through an FD on latent statistics centred on the clip's own ground truth. Reality matching enforces frame-level realism through an FD to real frames in a frozen self-supervised feature space, penalising the dark, washed-out and tiled artifacts towards which long rollouts otherwise drift. Because none of the three constraints compares a rollout against a long recorded future, long-horizon training no longer requires long videos. Generative anchoring regresses a short real window after a re-rendered history, context fidelity compares the final chunks of a 317-frame rollout against the corresponding span of its own clip, and reality matching compares generated frames against a population of real frames. Every training sample is a 381-frame clip, and long-horizon drift is suppressed by supervising the states that the model reaches and learns to correct within these rollouts. At deployment, the rollout extends for as long as the action stream that drives it. We validate on MiniWorld-1B~ zhao2026miniworld , a block-causal world model pretrained on 253-frame clips, across two distinct domains. After fine-tuning on 381-frame clips, its rollouts remain stable beyond 4,000 frames, over the pretraining horizon, in both robot manipulation on DROID and camera-controlled exploration on Sekai (Fig.~ fig:teaser ). Naive distribution matching on free rollouts fails in instructive ways. We analyse its training dynamics with three diagnostic probes that track whether outputs remain dependent on their context, whether gradients align with the required statistical correction, and whether an external perceptual judge agrees with the training objective ( sec:analysis , Fig.~ fig:dynamics ). This analysis reveals three distinct failure modes: matching a marginal FD pulls every rollout towards a dataset-average appearance (context decoupling), pooling statistics over the entire rollout forces the gradient-carrying tail to compensate for the detached prefix (gradient-statistic misalignment), and matching a low-order feature space admits degenerate frames that do not resemble real images (feature-space exploitation). The critical design choices are therefore where a rollout is scored and in which feature space: context fidelity scores clip-centred statistics solely on the gradient-carrying chunks, while reality matching provides a semantic feature space, making the two distributional constraints mutually complementary. Our analysis also uncovers a failure mode specific to training on self-generated history: when a re-rendered history does not meet the real target smoothly, the model learns to redraw the scene at every chunk boundary. We quantify this periodic redraw with a dedicated chunk-boundary flicker metric and eliminate it by ending the history on a single real chunk. In summary, our contributions are threefold: We propose , to our knowledge the first method that trains a streaming video world model on its own rollouts using Fr\'echet-distance objectives against real data. It requires no teacher, no online critic and no long videos, and fine-tunes the deployed multi-step sampler without modification. We analyse distribution matching on free rollouts to identify three distributional failure modes (context decoupling, gradient-statistic misalignment and feature-space exploitation) alongside chunk-boundary redraw induced by self-generated history, and derive the exact design choice that resolves each. title: RxGS: Relightable Gaussian Stylization via BRDF Decomposition
summary: Reference-based 3D scene stylization transfers the appearance of a reference image onto a reconstructed 3D scene while preserving scene geometry. Recent methods perform this transfer by optimizing the appearance representation of neural scene models including Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF) and 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS). These methods optimize an RGB appearance representation, in which a single per-point colour combines the effects of material reflectance, environment illumination, together with the shading it produces, and the viewing direction. When stylization modifies this combined colour, the illumination effects present during stylization are baked into the stored appearance, so the stylized scene cannot be rendered under different illumination. To address this limitation, we present RxGS, a relightable 3D scene stylization framework built on a Bidirectional Reflectance Distribution Function (BRDF)-aware 3D Gaussian representation. Rather than modifying a per-point RGB colour, RxGS optimizes only the diffuse albedo field recovered by inverse rendering, while leaving roughness, metallicity, surface normals, and the estimated environment lighting unchanged. As a result, the stylized scene keeps all the components a physically-based renderer needs other than the edited albedo, and can therefore still be relit. RxGS optimizes the albedo field using a nearest-neighbour feature matching loss together with a spatial smoothness prior over Gaussian centres. We evaluate the method using a Geometry Consistency Cost (GCC) based on optical-flow warping error. RxGS achieves the lowest GCC on all evaluated NeRF-Synthetic scenes and remains competitive on real-captured scenes, while additionally supporting relightable stylization, which existing reference-based 3D scene stylization methods do not provide.
full_text: RxGS: Relightable Gaussian Stylization via BRDF Decomposition , , , , , , , , , , Introduction sec:intro Reference-based 3D scene stylization transfers the appearance of an artistic reference image onto a reconstructed 3D scene while keeping the rendered result geometrically consistent across viewpoints. Recent neural rendering methods, in particular Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF) mildenhall2021nerf and 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) kerbl20233dgs , produce high-quality novel views and have prompted a growing body of 3D stylization work. These methods stylize a scene by modifying the RGB appearance representation that the neural scene model has learned. In many applications a scene must be stylized once and then rendered under several different lighting conditions without repeating the stylization. This requires the stylized scene to keep a representation that can be relit after the appearance transfer, a requirement the RGB representation does not meet, as the next paragraph argues. An RGB appearance representation stores, at each point, one colour that already combines material reflectance, the environment illumination together with the shading it produces, and view-dependent effects. Because these factors are not stored separately, a stylization process that edits this colour necessarily edits the illumination contribution together with the intrinsic material. The illumination present during stylization is thereby written into the stored appearance: when the scene is later rendered under a different illumination, the stored colour does not change, so no new shading or shadows appear. As illustrated in Fig.~ fig:relightVSRGB , stylization applied to an RGB appearance representation fixes the artistic appearance and the illumination contribution together, which prevents the result from responding to novel lighting. To remove this restriction we build on recent inverse rendering methods for 3D Gaussian representations. Such methods liang2024gsir recover separate scene attributes, namely diffuse albedo, material properties, and environment illumination, and so support relightable rendering and material editing. These separated representations have not previously been used for reference-based 3D scene stylization. We present RxGS, a relightable 3D scene stylization framework built on a Bidirectional Reflectance Distribution Function (BRDF)-aware Gaussian scene representation. Given a reconstructed scene, RxGS first applies inverse rendering decomposition to recover, per Gaussian, the diffuse albedo , the roughness , the metallicity , the surface normal , and one global environment lighting . Stylization then optimizes only the field of diffuse albedos and leaves and and all geometry unchanged. Relightability follows from this bookkeeping rather than from any claim that the albedo alone fixes the rendered colour. A physically-based renderer consumes the geometry, the per-Gaussian material attributes , and the environment lighting . RxGS changes only the albedo coefficients and holds every other input fixed, so all non-albedo inputs the renderer needs remain intact, and the same renderer can be re-run under any chosen to produce a relit image of the stylized scene. To optimize the albedo field, RxGS uses a nearest-neighbour feature matching (NNFM) loss in the VGG feature space together with a spatial smoothness term over Gaussian centres. We evaluate RxGS on synthetic and real-captured scenes, measuring cross-view geometric consistency with the Geometry Consistency Cost (GCC) defined in Section~ sec:experiments . RxGS attains the lowest GCC on every evaluated NeRF-Synthetic scene and remains competitive on real-captured scenes, while keeping a relightable scene representation after stylization. Our contributions are the following. We present RxGS, a relightable 3D scene stylization framework based on a BRDF-aware Gaussian scene representation. We formulate stylization as optimization of the diffuse albedo field alone in a logit parameterization, regularized by a smoothness term on a -nearest-neighbour graph over Gaussian centres, so that artistic appearance transfer leaves the material and illumination parameters required for relighting unchanged. We evaluate on synthetic and real-captured datasets, reporting cross-view geometric consistency (GCC) that is competitive with prior stylization methods together with relightable stylization that prior methods do not provide. Related work sec:related 3D Scene Representation and Rendering A 3D scene representation encodes scene geometry and appearance in a compact, learnable form that supports downstream tasks such as novel view synthesis, scene editing, relighting, and scene understanding. NeRF mildenhall2021nerf introduced an implicit neural representation that parameterizes volumetric density and radiance with multilayer perceptrons, achieving novel view synthesis from multi-view observations. NeRF requires dense volumetric sampling during both training and rendering, which is computationally expensive. To reduce this cost, later work introduced voxel grids, tensor factorizations, and multi-resolution encodings, including DVGO Sun22dvgo , Plenoxels Fridovich2022plenoxels , TensoRF Chen22TensoRF , and Instant-NGP muller2022instant . As scene editing and stylization tasks developed, several methods adopted surface-based representations that give a more explicit geometric correspondence than a purely volumetric field, including VolSDF Yariv2021VolSDF , NeuS Wang2021neus , NeuMesh Yang2022NeuMesh , and NeRF2Mesh Tang2023NeRF2Mesh . Among explicit representations, 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) kerbl20233dgs represents a scene with a set of anisotropic Gaussian primitives. Unlike volumetric methods that rely on dense ray sampling, 3DGS renders through differentiable Gaussian rasterization, which is fast enough for real-time rendering while still reconstructing scene geometry and appearance. Following 3DGS, many extensions adapt the representation to downstream tasks, including scene editing, relighting, and inverse rendering. The inverse rendering line, which recovers separate material and lighting attributes for each Gaussian, is the one RxGS builds upon, and we review it next. Inverse Rendering with 3D Gaussian Representations Inverse rendering recovers physically meaningful scene properties, namely geometry, material attributes, and illumination, from image observations. Several methods built this decomposition into neural rendering frameworks. NeRFactor zhang2021Nerfactor factorizes scene appearance into geometry, reflectance, visibility, and illumination for relightable rendering. PhySG zhang2021physg uses spherical Gaussian representations of the BRDF and of the illumination to put physically-based shading into neural rendering. TensorIR Jin2023tensorir introduces a tensor-based inverse rendering framework that makes scene decomposition and relightable rendering more efficient. After 3DGS, inverse rendering was extended to Gaussian representations by attaching material, normal, and illumination attributes to the Gaussian primitives. GaussianShader jiang2024gaussianshader adds a shading function to Gaussian rendering and estimates geometry-aware normals to improve reflective surfaces. Relightable 3D Gaussian gao2024relightable attaches BRDF attributes and incident lighting to each Gaussian and renders through differentiable physically-based rendering. GS-IR liang2024gsir formulates inverse rendering on a BRDF-aware Gaussian representation by jointly estimating scene geometry, material properties, and environment illumination from multi-view observations; RxGS takes the decomposition produced by GS-IR as its input. 3D Scene Stylization Neural style transfer was first developed for images gatys2016image, huang2017adain, Doyle2019LaplacianPyramid, Xu2024GlobalLocalStyle , where the goal is to synthesize an image that keeps the scene content of one input while matching the appearance of a reference style image. As 3D scene representations matured, stylization was extended from 2D images to 3D scenes. Before neural scene representations, 3D stylization operated on explicit representations such as meshes and point clouds hollein2022stylemesh, cao2020psnet, liu2018paparazzi , manipulating surface textures, geometric attributes, or rendered appearance directly. Neural scene representations let stylization act on a learned appearance representation, so that style is propagated consistently across viewpoints. Early NeRF-based methods modify the appearance field of a reconstructed scene while keeping the geometry fixed chiang2022stylizing, zhang2022arf, chen2024upst, nguyen2022snerf, goel2022styletrf, huang2022stylizednerf . ARF zhang2022arf optimizes the appearance field of a NeRF with a neural style transfer objective, giving multi-view consistent stylization, and ARF-plus li2025arfplus improves stylization quality and training stability through stronger appearance representations and optimization strategies. Ref-NPR zhang2023refnpr improves controllability by transferring appearance from reference images through geometry-aware feature correspondence, which enables localized stylization. LAE-NeRF radl2023laenerf lets a user mark target regions in a neural scene representation and propagates the edit through neighbouring volumetric regions. SNeRF nguyen2022snerf alternates between image-space stylization and scene reconstruction, transferring artistic appearance into the neural scene representation across iterations. Because 3DGS associates appearance attributes directly with individual primitives, it makes appearance manipulation explicit. StylizedGS zhang2025stylizedgs supports region-specific style transfer through semantic masks. ReGS mei2024ReGS adapts 3DGS to reference-based stylization with a texture-guided mechanism that adjusts local Gaussian arrangements to reproduce texture detail from the reference. StyleSplat segments individual objects in a Gaussian scene and fine-tunes the selected Gaussians for object-level stylization. Further methods match segmented regions across views before transfer to keep the style consistent over the whole scene Liu25abcgs , geometry-aware texture transfer liu2026gt2gs , diffusion-based stylization and distillation yang2026fantacy3d , and feed-forward or optimization-free stylization of Gaussian splats Liu2026Stylos, sablon2026optifree . All of these methods, whether NeRF-based or Gaussian-based, edit a per-point RGB appearance, and so produce a stylized scene that stores one fixed colour per point and cannot be relit. A smaller line of work stylizes a decomposed appearance representation rather than RGB colour. TANGO chen2022tango performs text-driven stylization by editing BRDF attributes on a relightable mesh, which allows appearance editing under varying illumination. RxGS differs from this mesh-based, text-driven setting: it performs reference-image stylization directly on a BRDF-aware Gaussian representation, editing only the diffuse albedo field of the Gaussians and keeping the rest of the decomposition fixed. Method sec:method The task is to modify the appearance of a 3D scene, reconstructed from posed multi-view images , so that it matches the style of a reference image , while keeping both the scene geometry and the physical rendering components that are needed to render the scene under novel illumination. Each Gaussian is parameterized by a centre , a scaling vector , a rotation quaternion , an opacity , and appearance-related attributes. title: Rethinking Sparse-View 3D Gaussian Splatting: A Few-Shot Learning Perspective on Overfitting Prevention
comment: 5 pages, 5 figures. First-place solution in the sparse-view track of the SIGGRAPH Asia 2025 Volumetric Video Challenge
summary:
Sparse-view novel view synthesis (NVS) is essential for AR/VR and real-time communication applications, yet remains challenging when reconstructing 3D scenes from limited viewpoints. While 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) excels in dense-view scenarios, it suffers from overfitting and geometry degradation under sparse inputs. Current approaches often tackle these problems from a local perspective, addressing either data quality or training regularization individually, lacking a unified and interpretable framework for systematic improvement.
  We introduce a new perspective that reframes sparse-view 3DGS from a few-shot learning viewpoint, treating each Gaussian primitive as a neuron and leveraging deep learning regularization techniques. Under this unified framework, our approach generates more effective supervision from scarce observations through two strategies: (1) data-related supervision enrichment via optical flow-guided pseudo-view synthesis and joint camera-scene optimization; and (2) training-time regularization via motion-aware dropout and early stopping, which suppress overfitting while preserving dynamic-scene stability. Extensive experiments on the SIGGRAPH Asia 2025 volumetric video challenge sparse-view dataset demonstrate significant improvements over state-of-the-art optimization-based and feed-forward baselines. Our system won first place in the sparse-view track of the SIGGRAPH Asia 2025 challenge.

Recent advances in differentiable rendering—most notably Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF) and 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS)—have driven substantial progress; in dense-view settings, 3DGS in particular offers fast convergence and high rendering efficiency and has been widely adopted kerbl20233d . However, under sparse inputs, even 3DGS often overfits the limited viewpoints, resulting in geometry degradation and unstable, artifact-prone appearance. Existing approaches address the sparse viewpoint problem through various strategies—synthesizing pseudo-views, incorporating external depth supervision, and applying training regularization bao2024loopsparsegs,yu2024lm,li2024dropgaussian,smith2024coadaptation —but lack a unified perspective. This motivates us to seek a principled viewpoint that organizes these strategies within a single methodology. We therefore ask: This question leads us to reframe sparse-view 3DGS from a few-shot learning perspective, making deep learning regularization principles directly applicable. In deep learning, Ying et al.\ ying2019overview attribute overfitting to three causes—noisy data, excessive model capacity, and insufficient data. We argue that a corresponding mapping to sparse-view 3DGS challenges is: camera miscalibration introduces noise, excessive and entangled Gaussians lead to overfitting and co-adaptation, and limited viewpoints provide insufficient supervision. Correspondingly, the four canonical overfitting prevention strategies in deep learning—early stopping, model reduction, data augmentation, and regularization—naturally apply to 3DGS to address these challenges. We therefore group them into the two pillars that structure our method: Supervision Enhancement (data-related) and Training Regularization (model-training-related). Our approach instantiates these pillars through: (1) Supervision Enhancement: data expansion via optical flow-guided pseudo-view synthesis and data augmentation via joint camera–scene optimization; (2) Training Regularization: motion-aware dropout (restricted to static regions to handle dynamic scenes) paired with early stopping. . Our work makes the following contributions: [leftmargin=*] To the best of our knowledge, we are the first to provide a principled reframing of sparse-view 3D Gaussian Splatting as a few-shot learning problem by interpreting each Gaussian primitive as a computational unit. This perspective yields an interpretable link between graphics optimization and well-established generalization mechanisms in deep learning. We instantiate the Supervision Enhancement component via a supervision scheme tailored to limited viewpoints that (i) synthesizes pseudo-views through optical flow, and (ii) performs adaptive joint camera–scene optimization based on reprojection error. We instantiate the Training Regularization component by coupling motion-aware dropout—selectively applied to static Gaussians—with early stopping, effectively reducing co-adaptation under sparse inputs. Experiments on the SIGGRAPH Asia 2025 sparse-view dataset demonstrate improvements over both feed-forward and optimization-based methods across quantitative metrics and visual quality. Methodology Our overall algorithm is illustrated in Figure fig:pipeline . Following the deep learning perspective outlined in the introduction, we organize our approach into two complementary categories: Supervision Enhancement and Training Regularization. This unified framework addresses the three fundamental causes of overfitting in sparse-view 3DGS: noisy data (corresponding to camera miscalibration), insufficient data, and excessive model capacity. In the following subsections, we detail each component. Supervision Enhancement To address insufficient supervision and noisy data in sparse-view 3DGS, we enhance the training data through two strategies: pseudo-view synthesis addresses insufficient data, while joint camera–scene optimization addresses noisy data. Optical Flow Guided Pseudo-view Synthesis sec:pseudo-view Given a predicted depth map with intrinsics , we synthesize a nearby view by applying a small in-plane translation . The induced pixel shifts are Rendering the translated pose produces , which we warp back via differentiable sampling: This optical-flow parameterization explicitly reasons about horizontal and vertical displacements, providing extra robustness along the vertical axis when the training views lie roughly on the same horizontal ring (a common sparse-view setting where vertical supervision is weak). Over the valid pixel set (visible and in-bounds), we measure the Charbonnier photometric consistency as where is a small constant. To regularize depth and the induced flow, we adopt total variation (TV) regularization for both depth and flow fields, along with edge-aware smoothing to preserve depth discontinuities at image edges. The final geometric objective combines the photometric consistency loss with these regularization terms: where and are total variation terms that encourage smoothness in depth and flow fields, respectively, and is an edge-aware term that reduces smoothing at image edges. The hyperparameters are . Joint Camera–Scene Optimization sec:camera-opt Camera poses are part of the input data; when their calibration is inaccurate, they act as noise that degrades sparse-view reconstructions. To address this, we jointly optimize both camera poses and scene geometry based on reprojection error. We parameterize camera poses using rotations and translations (SO3xR3), allowing the optimization to correct calibration errors while simultaneously refining the 3D Gaussian scene representation. To avoid unnecessary optimization when camera calibration is already accurate, we selectively enable camera pose optimization only for sequences with high reprojection errors, which indicates potential calibration issues. The camera optimizer is activated after an initial warmup period and frozen before geometric constraints are applied, ensuring stable convergence. This selective joint optimization effectively reduces the impact of noisy camera parameters on sparse-view reconstruction while preserving well-calibrated camera poses. Training Regularization To address excessive model capacity and prevent overfitting, we employ two regularization strategies: motion-aware dropout and early stopping. Motion-Aware Dropout sec:dropout Dropout requires that different subsets of Gaussians, after being dropped, yield comparable outcomes. However, this consistency assumption is often violated under fast motion. We therefore restrict dropout to static regions only. To define static and dynamic regions, we leverage dense initialization that combines optical flow estimation (PDCNet truong2023pdc ) and multi-view point cloud reconstruction (OpenMVS openmvs_github ). PDCNet provides a complete point cloud covering both static and dynamic regions, while OpenMVS, relying on multi-view consistency, primarily produces static point clouds. We compute the distance from each point in the PDCNet point cloud to the nearest point in the OpenMVS point cloud. Points close to OpenMVS (within a threshold) are assigned as static, while distant points are labeled as dynamic. During training, we apply motion-aware dropout: for each Gaussian, we determine whether it lies in a dynamic region based on the initial definition. Gaussians in dynamic regions are excluded from dropout to preserve rendering quality, while only static-region Gaussians are subject to dropout regularization. This selective application maintains the consistency assumption for dropout while protecting dynamic regions. Early Stopping sec:early-stopping To prevent overfitting, we employ early stopping based on validation metrics. We determine the optimal early-stopping point by evaluating checkpoints throughout training and computing rankings on novel view synthesis metrics (PSNR, SSIM, LPIPS). The optimal stopping point is determined as the checkpoint with the lowest average rank across all three metrics. This stopping criterion is determined using a validation sequence and then applied consistently across all experiments. title: CARNet: End-to-End Coupled Association-Recognition Network for Fine-Grained Multi-Drone Collaborative Detection
summary: Multi-drone collaborative detection aims to enhance target recognition by leveraging complementary observations from overlapping aerial viewpoints. Existing approaches typically follow a two-stage pipeline that first establishes cross-view correspondences and then performs fusion-based recognition. However, this decomposition suffers from inconsistent optimization objectives, redundant pairwise modeling, and irreversible error propagation, where incorrect associations inevitably undermine subsequent recognition performance. To overcome these limitations, we propose the Coupled Association-Recognition Network (CARNet), a unified framework that jointly optimizes cross-view target association and recognition fusion through a shared target-pair representation. To improve association reliability in densely populated scenes with visually similar targets, CARNet explicitly incorporates spatial cues into pairwise relation modeling. Moreover, we introduce two complementary causal-inspired intervention strategies: the first enhances cross-view association by emphasizing appearance-confusing pairs, while the second bolsters the robustness of fusion-based recognition by learning stable multi-view representations under incomplete visual evidence. In addition, we present MDMT-CD, a fine-grained extension of the MDMT dataset that enriches the original vehicle annotations with detailed category labels, providing the first benchmark specifically designed for multi-drone collaborative vehicle detection. Extensive experiments demonstrate that CARNet consistently outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods. The MDMT-CD dataset and source code will be available at https://github.com/bigdreaming11/CARNet.

Existing approaches typically follow a two-stage pipeline that first establishes cross-view correspondences and then performs fusion-based recognition. However, this decomposition suffers from inconsistent optimization objectives, redundant pairwise modeling, and irreversible error propagation, where incorrect associations inevitably undermine subsequent recognition performance. To overcome these limitations, we propose the Coupled Association-Recognition Network (CARNet), a unified framework that jointly optimizes cross-view target association and recognition fusion through a shared target-pair representation. To improve association reliability in densely populated scenes with visually similar targets, CARNet explicitly incorporates spatial cues into pairwise relation modeling. Moreover, we introduce two complementary causal-inspired intervention strategies: the first enhances cross-view association by emphasizing appearance-confusing pairs, while the second bolsters the robustness of fusion-based recognition by learning stable multi-view representations under incomplete visual evidence. In addition, we present MDMT-CD, a fine-grained extension of the MDMT dataset that enriches the original vehicle annotations with detailed category labels, providing the first benchmark specifically designed for multi-drone collaborative vehicle detection. Extensive experiments demonstrate that CARNet consistently outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods. The MDMT-CD dataset and source code will be available at . Multi-drone collaborative detection Cross-view target association Fine-grained object fusion recognition Causal-inspired intervention Introduction Single-drone object detection is prone to classification errors and struggles to handle challenging scenarios such as occlusion liu2026spformer . In contrast, multi-drone systems enable collaborative observation of the same target from different aerial viewpoints, providing complementary structural and appearance information liu2026topological . A natural implementation is a two-stage pipeline: an association network first establishes correspondences, and a subsequent fusion classifier recognizes each matched target peng2023skynet . However, the two stages are optimized with heterogeneous objectives, leading to inconsistencies in representation learning and redundant pairwise modeling across modules. Moreover, the cascade design introduces a structural bottleneck where association errors are irrevocably propagated to the recognition stage lu2026skyseg . Once the first stage incorrectly links two different vehicles, subsequent feature fusion inevitably aggregates conflicting evidence, making the final prediction unrecoverable. This design is also computationally redundant and inefficient due to duplicated pairwise modeling across stages. This motivates a unified formulation in which target association and fusion recognition are learned through the same target-pair representation. We address this bottleneck with a position-aware all-pairs relation. For every target in one drone view and every target in the other, we construct a fused relation by combining their cross-view visual descriptors. LGSGMM zhao2026two demonstrat , positional information provides valuable geometric cues that improve feature discriminability and correspondence estimation under appearance ambiguity. Motivated by this observation, we encode each target center using a learnable Fourier embedding and inject the resulting positional representation into the fused relation, allowing it to jointly model visual appearance and spatial consistency across views. Each fused target-pair relation is mapped to a distribution containing fine-grained vehicle categories and one no-match state. Consequently, the relation tensor serves as a unified target-pair representation that jointly performs cross-view target association and fusing recognition within a single prediction stage, eliminating the conventional separation between association and fusion-based recognition. This unified formulation enables CARNet to replace the conventional association network and fusion recognition with a single prediction stage. However, even with the unified target-pair modeling scheme, association learning may still struggle to capture discriminative correspondence evidence from challenging target pairs. Existing supervision paradigms typically optimize pairwise relations based on matching labels, while overlooking the varying discriminative difficulty among different target pairs. Since easy negative pairs provide straightforward optimization signals, the model tends to prioritize learning easily separable appearance patterns, whereas the fine-grained identity cues and critical correspondence evidence embedded in highly similar target pairs remain insufficiently explored, resulting in incorrect associations in complex scenarios. Motivated by Pearl’s causal hierarchy guyon2010causality , CARNet introduces two complementary intervention strategies to guide the model toward learning stable cross-view correspondence evidence. The first enhances cross-view correspondence by assigning greater learning emphasis to appearance-confusing non-matching target pairs, encouraging the model to devote more optimization capacity to challenging correspondence decisions. The second intervention perturbs the visual evidence within target pairs and enforces consistency between the original and intervened relation representations, encouraging the model to learn stable correspondence representations that remain robust under visual variations and incomplete observations. Our contributions are summarized as follows: We establish MDMT-CD, a fine-grained extension of the MDMT dataset by enriching the original single-category vehicle annotations with fine-grained category labels. We propose CARNet, a unified pairwise relation framework that integrates cross-view correspondence and fusion recognition in a single prediction stage. We propose two causal-inspired intervention strategies that improve cross-view correspondence in densely distributed scenes with appearance-similar targets while enhancing the robustness of multi-view fusion recognition. CARNet achieves state-of-the-art collaborative detection and cross-view association performance on the MDMT-CD datasets, the best association performance on the infrared and cross-modal subsets of M3Track, and further demonstrates excellent generalization on the cross-camera multi-object tracking benchmarks Wildtrack and MvMHAT. Related Work Multi-Drone Collaborative Perception Multi-drone collaborative perception exploits complementary observations from multiple UAVs to alleviate limited fields of view, occlusion, small object scales, and unstable imaging conditions. Early studies mainly focused on collaborative tracking. Zhu et al.~ zhu2021multidrone proposed an agent-sharing network that exchanges reliable target templates and performs view-aware fusion for multi-drone single-object tracking. Liu et al.~ liu2023robust introduced the MDMT benchmark and MIA-Net, which combine within-view tracking with cross-drone identity authentication to recover targets occluded in individual views. Wu et al.~ wu2025temporal further enhanced multi-drone multi-object tracking through temporal--spatial feature interaction. Beyond UAV-specific settings, Nguyen et al.~ nguyen2024multi formulated multi-camera multi-object tracking as a single-stage global association problem, jointly reasoning about detections and cross-camera correspondences in overlapping views. Zheng et al.~ zheng2024motion further improved multi-object association under occlusion through motion-guided cross-temporal aggregation and hierarchical matching. Recent research has increasingly investigated feature-level collaborative detection. DiscoNet~ li2021disconet learns a collaboration graph under teacher--student distillation, whereas Where2comm~ hu2022where2comm communicates only spatial regions with high perceptual confidence. V2X-ViT~ xu2022v2xvit , CoBEVT~ xu2023cobevt and CoBEVFlow~ wei2023cobevflow further address heterogeneous observations, sparse cross-agent fusion, communication redundancy, and temporal asynchrony. Although several of these methods were initially developed for vehicle-based agents, their feature alignment and communication mechanisms are also applicable to UAV collaboration. For UAV-specific three-dimensional perception, UAV3D~ ye2024uav3d provides benchmarks for collaborative 3D detection and tracking, while UCDNet~ tian2025ucdnet maps multi-UAV image features into a common 3D space using depth priors and geometric consistency. MCOP~ lin2025mcop extends collaboration from bounding-box detection to dense occupancy prediction with altitude-aware compression. V2U4Real~ li2026v2u4real studies real-world vehicle-to-UAV cooperative detection, and AirCopBench~ zha2026aircopbench evaluates multi-drone embodied perception and reasoning. Nevertheless, most existing methods output trajectories, boxes, or occupancy states, while target-level correspondence and fine-grained collaborative recognition remain insufficiently coupled. Cross-View Target Association Cross-view target association aims to determine whether targets observed by different UAVs correspond to the same physical object. Compared with conventional multi-object tracking, the task is considerably more challenging due to drastic viewpoint changes, severe rotations, scale variations, target occlusions, and dense distributions of visually similar objects. Existing UAV-oriented methods mainly exploit geometric consistency to establish cross-view correspondences. Li et al.~ li2022triangular represented each target using triangular topological sequences and performed globally consistent association through two-stage assignment. Liu et al.~ liu2023mdmt introduced the MDMT benchmark and proposed MIA-Net, which first establishes image-level correspondences using SIFT features and then associates tracked targets across UAVs through geometric verification. Qiao et al.~ qiao2024stca proposed STCA, which estimates inter-view transformations, identifies common visible regions, and performs bidirectional cross-drone association. Tan et al.~ tan2025gtanet further formulated target association as a graph matching problem and exploited reliable spatial relationships to improve robustness under missed and false detections. Besides these dedicated UAV-oriented methods, appearance-based ReID models and deep image matching networks are also widely adopted as association baselines. However, appearance-based methods such as Re-ID he2023fastreid , OSNet zhou2019omni , ReIDMamba gu2026reidmamba , CrossMOT hao2024divotrack , CT wieczorek2021unreasonable , AGW ye2021deep , mainly rely on visual similarity and therefore struggle to distinguish densely distributed targets with highly similar appearances. Deep image matching methods, such as SuperGlue~ sarlin2020superglue , LoFTR~ sun2021loftr and Roma~ edstedt2024roma , often experience noticeable performance degradation under the large rotation differences commonly encountered between UAV views. Moreover, MIA-Net depends on handcrafted SIFT features for image registration, resulting in relatively low computational efficiency. Furthermore, most existing methods perform target association as an independent preprocessing stage, making it difficult to jointly optimize cross-view association and downstream collaborative recognition. title: PrismWAM: Decoupling State Representations in World Action Models
summary: World Action Models (WAMs) typically represent the world through latent embeddings from pretrained video models, which entangle heterogeneous aspects of the world, from how it looks (e.g., texture and color) to how it is physically configured (e.g., occupancy and pose). This raises an underexplored question: $\textbf{what should constitute the state of a WAM?}$ We argue that the world state should separate how the world appears from how the world evolves under action: the former captures semantic context, while the latter is governed by physical state. To this end, we propose $\textbf{PrismWAM}$, which decouples physics from semantics while jointly modeling state and action. PrismWAM factorizes an embodied task into a $\mathrm{Semantic\ Planning}\rightarrow\mathrm{Physical\ Rollout}\rightarrow\mathrm{Executable\ Action}$ pipeline: given only the initial RGB observation, semantic planning learns to predict the final goal image, while physical rollout predicts the fine-grained evolution toward this goal in depth space; executable actions are then generated from the depth rollout. Without any embodied action pretraining or additional data augmentation, PrismWAM achieves strong manipulation performance in both simulation and the real world. Notably, PrismWAM even surpasses a broad range of models with large-scale embodied action pretraining (e.g., OpenWAM-$α$). More broadly, we reframe World Action Models from modeling how the world looks to how it responds to action, paving the way for action-centric world models grounded in occupancy, flow, tactile sensing, proprioception, and beyond.

This raises an underexplored question: We argue that the world state should separate how the world appears from how the world evolves under action: the former captures semantic context, while the latter is governed by physical state. To this end, we propose PrismWAM, which decouples physics from semantics while jointly modeling state and action. PrismWAM factorizes an embodied task into a pipeline: given only the initial RGB observation, semantic planning learns to predict the final goal image, while physical rollout predicts the fine-grained evolution toward this goal in depth space; executable actions are then generated from the depth rollout. Without any embodied action pretraining or additional data augmentation, PrismWAM achieves strong manipulation performance in both simulation and the real world. Notably, PrismWAM even surpasses a broad range of models with large-scale embodied action pretraining (e.g., OpenWAM- ). More broadly, we reframe World Action Models from modeling how the world looks to how it responds to action, paving the way for action-centric world models grounded in occupancy, flow, tactile sensing, proprioception, and beyond. Introduction World models have emerged as a promising paradigm for enabling autonomous agents to predict the consequences of their actions~ ha2018world,lecun2022path . By learning how the world evolves over time, these models aim to provide a foundation for planning and action~ hafner2019dream . Recent World Action Models (WAMs) extend this paradigm by jointly modeling video and action, often relying on pretrained video backbones to capture the rich visual dynamics of the physical world~ dreamzero,lingbot-va,gigaworld-policy . Yet, a key question remains underexplored: Our key observation is that video latents capture a mixture of factors that are not equally relevant to action generation~ cosmos-predict2.5 . While appearance and texture provide rich semantic context for understanding the scene, they are often invariant to the actions being modeled. For example, when an agent moves or grasps an object, its geometry and pose may change, while its color, texture, and intrinsic appearance typically remain unchanged. Therefore, video latents which entangles the physical state with the semantic context can make the representation substantially richer than what is necessary for modeling how the world evolves under action. This motivates a simple principle: a good state representation in WAMs should distinguish between physical state and semantic context . The physical state refers to action-relevant properties such as geometry, pose, occupancy, contact, and potentially dynamics, whereas semantic context provides the appearance information necessary to interpret that state, such as object identity, category, and texture; see~Fig.~ fig:teaser (a). The distinction is not between information that is useful and useless; rather, it decouples what actions can change from what helps us understand what is being acted upon . Therefore, we propose PrismWAM to separate semantic context from physical dynamics through a workflow (see~Fig.~ fig:teaser (b)), rather than treating a single video latent as a monolithic state. Semantic planning infers from RGB observations, physical rollout models toward the goal, and executable action determines . We instantiate this principle with a Mixture-of-Transformers (MoT) architecture built upon a pretrained video backbone~ wan2.2 , as shown in Fig.~ fig:method_architecture . During training, the semantic planner predicts the target from the initial RGB observation and transfers its task-level knowledge to the physical rollout via attention layers, while the action branch learns to map the predicted physical evolution to continuous actions. We use depth as the physical representation for its accessibility, physical grounding, and spatial alignment with RGB. Notably, the semantic planner serves only as a training-time teacher, with action inference relying solely on the initial RGB observation and learned depth rollout. Extensive experiments across diverse simulation and real-world benchmarks validate the effectiveness and efficiency of PrismWAM. (1)~Without action pretraining, PrismWAM substantially outperforms representative VLAs and WAMs under the same setting, improving the success rate over FastWAM by 43.82 percentage points ( vs. ) on RoboTwin-C2R and the score over starVLA by 29.83 points ( vs. ) on RoboDojo; see Fig.~ fig:teaser (c). (2)~PrismWAM outperforms several WAMs, including models with action pretraining, with particularly strong gains in precision manipulation and generalization: on RoboDojo Precision, it surpasses OpenWAM- by 21.37 points ( vs. ), while improving the success rate on RoboTwin-C2R by 14.62 percentage points ( vs. ), showing a higher ceiling for complex tasks and novel scenes. (3)~PrismWAM even matches or surpasses large-scale pretrained models on several benchmarks despite being trained with only 2,300 hours of depth data. On RoboDojo, it improves the score by 16.00 points over G0.5 ( vs. ) and 16.16 points over Xiaomi-Robotics-1 ( vs. ), showing that scaling action pretraining is not the only path to stronger embodied foundation models; principled architectural design offers a more data-efficient alternative. Our key contributions are listed as follows: [leftmargin=6mm] A decoupling principle for World Action Models. We identify the entanglement of semantics and physics in video latents as a fundamental limitation of existing WAMs, forcing action generation to disentangle high-level task planning from fine-grained physical state transitions. An effective and efficient WAM architecture. We instantiate the principle with a Mixture-of-Transformers (MoT), where an RGB semantic planner guides depth-based physical rollout, and develop a learning pipeline combining dense depth supervision with sparse RGB goal supervision, enabling fast inference without explicit RGB goal prediction. Strong performance and data efficiency. PrismWAM outperforms existing VLAs and WAMs, with particularly strong gains in precision manipulation and generalization. It also surpasses a number of models with large-scale action pretraining, demonstrating that principled architectural design offers a more data-efficient path toward stronger embodied foundation models. Related Works -Language-Action Policies. The general and embodied knowledge encoded in pretrained vision-language models (VLMs)~ gemini,qwen-vl,rynnbrain,hy-embodied,mimo-embodied provides a foundation for vision-language-action (VLA) models that map visual observations and language instructions to robot actions~ RT-2,openvla,pi_0,cogact,pi05,gr00t-n1,smolvla . Internet-scale image--text pretraining provides semantic priors for complex instruction understanding and long-horizon manipulation~ RT-2,pi_0,pi05,gr00t-n1,hi-robot . However, such pretraining emphasizes recognition and semantic alignment, with limited explicit supervision for continuous state transitions and how actions change the environment. Action Models. Advances in video generative models~ wan2.2,cosmos-predict2.5,cosmos3 have paved the way for world action models (WAMs), a promising paradigm that jointly models future states and robot actions for generalist robotic manipulation. Most jointly model future RGB observations and action sequences~ uwm,cosmos-policy . Some methods guide actions based on predicted future RGB observations~ videovla,motus,lingbot-va,dreamzero,next-forcing,lingbot-va2,openwam . Others use future prediction as training supervision and generate actions directly from observed context~ fastwam,gigaworld-policy,pfd,arps,meco-wam . Both approaches primarily learn state evolution in RGB appearance space, which entangles action-relevant geometry and pose with texture, illumination, and background. This requires modeling appearance details that may be irrelevant to control and inferring physical changes from visual variations that may not reflect motion~ agra,meco-wam . Representations for Manipulation. Physical or spatial representations support precise manipulation and spatial generalization~ peract,rvt,dp3,3d-diffuser-actor,spatialvla . Such information can directly guide action generation through depth or point-cloud features extracted from current observations~ depthvla,pointvla,3d-diffuser-actor . Complementary approaches introduce physical or spatial structure through supervision, including representation alignment~ spatial-forcing,lingbot-vla2,3dthinkvla,4d-wam and auxiliary prediction~ xwam,wam4d,meco-wam,dreamvla . Recent world action models take RGB and geometry as joint inputs and predict their future states together~ rynnworld-4d,sa-wam . This couples semantic and physical information, retaining the RGB-based modeling issues discussed above. PrismWAM separates their roles along a chain, distinguishing semantic task understanding from the physical state evolution that guides action execution. Method sec:method PrismWAM follows a chain for prediction and control. The RGB stream learns semantic planning representations from a sparse future-frame target, while the depth stream predicts a dense physical rollout that guides action generation. We first present the problem formulation ( sec:method_formulation ), then describe PrismWAM's architecture, training, and inference ( sec:method_architecture ). Problem Formulation sec:method_formulation We formulate a world--action model (WAM) that jointly predicts world-state evolution and the corresponding actions. Let denote the current world state, its future world state trajectory, and the corresponding action sequence. Given task context , comprising the language instruction and proprioceptive state , the policy can be expressed as Here, models how the current state may evolve over the prediction horizon, while predicts actions conditioned on the current state and a future state trajectory. Marginalizing over possible future world state trajectories yields the policy's action distribution. The future world state trajectory and action sequence cover the same time interval. Semantic Planning and Physical Rollout. We use historical and current RGB observations for semantic planning and the current depth observation as the initial physical state. Semantic planning captures task intent and the intended scene configuration, while physical rollout models the intermediate geometric changes needed for action execution. The resulting policy is PrismWAM sec:method_representation sec: arch sec:method_architecture Architecture with Sparse--Dense Temporal Supervision. Building on the pretrained video backbone WAN~ wan2.2 , PrismWAM uses RGB and depth streams with asymmetric temporal supervision, coupled to an action tower through a mixture-of-transformers (MoT) architecture (Fig.~ fig:method_architecture , left). The RGB stream predicts a single intended-future frame , a sparse target for learning task semantics. The depth stream predicts the denser sequence , providing intermediate spatial states that guide action evolution. This assigns semantic planning to sparse RGB prediction and physical rollout to dense geometric prediction, whose representation is less entangled with texture and illumination.
