title: SpatialScout: Can VLM Agents Actively Explore and Map 3D Scenes?
summary: Spatial intelligence requires agents to actively acquire visual evidence and integrate observations into a coherent representation of the three-dimensional world. Yet spatial question answering offers limited evidence of whether models can construct accurate metric maps through autonomous exploration. We introduce SpatialScout, a benchmark for evaluating vision-language model (VLM) agents on active object-level 3D mapping. SpatialScout comprises 80 diverse indoor scenes containing 3,140 target objects. Given an object inventory, RGB observations, camera calibration, and camera poses, agents control a camera to explore each scene and estimate object centers in a shared coordinate frame. The task requires coordinating viewpoint selection, cross-view association, geometric estimation, and map revision under bounded interaction budgets. Evaluation jointly measures localization accuracy and target coverage through object-scale overlap scores that penalize missing predictions. Experiments with frontier VLMs reveal substantial limitations: the strongest evaluated model, Claude Opus 5.5, achieves a mean overlap score of 41.71%, with 47.23% of targets exceeding an intersection-over-union (IoU) threshold of 0.5 and only 3.25% exceeding 0.9. These results reveal a substantial gap between recovering coarse object layouts and constructing complete, precise metric maps. SpatialScout provides a quantitative testbed for developing agents that build reliable 3D spatial representations through active perception. Code is available at https://github.com/JesseZZZZZ/SpatialScout.
full_text: Spatial intelligence requires agents to actively acquire visual evidence and integrate observations into a coherent representation of the three-dimensional world. However, spatial question answering provides limited evidence of whether models can construct accurate metric maps through autonomous exploration. We introduce SpatialScout, a benchmark for evaluating vision-language model (VLM) agents through active object-level 3D mapping. SpatialScout comprises 80 diverse indoor scenes containing 3,140 target objects. Given an object inventory, RGB observations, and camera calibration and poses, agents control a camera to explore each scene and estimate object centers in a shared coordinate frame. This task requires sustained coordination of viewpoint selection, cross-view association, geometric estimation, and map revision under bounded interaction budgets. Our evaluation jointly measures localization accuracy and target coverage, using object-scale overlap scores that penalize missing predictions. Experiments with frontier VLMs reveal substantial limitations: the strongest evaluated model, Claude Opus 5.5, achieves a mean overlap of 41.71 , with only 47.23 of targets exceeding an IoU threshold of 0.5 and 3.25 exceeding 0.9. These results expose a substantial gap between recovering coarse object layouts and constructing complete, precise metric maps. SpatialScout provides a quantitative testbed for developing agents that build reliable 3D spatial representations through active perception. Code is available at https://github.com/JesseZZZZZ/SpatialScout. Introduction sec:introduction Spatial intelligence is fundamental to embodied agents' ability to understand and act in 3D environments~ openeqa,conceptgraphs . It requires agents to actively observe their surroundings to resolve occlusion and perspective ambiguities, infer object locations and spatial relationships, and integrate evidence across views into a consistent 3D representation~ hartley2004,esi . Evaluating this entire process is central to assessing the spatial capabilities of vision-language models (VLMs). Existing spatial intelligence benchmarks widely adopt image- and video-based question answering (QA) to assess counting, direction, distance, and spatial relations~ vsi,site . Although these evaluations have revealed substantial model limitations, answer accuracy imposes only limited constraints on spatial understanding. Finite answer choices allow models to arrive at correct answers through guessing or elimination; language priors and biases in answer distributions may also enable correct responses based on non-spatial cues~ goyal2017vqa,agrawal2018priors . More importantly, spatial QA does not fully capture real-world demands: agents must autonomously gather evidence, update spatial representations, and use them to guide subsequent actions~ openeqa,theoryofspace . Evaluating frontier VLMs therefore requires end-to-end assessment of this multi-step process, beyond answer accuracy alone. Bridging this gap requires evaluating autonomous information acquisition and spatial representation construction within a single task, forming a closed loop of observation, reasoning, and decision-making. Recent benchmarks such as ESI-Bench~ esi and S -Bench~ s3 introduce active interaction into spatial QA, while Theory of Space~ theoryofspace examines the construction of discrete cognitive maps. Our key advance is to make the construction of object maps in continuous 3D space through active interaction a direct evaluation objective for spatial intelligence. Models must autonomously acquire visual evidence and recover the 3D positions of a target set in a common coordinate frame. This task couples active perception, cross-view association, geometric estimation, and scene modeling: the current spatial estimate determines what to observe next, while the selected viewpoint shapes the evidence available thereafter. Through spatial construction beyond QA, feedback-driven active exploration, and end-to-end task evaluation, we examine whether VLMs can transform local observations into accurate and complete metric spatial representations. To this end, we introduce SpatialScout, a benchmark for evaluating the spatial intelligence of vision-language agents through active object-level 3D mapping. Starting from an initial observation and a target inventory, an agent autonomously explores the scene and progressively constructs a 3D map of target object centers in a common coordinate frame. The benchmark has three core features: ~Explicit spatial construction. Models must output a set of 3D object positions, enabling quantitative evaluation of spatial representation quality through localization accuracy and target coverage. ~Closed-loop active exploration. Models select subsequent viewpoints based on existing observations and the current map, then update position estimates using new evidence, forming a feedback loop between the active acquisition of perceptual evidence and spatial understanding. ~Long-horizon end-to-end capability evaluation. Models coordinate observation planning, object recognition, cross-view association, geometric estimation, and map updates across multiple interaction steps, with overall performance measured by final map quality. This sustained coordination goes beyond QA tasks with short reasoning chains and better reflects real-world spatial understanding. SpatialScout comprises 80 indoor scenes and 3,140 target objects, with 30--40 targets per scene, spanning diverse spatial layouts, object scales, and repeated category instances. The benchmark provides a unified set of camera-control and geometric assistance tools, along with camera intrinsics and poses, and requires models to infer object centers from autonomously acquired visual evidence. Evaluation jointly measures geometric estimation error, localization accuracy relative to object scale, and target coverage. We also record map updates under a limited interaction budget to analyze how object-level spatial representations emerge as exploration proceeds. We evaluate frontier VLMs, including GPT-6 Astra and Claude Opus~5.5. The results show that models can recover parts of object layouts through autonomous exploration, but comprehensive coverage and precise localization remain challenging. Models differ substantially in target omissions and center localization accuracy, while the proportion of targets meeting stringent scale-relative accuracy criteria remains low. These findings indicate that recognizing objects or making coarse spatial judgments does not necessarily translate into constructing reliable metric maps. By exposing these limitations through measurable localization and coverage metrics, SpatialScout provides a unified benchmark for studying how models construct and understand the 3D world through autonomous interaction. SpatialScout Construction sec:method SpatialScout evaluates active object-center mapping by VLM agents. Given an object inventory and calibrated camera poses, an agent selects RGB views, associates objects across observations, and maintains a three-dimensional map of their centers. The benchmark combines a fixed scene catalog, a shared interaction interface, and object-level evaluation to measure the accuracy and completeness of the resulting map (Fig.~ fig:main ). Task Definition sec:method_task Inventory and map. A scene contains targets with public inventory : instance identifier , category , and equivalence group . During an episode, the agent maintains estimates for submitted identifiers . Evaluation compares multisets of center positions within each group, with identifiers serving as submission slots for individual estimates. Geometric target. Each target center is the midpoint of the tight world-axis-aligned bounding box (AABB) of its rendered geometry. For an articulated object, the box encloses the union of its rendered link geometries. Let denote the box corners and let be the initial camera's world position and camera-to-world rotation. The reference center in meters is The box is constructed in world coordinates; Eq.~ then expresses its midpoint in the task frame. This definition gives each asset a reproducible localization target, including assets whose internal origins are offset from their visible geometry. Center inference combines correspondence geometry with the object's observed spatial extent: a triangulated surface feature and the AABB center are generally different points. Coordinate frame and inputs. The task uses a fixed right-handed frame with origin at the initial camera, along its initial optical forward direction, to its initial left, and along its initial up direction. All absolute map positions and returned camera poses use this frame. An initially pitched camera gives a task up axis tilted relative to world vertical. The agent receives RGB images, the inventory, camera intrinsics, poses, and the target-region radius . Reference centers, boxes, and asset geometry remain in the evaluator. The supplied camera geometry and scene-level search bound support metric estimation, while the agent selects views, establishes correspondences, and infers object centers. Benchmark Construction sec:method_construction Scene diversity. Explicit geometric annotations and reproducible configurations support object-level scene evaluation~ ir3d,sceneact . We assemble 80 indoor scenes rendered with SAPIEN~ sapien through ManiSkill3~ maniskill3 : 32 iTHOR~ ai2thor , 12 RoboTHOR~ robothor , 10 ArchitecTHOR~ procthor , 6 ReplicaCAD~ habitat2 , and 30 ProcTHOR~ procthor scenes. The catalog spans individual rooms and apartments, retaining the source layouts and target placements; each source scene appears once. Complexity. Each scene contributes 30--40 targets. The catalog contains 12 scenes with 35 targets, and 68 with 40, totaling 3,410 instances. The target-region radius ranges from 1.95 to 9.23\,m. Across the catalog, 1,489 targets (43.3 ) belong to equivalence groups with multiple instances in the same scene. Target count controls inventory scale, while spatial extent and repeated categories vary the localization and association demands. Selection and initialization. Preparation prioritizes candidates with known semantic categories, then orders them by distance to the initial camera, using identifier order to break ties. This rule aligns the inventory with recognizable categories and concentrates targets around the exploration origin. Candidates must have rendered geometry, and each scene must supply the requested target count. Candidates outside the selected target subset are hidden in rendered observations; selected targets retain their source placements. Loaded object counts are checked against the source configuration with scene-builder exclusions accounted for. Each catalog entry fixes the source configuration, initial pose, and target count. Preparation saves the inventory, geometric annotations, and initial view, and verifies agreement between the camera-pose axes and projection matrix. Appendix~ sec:protocol_details specifies the manifest and cache checks. Evaluation sec:evaluation sec:experiments Evaluation Protocol sec:method_protocol sec:method_interaction sec:experiments_setup Setup We evaluate seven models on a common set of 80 catalog scenes, with one episode per model--scene pair: GPT-6 Astra~ openai2026gpt6astra , GPT-6 Sol~ openai2026gpt6sol , Claude Opus~5.5~ claude2026opus55 , Claude Sonnet 5.5~ claude2026sonnet55 , Kimi-K3~ team2026kimi , Qwen3.8-Max~ qwen2026-38max , and DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash~ ds2026-41flash . We impose no explicit limit on output or reasoning tokens. Interaction All agents use the ten tools in Table~ tab:method_tools through a shared interface~ embodiedbench . Starting from one RGB image, the agent queries the inventory and calibration, acquires further views, and submits or revises object centers (see Fig.~ fig:main ). title: PlanarCityLoc: Breaking Silhouette Ambiguity in LoD Aerial Localization via 3D Planes
summary: Aerial visual localization is crucial for autonomous drone navigation in urban environments where GNSS signals are often degraded. Lightweight textureless Level-of-Detail (LoD) city models provide a geometric map alternative to textured assets. Existing silhouette-based methods rely on image-space alignment, which can leave different camera poses indistinguishable and favor incorrect poses when segmentation errors distort the building outlines. We present PlanarCityLoc, which moves beyond silhouette overlap by leveraging the planar geometry of building facades and roofs. Following geometry-aware initialization, we match image-side planar patches to LoD model planes and use the resulting 3D-to-2D correspondences to refine pose with Perspective-n-Point (PnP). The framework uses off-the-shelf geometry and segmentation models without dataset-specific training or fine-tuning. Experiments on UAVD4L-LoDv2 and Swiss-EPFLv2 achieve state-of-the-art localization recall among the evaluated off-the-shelf LoD-based methods. By grounding image-space alignment in 3D planes, PlanarCityLoc enables more accurate aerial localization with lightweight, textureless city maps.
full_text: Aerial visual localization is crucial for autonomous drone navigation in urban environments where GNSS signals are often degraded. Lightweight textureless Level-of-Detail (LoD) city models provide a geometric map alternative to textured assets. Existing silhouette-based methods rely on image-space alignment, which can leave different camera poses indistinguishable and favor incorrect poses when segmentation errors distort the building outlines. We present PlanarCityLoc, which moves beyond silhouette overlap by leveraging the planar geometry of building facades and roofs. Following geometry-aware initialization, we match image-side planar patches to LoD model planes and use the resulting 3D-to-2D correspondences to refine pose with Perspective-n-Point (PnP). The framework uses off-the-shelf geometry and segmentation models without dataset-specific training or fine-tuning. Experiments on UAVD4L-LoDv2 and Swiss-EPFLv2 achieve state-of-the-art localization recall among the evaluated off-the-shelf LoD-based methods. By grounding image-space alignment in 3D planes, PlanarCityLoc enables more accurate aerial localization with lightweight, textureless city maps. Introduction sec:intro Aerial visual localization for , defined as estimating the precise 6-Degrees-of-Freedom (6DoF) camera pose from a single image, is essential for operations in -denied urban environments~ villa2020survey, cai2022review . Camera pose estimates also support geometry-guided annotation of aerial imagery~ gross2026segfly and semantic mapping for autonomous landing~ gross2026safeland . While matching images to textured 3D meshes~ schonberger2016structure, wu2024uavd4l is established, maintaining these assets globally is expensive and privacy-restricted~ nex2024usegeo . Textureless city models provide a compact geometric reference without storing facade appearance~ zhu2024lod, zhu2025lod, peng2026lod, wysocki2024reviewing, groger2012ogc . One way to bridge the appearance gap between images and textureless maps is to compare their structural projections. LoD-Loc~ zhu2024lod follows this approach by predicting building wireframes in the query image and aligning them with edges projected from the LoD model. LoD-Loc v2~ zhu2025lod instead compares building silhouettes, making alignment applicable to simpler LoD1 geometry ( (a)). LoD-Loc v3~ peng2026lod uses instance masks to distinguish buildings, reducing ambiguity and broad score plateaus caused by merged semantic silhouettes in dense scenes. These silhouette-based objectives still measure agreement in image space. Distinct camera poses can produce similar projections, and disjoint masks yield the same zero intersection-over-union over a range of poses. Segmentation errors introduce a further difficulty. Missing facades, displaced boundaries, or merged building instances change the target silhouette, so an incorrect pose can align better with the predicted mask than the true pose does. Consequently, even a distinct score maximum need not coincide with minimum pose error, as illustrated schematically in (c). Improving pose accuracy therefore calls for constraints beyond silhouette overlap alone. Our key observation is that building facades and roofs provide explicit 3D planar patches within models. In summary, our main contributions are: We formulate zero-shot -based aerial localization through explicit plane correspondences. We introduce iterative plane association between image patches and textureless map geometry for robust refinement of the camera pose. We evaluate on UAVD4L-LoDv2 and Swiss-EPFLv2, achieving state-of-the-art localization recall among the evaluated off-the-shelf LoD-based methods across all four splits, and analyze the contributions of geometric scoring and plane-based refinement through ablations. Related Work sec:related localization. Visual localization estimates the 6DoF camera pose relative to a known map. Traditional approaches match local features to a 3D point cloud constructed via Structure-from-Motion~ schonberger2016structure, pan2024global , pairing feature extractors~ detone2018superpoint with robust matchers~ sarlin2020superglue, sun2021loftr, edstedt2024roma, edstedt2025romav2 . Hierarchical pipelines~ sarlin2019coarse first retrieve relevant images before local feature matching. MeshLoc~ panek2022meshloc localizes directly on 3D meshes, while UAVLoc~ wu2024uavd4l uses posed reference images rendered from textured meshes for aerial localization. Render-and-compare approaches~ yan2023render offer another route to aerial pose estimation. MC-Loc~ trivigno2024unreasonable combines pretrained image features, a renderable scene representation, and particle filtering for pose refinement without task-specific training. Maintaining detailed appearance-bearing maps at city scale remains costly. AnyVisLoc~ ye2026anyvisloc , OrthoLoC~ dhaouadi2025ortholoc , and OrthoTrack~ dhaouadi2026orthotrack instead explore localization using overhead imagery and 2.5D surface maps. Our work focuses on textureless geometry, which provides a compact reference without storing facade appearance. -based localization. LoD-Loc~ zhu2024lod introduced the use of LoD city models for aerial localization through neural wireframe alignment. It predicts building edges in the query image, scores pose hypotheses using projected map wireframes, and refines the estimate through differentiable alignment. LoD-Loc v2~ zhu2025lod shifts from wireframes to semantic building silhouettes, supporting simpler LoD1 models through coarse pose search and particle-filter refinement. LoD-Loc v3~ peng2026lod further separates buildings using instance segmentation trained on synthetic aerial imagery. Instance-level alignment reduces the ambiguity of merged semantic masks in dense scenes, but remains sensitive to missing instances, incorrect boundaries, and merged or split predictions. Such errors can displace the overlap maximum from the true pose, even when the score has a distinct peak ( (c)). PlanarCityLoc complements silhouette alignment with explicit 3D plane correspondences.
